9 . Shri Jayant Tripathi opined that the AMASR Act need s to be amended to bring back its 
focus on the protection of monument and sites, and not on the areas outside the monuments and 
sites. The current focus, after the 2010 amendments , has resulted in the bulk of the amendments 
being aimed at the areas outside the monuments, which are not within the jurisdiction of the ASI, 
and fall in the domain of municipal laws and buildi ng bye-laws. He was of the view that the 100 
metre prohibited area rule needs to be revisited, a s the same is not based on any logical criteria. 
There can be no basis for saying that a kos minar i n the middle of an agricultural field requires 
the same protection as the Qutab Minar or the Puri Temple. If at all the 100 metre prohibition has 
to remain, then there has to be synergy between the  AMASR Act and the municipal building bye 
laws to introduce the concept of Transferrable Deve lopment Rights, which would enable persons 
who  cannot construct within the 100 metre /uni2015Prohibited Area /uni01C1, still being able to monetize the ir 
properties. This would reduce the resentment that t he 100 metre rule has generated, and would 
immediately nullify all court cases that have been filed on this aspect. He further submitted that 
the 2010 amendment was brought about without any in puts from the ASI, and needs to be 
revisited. He stated that the committee that propos ed the amendments did not even have a 
representative from the ASI, and comprised three pe rsons, none of whom had any expertise in  
the field of archaeology or the preservation of mon uments. He observed that the scheme of the 
Act, as it currently exists, has three aspects – th e monument or site itself (where ASI has 
exclusive authority), the Prohibited Area (where AS I is supposed to enforce the prohibition) and 
the Regulated Area – where the ASI, the NMA and the Competent Authority play different roles. 
He submitted that this multiplicity of authorities leads to confusion, and needs to be streamlined. 
He further submitted that the AMASR Act requires an  overhaul, keeping in mind the current 
situation and the threats to monuments on account o f population pressures, pollution and other 

12   
factors.

1 4 . In light of the observations made by various expert s on the subject and the lack of 
any specific reasoning behind the limit of 100 metr es and 300 metres around the CPMs as 
prohibited and regulated areas, the Committee is of  the strong view that the Ministry must 
undertake a holistic, in-depth review of the restri ctions imposed by the AMASR Act on 
construction activities near the CPMs since it does not seem logical to have restrictions on a 
uniform amount of area across the highly diverse ty pes of monuments under the protection 
of the Central Government. The Committee takes seri ous notice of the observation made  
by one of the experts that the 2010 amendment was b rought about without any inputs from 
the ASI and recommends that the review of the exist ing legislation should be carried out in 
consultation with existing and former senior officials of ASI, and other subject experts. The 
Committee recommends that the area to be deemed as prohibited and regulated area  
should not be set in stone for all the monuments and should instead be decided on a case-to- 
case basis, with due consideration to the individua l requirements of the monument/site. 
There is no denying the fact that there needs to be  a mechanism for keeping a check on the 
construction activities in the vicinity of a histor ical monument but utmost care must be 
taken to ensure that doing so causes least possible  disruption in the lives of people who 

15   
have had been living in harmony with the monuments since decades, duly factoring in the 
specific requirements for such checks given the uni que nature of the individual historical 
monuments. The Committee recommends that the Minist ry should urgently work towards 
creating a regulatory framework that has provisions  for the least possible restrictions on 
construction activities in a manner suitable to the  specific requirements for individual 
monuments while ensuring that no structural or visu al damage is caused to the monument 
by any construction activities and does not unneces sarily impinge on the rights of people 
living nearby the monuments.

embargo.

20

1 8 . The Committee takes note of the extensive list of s uggestions made by the expert 
regarding the new Rules/ Regulations/ Policies/ Leg islation/ Amendments that can be 
introduced in order to ensure better protection of the Historical Sites and Monuments. The 
Committee reiterates its recommendation made in Par a 14 of this Report and recommends 
that the Ministry may thoroughly examine the above- mentioned suggestions made by the 
expert while undertaking the review of the AMASR Act. The Ministry must ensure that the 
review of the existing legislation may factor in fe edback from experts in the field of 
conservation, preservation, archaeology, law as wel l as all the stakeholders who are 
impacted by the AMASR Act. 
 
 
 
Suggestions for creation of Regulatory Framework fo r protection of Historical Monuments 
presently not under the protection of both Central and State Governments 
1 9 . The Ministry informed the Committee that the State Governments and Union Territories 
have also declared the monuments/sites of State imp ortance under their respective Acts. The 
protection of monuments, sites and remains, which h ave not been declared by the Central 
Government as of national importance, fall under th e State List of the Constitution of India. As 
such, the protection of historical monuments and si tes is a responsibility being handled by 
Central Government as well as State Government for which legislative mechanism is available 
with Centre and State Governments. 

22   
2 0 . In this regard, Shri Jayant Tripathi, in his writte n note, has stated that Schedule VII to the 
Constitution contains appropriate entries in List I , List II and List III to provide protection to 
monuments and sites. These entries are extracted for ease of reference below:- 
List I (Union List) 
 
67. Ancient and historical monuments and records, a nd archaeological sites and 
remains, declared by or under law made by Parliamen t to be of national 
importance. 
List II (State List) 
 
12. Libraries, museums and other similar institutions controlled or financed by the 
State; ancient and historical monuments and records  other than those declared by 
or under law made by Parliament to be of national importance. 
List III (Concurrent List) 
 
40. Archaeological sites and remains other than tho se declared by or under law 
made by Parliament to be of national importance. 
2 1 . Shri Jayant Tripathi, in his written note, stated t hat monuments which do not fall within 
the above two categories are sometimes protected th rough local municipal laws by inserting 
provisions for the protection of heritage buildings . He further informed that there are two ways  
to achieve the objective of protection of Historical Monuments presently not under the protection 
of both Central and State Governments. The first wa y he suggested is the creation of an 
overarching non-binding Central policy regarding he ritage conservation, which States can adopt 
and legislate upon. He stated that the other way wo uld require a minor amendment in the 
Constitution, where the words  /uni2015hist orical buildings and sites/uni01C1 are added to Entry 40 of List III of 

23   
the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, which wou ld pave the way to bring about a Central 
Legislation for the protection of Historical Buildi ngs and Sites as well as archaeological sites 
which are not declared to be of national importance . This could then be governed by a separate 
Heritage Commission with offices in every State, an d can protect monuments that are  
overlooked by the State Governments. 
2 2 . The Committee notes that as per the division of pow ers laid down under the Constitution 
of India, the Parliament can enact laws for only th ose historical monuments that have been 
declared  to  be  of  national  importance.  Besides  that,  Parliament  can  enact  laws  only      for 
/uni2015Archaeological sites and remains other than those declared by or under law made by Parliament 
to be of national importance /uni01C1 but not for ancient and historical monuments. Alth ough the State 
Governments have been conferred the power to legislate for all ancient and historical monuments 
other than those declared to be of national importa nce, the Committee observes that there are 
many monuments across the country which do not make  it to the list of State-protected 
monuments either and are thus left totally neglecte d, falling victim to the vagaries of nature. The 
Committee feels that there is a pressing need to ta ke concrete action to ensure that such 
monuments are not damaged beyond repair and are kep t in a good state of conservation since 
they are a reflection of our rich and diverse histo rical heritage and going forward, could present 
opportunities for development of tourism in the local area as well. 
2 3 . The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Minis try may consider coming up 
with a legislation to amend the Constitution adding  /uni2015ancient and historical monuments 
other than those declared to be of national importa nce /uni01C1 to the Concurrent List, in order to 
permit the Central Government to enforce at least s ome set of provisions for the basic 
protection and conservation of archaeological monuments and sites which are presently not 

24   
under any sort of protection by Central and State G overnments. A separate Heritage 
Commission may thereafter be established to look af ter such monuments. Since a 
Constitutional amendment is a time-taking process, the Committee recommends that in the 
meanwhile, the Ministry may come up with policy gui delines which can be adopted by the 
State Governments across the country for looking af ter neglected archaeological sites and 
monuments. The Committee further recommends that th e Ministry may request for  
certain budgetary allocation to allow ASI to carry out urgent conservation measures at 
such miscellaneous monuments, possibly in coordination with concerned State Archaeology 
Departments. 
 
 
Efficacy of the existing Regulatory Framework to de al with the specific issue of 
encroachment of the Historical Sites and Monuments 
2 4 . On the issue of encroachment, the Ministry, in its written note, has informed that any 
construction, occupation of monument or part of mon ument by any means, installation of any 
kind, erection of any kind, temporary or permanent in nature, within the protected limit is 
considered as encroachment. The Section 19 of the AMASR Act even restricts the right of owner 
of the protected area to construct anything within the protected area and imposes condition to 
obtain permission from the Central Government. 
2 5 . In order to contain the encroachments, the Superint ending Archaeologist in charge of the 
Circles have been vested with the powers of an Esta te Officer to issue eviction notices/orders to 
the encroachers under Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. They  
are also delegated with the powers to issue notices  under the provisions of Ancient Monuments 
and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and Rules 1959 followed by an order to the 

25   
District Collector/Magistrate by Central Government  to remove such encroachment under  
section 19 (2) of the Act and Rules 38 (2) of the R ule. Assistance in containing and removing 
encroachments is also sought from the respective State Government/police force and where there 
are no fruitful results, actions are initiated agai nst the encroachers by filing cases in the court of  
law. 
2 6 . As and when construction activities are noticed/rep orted in the prohibited/regulated area 
the Superintending Archaeologist issues a notice to  the owner under rule 38 of the provisions of 
the Ancient Monuments, Archaeological Sites and Rem ains Rules, 1959 for removal of 
unauthorized building. Simultaneously, help from th e local police is also sought by lodging a 
complaint and by registering a FIR. On receipt of a  report from the field office, the Director 
General, Archaeological Survey of India , issues a notice to the erring party in pursuance of sub 
section 19(ii) and sub-rule 38(i) of Ancient Monume nts, Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 
1958, and Rules, 1959 respectively for removal of s uch unauthorized construction within a 
specified period. A copy of the notice issued by th e Director General is also sent to the District 
Collector with the request to demolish the illegal construction. In this regard, the assistance in 
containing and removing encroachments is sought fro m the respective State Government and 
where there are no fruitful results, action is initiated by filing cases in the court of law. 
2 7 . Shri Jayant Tripathi, in his written note, opined t hat the main reasons why sites and 
monuments are encroached upon can be summarized as under:- 
(i) Inadequate numbers of personnel guarding monuments to prevent encroachment or 
report encroachment as soon as it takes place; 
(ii) The lack of ownership of monuments with the ASI; 
 
(iii) Inadequate penal provisions in the AMASR Act. 

26   
2 8 . Shri Jayant Tripathi further stated that under the AMASR Act, in order to protect a 
monument or a site, a notification is issued in the  Gazette. Sometimes it may just be the physical 
monument that is notified, and sometimes adjacent l and may also be included in the notification. 
The Act recognizes such adjacent land as an integra l part of the monument, and extends 
protection to such additional land also. However, a fter notification as a monument of National 
Monument, the ownership of the monument is not auto matically transferred to the Government 
or the ASI. Had that been the case, the provisions of the Public Premises (Eviction of 
Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 could be utilized  to summarily throw out encroachers. In 
other cases, there are large areas surrounding monu ments which form a part of the monument, 
which are ripe for encroachment, one example being the Tughlaqabad Fort in Delhi. The lack of 
manpower to prevent the initial encroachment, and t he inadequacy in the law to adequately and 
swiftly punish such encroachment adds to the proble m. The only provision in the AMASR Act 
which provides punishment to persons who are encroa ching on monuments and sites is set out in 
Section 30. However, the wording of the same leaves  a lot to be desired, and there are loopholes 
which require rectification. Amendments are required in order to ensure that such encroachments 
are removed as fast as possible, in fast track cour ts, or by making the proceedings summary in 
nature. He submitted that the current regulatory fr amework, which was amended in 2010, does 
not provide adequate protection to sites and monuments. The amendments of 2010 actually focus 
more on the areas outside the monuments and sites, i.e., in the Prohibited and Regulated areas. 
Thus, the focus of the AMASR Act appears to have sh ifted from actually protecting monuments 
and sites to overseeing construction activities etc ., in the 300 metre area beyond the monuments. 
It is further submitted that this lack of focus nee ds to be remedied through legislative 
intervention,  in  order  to  ensure  that  monuments  and  sites  are  once  again  the  focus  of th e 

27   
AMASR Act, and the ASI can carry out work in its co re competency areas, rather than act as a 
chowkidar policing what is happening outside the monuments and sites. 
2 9 . Shri Vinay Ranjan, in his written note, stated that  provisions of the Ancient Monuments 
and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, are broug ht into motion only upon declaration of an 
ancient/historical monument/site/remains as of nati onal importance under the provisions of 
section 4 of the Act. Once the notification is duly  published in the Official Gazette under section 
4, all other provisions of the Act become applicabl e. However, in practice the notification is 
divided into two- preliminary and final. Alongwith the notification a revenue map/site map is 
also published for demarcation / delimitation of the boundaries of protection limits. In most cases 
the final notification is not done. Judicial ruling s have also held that in the absence of final 
notification, the preliminary notification may be d eemed as final and the same cannot be pressed 
into service as a disability. But the very purpose of the provision to verify the physical structure 
and to determine what portion, part or extent of the monument or the adjoining area is required to 
be within protected limits, is defeated by such lax ity to publish the final notification after due 
diligence. Again, in very many cases, the site map is missing as part of the preliminary 
notification. To moot the point, it is submitted th at if the final notification is published with due 
regard to delimitation /demarcation of the protecte d monument or the protected area, as the case 
may be, alongwith the site map, then the vexing que stion whether the limits of prohibited area or 
the regulated area is to be measured from the physi cal structure of the monument or its adjoining 
boundaries can be avoided from becoming the subject matter of vexatious litigation. On the other 
hand, it may be considered that publication of such  inchoate / inept notifications paves the way 
for subjective bureaucratic discretion which in tur n results in encroachments in and around the 
CPMs. Also, in focus would be the 16 th  June 1992 notification, which serves as    the cut-off date 

28   
for the ASI for the purpose of determining legality  or illegality of a construction. However, no 
modus or data is available pre and post the said cu t-off date to determine as which structures 
existed prior to such cut-off date and which constr uctions have come up thereafter. In the end, it 
often leads to default validation of the illegal co nstruction despite the legislative embargo for 
want of determinative and/or actionable data in this regard. Moreover, even when a  construction 
/ structure is identified as having been made in vi olation of the provisions of the AMASRA, 
1958, and the Rules made thereunder, the legislativ e gaps in the provisions of the Act and the 
Rules have resulted in beneficial litigation to off enders under the Act. For instance, the power to 
remove unauthorized construction in respect of a /uni2015protected area /uni01C1 and not ‗protected monument /uni01C1 
has been conferred upon the Central Government, by the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 
19 of the AMASRA, 1958. However, for the purpose of  removal of unauthorized construction 
with reference to /uni2015protected monument /uni01C1 or CPM,  the ASI has to fall upon the provisi ons  of Rule 
38 of the AMASR Rules, 1959. 
3 0 . Shri Vinay Ranjan informed that Rule 38 of the AMASR Rules 1959 states the following: 
 
" Removal of unauthorized buildings.— (1) The Central Government may, by order, 
direct the owner or occupier of an unauthorized bui lding in a prohibited area or in a 
regulated area or of a building or part thereof whi ch has been constructed in  
contravention of any of the conditions of a licence  granted under rule 35 to remove such 
building or part thereof within a period specified in that order. 
(2) If the owner or occupier refuses or fails to comply with an order made under sub-rule 
(1), the Central Government may direct the District Magistrate to    cause the building 

29   
or part thereof to be removed, and the owner or occupier shall be liable to pay the cost 
of such removal." 
3 1 . Shri Vinay Ranjan stated that the provisions of rul e 38 (1) do not envisage the situation 
for issue of demolition order where neither an appl ication for licence has been made under rule 
34 nor any licence has been granted under rule 35. Consequently, in such cases, the question or 
occasion for contravention of any condition of lice nce does not and cannot arise and hence the 
applicability of action under Rule 38(1) also can b e contended to be as of no effect. Further, the 
entire scheme of the provisions as contained in rul e 38 hinges upon building or part thereof 
which has been "constructed" and the removal of suc h "construction". "Construction" has been 
defined under section 2 (dc) of the AMASR Act 1958 and is as follows:- 
/uni20152… 
 
(dc) 'Construction'  means  any  erection  of  a  s tructure  or  a  building  including  any 
addition or extension thereto either vertically or horizontally, but does not include any re-  
construction, repair and renovation of an existing structure or building , or, construction 
maintenance and cleansing of drains and drainage wo rks and of public latrines, urinals 
and similar conveniences, or, the construction and maintenance of works meant for 
providing supply of water for public, or, the const ruction or maintenance, extension, 
management for supply and distribution of electrici ty to the public or provision  for 
similar facilities for public." 
He submitted that it appears from the provisions of  the rule 39 of the AMASR Rules, 1959 that 
whoever unlawfully undertakes any construction in a  regulated area or fails or refuses to comply 
with an order made under sub-rule (1) of rule 38, shall be punishable with imprisonment,   which 

30   
may extend to three months or with fine which may e xtend to five thousand rupees or with both. 
He further submitted that where there has been no c onstruction (as distinguished from 
reconstruction) but only repair and renovation, the  penal provisions in the ultimate analysis fail  
to serve the purpose. Therefore, it is apparent tha t all the penal provisions or prohibitory 
provisions of the Act or the Rules that such provis ions are primarily concerned with 
"construction" activities and not re-construction o r repair or renovation, often allowing 
construction through the modicum of misplaced/misco nceived subjective bureaucratic discretion 
under the garb of re-construction or repair or reno vation. He opined that the above instances are 
merely enumerative of some of the glitches and gaps  that need to be addressed for a better and 
efficacious implementation of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. 
3 2 . During the meeting of the Committee held on 9 th December, 2021, Adv. A.D.N. Rao 
opined that the powers available with ASI to deal w ith encroachment are not sufficient as they 
are dependent on local police, which sometimes work s in connivance with the encroachers. He 
suggested that ASI officers should have powers like  those given to District Forest Officers 
(DFOs) under The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and that granting power to ASI to seal the site 
of illegal construction by the time the demolition can be done, would be effective in curbing the 
issue of encroachment of monuments. 
3 3 . The Committee notes the existing provisions in plac e in order to deal with the issue 
of encroachment of Centrally Protected Monuments an d the loopholes/ gaps/ glitches 
pointed out by various experts. The Committee agree s with the suggestion made by one of 
the experts that amendments are required in order t o ensure that encroachment of 
monuments are removed as quick as possible in fast track courts. The Committee feels that 
doing so can permit the encroachment to be removed before any permanent structure is 

31   
constructed in the vicinity of the monument, thus p reventing any sort of possible damages 
to the monument. 
3 4 . The Committee is concerned to note that the final n otification of declaration of an 
ancient/historical monument/site/remains as of nati onal importance, is not published by 
ASI in most cases. The Committee recommends that a time-bound limit may be prescribed 
for ASI to publish the final notification, alongwit h the site map, for monuments under its 
protection since the purpose of the same is to verify the physical structure and to determine 
the portion/part/extent of the monument that is required to be within the protected limits. 
3 5 . The Committee recommends that the Ministry may unde rtake a thorough review of 
the AMASR Act as well as the AMASR Rules in terms o f the powers available with ASI to 
tackle the issue of encroachment of monuments, keep ing in view the various loopholes and 
gaps pointed out by legal experts. The Committee fe els that the Ministry should  
incorporate provisions similar to those relating to  encroachment in the Indian Forest Act, 
1927, in the AMASR Act in order to empower ASI to e ffectively deal with the issue of 
encroachment of monuments. The Committee further re commends that the AMASR Act 
should grant power to ASI to seal the site of illeg al construction till the time the demolition 
can be done, so that any delay in the same does not  cause any further damage to the 
monument and there is no incentive for encroachers to undertake any illegal construction 
near the monument. The Ministry should request the Ministry of Finance to provide it with 
separate budget to carry out the demolition of unau thorized constructions that have taken 
place in the vicinity of Centrally Protected Monuments. 
35A. The Committee recommends that wherever possibl e, the Ministry/ASI  should  
develop the area in the vicinity of the ancient monuments as green space with amenities for 

32   
tourists since doing so will not only curb encroach ment of that area but also  bolster 
tourism in the region. 
 
 
Review of existing provisions for grant of permissi on required for construction or repairs 
within the prohibited/ regulated areas of Centrally protected monuments 
3 6 . The Ministry, in its background note, has stated th at as per the AMASR Act 1958 
construction related activities are permitted withi n the prohibited and regulated area on 
permission from Competent Authority as per recommen dation of National  Monuments 
Authority. Such constructional work taken up withou t the permission from competent authority 
within regulated area of protected monument/site ar e considered as unauthorized construction. 
The Ministry further informed the Committee that in  order to undertake repairs or new 
constructions within the regulated areas or repair and renovation within prohibited area of any 
protected monument, prior permission from Competent  Authority is essential. For this purpose, 
Director of Archaeology of State Governments or Com missioners of States have been notified as 
Competent Authority. 
3 7 . Shri Jayant Tripathi, in his written note, informed  the Committee that the repair works 
listed in Rule 8 of the AMASR (Framing of Heritage Bye Laws and Other Functions of 
Competent  Authority)  Rules,  2011  include  /uni2015repairs   to  water  tanks,...re-plastering  of  building, 
...filling up of cracks...., replacement of windows ..., relaying the flooring, ....providing coat of 
white wash or colour wash or painting of walls.... /uni01C1 etc. Citing an example of the implications of 
this, he stated that if his home in Basti district in Uttar Pradesh were to be within 300 metres of a 
monument of national importance and he needed to re pair a broken window of his home or get 
his  home  whitewashed,  he  would  first  need  to  seek  prior  permission  from  the  Competent 

33   
Authority (CA) whose office is in Lucknow and if th e CA happened to refuse permission for any 
reason, an appeal will need to be filed to the NMA in New Delhi. Getting the window repaired or 
the home whitewashed without prior permission would  be liable to penal consequences,  
including imprisonment. He submitted that the above  example highlights the issue  of 
government interference in the day to day life of t he citizens in the name of protecting heritage, 
which ultimately has the result of turning citizens  against heritage, or worse still, ignoring or 
flouting the law. 
3 8 . In this regard, Shri Jayant Tripathi suggested that  the entire issue of granting permissions 
for repairs needs to be streamlined, and made as ea sy as possible, especially for minor repairs, in 
the same manner as municipal building bye-laws. If a citizen does not need permission to carry 
out certain repairs under the building bye-laws, th en the AMASR Rules should be, as far as 
practicable, in line with those building bye-laws. He suggested that a review of the AMASR 
Rules in this regard needs to be done keeping in mi nd the building bye-laws around the country, 
and with the intent of making the life of citizens easier, and less bound by red tape. He further 
submitted that the purpose of the AMASR Act was not , and should not be, controlling repairs in 
houses which are outside the notified area of the m onument. He opined that the expertise of the 
ASI, which is a valuable resource, should not be wa sted on deciding whether a citizen can 
replace a window, or whitewash a house. 
 
 
3 9 . The Committee fails to see why a person living in t he Regulated Area of a CPM 
should be required to seek permission from the Comp etent Authority under the AMASR 
Rules for carrying out innocuous maintenance activi ties such as filling of cracks, 
whitewashing, replacement of windows etc. The Commi ttee feels that such uncalled-for 

34   
interference makes lives harder for people living n earby the monuments and could slowly 
cause feelings of anguish towards the monument itse lf. Given the large number of 
monuments across the country and the limited budget ary resources available with the 
Government, it is pertinent that people residing ne ar the monuments are encouraged to 
look after the monuments and protect them. Besides,  placing such unnecessary curbs and 
implementing them is a wastage of limited Government resources and turns the focus away 
from where it should be - actually protecting and p reserving the monument itself. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may undertake a thorough review of 
the AMASR Act and Rules and omit any provisions tha t provide for seeking permissions 
for minor works where the same is not actually need ed and streamline the process for 
applying for permission in case where the same is a ctually needed. Steps may urgently be 
taken to make it possible for the entire process fo r seeking permission for construction 
activities in prohibited and regulated areas, to be  completed online so as to not cause any 
hassle to bona fide residents living near the monuments. 
 
 
Evolving ways for participation of municipalities a nd village panchayats in the process of 
protection of regional Historical Sites and Monuments 
4 0 . Shri Jayant Tripathi, in his written note, stated t hat the examples from Delhi and Mumbai 
show that municipal laws and building bye-laws can be used as effective tools for ensuring 
protection of regional historical monuments and bui ldings. It has to be kept in mind that this 
aspect would fall within the legislative competence  enumerated in List II of the Seventh 
Schedule, and as such it may not be possible to cre ate a dedicated body which can regulate such  
a  framework  on  a  pan-India  basis.  He  suggested  that  if  there  is  a  minor      Constitution al 

35   
Amendment as proposed by him earlier (para 21 of th is Report), protection of regional 
monuments and sites would be possible through a Centrally enacted regulatory legislation. 
4 1 . Given the large number of historical monuments and sites located across the 
country, many of which are not under any sort of pr otection from the Central/State 
Governments, the Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para 5.7.23 of its 294 th 
Report on the subject ‗Development and Conservation of Museums and Archaeo logical 
sites - Challenges and Opportunities‘ and  recommends that the Ministry should find  ways 
to institutionally integrate municipalities and vil lage panchayats in the process of 
protection of historical monuments and sites across  the country and if needed, create a 
dedicated body to implement the regulatory framework for the same. 
 
 
Preparation of monument-specific conservation plan and bye-laws for all Centrally 
Protected Monuments across the country 
4 2 . Appearing  before  the  Committee  in  the  capacity  of  a  domain  expert  on  the subject 
 
‗Creation of Regulatory Framework for protection of Historical Sites and Monuments‘ in its 
meeting held on 9 th December, 2021, Prof. Alok Tripathi, Additional Dir ector General, ASI 
opined that having monument-specific bye-laws, depe nding on their nature, date and kind of 
structure etc. will help ASI in protecting the monuments more effectively.. 
4 3 . The Committee opines that the Ministry/ASI/NMA shou ld carry out an exercise to 
prepare monument-specific conservation plans and he ritage bye-laws for all Centrally 
Protected Monuments across the country, since there  cannot be a uniform plan for all the 
monuments and the unique conservation requirements of each monument can only be 
reflected through dedicated conservation plan for each monument. Such an exercise  would 

36   
undoubtedly require sufficient manpower and resourc es. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry should ensure that swift action is tak en to ensure that ASI is adequately 
staffed at all times and staffing requirements shou ld be anticipated well in advance since 
recruitment of quality personnel is often a time-ta king exercise. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry should formulate the b udgetary requirements for creation  
of dedicated conservation plans for all CPMs and re quest the Ministry of Finance to grant 
the same as a special one-time grant. 
 
 
 
Security policy for all Centrally Protected Monuments 
 
4 4 . Security of the monuments is being looked after by ASI by deploying round the clock 
watch and ward through MTS. Besides, additional sec urity is provided with the Central 
Industrial Security Force at Red Fort and Taj Mahal  and private security guards at selected 
monuments. 
4 5 . Additional Director General, ASI further informed t he Committee about the issue of lack 
of manpower faced by the ASI in the protection of h istorical monuments across the country. He 
was of the view that having regular staff at all Ce ntrally Protected Monuments can allow ASI to 
stop encroachments at the early stage before any illegal construction has taken place. 
4 6 . Shri Jayant Tripathi, in his written note, stated t hat it would require an in-depth study 
regarding the security requirements of each monumen t and a subsequent overarching policy. 
However, any policy would need to be sufficiently f lexible to take into account specific needs of 
monuments, as well as changes that may occur with t he passage of time. He opined that in the 

37

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS – AT A GLANCE  
 
 
The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (AMASR) Act, 1958 
In light of the observations made by various expert s on the subject and the lack of 
any specific reasoning behind the limit of 100 metr es and 300 metres around the CPMs as 
prohibited and regulated areas, the Committee is of  the strong view that the Ministry must 
undertake a holistic, in-depth review of the restri ctions imposed by the AMASR Act on 
construction activities near the CPMs since it does not seem logical to have restrictions on a 
uniform amount of area across the highly diverse ty pes of monuments under the protection 
of the Central Government. The Committee takes seri ous notice of the observation made  
by one of the experts that the 2010 amendment was b rought about without any inputs from 
the ASI and recommends that the review of the exist ing legislation should be carried out in 
consultation with existing and former senior officials of ASI, and other subject experts. The 
Committee recommends that the area to be deemed as prohibited and regulated area  
should not be set in stone for all the monuments and should instead be decided on a case-to- 
case basis, with due consideration to the individua l requirements of the monument/site. 
There is no denying the fact that there needs to be  a mechanism for keeping a check on the 
construction activities in the vicinity of a histor ical monument but utmost care must be 
taken to ensure that doing so causes least possible  disruption in the lives of people who  
have had been living in harmony with the monuments since decades, duly factoring in the 
specific requirements for such checks given the uni que nature of the individual historical 
monuments. The Committee recommends that the Minist ry should urgently work towards 
creating a regulatory framework that has provisions  for the least possible restrictions on 
construction activities in a manner suitable to the  specific requirements for individual 
monuments while ensuring that no structural or visu al damage is caused to the monument 
by any construction activities and does not unneces sarily impinge on the rights of people 
living nearby the monuments. 
(Para 14) 
 
 
The Committee agrees with the concerns raised by one of the experts regarding the 
prohibitions  imposed  by  the  AMASR  (Amendment)  Act,  2010  on  appointment  of any 

41   
person who has held any post with the ASI or the Mi nistry of Culture, as the Chairman or 
member of the NMA. The Committee feels that having the services of personnel who have 
had actual field experience working for the preserv ation and protection of the historical 
monuments and sites, could help NMA fulfill its man date in a more effective manner but 
many people with such experience would be those who  have had worked with the ASI or 
Ministry of Culture and thus would be deemed inelig ible to be appointed as the Chairman 
or member of the NMA as per the existing provisions  of the AMASR Act. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may revisit the ration ale behind the restrictions imposed by 
Section 20F(3) of the AMASR (Amendment and Validati on) Act, 2010 and consider the 
pros and cons behind imposing such a restriction on  the appointment of Chairman and 
members of the NMA. Further, the Committee notes th at the NMA has also been given the 
responsibility of classification and gradation of m onuments in consultation with ASI. The 
Committee recommends that NMA may complete the clas sification and gradation exercise 
at the earliest. The Committee feels that doing so,  alongwith preparation of heritage bye- 
laws for all CPMs, would permit the Ministry to com e up with provisions for restrictions 
best suited for each monument instead of blanket ba ns that fail to serve the intended 
purpose. 
 
(Para 15) 
 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may intr oduce the concept of 
Transferable Development Rights to enable people ha ving properties in the vicinity of the 
monuments to monetize their properties. The Committ ee feels that this would act as a 
deterrent to encroachment of monuments, especially in case the monument is located in a 
congested urban area. 
 
(Para 16) 
 
The Committee takes note of the extensive list of s uggestions made by the expert 
regarding the new Rules/ Regulations/ Policies/ Leg islation/ Amendments that can be 
introduced in order to ensure better protection of the Historical Sites and Monuments. The 
Committee reiterates its recommendation made in Para 14 of this Report and recommends 

42   
that the Ministry may thoroughly examine the above- mentioned suggestions made by the 
expert while undertaking the review of the AMASR Act. The Ministry must ensure that the 
review of the existing legislation may factor in fe edback from experts in the field of 
conservation, preservation, archaeology, law as wel l as all the stakeholders who are 
impacted by the AMASR Act. 
(Para 18) 
 
Suggestions for creation of Regulatory Framework fo r protection of Historical Monuments 
presently not under the protection of both Central and State Governments 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Minis try may consider coming up 
with a legislation to amend the Constitution adding  /uni2015ancient and historical monuments 
other than those declared to be of national importa nce /uni01C1 to the Concurrent List, in order to 
permit the Central Government to enforce at least s ome set of provisions for the basic 
protection and conservation of archaeological monuments and sites which are presently not 
under any sort of protection by Central and State G overnments. A separate Heritage 
Commission may thereafter be established to look af ter such monuments. Since a 
Constitutional amendment is a time-taking process, the Committee recommends that in the 
meanwhile, the Ministry may come up with policy gui delines which can be adopted by the 
State Governments across the country for looking af ter neglected archaeological sites and 
monuments. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may request for certain 
budgetary allocation to allow ASI to carry out urge nt conservation measures at such 
miscellaneous monuments, possibly in coordination w ith concerned State Archaeology 
Departments. 
(Para 23) 
 
Efficacy of the existing Regulatory Framework to deal with the specific issue of 
encroachment of the Historical Sites and Monuments 
The Committee notes the existing provisions in plac e in order to deal with the issue 
of encroachment of Centrally Protected Monuments an d the loopholes/ gaps/ glitches 
pointed out by various experts. The Committee agrees with the suggestion made by one   of 

43   
the experts that amendments are required in order t o ensure that encroachment of 
monuments are removed as quick as possible in fast track courts. The Committee feels that 
doing so can permit the encroachment to be removed before any permanent structure is 
constructed in the vicinity of the monument, thus p reventing any sort of possible damages 
to the monument. 
(Para 33) 
 
The Committee is concerned to note that the final n otification of declaration of an 
ancient/historical monument/site/remains as of nati onal importance, is not published by 
ASI in most cases. The Committee recommends that a time-bound limit may be prescribed 
for ASI to publish the final notification, alongwit h the site map, for monuments under its 
protection since the purpose of the same is to verify the physical structure and to determine 
the portion/part/extent of the monument that is required to be within the protected limits. 
 
(Para 34) 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may unde rtake a thorough review of 
the AMASR Act as well as the AMASR Rules in terms o f the powers available with ASI to 
tackle the issue of encroachment of monuments, keep ing in view the various loopholes and 
gaps pointed out by legal experts. The Committee fe els that the Ministry should  
incorporate provisions similar to those relating to  encroachment in the Indian Forest Act, 
1927, in the AMASR Act in order to empower ASI to e ffectively deal with the issue of 
encroachment of monuments. The Committee further re commends that the AMASR Act 
should grant power to ASI to seal the site of illeg al construction till the time the demolition 
can be done, so that any delay in the same does not  cause any further damage to the 
monument and there is no incentive for encroachers to undertake any illegal construction 
near the monument. The Ministry should request the Ministry of Finance to provide it with 
separate budget to carry out the demolition of unau thorized constructions that have taken 
place in the vicinity of Centrally Protected Monuments. 
 
(Para 35) 

44   
The Committee recommends that wherever possible, th e Ministry/ASI should 
develop the area in the vicinity of the ancient mon uments as green space with amenities for 
tourists since doing so will not only curb encroach ment of that area but  also  bolster 
tourism in the region.

Review of existing provisions for grant of permission required for construction or repairs 
within the prohibited/ regulated areas of Centrally protected monuments 
The Committee fails to see why a person living in t he Regulated Area of a CPM 
should be required to seek permission from the Comp etent Authority under the AMASR 
Rules for carrying out innocuous maintenance activi ties such as filling of cracks, 
whitewashing, replacement of windows etc. The Commi ttee feels that such uncalled-for 
interference makes lives harder for people living n earby the monuments and could slowly 
cause feelings of anguish towards the monument itse lf. Given the large number of 
monuments across the country and the limited budget ary resources available with the 
Government, it is pertinent that people residing ne ar the monuments are encouraged to 
look after the monuments and protect them. Besides,  placing such unnecessary curbs and 
implementing them is a wastage of limited Governmen t resources and turns the focus away 
from where it should be - actually protecting and p reserving the monument itself. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may undertake a thorough review of 
the AMASR Act and Rules and omit any provisions tha t provide for seeking permissions 
for minor works where the same is not actually need ed and streamline the process for 
applying for permission in case where the same is a ctually needed. Steps may urgently be 
taken to make it possible for the entire process fo r seeking permission for construction 
activities in prohibited and regulated areas, to be  completed online so as to not cause any 
hassle to bona fide residents living near the monuments.

REPORT 
 
Review of Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) Works 
 
 India has one of the largest road networks in the world. Having a well -maintained, robust 
road network spanning across the country is a crucial prerequisite for fast -paced economic 
growth of any country. The development and maintenance of National Highways in India is in -
part funded by the collection of cess, a duty of excise customs on petrol and high speed diesel 
oil. The Central Road Fund Act, 2000 was enacted to give statutory st atus to the existing Central 
Road Fund governed by the Resolution of Parliament passed in 1988, for development and 
maintenance of national highways and improvement of safety at railway crossings, and for these 
purposes to levy and collect by way of cess, a duty of excise and duty of customs on motor spirit 
commonly known as petrol, high speed diesel oil and for other matters connected therewith. The 
CRF Act, 2000 has been replaced by the Central Road and Infrastructure Fund, 2000 through 
Finance Act, 2018.  Given the large number of road highway works taken up across the country 
under the Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF), the Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture decided to take up the subject ‘Revie w 
of Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) works’ for detailed examination and Report 
thereon. 
2. In this connection, the Committee heard the views of the Director -General (Road 
Development) and Special Secretary (DG (RD) & SS), Ministry of Road Tran sport and 
Highways in its meeting held on 16 th December, 2021. The Committee held discussions with the 
officials of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, State Government of Tamil Nadu and 
State Government of Kerala on this subject during its Study Visi t to Chennai and Kochi from 

 
2 
12th - 16th July, 2021. The Committee also heard the officials of Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways and State Government of Rajasthan on the subject during its Study Visit to Jaisalmer 
on 15th November, 2021. 
 
Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) 
3. The Ministry, in its background note on the subject, informed the Committee that CRF 
was available for Road Sector (National Highways, Rural roads under PMGSY and State Roads) 
and only for ROBs/ RUBs and safety works at u nmanned Railway Level Crossings as per the 
initial Central Road Fund (CRF) Act of 2000. Vide amendment through Finance Act, 2016, 
Railway capital works (Gauge conversion, electrification, etc.) were also included under the Act. 
4. The Central Road Fund Act, 2000 has been replaced by “Central Road and Infrastructure 
Fund” (CRIF) through Finance Act, 2018.  More sectors were included through amendment of 
2018, viz. Ports, Shipyards, Inland Waterways, Airports, Railway track & Commercial 
Infrastructure/ Stations, Urban Public Transport, etc., in Transport Sector besides other Sectors 
(Energy, Water and Sanitation, Communication, Social and Commercial Infrastructure). 
5. The CRIF Act, 2000 was further amended vide Finance Act, 2019. Now the fund is 
earmarked as p er Section 7A of the amended Act by a Committee headed by the Hon’ble 
Finance Minister and there is no fixed share of apportionment now, for this a committee is 
constituted as per Gazette Notification No. S.O.3226(E) dated 02.07.2018. The Act is 
administered by the Department of Economic Affairs as per the amendments to the Government 
of India (Allocation and Business) Rules, 1961 dated 26.07.2018.  
6. The Ministry furnished the below comparison of cess distribution before 01.06.2016, 
after 01.06.2016 and b efore 31.03.2018 and as per CRF Act, 2000 amended to CRIF Act, 2000 
by the Finance Act, 2018:

7. The funds under CRIF are allocated for development and maintenance of National 
Highway works including Bharatmala projects, Road Transport projects, works on State roads 
including EI&ISC works, etc. Total budget of Ministry, IEBR and Pvt. Sector Investment since 
2014-15 is at Annexure -I. The details of CRIF share used for NHs, Road Transport and State 
roads including EI&ISC since 2014 -15 is at Annexure -II. The scheme -wise Outstanding 
liabilities of sanctioned projects/ Bank of Sanction (BOS) of various works of the Ministry as on 
01.04.2021 is at Annexure-III. 
8. The Committee notes that through the amendment made by F inance Act, 2018, 
more sectors viz., Ports, Shipyards, Inland Waterways, Airports, Railway track and 
Commercial Infrastructure/ Stations, Urban Public Transport, etc., in Transport Sector 
besides other Sectors (Energy, Water and Sanitation, Communication, Social and 
Commercial Infrastructure), have been included under the CRIF. The Committee feels 
that the budgetary support that CRIF now provides to all these crucial sectors will help in 
achieving all round growth of the Indian economy. The Committee furthe r notes that the 
distribution under CRIF has been made more transparent as it is to now be decided by a 

 
5 
Committee headed by Hon’ble Finance Minister as per Section 7A of the CRIF Act, 2000 
depending on the priorities of the project. 
 
CRIF State Roads 
9. The Ministry informed the Committee that it allocates funds for State Roads under the 
Central Road and Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) Scheme and Economic Importance and Inter State 
Connectivity (EI&ISC) Schemes as per the provisions of the CRIF Act, 2000 amended  by the 
Finance Act from time to time. As per the CRIF Act, 2000 and its amendment vide the Finance 
Act, 2019. 
■ Central Government is no longer responsible for:- 
● Sanctioning of schemes; State to sanction works 
● Monitoring of State road projects and expenditu re incurred thereon; for release 
of funds to States 
● Formulation of rules for State roads. 
■ Central Govt. to formulate criteria for allocation of funds for such roads. 
10. The Committee notes that as per the CRIF Act, 2000 and its amendment vide the 
Finance Act, 2019, the Central Government is no longer responsible for formulation of 
rules for State roads. The Committee feels that the Ministry should specify the guidelines 
and technical specifications that must be followed by States to construct State roads f unded 
by CRIF. The Committee recommends that a mechanism should be put in place by the 
Ministry to carry out random checks regarding the quality of such State roads. This would 
go a long way in improving the quality of State roads being constructed by using CRIF. 

 
6 
11. The Ministry further informed the Committee that the criteria for CRF State Roads was 
proposed by the MoRT&H with the approval of Hon’ble Minister (RT&H); these have been 
finalized by M/o Finance with approval of Hon’ble Finance Minister; issued on 31.01.2020 
(Annexure-IV). 
12. The Ministry apprised the Committee about the following major aspects of the criteria for 
State roads under CRIF Act, 2000:- 
○ Criteria for allocation of funds is based on 30% weightage to fuel consumption and 70% 
weightage to geographical area of the State/ UT. 10% of such allocation to be 
earmarked for road safety works.  
○ Considering the limited available budgetary resources, aspirations of the Government, 
financing of State road projects in the second phase after com pletion of the Phase -I of 
Bharatmala under CRIF shall be duly considered.     
○ Fund shall be available for clearing outstanding liability of works sanctioned by the 
MoRT&H under CRIF (including Economic Importance & Inter -State Connectivity 
(EI&ISC) Schemes). 
○ Construction of roads connecting 'economic corridors', 'connecting roads under 
Bharatmala', 'roads connecting ports' and 'roads connecting commercial hubs' shall be 
funded under CRIF. 
○ The sanction of EI&ISC works would be similar as CRIF works.  
○ Total c ost of the schemes to be approved to be limited to the bank of sanctions of 
generally three times  of the annual allocation, except for hill States and North -East 
States (where working season is limited) for which this is to be generally be four times 
of the annual allocation for the year for the State/ UT. 

 
7 
○ Land acquisition (LA) was not being permitted earlier for State road projects except for 
pre-construction activities for ring -roads or bypasses or service roads along NHs. LA is 
now also to be allow ed for development of NHs as States’/ UTs’ contributions to share 
of Land Costs. This would facilitate participation/ contribution of States in LA cost as 
envisaged under “Grand Challenge” mechanism. 
○ Projects on de-notified/ reverted back to States/ UTs on  account of construction of NH 
bypasses, potential roads for declaration as new NHs, economically important roads, 
roads connecting NHs with particular focus on safety aspects.  
○ Road safety works, construction of ROBs/ RUBs, bridges, etc. 
○ State Governments/ UTs shall forward list of projects along with the relevant details to 
this Ministry for consideration of finalizing the same.  
○ State Govts./ UTs shall accord Administrative Approval for the projects after 
finalization of list by the Ministry. 
○ State/ UT PWDs, Road Construction Department/ Corporation, etc., to accord Technical 
Approval and Financial Sanction (TA&FS).   
○ Upto 10% of excess cost over administratively approved cost allowed. 
○ MoRT&H to release funds to State Govts./ UTs in Quarterly instalments linked to 
submission of Utilization Certificates (UCs).  
○ One third of accrual for the State/ UT for the year shall be maintained as a revolving 
balance with State/ UT while releasing funds.      
○ State Governments/ UTs to further release funds to concerned executive agencies (e.g. 
PWDs, Road Construction Department/ Corporation, etc.) within 7 days of release of 
funds by Ministry. 
○ Fund provided under CRIF shall not lapse at the end of the financial year. 

 
8 
13. The Ministry furnished details about the State / U T – wise accrual and release made for 
CRIF State roads since 2014-15 including Outstanding liabilities of sanctioned projects/ Bank of 
Sanction (BOS) as on 01.04.2021 (attached at Annexure -V). The State / UT – wise allocation 
and expenditure made for EI&IS C works since 2014 -15 including BOS as on 01.04.2021 is 
attached at Annexure-VI.  
14. During the meeting of the Committee held on 16 th  December, 2021, DG(RD)&SS 
informed that the total cost of scheme which can be sanctioned under a particular State, is limited 
to Bank of Sanctions which is limited to three times of the annual accrual/allocations in plain 
areas and four times in hilly and North -Eastern Areas. He stated that the sanction process has 
been further modified and as per the amended Act, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
only approves the projects which are identified and submitted by the State Governments. After 
the approval, it is the responsibility of the State Government to accord administrative approvals 
and financial sanctions and to mo nitor the progress of projects. He apprised the Committee that 
based on the progress of work, State Governments submit a utilization certificate duly audited by 
the audit committee, based on which, the Ministry releases the funds to the State Governments. 
He stated that there was no lack of clarity between the States and the Centre and that delays in 
the progress of works used to be present in many States a few years back but that now most 
States are completing projects in 3 -4 years, except some North -Eastern States where projects 
take more time because of rains and other issues. He pointed out the issue of delay in submission 
of utilization certificates by the State Governments. Another problem he highlighted upon was 
that the bank of sanctions is already h igh and the Ministry does not have any funds for further 
release as the unspent balance and current accruals of State Governments have been completely 
released. 

 
9 
15. Chief Engineer, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, during his presentation 
before the Committee on 16th December, 2021, furnished the following details regarding projects

17. The Committee notes the State / UT – wise accrual and release made for CRIF State 
roads since 2014-15 and the State / UT – wise allocation and expenditure made for EI&ISC 
works since 2014-15 including BOS as on 01.04.2021. The Committee feels that most of the 
States are making efficient use of the CRIF funds. Since the CRIF fund i s non-lapsable in 
nature, the Committee recommends that the Ministry must take up the issue of  inordinate 
delays in submitting the utilization certificates with the State Government, at the top -most 
level. The Ministry must impress upon the State Governme nts that sincere efforts have to 
be made to ensure that the projects sanctioned under CRIF are completed on time and the 
available funds are timely utilized.  
18. The Committee takes note of the issue highlighted by the Ministry regarding Bank 
of Sanctions already being high and the Ministry not having any funds for further release 
as the unspent balance and current accruals of State Governments have been completely 
released. Considering the backlog of funds to be released under CRIF which has been 
caused by Bank of Sanctions being high, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
make efforts to keep the Bank of Sanctions within the prescribed limits so that the funds 
for the sanctioned projects can be released to the State Governments on time.  
19. The Committee observes a major negative impact that the Coronavirus pandemic 
has had on the number of projects sanctioned under CRIF during 2020 -21 and 2021 -22. 
The Committee hopes that the subsequent waves, if any, of the pandemic do not have a 
significant impact on the road projects across the country and that the Ministry would be 
able to sanction a greater number of works under CRIF in the coming years.  
20. On the issue of Bank of Sanctions (BOS), the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation made in para 376 of its 296 th Report on ‘Role of Highways in Nation 
Building’, which states the following:  

 
11 
 “The Committee is of the view that the existing mechanism of bank of sanctions is 
causing a visible lack of clarity between the State Government Departments concerned and the 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, regarding the amount that the State is yet to be 
awarded. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may look into the issue and come up 
with suitable guidelines to ensure that there is no confusion among t he State Government 
Departments and the Ministry, regarding the share of funds to be received by the State, in any 
particular year, after factoring in the Bank of Sanctions.”  
21. The Committee observes that 10% of the allocation made to States under CRIF is to 
be earmarked for road safety works. Keeping in mind that India has the highest number of 
deaths in the world on account of road accidents and the immeasurable impact that the 
same has on countless families as well as on the overall Indian economy, th e Committee 
feels that the efforts being made by the Ministry in this regard would give a big boost if a 
higher share of CRIF funds allocated to the State Governments are earmarked for 
carrying out road safety works. The Committee, therefore, recommends th at the Ministry 
may consider increasing the percentage of funds that are earmarked for road safety works 
under CRIF, from the existing 10 percent. Further, the Ministry may evolve an effective 
mechanism to oversee and monitor optimal utilization of the fun ds earmarked for road 
safety works under CRIF.

viz., diversion of CAL A by the State Governments during general elections, pandemic, natural 
calamities, etc., absence of suitable provision in NH Act 1956 in connection with the deposit 
money before the competent court in such cases of unwilling/absentee/ untraceable land owne rs, 
land owners approaching arbitration for more compensation, enhancement of compensation by 

 
12 
the Arbitrator , protests by land owners for higher rates, alignment mismatch  leading to shift in

Governments should have dedicated Land Acquisition Department for speedy execution of road 
projects and informed that NHAI has given all powers to Regional Officers (ROs) to execute the 
projects. It was informed that for  Tamil nadu, the annual accrual of funds is Rs. 350 crores for 
the year 2021-22 and 1/3rd of the project value had been released as advance, till that time.

Public Wo rks Department, State Government of Kerala opined that the State receives low 
allocation of CRIF funds because of its small area, despite having a high density road network 
because the CRIF guidelines give 70% weightage to area of the State and only 30% we ightage to 
fuel consumption in the State. He briefed the Committee about the delayed NH projects in Kerala 
and stated that the State however is receiving good support from NHAI. Representatives of the 
State Government of Kerala, informed the Committee that  about Rs. 700 crores of funds under 
CRF/CRIF are yet to be received whereas the representatives of Ministry of Road Transport & 
Highways stated that about Rs. 126 crores are yet to be disbursed to the Government of Kerala 
and that utilization certificates for the same are yet to be received.  
24. The Committee takes note of the issue highlighted by the representatives of State 
Government of Kerala regarding the criteria for allocation of CRIF funds based on 70% 
weightage to area of the State and 30% weight age to fuel consumption in the State, and 
recommends that the criteria may be reassessed to ensure that there is a logical, equitable 
distribution of CRIF funds and smaller States are not at a disadvantage in terms of the 
CRIF allocation that they receive.  The Committee feels that the existing criteria might be 
resulting into very low allocation of CRIF funds to the North -Eastern States since they are 
smaller in area and the traffic plying in those States is also on the lower side. The 

 
13 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may consider making some special changes to 
the existing criteria to permit higher allocation under CRIF to the North -Eastern States 
given their sensitive location and difficult terrain.

coordinate to address the issues being faced regarding the disbursal of CRIF funds to the 
State. A high -level meeting of officials of the Ministry and the State Governments should 
take place every month to resolve issues pertainin g to land acquisition, forest clearances, 
CRIF disbursal, and other problems being faced in the development of NHs in the State. 
The Committee further recommends that a comprehensive Master Plan should be 
formulated for improving road connectivity to impor tant tourism places, cultural places, 
ports etc. across the country and that CRIF funds may be utilized for implementing the 
same. The Committee recommends that the criteria for sanction of road projects under 
CRIF may be modified so as to give higher prio rity for sanctions to roads that provide 
connectivity to places of tourism and cultural significance and last -mile connectivity to 
ports.

that the Ministry should have a syste m to identify the pending issues with State and 
Central Governments and the same should be followed up with the Chief Secretary of the 
States. CRIF funds should also be recommended for linkage of inner state roads, small 
towns to nearby NH roads and when l inkage between two states is being worked out, it 
should be ensured that both States cooperate for executing the works on time. The 
Committee further recommends that all concerned Ministries/State Departments viz., 
tourism, culture, airport, shipping, rail ways, etc. should formulate a master plan and plan

of action for their respective sector and convene periodical meetings to carry out the same 
in a time-bound manner.

CRIF. He queried about the quality monitoring mechanism for the same and highlighted a road

involved and action must be taken by the Ministry after due investigation. DG (RD)&SS

good. A Member of the Committee suggested that a benchmark c ost of road projects should be

 The Committee notes that through the amendment made by Finance Act, 2018, 
more sectors viz., Ports, Shipyards, Inland Waterways, Airports, Railway track and 
Commercial Infrastructure/ Stations, Urban Public Transport, etc., in Transport Sector 
besides other Sectors (Energy, Water and Sanitation, Communication, Social and 
Commercial Infrastructure), have been included under the CRIF. The Committee feels 
that the budgetary support that CRIF now provides to all these crucial sectors will help in

and other senior representatives of the Ministry to  the meeting, apprising them of the agenda of 
the meeting i.e.  to deliberate on ‘Review of Central Road and Infra structure Fund (CRIF) 
Works’. 
2.         In his opening remarks, the Chairman sta ted that the amendment of the Central Road 
Infrastructure Fund (CRIF) Act, 2000 through the Fi nance Act, 2018 and replacing the earlier 
Act with the CRIF Act, 2000 has been done to use th e proceeds of the road cess under CRIF to 
finance other infrastructure projects including por ts, shipyards, waterways, some portion of the 
railway infrastructure and even social infrastructu re including educational institutions, medical 
22

 
colleges etc. He asked the Director General (Road D evelopment) & Special Secretary to 
highlight the impact of the recent amendments of the CRIF Act, 2000. He queried about the bank 
of sanctions issued and amount of funds released to  the State Governments under CRIF during 
the last three years. He enquired about the rationa lity of the existing criteria for allocation of 
funds under CRIF Act, 2000, which is based on 30% w eightage to fuel consumption and 70% 
weightage to geographical area of the State/UT. He further sought information regarding the 
present mechanism with regard to allocation, accrua l and release of CRIF funds to the State/UT 
Governments and any delays that State/UT Government s might be facing in release of funds by 
the Government of India, under CRIF. 
3.         The DG (RD)&SS, Ministry of Road Transpo rt and Highways began his deposition by 
informing the Committee that the earlier CRF Act, 2 000 came into effect in the year 2000 and 
was amended through the Finance Act, 2018 and renam ed as Central Road Infrastructure Fund. 
He further stated that as per the Finance Act, 2018, CRIF is to be administered by the Ministry of 
Finance through the Department of Economic Affairs.  He further elaborated that earlier, 41.5 
percent of the cess was given for the National High ways, 10 percent for the State Roads and the 
rest for other infrastructure, however, after 1 st  April, 2018, a Committee headed by the Finance 
Minister and aided by a Committee of Secretaries, d ecided upon the distribution of the CRIF 
among the various Ministries/Organizations. He appr ised the Committee that the total cost of 
scheme which can be sanctioned under a particular S tate, is limited to Bank of Sanctions which 
is limited to three times of the annual accrual/all ocations in plain areas and four times in hilly 
and North-Eastern Areas. He stated that the sanctio n process has been further modified and as 
per the amended Act, Ministry of Road Transport and  Highways only approves the projects 
which are identified and submitted by the State Gov ernments. After the approval, it is the 
responsibility of the State Government to accord administrative approvals and financial sanctions 
and to monitor the progress of projects. He apprise d the Committee that based on the progress of 
work, State Governments submit a utilization certif icate duly audited by the audit committee, 
23

 
based on which, the Ministry releases the funds to the State Governments. He stated that there 
was no lack of clarity between the States and the C entre and that delays in the progress of works 
used to be present in many States a few years back but that now most States are completing 
projects in 3-4 years, except some North-Eastern St ates where projects take more time because 
of rains and other issues. He pointed out the issue  of delay in submission of utilization 
certificates by the State Governments. Another problem he highlighted upon was that the bank of 
sanctions is already high and the Ministry does not  have any funds for further release as the 
unspent balance and current accruals of State Governments has been completely released.

Committee that CRIF is non-lapsable and there is no  provision to withhold and earmark the fund

investigation. DG (RD)&SS informed the Committee th at the State Governments are responsible

construction issued by the Ministry and the Indian Roads Congress. As for quality of roads of 
National Highways are concerned, Ministry of Road t ransport and Highways is responsible.

questioned about how the quality of roads construct ed by such bidders can be expected to be 
good. A Member of the Committee suggested that a be nchmark cost of road projects should be 
calculated by the Ministry and that in case of proj ects being awarded to bids lower than the 
benchmark costs, such projects must be flagged and frequent inspection visits must be made to 
check the quality of construction of such flagged road projects.

DG (RD)&SS and other representatives of the Ministr y. The Chairman then directed that written 
replies to the queries which remained unanswered may be sent to the Secretariat within a week.

presently, inter-alia , examining the subject ‘Issues related to land acq uisition at Bagdogra 
Airport’. The Chairman stated that during its Study Visit to Kolkata on 18 th  November, 2021, the 
Committee had discussed the issues relating to the functioning of Airports in West Bengal 
wherein the issue of land transfer by the Ministry of Defence to Airports Authority of India to 
expand the Bagdogra Airport was raised. Though the State Government and Airports Authority 
of India were keen to develop/expand the said airpo rt, the key hindrance for it is the non-transfer 
25

 
of 3.5 acres of land which is currently under the p ossession of Ministry of Defence. The 
Committee directed the authorities to solve the iss ue between themselves so that the airport can 
be expanded/developed. Both the State Government of  West Bengal and Airports Authority of 
India are willing to fully compensate the Ministry of Defence for acquiring this piece of land. 
However, inter-Ministerial differences still persis t. On earlier occasions, when such disputes

Committee decided to call for written views/suggest ions of State Governments and hear their 
officials on the subject. Accordingly, the Committe e authorized the Chairman to obtain 
necessary orders from Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha in this regard.

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee to the first meeting 
of the reconstituted Committee and apprised them of  the agenda of the meeting, i;.e. (i) oral 
evidence of Secretary, Ministry of Tourism on the s ubjects - * * * and "Promotion of Indian

(i) Oral Evidence of Secretary, Ministry of Tourism 
2.         Thereafter, the Chairman invited the Sec retary, Ministry of Tourism to make a 
presentation on the above subjects which are instru mental in promoting tourism in the country. 
The Secretary,   Ministry of Tourism during the cou rse of his deposition made a detailed 
presentation on Tourism Infrastructure Development Schemes. While making the presentation, 
the Secretary elaborated on the Schemes of the Mini stry viz. ‘ Swadesh Darshan,’ ‘PRASHAD,’ 
‘Assistance to Central Agencies’ and ‘Adopt a Herit age.’ He informed that the ‘Swadesh 
Darshan’ Scheme aimed to develop a theme-based inte grated tourism infrastructure with 15 
thematic circuits identified for development of 76 sanctioned projects across 31 States and UTs 
with a budgetary allocation of Rs. 5526.71 Crore for the year 2021-22 and that the Ministry  
 
*Relates to other matters.  

 
24 
 
completed projects in Tehri (Uttarakhand), Khajuraho (M.P.) and Thenzawl (Mizoram) under the 
Scheme. He further stated that the PRASHAD Scheme a ims to develop Ghats, tourist Reception/ 
Facilitation Centers, Public amenities, open-air am phitheatres, museums, medicine centers, 
external infrastructure such as water supply, sewag e, drainage, electricity, roads and use of 
renewable sources. The Secretary also informed the Committee that under the PRASHAD 
Scheme, 61 sites have been identified for developme nt of tourism infrastructure and 37 projects 
have been sanctioned for an amount of Rs. 1214.19 c rore. Highlighting the challenges faced in 
execution of the tourism infrastructure projects, t he Secretary made a mention of the delay in 
land availability and statutory clearances, delayed  tendering and slow project implementation by 
State Governments. The Secretary also apprised the Committee that the Scheme ‘Assistance to 
Central Agencies' aims to develop and upgrade basic  tourism infrastructure and has 55 projects 
in pipeline with budgetary allocation of Rs. 629.06 Crore and has 19 completed projects in its lap 
till date. The Committee was further informed that under the ‘Adopt a Heritage Scheme’ which 
aimed at increasing awareness about heritage and in volved community participation as well as 
development of hard and soft interventions at the s ites, 27 MoUs (Memorandum of 
Understanding) have been signed for 27 sites.  
3.         The Chairman emphasized the need for inc reasing connectivity to tourist spots by road, 
rail, air and waterways and suggested that CSIR fun ds/ state govt. funds should be used for 
improvement of the same. He stated that the coopera tion on part of Indian embassies in 
promotion of tourism in overseas markets is almost non – existent and emphasized that in order 
to boost the GDP of our country, the overseas promo tion and publicity of Indian tourism should 
be revamped to derive maximum advantage from the to urism generating markets. He also 
suggested that a master-plan should be prepared  fo r better connectivity to all the tourists 
destinations. 

 
25 
 
4.        The Chairman also suggested that various unexplored/lesser known tourist spots may be 
added / highlighted on the Ministry’s website porta l so as to attract more tourists to different 
destinations and facilities. 
5.         Replying to the query regarding the role  played by Indian Embassies in increasing India's 
share of the global tourism market, the Secretary informed the Committee that the Ministry had a 
discussion with the Ministry of External Affairs (M EA) regarding separate listings of top ten 
countries from which India has a good tourist rush and another list of top ten countries from 
where heavy tourist rush is expected for India and that the MEA has already appointed twenty 
earmarked nodal officers in these countries to deal  with the issue of tourism. Upon the question 
of using Central Road Fund (CRF) for tourist places  with the help/ cooperation of Ministry of 
Transport, the Secretary stated that the process to  develop highways and roads out of CRF 
money was an ongoing process and some of the connec tivity projects  had already been 
undertaken by NHAI. 
6.         Members of the Committee raised various queries on need of tourism infrastructure 
development in various States; identification and d evelopment of revenue-generating domestic 
tourist destinations in States; establishing Souven ir Shops selling miniatures of historical 
monuments, development of Haats, identifying and tr aining local families willing to provide 
local homemade food and home-stay facilities in the ir abodes to the tourists; creating revenue 
potential through promotion of Seaport tourism; pro motion of cruise tourism and Monsoon 
tourism; assessment and pre-listing of privately–ow ned culturally rich buildings and taking steps 
towards their preservation; assessment of tourist o ffices abroad; making Tourist Information 
Centers accessible; lack of funds for assistance to the States in capacity building, etc.  Some of  
  

 
26 
 
the queries were replied to by the Secretary. The C hairman then directed that written replies to 
the queries which remained unanswered may be sent to the Secretariat within a week.
