courses to be offered, curriculum etc. In the long- term plan of action, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may also look into the  feasibility of opening regional 
centres of IIH in various regions of the country. 
(Para 31) 
 
 
LIBRARIES AND ARCHIVES 
The Committee finds that budget allocation under de velopment of Libraries and 
Archives has been increased from Rs. 100.07 crores in BE 2021-22 to Rs. 127.76 crores  
in BE 2022-23. While the Committee appreciates the near 28 percent increase in 
allocation under this head, it feels that the alloc ation is not sufficient and needs to be 
enhanced comprehensively, considering the importanc e of Libraries Sector in 
disseminating information and the vast scope that l ies in developing it rapidly. Facility  
of Libraries needs to be expanded to the village le vel to educate the masses. Therefore, 
every village needs to be facilitated with Library facilities for generations to reap its 
benefits from year to year. The Committee, therefor e, recommends that more funds 
should be allocated to promote this sector. 
(Para 33) 
 
 
VACANCIES IN VARIOUS ORGANIZATIONS OF THE MINISTRY 
The Ministry in its written reply has furnished the  details of the vacancies and the steps 
taken to fill them in ASI (placed at Annexure-I) an d other organizations (Annexure-II) 
of the Ministry. The Committee feels that the vacan cy details reflect a very pathetic  
state of affairs in all the organizations of the Ministry. In the Archaeology Cadre of ASI, 
against the total sanctioned strength of 420, the vacant positions are 166, similarly in the 
Conservation Cadre, against the total strength of 9 18 there is a mammoth vacancy of 
452 positions. The situation is not any better in o ther Cadres of ASI or other 
organisations of the Ministry. The Committee thus f inds it difficult to understand how 
the Ministry can ensure the efficiency of its organ izations and manage to meet the 

34   
present human resource needs of the respective orga nisations, leave alone there being 
any scope for new initiatives by the organisations. The Committee strongly recommends 
that the Ministry may set up a foolproof mechanism in place to ensure that the staffing 
requirements of all its organizations are met at al l times, so as to enable them to carry 
out their mandate in letter and spirit. 
(Para 35) 
 
 
The Committee is anguished to note the large scale vacancies in all the organizations of 
the Ministry for years together and shocked to find  that in some cadres the vacancies 
are more than 50% of the sanctioned strength. It fa ils to understand how the Ministry 
will achieve the task of conserving the culture and  heritage of such a vast country with 
less than 50% of the sanctioned strength. 
(Para 36) 
 
 
The Committee notes with concern that a large numbe r of vacancies in important 
organizations like ASI, National Archives, Anthropo logical Survey of India etc. are 
vacant for a considerable period of time. The Commi ttee, therefore, strongly comments 
that concerted efforts be taken to fill up the vaca ncies at a fast pace to improve the 
organisational functioning. It is observed that due  to not filling up the vacancies 
regularly the organizations are facing deemed aboli tion of several posts which have 
many other ramifications. The Committee feels that most of the organizations in the 
Ministry require specialized qualifications and the  students/candidates who study these 
subjects do not have many other opportunities and i f the posts are not filled timely, 
many qualified and talented candidates would be age  barred, thus causing loss to the 
Government by spending in their education and not a vailing the benefits of their 
knowledge/expertise as well as career of the candid ates. Similarly delayed promotions 
also play a negative role in the morale of the offi cials. The Committee is, therefore, of  
the considered opinion that all the vacancies to be  filled by promotions must be filled, at 
the earliest within a span of six months and the Di rect Recruitment vacancies be filled 
up within a year. The Committee also recommends tha t the organisations should 
identify the anticipated vacancies of Direct Recrui tment and request UPSC/SSC in 
advance to initiate action to fill up the vacancies  which will enable the organisations to 
serve better for the purpose for which they have been established. 
(Para 37) 

35   
NORTH-EASTERN AREAS 
The Committee would like to know about the expendit ure pattern under the head 
‘North-Eastern Areas’ for the last 5 years and how the same compares with the 
expenditure pattern of the overall allocation made to the Ministry during the same 
period. 
(Para 44) 
 
 
The Committee is pleased to note that ASI has creat ed a new North Eastern Region 
Division and that a Joint Director General has been posted there. This was long overdue 
given the rich and varied heritage of the region an d would certainly add fresh impetus  
to the conservation and development of archaeologic al sites and monuments in the 
region. It recommends that the Ministry and ASI may  ensure that the North Eastern 
Region is not neglected in terms of budgetary alloc ation for preservation and 
development of tangible heritage in the region. The  Committee desired to be apprised 
about the sites/monuments in the North Eastern Regi on that are being considered for 
inclusion under the list of monuments under the protection of ASI. 
(Para 45) 
 
 
NATIONAL MONUMENTS AUTHORITY 
The Committee observes that main roadblocks in spee dy preparation of HBLs are lack 
of qualified staff in the offices of the Regional D irectors of ASI, less number of Heritage 
Bodies for heritage consultation and the quantum of  fees payable to these  notified 
bodies for heritage consultation. The Committee, th erefore, recommends that urgent 
steps should be taken to remove all the bottlenecks  being faced in the preparation of 
HBLs, such as meeting the staff requirements of Reg ional Director Offices of ASI, 
enlarging the list of notified expert heritage bodi es and recruitment of Hindi 
Translators, in order to prevent further damage to invaluable national heritage due to 
lack of heritage bye-laws. 
(Para 50) 
 
 
GLOBAL ENGAGEMENT AND INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 
The Committee observes that out of total allocation  of Rs. 10.50 crores in R.E. 2021-22 
actual expenditure incurred was Rs. 5.76 crores whi ch works out to a little more than 
50% only. The Committee further finds that out of the total allocation of Rs. 13.57 crore 

36   
made in BE 2022-23 for the head ‘Global Engagement and International Cooperation’, 
an allocation of Rs. 11.38 crores has been made for  the Scheme for Promotion of 
International Cultural Relations, Rs. 69 lakhs for Project Mausam and Rs. 1.5 crores  
for contribution to international organizations. Th e Committee recommends that 
maximum utilization of funds should be achieved for cultural festivals to be held abroad 
in order to promote and strengthen Indian culture a broad by sanctioning grant-in-aid  
to Indo-foreign friendship cultural societies for achieving the desired results. 
(Para 52) 
 
 
The Committee notes that as against the BE 2021-22 allocation of Rs 9.90 crores, the RE 
allocation has been increased to Rs. 10.50 crores i n RE 21-22. But the  actual 
expenditure till 31.01.2022 is only Rs 5.11 crores,  i.e., less than 50%. The Committee 
desired to be apprised of the reasons for less than  50% utilisation under this head and 
the basis on which the budget allocation is being i ncreased. The Committee also  
requests that the Ministry should also ensure that the balance 50% of funds are spent 
fully. The Ministry also must ensure that in future , funds are spent evenly throughout 
the year. 
(Para 53) 
 
 
NATIONAL MISSION FOR PRESERVATION OF MANUSCRIPTS 
The Committee notes that Rs. 3.28 crores was alloca ted in B.E. 2021-22 but it is 
surprised to note that there is no allocation in R. E. 2021-22 and BE 2022-23. The 
Committee fails to understand the reasons for the s ame. The Committee recommends 
that proper allocation be made in future for such a n important area so that a national 
resource base for manuscripts can be preserved and created. 
(Para 55) 
 
 
NATIONAL MISSION ON CULTURAL MAPPING AND ROADMAP 
The Committee is pleased to note that an allocation  of Rs. 19.13 crore on account of 
National Mission on Cultural Mapping and Roadmap ha s been made in BE 2022-23. 
This will go a long way in achieving its aims. The Committee hopes the fund allocated 
for the same will be utilised in the most prudent, planned and beneficial manner and 
would like to be apprised of the actual spendings under this head in the last few years. 
(Para 57) 

37   
SUPPORT TO ACADEMIES, MUSEUMS, LIBRARIES, BUDDHIST TIBETAN 
INSTITUTIONS AND MEMORIALS 
The Committee notes that the BE 2022-23 allocation to these Akademies, Museums, 
Libraries, BTI and Memorials is more or less the sa me as in BE 21-22 with slight 
increase/ slight decrease. But the actual expenditu re in 21-22 till 31.1.22 in respect of 
Akademies, Libraries and BTI Memorials is quite low  as compared to BE allocation. It 
is especially very low in case of Akademies while t he RE allocation for 2021-22 is Rs. 8 
crores higher than BE allocation, the actual expenditure is only Rs. 239.45 (till   31.1.22) 
i.e. only 68.5% of the RE allocation. The Committee  notes that even when the actual 
expenditure in these and some other cases are low, the allocations have been increased 
significantly in RE. 
(Para 60) 
 
 
The Committee hopes and urges the Ministry of Culture to ensure that allocations are 
fully spent and not surrendered at the last moment. 
(Para 61) 
 
 
ARTISTS PENSION SCHEME AND WELFARE FUND 
The Committee, therefore, strongly reiterates that the pension amount needs to be 
reviewed without further delay and it should be mad e respectable for a person who has 
contributed to the society and country in continuing the various art forms. 
(Para 63) 
 
 
It is very saddening that instead of intensifying t he efforts in recognizing the artists in 
the 75 th year of Independence, the Ministry of Culture is re ducing the number of 
beneficiaries of this scheme since 2018-19, when it  reached the highest level of 4120 
beneficiaries. The Ministry has informed that due t o COVID-19, the beneficiaries have 
not been able to submit the desired documents, henc e the disbursements have been 
delayed. 
(Para 65) 
 
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the reason adva nced by the Ministry and 
recommends that the Ministry should be rather proac tive in such difficult  
circumstances  in  providing  financial  and  medical  support  to  artists  who  might  be 

38   
struggling for their survival. The Ministry should take help from its Zonal Cultural 
Centers or the bankers of the pensioners, besides r eaching to the beneficiaries directly 
for providing them with the financial support. 
(Para 66) 
 
 
SCHEME FOR THE AWARD OF SENIOR/JUNIOR FELLOWSHIPS T O 
OUTSTANDING PERSONS IN THE FIELDS OF CULTURE 
The Committee is shocked to find the inordinate del ay in release of payments to the 
junior and senior fellows under the scheme. It is p ained to know that despite strong 
recommendations made on the subject the Ministry is  not able to release the pending 
fellowships to all the fellows of the scheme in the last one year. 
(Para 69) 
 
 
As these fellows are basically full time researcher s in the field of art and music, the 
Committee feels that they should be supported by th e Ministry in their endeavor to 
preserve and continue our cultural heritage in a be tter and respectable manner. The 
Committee therefore recommends that in view of the rising inflation the fellowship 
amount should also be reviewed from Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 20,000 per month, respectively, 
to Junior and Senior fellows, which was fixed a long time back. 
(Para 70) 
 
 
The Committee also feels that centralizing the disb ursement of the fellowship has also 
affected the timely disbursement of the fellowship.  It should be disbursed by the CCRT 
as was done a few years back. The Committee also re commends that the Research 
papers of their scheme should be sent to art colleg es/schools on rotation basis so that 
they are utilized by future generations. 
(Para 71) 
 
 
CULTURAL FUNCTION AND PRODUCTION GRANT (CFPG) AND R EPERTORY 
GRANT 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should p repare a mechanism to 
individually intimate about the sanction of the gra nt to the organisations through their 
emails and requirement of any document should also be communicated. A nodal  officer 

39   
should be nominated to coordinate with these organisations to resolve any query on 
documentation. 
(Para 74) 
 
 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in  para 64 of this Report that since 
the beneficiaries of this scheme are the people inv olved in preserving the intangible 
cultural heritage of the country while devoting the ir life to the art forms and 
propagating it further, they should be honored in a respectable manner. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should review the amou nt of CFPG  and  Repertory 
Grant as well as keep increasing the number of gran tees, so that more and more people 
in the country, especially from rural background, h ave the opportunity to perform and 
enrich our culture, while earning a respectable liv elihood by showcasing their artistic 
skills. 
(Para 75) 
 
 
INCLUSION OF MONUMENTS IN THE LIST OF CENTRALLY PRO TECTED 
MOVEMENTS 
The  Committee  reiterates  the  recommendation  it  made  in  its   289 
th    Report      that 
important historical monuments and sites such as Ra ma Temple at Peddathumbalem 
Village, Adoni Taluka, Kethavaram Rock arts, and Behim caves in Kurnool be included 
in the list of Centrally Protected Monuments in Con sultation with State Governments. 
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should expedite the process of 
identifying the important historical sites/monument s for requiring protection on 
priority, adding to the list of the 1.84 lakh Built  Heritage and Sites (BHS) that have 
already been documented by National Mission of Monu ment and Antiquities (NMMA) 
in the last 15 years. 
(Para 76) 
 
 
The Committee further recommends that the list of s tolen properties of the 
monuments/historical sites also be prepared and the  cases filed in these respect should 
be vigorously pursued, if it has not been filed the n the Ministry should take steps to file 
cases for stolen properties and recover them. 
(Para 78) 

40   
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should p ursue the matter of exploration 
of Ram Setu in the right earnest with priority inst ead of waiting for the proposal from 
the National Institute of Oceanography for exploration. The Committee also wants to be 
updated about the progress in the matter as well as  the project of ASI on underwater 
exploration in Dwarka. 
(Para 80) 
 
 
UTILISATION OF FUNDS COLLECTED FOR LIBRARIES BY STA TE 
GOVERNMENT 
The  Committee  reiterates  its  recommendation  made  in  para  42  of  its 310 
th  Report, 
which is as follows: 
'The State Governments may be guided to frame rules/ recommendations in the Act 
in a manner that money collected for the purpose is  utilized properly and spent only 
for the libraries. It should not go to the other St ate accounts and be used for other 
purposes. ' 
(Para 82) 
 
 
AZADI KA AMRIT MAHOTSAV 
The Committee appreciates the celebration and comme moration of the 75 years of 
progressive India and its glorious history. The use  of low cost initiatives and social  
media with a view to involve one and all is an exce llent approach towards this 
celebration of AKAM, which will maximize the outrea ch of the programme among the 
general public without straining the limited budget ary resources available with the 
Ministry. The Committee recommends that the Ministr y may ensure high levels of 
coordination with other Ministries and help them co me up with innovative ways to 
celebrate the AKAM. Efforts may also be made to rop e in State Government 
Departments to ensure even higher outreach of the celebrations. 
(Para 84) 
 
 
VISION OF THE MINISTRY FOR INDIA@2047 
The Committee is of the considered view that the Vi sion 2047 of the Ministry is very 
encouraging, however to achieve those, the Ministry  needs to intensify its efforts from 
the beginning itself. In this direction, the Minist ry needs to optimize the utilization of 
funds and plan more proposals with demand for more funds at the RE stage. 

41   
(Para 86) 
 
 
The Committee appreciates the long-term vision of t he Ministry of Culture to move 
towards a holistic model of cultural governance tha t goes beyond the Ministry  itself. 
The Committee feels that a significant part of the cultural heritage of the country is 
intangible, and as such, promotion and preservation  of the same for years to come can 
only be made possible when the policies of the Mini stry work in tandem with  the 
policies of other Central Ministries , State Govern ment Departments, Local Bodies, 
Societies and NGOs, International Organizations etc . The Committee therefore 
recommends that the Ministry may start working on b ringing this envisioned holistic 
model of cultural governance to reality, in a gradu al manner, since doing so would not 
only promote and preserve our cultural heritage, but also increase the cultural influence 
of the country and further its tourism prospects as well. 
(Para 88) 
 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
Co-ordination with State Governments 
The Committee reiterates the recommendations made in para 116 of its 289 
th Report on 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry, which is as follows: 
‘The Committee feels that many of the State Governme nts often do not look after 
their protected monuments. The apathy of the State Governments towards the 
cultural heritage falling under their jurisdiction,  sometimes causes irreparable 
damage to the same. The Committee desires the Minis try to look into cases of 
neglect of historical monuments and sites by the St ate Governments, take it up with 
the concerned State Department, provide technical a ssistance to them and if  
needed, consider taking over the responsibility of development and upkeep of select 
State-protected monuments in cases of extreme neglect. ’ 
(Para 89) 
 
 
Conservation of Regional Cultures, Languages, Traditions, Art and Dance forms 
The Committee is concerned to note that although In dia is home to a plethora of rich 
and distinct regional cultures, languages, traditions, art and dance forms, many of these 
are getting lost under modern influence, without be ing recorded or preserved. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should take all possible steps to protect and 

42   
preserve the intangible culture, languages, dialect s, traditions, art and dance forms of 
regional/local communities and tribes, including th ose in North-Eastern Areas  and 
other parts of the country, so that the unique rich ness of these cultures can be passed 
onto future generations. 
(Para 90)

The Indian Shipping Sector, with about 212 ports (1 2 Major and 200 Minor ports)  
along its 7,517 km coastline, has strengthened subs tantially in the last two decades. Over the 
years, the development of other aspects of shipping , such as containerization, multi-modal 
transport services, advancement of marine engineeri ng technology etc. has enabled  
infrastructural improvement in the Indian shipping industry. Roads, rails, airports and seaports 
together with the optimum storage capacity to move large shipments have placed the industry in 
a very advantageous position. The Ministry of Ports , Shipping & Waterways has been entrusted 
with the responsibility of formulation and implemen tation of various policies and programmes  
on development of Major & Minor Ports and harbours,  maritime safety, training & skill 
development, human resource, finance etc. Approximately 95% of the country /uni201Fs trade by volume 
and 68% by value, is moved through maritime transport.

projected  demand  of  Rs.  690  crores,  the  allo cation  made  under  the  head

Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may approach the Ministry of 
Finance for higher allocation under this head at th e R.E. stage so that the progress 
envisaged by the Ministry under the Sagarmala Programme for the Financial Year 2022-23 
can be achieved as per targets.

PERFORMANCE OF PORTS 
19. During the meeting of the Committee held on 18 th February, 2022 on Demands for Grants (2022-
23) of the Ministry, the Secretary, MoPSW, through a powerpoint presentation, shared the 
following information regarding the comparative per formance of Major and Non- Major Ports in 
the country in the last few years: 

16   
 
 
20. The Committee observes that the cargo handling capa city of Major Ports in the country 
has increased by about 79 percent between the years  2014-15 and 2020-21  (ignoring the 
incomplete data for the year 2021-22 since it is ye t to be finalized), which is an annualized 
growth rate of about 10.2 percent. As compared to t his, the gross cargo  handling capacity 
of Non-Major Ports has increased by only about 52 p ercent, with an annualized growth 
rate of just 7.2 percent. In terms of Traffic handl ed, however, Non- Major Ports registered 
a growth of about 30 percent ( ∼∼ ∼∼6.7 percent annualized) between the years 2015-16 a nd 
2019-20 (excluding the Covid affected year 2020-21 and ongoing year 2021-22) whereas 
Major Ports in the country only managed a minor inc rease of about 16 percent ( ∼∼ ∼∼3.8 
percent annualized) during the same period. This da ta points to the fact that while Major 
Ports across the country have managed to increase t heir capacity at a satisfactory pace, 
which is higher than that of Non-Major Ports, the s tatistics pertaining to traffic handled at 
ports across the country do not portray a robust picture for the Major Ports in the country. 
While Non-Major Ports have managed to increase the volume of traffic handled at nearly 
the same pace at which their capacity is increasing, Major Ports paint a contrasting picture 
with annual growth in traffic handled at a mere 3.8  percent as against the capacity growth 
rate of about 10.2 percent. The Committee, therefor e, recommends the Ministry to review 
the possible reasons behind the comparative stagnan cy in the volume growth of traffic 
handled at Major Ports in the country. The Ministry  may also come up with an effective 
plan of action to further improve the growth rate o f cargo handling capacity of Non-Major

RESPONSE TO OIL SPILL HAZARDS 
45. Upon the Committee /uni201Fs query on oil spill hazards, the Ministry apprised  that a National Oil Spill 
Disaster Contingency Plan (NOSDCP) has been in plac e in order to prevent oil spill generated 
impacts on marine species and ecosystem. The NOSDCP  works with different stakeholders such 
as Ports, State Governments. The Indian Coast Guard  has been declared as National  
Coordinating Agency for coordination of oil spill r esponse action. Under NOSDCP, spills 
occurring within Notified Port areas are dealt by i ndividual ports, and in turn MoPSW is taking 
action to strengthen oil spill response capability of ports in the country. In this regard, the 
Ministry had already executed a scheme of 50% finan cial assistance for procurement of Tier-1 
Oil Spill Response Equipment to Oil handling Major Ports & Non -Major Ports which continued 
till December 2020. Most of the Oil handling ports are equipped with Tier -I Oil Spill Response 
Facility. 
46. Subsequently, the Ministry has come out with the co ncept of developing 5 Regional Oil  
Response Centers (ROSRC) along the coastline coveri ng all major and non-major ports. 
ROSRCs shall provide enhanced capability and bring domain expertise and professional 
competence required to deal with oil spills in shor test possible time and minimizing the Overall 
Impact on ecosystem. The Ministry also provided the following information: 
 
a) Annex 1 of the International Convention for the Pre vention of Pollution from Ships 
(MARPOL) convention to which India is party to, deals with Prevention of Pollution by Oil. The 
aforesaid convention besides mandating the construction and operational requirement for ships to 
prevent pollution by oil, also specifies the requir ements for emergency response in case of oil 
spill. Indian ships are surveyed at periodic interv als to ensure compliance with the requirement  
of the MARPOL Convention. 
 
b) Part XI-A of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and M erchant Shipping (Prevention of 
Pollution by Oil from Ships) Rules, 2010, deals with aspects related to prevention of oil pollution 
by ships. 
 
c) In addition, to discourage operation of sub-standar d vessels in Indian water, Flag State 
Inspections (FSI) and Port State Control (PSC) Insp ections of ships in Indian ports are carried  
out to ensure compliance of ships with applicable regulation for prevention of pollution by oil. 

27   
d) Merchant Shipping (Regulations of Entry of Ships in to Ports, Anchorages and Offshore 
Facilities) Rules, 2012 has provisions that require  older vessels to conform to standards of 
members of the Association of International Classif ication Societies, so that possibility of oil- 
spill from such vessel is minimized. 
 
e) National response mechanism to deal with oil spill incidents has been prepared (NOS-DCP). 
In addition, to deal with compensation matters in c ase of an oil-spill from certain types of oil, 
India has become a party to the International Civil  Liability Convention (CLC-92) and the 
International Fund Convention (known as 1992 Fund). 
 
47. The Committee appreciates that a specialized agency  viz., National Oil Spill Disaster 
Contingency Plan (NOSDCP) has been established to p revent oil spill, which coordinates 
with ports, state governments and the Indian Coast Guard and that the Ministry is 
implementing sufficient measures to prevent oil spi ll hazards and their impact on marine 
species. The Committee desires to know the financia l allocation provided to NASDCP and

has been allocated /Rupee/Rupee /Rupee/Rupee 412.79 Crores in the B.E. 2022-23 against the proj ected demand of

500 Crores, which is about 17% less than the projec ted demand. The ambitious 
programme aims to promote port-led development in t he country and reduce logistics 
cost for both domestic and EXIM cargo. The Committe e, therefore, recommends that 
more financial resources need to be allocated for S agarmala at RE 2022-23 stage so that 
the vision of increasing competitiveness of Indian exports and improving the overall 
efficiency of the economy could be translated into reality. 
(Para 29) 
The Committee is unable to understand that no allocations have been made in the 
B.E.  2022-23  under  the  heads  „Sagarmala  Development  Company  (SDCL) /uni201F        and 
„Transfer to Central Road and Infrastructure Fund ( CRIF) /uni201F against the projected

growth of India in the coming years and the Sagarmala Development Company as well 

44   
as CRIF funds, are both crucial to the timely compl etion of the objectives envisaged 
under the Sagarmala programme. The Committee desire s to be apprised of the 
reasoning, if any, provided by the Ministry of Fina nce for effecting these cuts and 
recommends that the Ministry may make a strong case  for budgetary allocation under 
these heads at the RE 2022-23 stage. 
(Para 31)  
The Committee also desires to know the amount of unspent capital available with 
SDCL for investment in maritime sector infrastructure development projects. 
 
 
(Para 32)  
The Committee may be apprised of the reasons behind the 23.9% reduction in the 
allocation  for  ALHW  under  capital  head  at  RE  2021-22  stage,  as  compared  to the 
allocation made in BE 2021-22. 
(Para 34)  
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should put in place a rigorous  monitoring 
mechanism for the ongoing projects under the head „Sagarmala /uni201F and ensure that the 
scarce resources available with the Ministry for th e given year are utilized  efficiently 
and optimally. This would also ensure that the RE 2022-23 allocation of the  Ministry 
would not face any cuts under this head which is of utmost importance given its  crucial 
significance for the overall growth of the Port and Shipping sector in the country 
through port-led development. 
(Para 35) 
The Committee feels that having a Special Purpose V ehicle to improve the road 
and rail connectivity to Ports across the country w ould be very effective in addressing  
the bottleneck of poor connectivity that is faced b y almost all Ports, stifling their 
throughput. Having robust rail and road connectivit y at ports is crucial to ease 
congestion of cargo coming in and out of ports. The  Committee may be apprised of the 
progress being made with regard to the creation of this proposed SPV. The proposed 
SPV may recruit officials having prior experience i n execution of rail and road projects 
as well as in coordination with concerned agencies for this purpose. 
(Para 37) 
 
 
DEVELOPMENT OF PORTS 
The Committee welcomes the enactment of MPA Act, 2021 in addition to the 

45   
Policy Guidelines, 2014, to regulate land allotment  of Major Ports. It is of the opinion 
that it will give a new direction to the regulation , operation and planning of Major Ports 
in India. The Committee also notes that the Policy guidelines for Land/Township area 
management to set up port-based industries, is unde r consideration with the 
Government. The Committee urges the Ministry to exp edite the framing of the policy 
guidelines for land Management/township area Manage ment to set up port-based 
industries. The Committee is of the firm opinion th at integrating the port-based and 
other ancillary industries in the township areas of  the Major ports will boost the 
employment potential  and economy of the areas near the ports. 
(Para 40) 
The Committee also notes the initiation of the new „Landlord Model /uni201F through 
PPP mode. The Committee feels that since Port Devel opment and Modernisation is 
highly capital intensive, efforts of both the Publi c and Private sector are the need of the 
hour. In this direction, PPP mode should be encoura ged by the Ministry as the Private 
sector has the requisite capital and has already sh own competence in setting up modern 
ports. The Committee also desires to know the details of the proposed „Landlord Model /uni201F 
and how it will prove to be more advantageous in po rt development vis-à-vis the existing 
system. While appreciating the major initiatives ta ken to improve private sector 
participation in the port sector, the Committee sug gests that the example of the aviation 
sector where private players have changed the face of the aviation industry may be 
studied and impetus may be provided for more PPP pr ojects in the seaports. The 
Committee also desires to know the details regardin g ongoing/proposed PPP projects at 
Major ports for the year 2022-23. 
(Para 41) 
MARITIME RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT 
The Committee notes with concern about the meager a llocation of Rs. 1 crore 
which had been allocated both at B.E. and R.E.2021- 22 and again it was allocated the 
same amount of Rs. 1 crore at B.E. 2022-23, without any significant increase. Besides, the 
grants for research projects have been given to onl y three R&D Projects and that too 
only to three technical institutes. The Committee i s aware that India has a vast coastline 
and an Exclusive Economic Zone, which assumes great  significance in the growth of our 
economy. Research and innovation are a vital compon ent of the Maritime Sector 
worldwide. In order to become a leader in Maritime Sector, India needs to enhance 
maritime  research  &  development  and  education  in  marine  geology,  environmental 

46   
science, etc. Hence, the Ministry should plan towar ds increasing research and 
development capacities and also increase the number  of institutes involved in research  
on maritime sciences as new technology can propel the growth of the upcoming maritime 
sector in the country and help in the advancement o f career of many maritime 
researchers as well. 
(Para 44) 
RESPONSE TO OIL SPILL HAZARDS 
The Committee appreciates that a specialized agency  viz., National Oil Spill 
Disaster Contingency Plan (NOSDCP) has been establi shed to prevent oil spill, which 
coordinates with ports, state governments and the I ndian Coast Guard and that the 
Ministry is implementing sufficient measures to pre vent oil spill hazards and their 
impact on marine species. The Committee desires to know the financial allocation 
provided to NASDCP and whether it is sufficient to provide for purchasing oil spill 
prevention equipments of international standards. T he Committee would also like to be 
apprised of the recent oil spill incidents and whet her the response of the NOSDCP was 
found to be adequate to address such disaster. 
(Para 47) 
INSTALLATION OF HIGH TECH EQUIPMENTS AT PORTS 
The Committee observes that earlier CBIC was handli ng the matter of  
installation of container scanners at Major Ports. Thereafter, as per the decision of the 
Committee of Secretaries, the responsibility of pro curing scanners was shifted to the 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways in December , 2015. However, now the 
responsibility has again been shifted back to CBIC.  The Committee deplores this 
frequent shifting of responsibility of the importan t security aspect, such as the 
installation of scanners, between the CBIC and the Ministry and feels that there has  
been no long term planning on this crucial issue. T he Committee desires to know the 
reasons for this frequent change of responsibility and recommends that immediate steps 
may be taken to resolve this issue. It also recomme nds that the Ministry should explore 
the best technical equipments available and install ed at international ports abroad and 
install the same at all ports in the country. As regards installation of Drive through Road 
and Rail Scanners, the Committee recommends that al l the procedural and operational 
issues may be resolved, so that the concerned ports  can benefit at the earliest. The 
Committee also recommends that a long term policy s hould be framed for installation of 
high tech security apparatus at all ports in the country, in view of the increased  security 

47   
threats faced by the country. 
 
 
SHIPBUILDING AND ITS POTENTIAL IN INDIA 
 
(Para 50) 
The Committee notes that Shipbuilding has been iden tified as one of the key 
sectors under the “Make in India” Programme of the GOI. The Committee notes that 
though the existing shipbuilding industry comprises  both Central and State PSUs, and 
also 14 private sector shipyards, India /uni201Fs share in the global shipbuilding market is very 
less. The Committee is of the opinion that shipbuil ding is a manufacturing industry and  
a core sector with one of the highest job multiplie rs and therefore, there is a huge 
potential for the growth of the shipbuilding indust ry in India, which can also generate 
growth in employment. Though the Indian Shipbuildin g industry comprising both the 
Public and Private sectors have been in existence s ince a long time, however, due to the 
global competition, global downturn in the shipbuil ding industry and the unavailability 
of skilled workforce and state-of-the-art technolog y, Indian shipbuilding industry has 
lagged behind in its prospective growth. In this direction, the Committee appreciates the 
„Atmanirbhar Bharat /uni201F initiative, which lays emphasis on the indigenizat ion of 
shipbuilding. The Committee recommends that detaile d and futuristic planning should 
be made for growth of the industry in all the ident ified segments of shipbuilding and an 
effort should be made to develop India as a shipbuilding hub. 
 
(Para 52) 
DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF LIGHTHOUSE AND LIGHTSHIPS 
 
The Committee notes that out of the RE 2021-22 allo cation of Rs. 410 crores  
under the head „Directorate General of Lighthouse a nd Lightships /uni201F, the Ministry has 
only been able to spend Rs. 280 crores, i.e., about  68 percent of the total allocation, till 
7th February, 2022. The Committee feels that this slow pace of expenditure will certainly 
lead to time and cost overruns and will have an adv erse impact on the various projects 
carried out under this head. Given the important ro le played by Lighthouses in meeting 
the commercial and security needs of the country, t he timely execution of  projects 
related to development and maintenance of Lighthous es is extremely important. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Directorate  General of Lighthouses and 
Lightships may look into the reasons behind the slo w progress of its projects/schemes  
and take necessary remedial measures at the earliest. 

48   
(Para 55)  
The Committee, while welcoming the initiative of the Ministry to promote Lighthouses 
as tourist destinations, observes that tourism is a multi-sector activity. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that a formal link should be developed between all 
stakeholders so that Lighthouses could be promoted as attractive tourist destinations.  
The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may come up with innovative  
plans to promote tourism at Lighthouses in coordination with Ministry of Tourism and  
State Tourism Departments and provisions for tourist amenities and proper connectivity 
should be ensured. 
(Para 56) 
INLAND WATERWAYS 
The Committee is concerned to note that only about 63 percent of the funds 
allocated under the head – „Capital outlay on Inlan d Water Transport /uni201F for FY 2021-22 
have been spent till 7th February, 2022. The Commit tee feels that it might  not  be 
possible to utilize the entire amount of funds avai lable with it under this head for FY 
2021-22 and therefore, desires to be apprised of th e actions being taken by the Ministry 
in order to improve the expenditure pattern under this head. 
(Para 58)  
The Committee desires to know from the Ministry regarding the process being followed 
to develop Inland Waterways across the country and whether any consultants  are 
appointed for preparation of DPR of the projects. The Committee strongly recommends 
that the Ministry may follow due procedure and well-established norms for the 
development of inland waterways across the country with a long-term vision in mind, 
since waterways is a cost-effective, environment-friendly mode of transportation which  
can decrease the existing load on roads in the country. The Committee further desires  
that the Ministry may coordinate with the State Governments for development of inland  
waterways since the State Governments may not be having the necessary expertise for 
the same. Close coordination may also be established with the Ministry of Road  
Transport and Highways and State Public Works Departments to ensure that the road 
bridges constructed over waterways do not obstruct the passage of ships and boats, as 
far as possible. 
(Para 59) 
 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 

49   
Draught-related issues at Kolkata Port and other Ports  
The Committee notes with serious concerns that even  though PIB had approved 
an amount of Rs. 256 crores for dredging subsidy to  SMPK during FY 2022-23, a 24% 
lower allocation of Rs. 195.10 crore has been made for the same in BE 2022-23. The 
Committee recommends that the subsidy amount may be  reviewed at the RE stage in 
order to ensure that dredging operations at SMPK ca n achieve sufficient draft, so that 
the port can function as per its targets for the FY 22-23. 
(Para 62) 
 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may unde rtake a detailed exercise 
about the dredging requirements of all the major po rts along with cost-benefit analysis 
for the investment required to ensure improved draf t levels at the ports. The Ministry 
may analyze the viability of monetizing the sand an d other raw materials of any  
potential value, that are obtained as an outcome of  dredging at ports and utilizing this 
amount for funding more dredging projects at seaports as well as riverine ports. If found 
feasible, this would finance enhanced dredging effo rts which in turn would permit the 
ports to handle vessels of much bigger size and boo st the growth potential of the India /uni201Fs 
maritime sector at large. It would also put a check  on the illegal mining of sand that is 
presently taking place at sea and river basins. The  Committee, therefore, recommends 
that sufficient funds may be allocated by Ministry for carrying out research into this 
area in a time-bound manner and if possible, a policy may be brought out in this regard. 
(Para 64) 
 
 
Buckingham Canal  
The Committee notes that a canal route namely, the Buckingham Canal in 
Andhra Pradesh, existed in the past and was used fo r travel/ transport from 
Visakhapatnam to Chennai during British period, whi ch seems to have been completely 
forgotten and not being used in the present times. The Committee is aware that the 
Ministry is going in for Canal Transport System and  would like to be apprised whether 
feasibility of revival of this historical Buckingha m canal route, possibly with private 
partnership, has been looked into by the Ministry, and if not, the reasons for not 
exploring the same. 
(Para 65) 

50   
Cruise Tourism  
The Committee notes the steps being taken by the Mi nistry to promote cruise 
tourism in the country. Now that the Coronavirus pa ndemic restrictions are slowly 
easing across the country, the Committee recommends  that the Ministry may come up 
with a detailed plan of action to develop ocean, co astal and island cruise hub in India by 
undertaking development of world-class cruise terminals at various ports in the country. 
The Ministry may hold discussions with the private players in the cruise tourism  
industry in order to understand their needs and cha lk out a plan to address their 
requirements. The Committee desires the Ministry to  work in close co-ordination with 
the Ministry of Tourism and relevant State Government Departments to address various 
issues pertaining to cruise shipping and formulate a cohesive cruise tourism promotion 
policy across the country. 
(Para 68) 
Seaplanes  
The Committee notes that 78 Seaplane routes have be en introduced in UDAN 4.1 
and desires to know how many of these routes are op erational at present.  The 
Committee feels that seaplanes can play an importan t role in promotion of tourism and 
enhancing connectivity in the country, and therefor e recommends that the Ministry may 
work towards operationalization of more seaplane ro utes across the country. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry may take steps to increase 
participation of the private sector in this regard. 
(Para 70) 
Clearance time at Customs  
The Committee commends the decrease in the turnarou nd time of containers at 
ports across the country. However, the Committee fe els that the time taken for customs 
clearance at the ports should be further reduced in  order to minimize traffic congestion 
at the ports as well as to further reduce the overa ll transportation time of goods. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may take up the issue of customs 
clearance may be taken up with the Ministry of Fina nce so that the process of customs 
clearance becomes hassle-free and streamlined and t he time taken for the same is 
reduced. 
(Para 71)

REPORT  
 
BRIEF BACKGROUND 
 
 
An intricate, robust and well-maintained road network spanning the length and breadth of 
a country, acts as a fundamental enabler for its ov erall economic and social development by 
permitting efficacious movement of freight as well as passengers. Road transport handles bulk of 
countrywide passenger and freight traffic in India,  while also complementing other modes of 
transport by providing and ensuring last-mile connectivity. 
2. India has the second largest road network in the wo rld of about 63.72 lakh kilometers, 
consisting of National Highways, Expressways, State  Highways, Major District Roads, Other 
District Roads and Village Roads. The bifurcation of it is as under:- 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(As on 31 st January, 2022) 
 
3. The tasks and responsibilities of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) 
encompass, inter alia, construction and maintenance of National Highways (NHs); administration 
of the National Highways Act, 1956; National Highwa ys Authority of India Act, 1988; National 
Highways Fee (Determination of Rates and Collection ) Rules, 2008; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988; 
and Central Motor Vehicles Rules 1989, as also form ulation of broad policies relating to road 
transport and automotive norms, besides making arra ngements for movement of vehicular traffic 
with neighbouring countries. 
4. The associated offices under the Ministry of Road T ransport and Highways are as 
follows: 
I. National Highways Authority of India 
National Highways 1,41,190 km 
State Highways 1,70,844 km 
Other Roads 60,59,813 km 
Total 63,71,847 km 

2  
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) was  set up through an Act of 
Parliament, namely the National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988. The NHAI is 
responsible for the development, maintenance and ma nagement of the National  
Highways entrusted to it and for matters related or  incidental thereto. The NHAI became 
operational in February, 1995. 
II. National Highways & Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. (NHIDCL) 
 
The Cabinet, in its meeting held on 13.03.2014, app roved the setting up and 
operationalization of a new corporate entity, the N HIDCL, under the Ministry to 
exclusively carry out the task of construction/ upg rading/widening of National Highways 
in parts of the country which share international b oundaries with neighbouring countries 
in order to promote regional connectivity on a sustainable basis. 
III. Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE) 
 
The Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE) is a  registered Society under the 
administrative control of the Ministry. It is a col laborative body which was set up in the 
year 1983 with the objective of fulfilling the long  felt need for training of Highway 
Engineers in the country, both at the entry level and during their service period. 
IV. Indian Road Congress (IRC) 
 
The IRC was formally registered as a Society on 24t h September 1937 under the 
Societies Registration Act of 1860 for periodical h olding of road conferences to discuss 
issues related to road construction, maintenance & development. IRC has over 16,850 
registered members comprising engineers & professio nals of all Stakeholders of the road 
sector, from Central and State Governments; Public Sector; Research Institutions; 
Academic Institutions, Local bodies; Private sector ; Concessionaires; Contractors; 
Consultants; Equipment manufacturers; Machinery man ufacturers; Material producers & 
suppliers; Industrial Associations; and Multilatera l & Institutional organizations like 
World Bank, Asian Development Bank (ADB), Japan Int ernational Cooperation Agency 
(JICA), Japan Road Association (JRA), International Road Federation (IRF) etc. 
V. National Highway Logistics Management Limited (NHLML) 

3  
The National Highways Logistics Management Limited (NHLML) is a 100% owned 
subsidiary company of NHAI. It is a Special Purpose  Vehicle (SPV) company 
incorporated by the Ministry in the year 2020 with the intent of spearheading the 
development and inter-departmental coordination pertaining to the Multi-Modal Logistics 
Parks (MMLPs) for Cargo Traffic and first/last mile  Port Connectivity Road projects 
under the Bharatmala Pariyojana. NHLML has also bee n delegated by the Ministry for 
development of other allied highway infrastructure such as Inter-modal Stations for 
passenger traffic and development operations and ma nagement of way-side amenities 
along National Highways, Utility corridor along Nat ional Highways. NHLML has been 
pivotal in accelerating the pace of coordination wi th State Governments and Partner 
Government Agencies in terms of on-boarding them as  equity stakeholders for 
development of MMLPs and signing of MoUs with vario us agencies. Since its inception, 
the organization, under the supervision of Ministry, has prioritized action on fast tracking 
first/last mile direct road connectivity for variou s major and non-major ports and Inland 
Waterway Terminals under Bharatmala Pariyojana, in coordination with the Ministry of 
Ports, Waterways and Shipping and various Port agencies.

6. The Committee observes that by January, 2022, the M inistry has managed to spend 
about 77.8 percent of the funds allocated to it at the Revised Estimates (2021-22) stage, 
which was about 11 percent more than the amount all ocated to the Ministry at the Budget 
Estimates (2021-22) stage. While the Committee is p leased to note the overall pace of 
utilization of funds by the Ministry, a closer inspection shows that the utilization figures for 
several important heads viz. , ‘Externally Aided Projects’, ‘Development of IT’,  ‘R&D 
Planning Studies’, ‘Bharatmala Pariyojana - work un der State PWDs/NHIDCL/BRO etc.’, 
‘Maintenance of NHs including Swachhta Action Plan and PIARC’, ‘Tribal Sub-Plan - NH 
works in NE States, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jh arkhand, etc.’, and  ‘Road  
Transport’ has been very low. All these heads are a lready receiving comparatively lower 
amount of funds, especially keeping in mind the vastness of the National Highways network 
in the country coupled with the discernible pattern of underutilization of funds under these 

6  
heads, the Committee feels that the Ministry’s focus has been only on increasing the pace of 
construction of Highways and not so much on the oth er areas, which are equally  
important, if not more. Given the crucial role play ed by the activities carried out under 
these heads, for having a safe and pliable National  Highways network across the country, 
the Committee is of the strong view that the Minist ry should look into the reasons behind 
the underutilization of funds under these various k ey heads and resolve the bottlenecks, if 
any, in order to ensure optimal utilization of the limited budgetary resources available. 
7. The Committee is especially concerned to note the e xtremely low expenditure made 
under the head Road Transport which has important s ub-heads like ‘Research, Training,

35. The Committee is highly distressed to note that des pite the recommendations to the 
Ministry year after year, NHAI, with a budgetary al location of Rs. 134,015 crores, is still 
operating with only 61.2 percent of its sanctioned strength. The Committee fails to 
understand how NHAI will be able to do justice to its mandate with more than a third of its 

18   
sanctioned strength being vacant. The Committee str ongly recommends that the Ministry 
should take immediate measures to fill the vacancies in NHAI at shortest possible time. 
36. It has come to the notice of the Committee that the  first Recruitment Rules (RR) of 
NHAI had provisions for direct recruitment of offic ials up to General Manager (GM) level, 
both in Technical and Finance division. However, ov er time, these seats were commuted 
into promotion and deputation seats by removing the  provision of direct recruitment from 
GM to Manager levels, which might be because of inc reased influence of officials on 
deputation in NHAI. 
 
37. The Committee is of the view that commuting the Dir ect Recruitment posts to only 
promotion and deputation posts has caused a lot of difficulty in the efficient functioning of 
NHAI, especially in finance wing, as there is a dea rth of candidates eligible for deputation 
because of various reasons, such as: 
 
a. NHAI follows Double Entry Accounting pattern whereas Government 
agencies follow Single Entry Accounting 
b. Disparity in pay scale as NHAI and PSUs follow different pay pattern 
c. Non-willingness of Central/State PSUs to spare their officials as they 
themselves face shortage of officials 
d. Ineligibility of internal candidates for promotion 
 
38. The Committee observes that because of these issues , an Expert Committee was 
formed to redress the issue and Draft Recruitment R ules, 2017 were formulated re- 
introducing the provision for Direct Recruitment up to DGM level in Finance cadre, by 
reducing quota for deputation and promotion for thr ee years until equilibrium was 
reached in the hierarchy. It has come to the notice  of the Committee that lobbies of 
deputation officials working in NHAI got the provis ions changed before the draft RR could 
be placed for board approval and in the end, only c hanges made in the new RR were 
linguistic and a reduction of promotion time period  from 5 years to 4 years. In this regard, 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry may furn ish details regarding the exact 
changes made in the existing RR by the Expert Committee in 2017. 

19   
39. The Committee took up this issue in its 296 th Report on ‘Role of Highways in 
Nation Building’. In the Action Taken Replies furni shed by the Ministry on the 296 th 
Report of the Committee, it has been observed that a large number of vacancies exist in 
NHAI from Deputy Manager level to GM level in Finan ce cadre, which implies that 
NHAI is mostly functioning with Junior Accountants and Young Professionals (YP)  
who neither have appropriate educational qualificat ions nor experience, but are 
handling thousands of crores of public money possib ly serving the vested interests of  
the contractors. The Committee further notes that d espite several advertisement for 
deputation in Finance wing, no applications were re ceived for eligible candidates and 
NHAI kept rolling on the advertisement. 
40. The Committee is surprised to note that in para 5.1  of Chapter III of the 307 th 
Report of the Committee, NHAI has clearly indicated  various problems in recruiting 
officials under deputation quota, but still NHAI fr ames policy for recruitment under 
deputation only. It may also be noted that under pa ra 5.2 of Chapter III of that Report, 
NHAI has replied that review of Finance cadre RR wa s recently done and accordingly, 
new advertisement has been made. The Committee may be apprised of the various 
changes made in the RR after this review. 
41. In para 6.1 of Chapter III of the 307 th Report of the Committee, NHAI has 
mentioned that while vacancies from CGM to Deputy M anager in Finance cadre range 
from 50 percent to 90 percent, the employee strength is maximum at Junior Accountant 
level. The Committee fails to understand how an org anization managing public money 
to the tune of lakhs of crores rupees can be run th rough Junior Accountants, with huge 
vacancies existing at higher levels. In para 9.1 an d para 9.2 of the abovementioned 
Report, it has been stated that direct recruitment above Deputy Manager level will lead 
to loss of promotion avenues to the Junior Accounta nts. In this regard, the Committee 
feels that since at present, promotion seats are 50  percent whereas deputation seats are 
50 percent as well, for which NHAI is not able to r eceive any eligible applications, 
NHAI may fill the deputation seats through direct r ecruitment, for which eligible and 
efficient officials at lower level can apply as wel l, further improving their promotion 
prospects. 

20   
42. In this regard, it is further observed that Railway s has its own cadre because huge 
funds are involved, so a responsible cadre is requi red and outsiders at such lower level 
who will come for few years and go, cannot be relie d upon with huge financial stake, in 
view of accountability issues. It may also be noted  that all Central PSUs, whether 
ONGC, PFC, GAIL, SAIL etc., recruit around 35 perce nt of their officials on direct 
basis at all levels, to have experienced candidates  from the market and bring 
equilibrium in the system, also helping eligible in ternal candidates to rise to higher 
ranks. 
 
43. In view of the above, the Committee recommends that  the following suggestion 
may be considered with the permissible framework of NHAI: 
 
a. NHAI needs to amend and improve the way it is being  run at present. It 
should take appropriate steps to ensure that it is not managing its huge 
budgetary allocation through Junior Accountants alo ne, with a drastic 
number of vacancies existing at higher levels. 
 
b. RRs for Technical and Financial cadres were amended  together in the 
past but now NHAI is revisiting amendment in techni cal cadre alone but 
not in Finance cadre, giving the reason that the am endment in Finance 
cadre RRs was recently done, which is contradictory . NHAI should bring 
transparency in its policy formulation. 
 
c. A committee may be set up comprising senior officia ls of relevant 
discipline, to formulate new RRs for filling up all  posts presently under 
deputation mode, via Direct Recruitment, taking pro vision of three years 
which will generate equilibrium in the hierarchy of  the cadre by filling all 
such posts. 
 
d. NHAI should correct the blunder it has made by corr elating B.Com. with 
higher qualifications like CA/ICWA/MBA(F) in its el igibility for 
Deputation Mode, since it was unable to get enough applications for 
highly qualified candidates under the Deputation Mode earlier. Having  a 

21   
workforce with higher qualifications and experience will help NHAI 
utilize its budgetary allocation in a more efficient manner. 
 
e. With Direct Recruitment, the stay of Orissa High Court for not recruiting 
on Deputation mode can be got vacated and eligible internal candidates 
can also apply for these DR posts. 
 
f. Since the education qualification of already recrui ted candidates in 
Finance is only B.Com. with no requisite qualificat ion and experience, 
their higher promotions should not be done blindly,  rather it should be as 
per their efficiency and acquiring higher qualifications. 
 
g. Till new Recruitment Rules are framed to resolve th ese issues, all present 
advertisements may be put into abeyance. 
 
44. The Committee feels that NHAI can resolve a lot of issues with these amendments and 
bring transparency and efficiency in its system.

the fact that budgetary allocation for the highway network of a developed economy like

National Highway network at a rapid pace, the conce ntration on expansion of the NH 
network alone cannot be permitted to sideline the n eed for high-quality maintenance of the 
existing NH network in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry should carry out an overhaul of the existi ng mechanism for inspection and 
monitoring of maintenance & repair requirements on National Highways across the 
country. Given the poor state of National Highways often observed around the country and 
the direct adversary effect of the same on road safety as well as average speed of the traffic, 
it is imperative that the Ministry/NHAI may put in efforts to ensure that routine M&R 
activities are carried out on National Highways in a proactive manner, without waiting for 
the NHs to reach conditions that would require imme diate intervention. The Committee, 
with a view to effectuate the same, recommends that  a mechanism may be developed to 
quantify the condition of all NH stretches in an ob jective manner, using international 
standards as a benchmark for such quantification.

It stated that apart from the above, NHAI has taken  up 14 nos. of R&D schemes costing about

the purpose.  
 
87. The Ministry has stated the reason for reduction of  funds for several schemes under 
this head at RE 2021-22 stage is due to the fact th at they are under third party evaluation. 
The Committee feels that the Ministry should conduc t this third party evaluation before  
the activities under the existing approved scheme h ave been completed so that schemes 
working to improve road safety through various mean s, are not totally stalled because of 
such evaluations. 
 
88. The Committee is anguished to note the poor expendi ture pattern under the crucial 
head ‘Research, Training, Studies and Other Road Sa fety Schemes’ since the past several 
years.  The  various  activities  under  this  heads  viz.,  Training  of  drivers,  Publicity   and 

44   
awareness, National Highways Accident Relief Servic e Scheme, Road Safety & Pollution 
Testing Equipment, etc. are crucial for improving t he scenario of road safety on National 
Highways across the country and to offset the huge death toll faced by the country each 
year due to road accidents. The Committee is not sa tisfied with the reasons furnished by  
the Ministry for the poor expenditure pattern under  this head and feels remedial measures 
should be taken to make maximum utilization of the limited funds available under this 
head. This pattern questions the commitment of the Ministry to make earnest efforts to 
minimize the deaths caused due to road accidents ea ch year. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry may cull out all the issues causi ng under-utilization under this important 
head at the earliest so that due focus is laid on road safety in the coming years. 
 
89. The Committee is surprised to note that the Ministr y has sanctioned just 5 R&D 
schemes worth merely Rs. 2.04 crores during the las t 3 financial years. For comparison, 
United States’ Federal Highway Administration (FHWA ) had an annual budget of about 
US$47 billion for the FY 2020 (compared to MoRTH’s R.E. 2021-22 allocation of Rs. 
131,149 crores i.e. roughly US$ 17.33 billion) and the fund allocated for ‘Research, 
Technology, and Education Program’ is $420 million (i.e., about Rs. 3177 crores). While  
the Committee appreciates that such comparisons can not be directly made between such 
differing economies owing to differences in require ments and present focus, the magnitude 
of difference in the importance being given to R&D and related activities points to the need 
for the Ministry to have a major rethink about its missing focus on R&D in the road sector. 
The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry  may strive to sanction more and 
more R&D schemes and work with best global institutions in this field in order to carve out 
niche solutions for the varied problems plaguing th e Indian road sector at present. The 
Committee feels that the same would also help the M inistry to have a better, clearer long- 
term vision in creating a safe, robust, well-mainta ined NH network across the diverse 
geographies of the country.

1 21. On the question, whether the Ministry has taken any  steps to review the present  
procedure of selection of lowest bids for awarding of road projects, without having any lower 
cap for such bidding, often causes the project to be awarded to shoddy contractors which leads to 
avoidable delays in road projects and/or poor construction quality.

1 22. The Ministry, in its written reply, informed the Co mmittee that at present, projects are 
awarded on the following criteria under different m odes of construction considering the base 
guidelines issued by the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC).  
• In case of EPC (Engineering, Procurement and Constr uction) Projects, the Bidder 
whose bid is adjudged as responsive against the tes t of Responsiveness mentioned in the 
RFP (Request for Proposal) documents and whose avai lable bid capacity is more than the 
Total Bid value and who quotes lowest price is declared as the selected bidder.  
• In case of HAM (Hybrid Annuity Mode) Projects, the Bidder whose bid is 
adjudged as responsive against the test of Responsi veness mentioned in the RFP 
documents and who fulfills the criteria of Technica l Capacity and Financial Capacity and 
whose assessed bid price is lowest is declared as the selected bidder.  
1 23. Information available regarding black listing / deb arment of Contractors /  
Concessionaires on various grounds including Qualit y of Works implemented are duly 
considered while awarding works.

Vacancies in NHAI 
 
The Committee is highly distressed to note that des pite the recommendations to the 
Ministry year after year, NHAI, with a budgetary al location of Rs. 134,015 crores, is still 
operating with only 61.2 percent of its sanctioned strength. The Committee fails to 
understand how NHAI will be able to do justice to its mandate with more than a third of its 

72   
sanctioned strength being vacant. The Committee str ongly recommends that the Ministry 
should take immediate measures to fill the vacancies in NHAI at shortest possible time. 
(Para 35) 
It has come to the notice of the Committee that the  first Recruitment Rules (RR) of NHAI 
had provisions for direct recruitment of officials up to General Manager (GM) level, both  
in Technical and Finance division. However, over ti me, these seats were commuted into 
promotion and deputation seats by removing the prov ision of direct recruitment from GM 
to Manager levels, which might be because of increa sed influence of officials on deputation 
in NHAI. 
(Para 36) 
 
The Committee is of the view that commuting the Dir ect Recruitment posts to only 
promotion and deputation posts has caused a lot of difficulty in the efficient functioning of 
NHAI, especially in finance wing, as there is a dea rth of candidates eligible for deputation 
because of various reasons, such as: 
 
a. NHAI follows Double Entry Accounting pattern wherea s Government agencies 
follow Single Entry Accounting 
b. Disparity in pay scale as NHAI and PSUs follow different pay pattern 
c. Non-willingness of Central/State PSUs to spare their officials as they themselves face 
shortage of officials 
d. Ineligibility of internal candidates for promotion 
 
(Para 37) 
 
The Committee observes that because of these issues , an Expert Committee was formed to 
redress the issue and Draft Recruitment Rules, 2017  were formulated re-introducing the 
provision for Direct Recruitment upto DGM level in Finance cadre, by reducing quota for 
deputation and promotion for three years until equi librium was reached in the hierarchy. 
It has come to the notice of the Committee that lob bies of deputation officials working in 
NHAI got the provisions changed before the draft RR  could be placed for board approval 
and in the end, only changes   made in the new RR w ere linguistic and a reduction of 

73   
promotion time period from 5 years to 4 years. In t his regard, the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry may furnish details regarding the  exact changes made in the existing RR 
by the Expert Committee in 2017. 
 
(Para 38) 
 
The Committee took up this issue in its 296 th Report on ‘Role of Highways in Nation 
Building’. In the Action Taken Replies furnished by  the Ministry on the 296 th Report of the 
Committee, it has been observed that a large number  of vacancies exist in NHAI from 
Deputy Manager level to GM level in Finance cadre, which implies that NHAI is mostly 
functioning with Junior Accountants and Young Profe ssionals (YP) who neither have 
appropriate  educational  qualifications  nor  experience,  but  are  handling  thousands   of 
crores of public money possibly serving the vested interests of the contractors. The 
Committee further notes that despite several advertisement for deputation in Finance wing, 
no applications were received for eligible candidat es and NHAI kept rolling on the 
advertisement. 
 
(Para 39) 
 
The Committee is surprised to note that in para 5.1  of Chapter III of the 307 th Report of  
the Committee, NHAI has clearly indicated various p roblems in recruiting officials under 
deputation quota, but still NHAI frames policy for recruitment under deputation only. It 
may also be noted that under para 5.2 of Chapter II I of that Report, NHAI has replied that 
review of Finance cadre RR was recently done and ac cordingly, new advertisement has 
been made. The Committee may be apprised of the var ious changes made in the RR after 
this review. 
 
(Para 40) 
 
In para 6.1 of Chapter III of the 307 th Report of the Committee, NHAI has mentioned that 
while vacancies from CGM to Deputy Manager in Finan ce cadre range from 50 percent to 
90 percent, the employee strength is maximum at Jun ior Accountant level. The Committee 
fails to understand how an organization managing public money to the tune of lakhs of 

74   
crores rupees can be run through Junior Accountants , with huge vacancies existing at 
higher levels. In para 9.1 and para 9.2 of the abov ementioned Report, it has been stated 
that direct recruitment above Deputy Manager level will lead to loss of promotion avenues 
to the Junior Accountants. In this regard, the Comm ittee feels that since at present, 
promotion seats are 50 percent whereas deputation s eats are 50 percent as well, for which 
NHAI is not able to receive any eligible applicatio ns, NHAI may fill the deputation seats 
through direct recruitment, for which eligible and efficient officials at lower level can apply 
as well, further improving their promotion prospects. 
 
(Para 41) 
 
In this regard, it is further observed that Railway s has its own cadre because huge funds 
are involved, so a responsible cadre is required an d outsiders at such lower level who will 
come for few years and go, cannot be relied upon wi th huge financial stake, in view of 
accountability issues. It may also be noted that al l Central PSUs, whether ONGC, PFC, 
GAIL, SAIL etc., recruit around 35 percent of their  officials on direct basis at all levels, to 
have experienced candidates from the market and bri ng equilibrium in the system, also 
helping eligible internal candidates to rise to higher ranks. 
 
(Para 42) 
 
In view of the above, the Committee recommends that  the following suggestion may be 
considered with the permissible framework of NHAI: 
 
a. NHAI needs to amend and improve the way it is being  run at present. It 
should take appropriate steps to ensure that it is not managing its huge 
budgetary allocation through Junior Accountants alo ne, with a drastic 
number of vacancies existing at higher levels. 
 
b. RRs for Technical and Financial cadres were amended  together in the past 
but now NHAI is revisiting amendment in technical c adre alone but not in 
Finance cadre, giving the reason  that the amendment in Finance cadre RRs 

75   
was recently done, which is contradictory. NHAI should bring transparency 
in its policy formulation. 
 
c. A committee may be set up comprising senior officials of relevant discipline, 
to formulate new RRs for filling up all posts prese ntly under deputation

higher qualifications like CA/ICWA/MBA(F) in its eligibility for Deputation

g. Till new Recruitment Rules are framed to resolve th ese issues, all present 
advertisements may be put into abeyance. 
 
(Para 43) 
 
The Committee feels that NHAI can resolve a lot of issues with these amendments and
