would mean issues would be faced in connecting to e mergency services as well. Besides the 
safety aspect, the Committee feels that having basi c mobile connectivity while travelling is 
getting more and more important in the modern times , with navigational services and 
several other forms of important communications rel y on on-the-go mobile connectivity. 
While it is understood that the installation of cel l towers is carried out by 
telecommunication companies on the basis of the num ber of users in the area, the 
Committee feels that given the high volume of traffic plying on National Highways across 

86   
the country, many such stretches might be having su fficient demand from users for good 
internet connectivity. The Committee, therefore, re commends that the Ministry may look 
into this matter and if feasible, suitable measures  may be taken to ensure good mobile 
connectivity for NH users, in coordination with the  Department of Telecommunications 
and other organizations concerned. 
(Para 109) 
 
 
 
SCHEMES OF STATES AND UTs FINANCED FROM CRIF 
 
The Committee is surprised to note that road projec ts pertaining to only 10 States/UTs 
have been approved under the heads ‘Schemes of Stat es financed from CRIF’ and 
‘Schemes of UTs financed from CRIF’ during the ongo ing FY 2021-22. The Committee 
desires to be apprised of the reasons behind the sa me. The Committee has submitted a 
detailed report on CRIF. The recommendation made in  that report may be followed 
scrupulously. 
 
(Para 111) 
MISCELLANEOUS 
 
 
Indian Roads Congress and Central Road Research Institute  
 
The Committee observes that the construction of Nat ional Highways is carried out as per 
the standards and specifications laid down in vario us IRC standards. It is evident that the 
codes and standards published by IRC are of extreme  significance, with the quality of 
construction of NHs across the country directly dep endent on the same. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may submit information regarding the various 
issues being faced at present in construction of NH s in the country to the committee set up 
by IRC to aid in its exercise for identification of  important pilot research projects and 
ensure that sufficient allocation is made available  to IRC in order to carry out  such 
projects through eminent research organizations and academic institutions of repute. 
 
(Para 113) 

87   
The Committee observes that the activities carried out by CRRI are of great significance 
for the effective development and maintenance of an  intricate road network in India 
through its activities pertaining to Research and D evelopment in the road sector as well as 
its national and international training programmes for capacity building of human 
resources in the area of highway engineering. The C ommittee expresses its apprehensions 
that since CRRI is a constituent of CSIR, which is an autonomous body under the 
administrative supervision of the Ministry of Scien ce and Technology, there might be a  
lack of cohesive and concerted efforts between CRRI  and the R&D and HR training 
institutes of the Ministry of Road Transport and Hi ghways viz., IAHE, IRC and NHAI’s 
SRD&Q Division. The Committee recommends that the M inistry may ensure that  
sufficient budgetary allocation is made available to fund the activities carried out by CRRI, 
IRC, SRD&Q Division and IAHE so as to bolster the R &D and HR training aspects of the 
Indian road sector. Efforts may also be made to ens ure that there is strong coordination 
between all these agencies to complement each other ’s efforts for the overall improvement 
of the road sector in the country. The knowledge ga ined by these research and training 
agencies may be freely shared with the various road  construction agencies in the country, 
including State PWDs. 
 
(Para 115) 
 
The Committee recommends that IRC may collaborate w ith CRRI and conduct research  
on usage of innovative materials for road construct ion and strengthening road safety 
through improved design and construction techniques , particularly looking into road 
accidents that take place at entry and exit points of highways. 
(Para 116) 
Provisions for service roads  
The Committee observes that the lack of service roa ds alongside National Highways causes 
inconvenience to local residents and is, at times, the cause of road accidents. The land 
required for development of National Highways is ac quired from the local people and they 
should be given the benefits of service roads along National Highways. The Committee feels 
that service roads are an integral part of National  Highways and therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may make it mandatory to have service roads along NHs to the extent 

88   
possible and provisions for the same may be included in the tender document for NH 
projects. 
(Para 117) 
Five Year Vision Plan for Infrastructure Sector  
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take  undertake concerted measures to 
achieve the ambitious goals laid out in the Five Ye ar Vision Plan (2019-24) for 
Infrastructure Sector, prepared by the Sectoral Gro up of Secretaries, which include 
targeting reduction of accident fatalities by at le ast 25%, strengthening public transport 
and shared mobility through regulatory reforms, str engthening connectivity to top 100 
tourist destinations, development of helipads near Highways for victim evacuation and 
commercial purposes, development of contractors dat abase to identify underperformers 
and habitual litigants, etc. A robust monitoring me chanism may be put in place in order to 
assess the progress being made in regard of all the  goals and targets laid out under the Five 
Year Vision Plan. 
 
(Para 118) 
CAG Audit Paras  
The Committee is distressed to note that the reply is awaited from NHAI and matter is 
pending with the Ministry relating to CAG Audit Par as dating back to as far back as 2017. 
The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry  and NHAI may take immediate 
action based on observations made by CAG in its Rep orts since time lost in such matters 
can cause loss of valuable information which could otherwise pinpoint culprits involved in 
giving undue benefits to concessionaires or causing loss of revenue to NHAI. 
(Para 120) 
 
 
Awarding of road projects  
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may star t maintaining a score of 
performance of road concessionaires across the coun try based on the construction quality, 
timely completion etc. of the road projects worked upon by them. This database based on 
work history of road concessionaires may be used as one of the criterias based on which 

89   
new road projects are awarded, giving priority to c oncessionaires with excellent project 
history as long as their financial capacities allow the same. 
(Para 125) 
 
The Committee takes serious view of the issues poin ted out by one of its Members 
regarding the possible connivance of the officials,  concessionaires and consultants  etc. 
which leads to poor quality NHs being constructed a cross the country. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may set up an enquiry committee to look into the above 
mentioned issues and to devise a mechanism to plug the loopholes present in the existing 
system which may be leading to the possibility of s uch corrupt practices. The Committee 
further recommends that the Ministry may review the  requirements presently in place to 
effectuate a change of scope in a road project and ensure that change of scope is permitted 
only in rare cases where alternative solutions are not possible. 
(Para 127) 
 
The Committee desires to know the number of road pr ojects awarded in which a ‘Change 
of Scope’ has happened during the last 5 years and the total number of road projects 
awarded during this period. Similarly, the Committe e may be apprised of the number of 
road projects which have been awarded for more than  20 percent below the official 
estimated cost and underwent a ‘Change of Scope’ du ring the last 5 years; and the total 
number of road projects which have been awarded for  more than 20 percent below the 
official estimated during this period. 
(Para 128) 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry may exam ine the feasibility of prescribing 
upper/lower limits for submission of bids for road projects. Till the time that is done, or if 
the same is not found to be a feasible alternative,  the Ministry may establish a specialized 
mechanism for closer scrutiny of the road projects that are awarded at substantially lower 
bids than the official estimates of the Ministry/NHAI. 
(Para 129) 
Promotion of Electric Vehicles  

90   
The Committee notes the steps taken by the Ministry  for promotion of electric vehicles in 
the country and feels that a lot still needs to be done in order to speed up the shift of 
vehicle-owners towards electric vehicles since EVs come with a huge set of benefits, 
especially in light of the dire air pollution issue s faced in a large number of Indian cities. 
The shift to electric vehicles will also reduce the  dependency of our country on petroleum 
product imports. The Committee, therefore, recommen ds that the Ministry may take more 
steps to promote the usage of electric vehicles in the country and work on creation of 
charging infrastructure for the same alongside Nati onal Highways, in coordination with 
concerned Ministries/organizations. The Ministry ma y also consider exempting electric 
vehicles from road tax, offering some discount at t oll plazas. The Ministry should work 
towards undertaking initiatives to boost and promot e the production of electric vehicles in 
the country should also be taken, in close cooperat ion with concerned 
Ministries/Departments as well as vehicle manufacturers. 
(Para 131) 
 
 
Driving Training Centres  
The Committee desires to be apprised of the number of districts in the country where 
Driving Training Centres are functional and the num ber of applications received and 
approved by the Ministry so far for the one-time as sistance scheme for setting up of model 
DTCs in the country. 
(Para 134) 
Laying of integrated utility corridors along greenfield National Highways  
The Committee is glad to note that bids have been i nvited for laying OFC ducts for a total 
length of about 1350 km. The Committee hopes that t he Ministry will utilize the experience 
gained from this exercise to make provisions for ut ility ducts alongside more upcoming 
Greenfield Highways/ Expressways. 
(Para 137)  
Weigh-in-Motion Systems at Toll Plazas  
 
The Committee recommends that a timeline may be dev ised to equip the remaining toll 
plazas on NHs with Weigh-in-Motion systems as well and the details of the timeline may be 
shared  with  the Committee,  since the system can  help  curb  the practice of     overloaded 

91   
vehicles which not only cause damage to NHs, but also pose great safety risks to other 
vehicles. 
(Para 139) 
 
Flyovers over Highways  
 
The Committee would like to know from the Ministry the reasons for lifting the existing 
MDR/ODR/VR over National Highways instead of liftin g the multi-lane NHs over the 
MDR/ODR/VR. 
(Para 141)

I. BRIEF BACKGROUND 
 
1. Tourism plays a key role in socio-economic progress through employment generation, 
creation of infrastructure and revenue earnings. Not only does the tourism sector spearhead 
growth, it also improves the quality of people‟s lives with its capacity to create large scale 
employment of diverse kind.  
 
2. Ministry of Tourism is the nodal agency to formulate national policies and 
programmes for the development and promotion of tourism. In the process, the Ministry 
consults and collaborates with other stakeholders in the sector including various Central 
Ministries/ Agencies, State Governments/ Union Territory Administrations and the 
representatives of the private sector.  The Committee has been informed that Facilitation as 
well as strengthening of tourism in India is the main objective of the Ministry. Augmenting 
tourism infrastructure, easing of visa regime, assurance of quality standards in services of 
tourism service providers, projection of the country as a 365 days‟ tourist destination , 
promotion of sustainable tourism etc. are some of the policy areas which need to be 
constantly worked upon to increase and facilitate tourism in our country. 
 
3. Secretary (Tourism) is the executive chief of the Ministry. The Directorate General of 
Tourism has 20 Domestic field offices and an Indian Institute of Skiing and Mountaineering 
within the country and 08 overseas offices. The overseas offices promote I ndian tourism in 
the markets abroad. 
 
4. The domestic field offices also play a vital role for promotion of tourism sector in the 
country. They are also involved in monitoring the progress of implementation of projects 
sanctioned by the Ministry to the State Governments/Union Territories. 
 
5. India Tourism Development Corporation (ITDC) is the only public sector undertaking 
under the charge of the Ministry of Tourism.

19. The Committee notes that although there has been marginal increase in the 
budgetary outlay for the Ministry from Rs. 2026.77 crore for FY 2021 -22 to Rs. 2400.00 
crore for FY 2022 -23, it is still lesser than the BE 2020 -21 allocation of Rs. 2499.83 
crore. Though the BE 2022 -23 allocation is 18 -41% higher than the BE 2021 -22 outlay, 
there is a substantial shortfall of Rs. 537.92 crore vis -à-vis the projected demand of Rs. 
2937.92 crore by the Ministry for FY 2022 -23 and that too at a time when this sector is 
reeling under losses in the wake of COVID -19 pandemic. The Committee notes that this 
budgetary outlay for 2022 -23 has been reduced to Rs 416 crore  as compared to the BE 
2021-22 of Rs. 668.72 crore under the head- Promotion and Publicity . The Committee 
finds this reduction alarming because the tourism and hospitality sector has been hit the 
hardest by COVID-19 pandemic and with massive job and revenue losses, it is essential 
that the Government promotes India on all possible platforms, both national and 
international, as a safe and must -visit destination and for this, instilling confidence  
among touriststhrough use of technology with the help of skilled manpower, investment 
in skilling, reskilling and upskilling is an imperative need. The Committee, therefore , 
apprehends that the marginal increase of Rs. 333.77 crore in the budgetary allocation 
for 2022 -23 is inadequate as it will be consumed by inflation. The Committee is 
simultaneously appreciative of the fiscal constraints faced by the Ministry of Finance 
due to deceleration in the growth rate in the Indian economy on account of global and 
domestic slowdown in the aftermath of COVID -19 pandemic. The Committee observes 
that with the accelerated pace of vaccine roll -out and easing of restrictions, the Indian 
economy has started to rebound and the additional resources would become available as 
a result of revenue buoyancy in FY 2022 -23. Given t he fact that the activities of the 
Ministry harness the direct and multiplier effect on economic development and 
employment generation in the country and integrated development of infrastructure 

 
10 
 
and facilities through effective partnerships and convergence  with stakeholders can 
propel India to a higher growth trajectory, the Committee recommends that depending 
on better financial performance and greater absorption capacity of the Ministry, 
quantum of funding for the Ministry of Tourism be enhanced at the RE  2022-23 stage. 
Simultaneously, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should initiate and 
implement better fiscal discipline and ensure that the scarce financial resources do not 
remain parked idelling. 
 
20. From a perusal of Table No. 2, the Committee is constrained to note that there is 
a substantial underutilization of the budgeted funds during the FY 2021 -22. Against the 
RE 2021-22 allocation of Rs. 969.80 crore, only 47.70% amounting to Rs. 462.55 crore 
could be spent till the 31 st January, 2022 . It m eans that the remaining expenditure 
would have to be squeezed in the last two months of FY 2021 -22. Since as per norms 
stipulated by the Ministry of Finance, there is a ceiling of 25% on expenditure in the 
last quarter, occurrence of huge savings is a cert ainty. It may be pertinent to mention 
here that a zero based budgeting exercise which requires that budget request be 
evaluated thoroughly, starting from zero base, is in practice and the financial outlays 
are earmarked based on factors like past trend of expenditure, stages of 
formulation/implementation of various projects, the pre -projects approvals etc. 
Therefore, savings of Rs. 1056.97 crore vis -à-vis the BE 2021 -22 allocation not only 
betrays fiscal indiscipline by way of underutilization of the earmar ked funds which will 
have an adverse bearing on infrastructure development oriented activities of the 
Ministry, but is also indicative of shortcomings in budgetary planning and monitoring 
of the budgeted funds. The Committee observes that a resource constrained country like 
India cannot afford to keep a vast chunk of its resources locked up and surrendered 
towards the end of the financial year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
realistic projection of fund requirements should be given utmost priorit y at the highest 
level of the Ministry so that the Budget Estimates are formulated with application of 
proper financial yardsticks and large variations between the Budget Estimates, Revised 
Estimates and Actual Expenditure needs to be  avoided. The Ministry  must also pay 
attention to streamlining its monitoring mechanism and ensure optimal and more 
efficient deployment and utilization of its financial resources for smooth execution of its 
programmes within the approved cost and designated timeline. 

 
11 
 
21. The Committee also takes a serious note of keeping the unspent provision of Rs. 
1056.97 crore till the close of financial year 2021 -22 despite reduction in the budgetary 
outlay at the RE 2021 -22 stage, in disregard of the provisions of General Financial 
Rules requiring the unspent provisions in a grant to be surrendered to the Ministry of 
Finance as soon as these are foreseen, without waiting for the last day of the financial 
year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should exercise greater 
fiscal prudence, and ensure that unspent budgetary provisions are surrendered timely 
in future.

30. The Committee notes that as per the World Travel and Tourism Council 
(WTTC), prior to the COVID -19 pandemic, Travel and Tourism accounted for 10.4% 
of global GDP. In many parts of the world, tourism is a major engine of growth. The 
Committee in its 275 th Report presented to the Parliament on the 3 rd March 2020 had 
noted that the contribution of tourism to nationa l GDP was over 10% for most 
countries where tourism happens to be the main driver of national economy. However, 
in India which has unique endowments of biodiversity, forests, rivers, its rich culture 
and heritage and many World Heritage sites, the tourism sector has not proved to be 
the proverbial engine of growth for our economy. This is evident from the fact that 
India's total share in global international arrivals remains a modest 1.57% against the 
target of 3 per cent set by the NITI Aayog to be achieve d by 2022. Similarly, the 
contribution (direct and indirect) of tourism in the GDP and the total jobs in the 
country are estimated to be 5.16 per cent and 15.34 per cent respectively during 2019 -
20. The Committee is of the firm view that if India has to mo ve towards becoming USD 
5 trillion economy and a global economic powerhouse, as envisioned by our Hon'ble PM 
Shri Narendra Modi, then the contribution of tourism to India's GDP has to be raised 
from the current 5.16% to 10% in the next five years. The Comm ittee, while welcoming 
the various measures taken by the Ministry to double the contribution of tourism to 
India's GDP, feels that the vast untapped potential of India as a tourism destination 
cannot be realized unless tourism is included in the Concurrent  List of the Constitution 
of India. Taking note of the fact that Travel and Tourism does not figure in the Centre, 
State or Concurrent Lists and since in a federal polity like ours, the responsibility for 
policy making and implementation of tourism project s are fragmented across different

levels - Central and State Governments and coordination between them is often lacking 
due to absence of clearly defined mandate, the Committee in its 288 th Report had 
recommended inclusion of tourism in the Concurrent List . Since tourism is yet to be 
included in the Concurrent List, the Committee reiterates its recommendation for 
inclusion of tourism in the Concurrent List of the Constitution of India. The Committee 
is convinced that this will go a long way in channelising the development of tourism and 
positioning and maintaining tourism development as a national priority.  
 
31. The Committee observes that Emirate of Dubai does not have the abundant 
wealth of natural oil reserves and nor does it have a pre -existing plethora of natural, 
historical and internationally significant tourist sites. Despite that, it has emerged as a 
multi-billion dollar economy and amongst the world's most visited tourist destinations, 
all based on the Government's tourism centric approach towards nati onal policy 
making. The Committee wishes that India should also endeavour to imbibe creating 
potential for tourism in the very core of its policy making. Although tourism is an 
important activity in India, its share in global market is extremely small and the 
potential of tourism sector in India is yet to be unleashed. The actual implementation of 
tourist projects takes place at State/UT level but in most of the States/UTs , the outlay 
for Department of Tourism is meagre. The Committee, therefore, recommends  that in 
order to give policy push to the tourism industry, a National Tourism Counc il chaired 
by the Prime Minister  and composed of Chief Ministers or Tourism Ministers of all 
States should be established. This National Council should be an empowered legi slative 
body on the lines of GST Council. This will enable fast -track Centre-State level tourism 
decision making, leveraging and utilising full synergies of India's tourism potential 
across all our States. 
 
32. The Committee observes that despite the fact that India offers a diverse portfolio 
for travel and tourism, the share of India's International Tourist Arrivals (ITAs) in the 
ITAs of the world was merely 1.57 per cent in 2020. There is increased competition 
among various countries to attract foreign visitors. There is, therefore, an imperative 
need for India to prepare suitable market strategy to attract foreign visitors. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry in collaboration with a 
professional body should carry out market research of foreign tourist source markets to 

 
18 
 
identify the expectations, requirements, psychographics, demographics and many other 
aspects of a foreign tourist willing to travel to India, thereby enabling to create a 
strategic plan to revive inbound tourism. The research should be conducted with an 
objective to provide an authentic feedback, roadmap and recommendations to the 
Ministry of Tourism with respect to inbound tourism in India and provide a blueprint 
on the various policy objectives and infrastructure development needed to strengthen 
inbound tourism in the country.

35. In reply to a question t he Ministry has informed the Committee that to assess the 
impact of Covid-19 pandemic on the tourism sector, the Ministry of Tourism, Government of 
India got conducted study on “India and the Corona Virus Pandemic: Economic Losses for 
Households Engaged in Tourism and Policies for Recovery”. Th is study captures the 
economic losses considering the changes experienced during the entire period of this 
pandemic situation with the help of data from different sources that reflects changes over the 
said period. The study also probed into the likely rec overy phases of the tourism sector post 
pandemic to understand how the sector would regain its pre- pandemic position.  
 
Objectives of the study 
36. This study aims to assess the estimated loss to the economy and to the income of 
households because of Covid-19 pandemic. The key objectives are: 
(i) Quantify the sector -wise (or industry -wise) direct and indirect impact of tourism 
activities on overall economy as a whole and especially on household income, which 
may be further disaggregated into different types of hou seholds like formal and 
informal. 
(ii) Quantify the loss in income, sector -wise and in the overall economy and of the 
household sector; and also the loss in jobs, due to the impact of Coronavirus 
pandemic on the tourism sector.  
(iii)Estimate the impact of gradual o pening up of domestic tourism activities and the 
sectors related to tourism.  
(iv) Estimate the likely impact of opening of international tourism, in a phased manner.  


 
21 
 
(v) Propose policy measures appropriate to provide relief to the tourism sector, in 
general, and households involved in tourism related activities, in particular, based 
on feedback received from various stakeholders.  
 
Key Findings 
Tourism Economy in a normal situation 
37. The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) is an important tool to estimate the 
contributions of Tourism to the economy. According to the second and third TSAs, tourism 
sector contributed as much as 6.8 percent and 5.2 percent directly and indirectly to the 
country‟s total GDP. The direct shares for these years were 3.7 percent and 2. 7 percent 
respectively. 
 
38. For the present study, we have also derived the income multiplier to estimate the 
impact of increase in tourism demand on overall household income of the economy through 
the preparation of Social Accounting Matrix (SAM). This is be cause SAM constitutes not 
only the production account but, in addition, also incorporates the household account. Hence, 
it presents the transactions between production sectors and the households drawing income 
from these sectors. The SAM based multiplier a nalysis reveals that the income multiplier of 
the tourism sector is 1.6332. Hence if the tourism demand or tourism expenditure increases 
by, say, Rs. 1 crore, then owing to the direct and indirect linkages among the sectors of the 
economy, the overall hous ehold income of the economy is expected to increase by Rs. 1.63 
crore.  
 
Tourism Economy during Covid-19 pandemic   
39. The impact of pandemic on tourism, through the estimation of TDGVA, is captured 
for all of these three quarters and across the following asp ects so that the impact of pandemic 
due to different types of shocks is separately captured. 
 
40. Impact due to supply side shock:  This relates to the overall economic slowdown 
during 2020-21 and assumes that tourism was rather resilient and continued as before. Hence, 
this scenario takes into account only the supply side shock. Therefore, for all the quarters of 
2020-21, Tourism Industry Ratios (TIRs) are assumed to remain the same as those for pre -
pandemic years. The findings are: 

 
22 
 
 While overall economy fell b y 20.1 percent in Q1; 5.1 percent in Q2 and grew at a 
positive rate of 4.3 percent in Q3, all in nominal terms, tourism economy or TDGVA 
saw a much greater fall of 42.8 percent in Q1; 15.5 percent in Q2 and continued to 
suffer from the negative growth even in Q3, with a fall of 1.1 percent. 
 
41. Impact due to demand side shock : This refers to the impact of pandemic on tourism 
economy given both supply side shock coming from the economic slowdown and demand 
side shock resulting from the limited tourism activity in the country during the three quarters 
of study. The limited tourism activity translates to huge reduction in tourism expenditure 
incurred by all types of tourists – inbound, domestic and outbound. Hence these estimates 
reflect the most likely loss in TDGVA. The findings are: 
 It is estimated that TDGVA plummeted by as much as 93.3 percent in Q1 of 2020 -21 
over its level in the same quarter of previous year. It picked up slightly to post a fall 
of 79.5 percent in Q2 and that of 64.3 percent in Q3, but continued to be at extremely 
low level in negative territory while overall economy posted a positive growth of 4.3 
percent in Q3. 
 
42. Impact due to inbound demand side shock:  This refers to the independent impact of 
fall in inbound tourism expenditure, assumi ng that all other forms of tourism remained the 
same during the study reference period. The TDGVA is estimated to have decreased by 61.7 
percent in Q2 of 2020 -21 over the same quarter of 2019 -20. Going forward, this is estimated 
to have fallen by 38.0 percent in Q2 and 25.7 percent in Q3. 
 
43. Impact due to domestic demand side shock : This refers to the independent impact of 
fall in domestic tourism expenditure, assuming that all other forms of tourism remained the 
same. Notably, the negative impact of fall in domestic tourism activity is much more 
significant than that of inbound tourism activity. The fall in all the three quarters is estimated 
to be 20 to 30 percentage points higher than that in the case of inbound tourism. 
 
44. Estimated loss in jobs during Covid 19 pandemic:  A significant number of jobs were 
lost in the tourism sector once the lockdown was implemented. However, recovery was fast 
once the unlock phases started and the economy was opened up. The findings are: 
 

 
23 
 
45. As many as 14.5 million jobs, out of a n estimated 34.8 million jobs in the pre -
pandemic period of 2019, are expected to have lost as a repercussion of the pandemic and the 
resultant lockdown in the first quarter of 2020-21. This is equivalent to a fall of 41.7 percent. 
 
46. In terms of absolute nu mber, the loss of jobs is more pronounced in the case of 
salary/wage earners, 7.8 million of whom were left without job during Q1. However, in terms 
of percent fall, those with the status of self -employed were hit harder as their number fell by 
42.8 percent, as compared with employees, whose number shrunk by 40.7 percent.  
 
47. As the economy, in general, and tourism activity, in particular, started picking up in 
the subsequent quarters, many jobs are estimated to have gradually returned in these quarters. 
Till the third quarter, however, the number of tourism jobs is still estim ated to run a deficit of 
1.8 million.   
 
Estimated loss in household income during Covid19 pandemic 
48. The impact on income is estimated to be much more severe as compared with the 
impact on loss in jobs. This might owe to the cut in salaries, explaining huge  loss in wage 
income and much higher loss in non -wage income among business owners who not just paid 
salaries but were also required to incur other committed expenditures like payment towards 
rent, bills for utility services and so on.   
 
49. While wage income  fell by 41.6 percent in Q1, non -wage income, that is, income of 
the self -employed or business owners nosedived by 124.4 percent. This shows not many 
businesses not just witnessed a severe fall in income but also posted a deficit in Q1. 
 
50. Going forward, wit h the pickup in activities, the income levels also showed an 
improvement but continued to post a negative growth of 3.4 percent in the case of wage 
income and 21.2 percent in the case of non-wage income, both in Q3. 
 
51. On the other hand, in sharp contrast wi th the tourism household income, total 
household income saw a steeper drop in income level in the case of wage income or salary 
income of the employees. This is because while tourism industries are mostly service 
industries, overall economy also includes a  large proportion of primary sector and 

 
24 
 
manufacturing industries, both of which are highly labour intensive.  
 
Tourism Economy going forward – Future Outlook 
52. With the gradual opening of international borders, regain in confidence to travel, 
successful vacc ination drive and lessons learnt from previous waves of infections, tourism 
activity is expected to move towards normalcy soon. In order to put forward our outlook, we 
have built following three scenarios for all forms of tourism, that is, inbound, domesti c, 
outbound and also outbound tourists diverted to domestic trips: 
a. Optimistic  
b. Most likely 
c. Pessimistic 
 
53. These scenarios are based on the assumptions using our judgement of the likely 
situation going forward. The key findings are: 
 
54. It is expected that tourism economy, in terms of tourism expenditure, will regain its 
pre-pandemic level by 2024 -25, primarily driven by domestic tourism. With respect to 
inbound tourism, the revival is expected to be slower and it is likely to reach the pre -
pandemic level not sooner than 2026-27, even in optimistic scenario. 
 
55. On the other hand, even in pessimistic scenario, domestic tourism (complemented by 
the outbound-turned domestic tourism) is likely to reach the pre-pandemic level much sooner, 
by 2024-25.  
 
Recommendations for the revival of Tourism in India 
The proposed recommendations are as follows: 
56. Promotion of Domestic Tourism: while an average domestic trip costs the least, only 
Rs. 5429, as compared with the cost of an inbound trip (Rs. 2.10 lakh) and an outbound trip 
(Rs. 14,286 as pre-trip and about Rs. 60,000 on-trip), but given its huge volume in number of 
trips, the total tourism expenditure incurred by domestic tourists is over 70 percent of total 
internal tourism expenditure. Hence, whatever tour ism contributes to the economy is mainly 
on account of domestic tourism. 
 

 
25 
 
57. Diverting outbound tourists to domestic trips: by creating an enticing bucket for 
domestic destinations; developing new approach through working holidays; and promoting 
regional or local destinations.  
 
58. Target incentives to industries contributing most to tourism economy: The data on 
tourism expenditure reveal that of all the tourism characteristic products and services, food 
providing services, road transport services and healthcare providing services account for 
close to 80 percent of the total tourism expenditure. Hence, the government policies need to 
be prioritised and targeted towards these important industries. 
 
59. Other broad recommendations include: 
a. Re-establish trust in travel and tourism 
b. Adherence to safety and mandatory health and hygiene protocols to the highest 
standards possible 
c. Protocols should be mandatory for tourists also. 
d. High-value, low-volume (HVLV) approach (as followed in Bhutan) 
e. Government responsiveness towards preparing Tourism Recovery Plan 
f. Provide tax benefits, subsidies and incentives to industry players so that they can 
survive and overcome this pandemic shock 
g. Integrate Public Health with Tourism  
h. Issuance of vaccine certificates 
i. Create healthy environment which is a natural barrier to future pandemics 
j. Technology innovation, like digital marketing, virtual tours etc. 
k. Use of digital services to improve the customer safety experience and adapt quickly if 
the health context in local area changes. 
l. Targeted support for vulnerable communities 
m. Support businesses in diversifying revenue sources 
n. Identify and target diverse customer base  
o. Maintain customer and employee confidence 
 
60. It is imperative that the policy measures need to include all above key areas which are 
identified in the proposed recommendations, in order to foster growth of the tourism industry 
in the country.

Department of Economic Affairs since long. The Committee observes that construction 
of hotels is highly capital intensive and it takes long for hotel projects to reach 
operational profitability. COVID has aggravated this and the current crisis is 
threatening the existe nce of hotel business for organizations in the Hospitality Sector 
because availability of lending by banks and financial institutions who have turned risk 
averse, especially towards hospitality sector, have reduced for contact -intensive sectors. 
The Commit tee, therefore, recommends that hotel projects with capex above Rs. 25 
crore (excluding land) be accorded infrastructure status and included in the 
Infrastructure list of the RBI so that long term funds are accessible at lower interest 
rates and the gap between return expectations and debt cost is bridged. The Committee 
is of the view that according of infrastructure status to hotel projects with capex above 
Rs. 25 crore will not only help build quality accommodation supply, but will also have 
an enormous e conomic multiplier effect across the length and breadth of the country. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the policy stance of the Government in this 
matter be spelt out within three months from the presentation of this Report.  
67. The Committee takes  note of the submissions made for relief measures for the 
survival of the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry. The Committee is aware that 
the Reserve Bank of India had constituted an Expert Committee with Shri K.V. 
Kamath as the Chairman to make reco mmendations on the required financial 
parameters in respect of borrowers eligible under the COVID Resolution Framework 

 
34 
 
and the recommendations of the Expert Committee on the key financial parameters, i.e., 
Total Outsid e Liabilities/ Adjusted Total  Net Wort h; Total Debt/ EBITA; Current 
Ratio; Debt Service Coverage Ratio; and Average Debit Service Coverage Ratio had 
been accepted by the Reserve Bank of India. The Committee has been informed that the 
timeline to achieve the four ratios has been moved from Marc h, 2022 to September, 
2022. However, the deadline for the most important financial metric, i.e., Total Outside 
Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net Worth has remained unchanged, i.e., March 2022. The 
Committee observes that the Indian economy has encountered a "once in a century" 
crisis due to COVID -19 pandemic and the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry is 
one of the hardest hit, revival from which is unlikely to happen for the next 3 -4 years 
because India is already facing a third wave of infections driven by the Omicron variant 
and tourists' footfall has come down significantly due to the vicious cycle of restrictions 
in the wake of COVID-19. The possibility of many more such waves and new variants of 
Coronavirus emerging in India cannot be ruled out. On account of the above factors, 
the Travel and Hospitality Industry has witnessed a huge dip in business. Since the 
Tourism and Hospitality Sector is a major engine of economic growth in terms of 
growth of GDP, forex earnings and employment generation, it is  imperative that the 
revival of this sector should be at the forefront of the efforts of the Government. There 
is, therefore, an imperative need for Government to pull this sector out of the COVID -
19 recessionary conditions. The Committee, therefore, lends  its Parliamentary support 
to the demand of the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality industry and recommends that in 
view of the adverse impact of the third wave of COVID -19 pandemic and the resultant 
recessionary conditions and the difficulties faced in reviva l of businesses and meeting 
the operational requirements, the deadline for achievement of all five financial 
parameters, i.e., (i) Total Outside Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net worth, (ii) Total Debt/ 
EBITA, (iii) Current Ratio, (iv) Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) and (v) Average 
Debt Service Coverage Ratio under the Resolution Framework relating to operational 
performance of borrowing entities be deferred to September, 2023 and the repayment 
schedule be extended from December 2022 to December, 2023. 
 
68. Taking into account the fact that one of the bottlenecks in tapping the full 
potential of the hospitality sector is the high incidence and multiplicity of taxes in the 
country which has led to tourist packages being outpriced in comparison to those 

 
35 
 
available in competing destinations, the Committee in its 288 th Report had 
recommended that policy measures for according Industry status to hotels be initiated. 
The Committee notes that though some states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Kerala, 
Madhya Pradesh, etc., h ave accorded Industry status to hospitality sector, there is no 
uniformity in the tax structure across States. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry of Tourism should work out a strategy for inclusion of Hospitality 
Sector in the State and Central industrial policy so that this sector is conferred Industry 
Status by all the States. The Committee is of the firm view that conferring of Industry 
status will give a big boost to this Sector and help its faster recovery as it will allow the 
Sector to avail lower electricity and water tariff, lower property tax, rationalization of 
license fees and simplified approval process for hotel projects and operations. The 
Committee desires to be kept apprised of the specific measures taken by the 
Government in this regard and the outcome thereof. 
 
69. The Committee in its 288th Report had recommended that to provide relief to the 
tourism and hospitality sector so as to enhance export competitiveness of Indian 
tourism, the payments received by all the tourism and  hospitality entities in convertible 
foreign exchange be considered as "deemed export" and exempted from GST and the 
concept of zero rating be applied to tourism foreign exchange earnings. In this 
connection, the Ministry in its action Taken Notes had stat ed that "…this is a policy 
decision to be taken by GST Council, a reference from Ministry of Tourism is being 
made to GST Council in this regard…" The Committee reiterates its recommendation 
that tourism services provided to foreign tourists in India on receipt of foreign exchange 
should be treated as "deemed export" and such transactions should be zero -rated for 
GST without stopping the flow of input credits. 
 
70. The Committee notes that Finance Act, 2020 which was announced just before 
the start of COVID -19 crisis, inter alia, came up with new insertion of Tax Collected at 
Source (TCS) provisions under Section 206C  (1G)(a) of Income Tax Act, 1961  
pertaining to TCS @ 5% on foreign remittance through Liberalized Remittance  
Scheme (LRS) and under Section 206 C (1G)(b) pertaining to TCS@5% on selling of 
overseas tour packages by tour operators. The Indian Tour Operators face challenges to 
match the prices offered for outbound tours in comparison to foreign tour service 

 
36 
 
providers due to additional burden of taxes which include GST and newly inserted TCS 
provisions under Section 206C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 because overseas agents and 
Online Travel Agents (OTAs) do not charge the same since their base is out of India. 
The Committee is of the view that the above TCS provisions will not only increase the 
cost of packages sold by Indian tour operators, they will also shift all sales of outbound 
tourism to overseas suppliers, thereby denying the Government of income tax and GST 
revenue. These newly inserted TCS provi sions, therefore, are detrimental to tourism 
business in India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to allow 
domestic tour operators a level playing field in comparison with foreign tour operators 
in the market of outbound tourism, the above mentioned TCS provisions be rolled back. 
The Committee is of the view that once TCS on outbound tourism is withdrawn, it will 
enable the Indian Travel Agents and Tour Operators to stage a recovery post the 
pandemic. 
 
71. The Committee in its 288 th Report had observed that under the Service Exports 
from India Scheme (SEIS) the Government  offered domestic exports duty credit scripts 
in the range of 5% to 7% of the net foreign exchange earned depending upon the nature 
of services and recommended that at a time when the tourism sector is faced with the 
crisis of the century, the notified services be incentivized at an enhanced rate of 10% for 
both tour operators and hotels in order to provide them with cash flow support. The 
Committee notes that the much awaited extension and the details on the Services 
Exports from India Scheme for FY 2019 -20 have been notified by the Directorate 
General of Foreign Trade  vide notification No. 29/2015 -20 dated September 23, 2021. 
The Committee is, however, disappointed to note that SEIS benefits for the tourism 
sector has been granted  at 5 per cent on net fore ign exchange earnings as opposed to 
earlier 7 per cent. SEIS rates for hotels have been reduced to 3 per cent from earlier 
specified rate of 5 per cent. Entitlement under SEIS for services exports has also been 
capped at Rs. 5 crore per exporter. The Commi ttee observes that the reduction in 
percentage of SEIS benefits comes at a time when the tourism and hospitality industry 
is struggling to recover their losses or even to stay afloat in many cases. The Committee 
would like to point out that the travel and hospitality businesses are expected to be very 
subdued due to the decline in business scenario post COVID -19 pandemic and there is 
an imperative need to infuse some liquidity into this cash -strapped sector. The 

 
37 
 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Min istry of Tourism should take the SEIS 
rate reduction issue with the Ministry of Commerce and impress upon them that the 
dependency of the hospitality industry is high on import of goods to maintain global 
standards which warrants SEIS benefits to be lucrat ive to reduce the import cost and, 
therefore, the scrips generated by the travel and hospitality sector should be allowed at 
the rate  of 10% vis -à-vis the existing rates and the SEIS benefits should also be 
extended for further period of two-three years for enabling cost savings. 
 
72. The Committee also observes that SEIS is the only incentive for service exporters 
and, therefore, imposing a limit on the total entitlement under the SEIS at Rs 5 crore 
per exporter will impact top revenue producers adversely. Lar ger organisations fetch 
volume based on higher reliability and are necessary to increase the footfall in India. 
Capping the SEIS benefit at Rs. 5 crore will force companies to split up entities to 
continue to avail full benefits which will not be helpful. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should take up with the Ministry of 
Commerce this issue so that the capping of Rs 5 crore for SEIS benefit is removed.

along rivers. The Ministry of Tourism has also sanctioned various projects for th e 
development of Cruise Terminals and related infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh, Goa, 
Maharashtra, Kerala and Tamil Nadu at the major ports for Rs. 151.79 Crore under the 
Scheme for „Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development‟. Th e 

 
45 
 
coastline of the country and its inland waterways have enormous potential to develop cruise 
tourism, both international and domestic. To harness this, a Task Force has been constituted

External Affairs, Customs, CISF, Coastal States, etc. and meets  regularly. On the 
recommendation of the Task Force, Ministry of Shipping and Mi nistry of Tourism have 
jointly appointed a consultant for preparing Action Plan for the development of Cruise 
Tourism in India. The Consultant has prepared a report which provides a roadmap and action 
plan that is needed to move India from its current posi tion to become a preferred cruise 
destination in the world.  On the recommendation of Taskf orce, the following measures were 
taken for the development of cruise tourism:  
 Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) have been formulated to be followed by the 
various agencies for handling cruise ships.  
 The SOPs have been revised during November, 2017 and since operationalized at 
all major ports.  
 The facility for e -tourist visa has been extended to passengers arriving at these 
ports of Mumbai, Mormugao, Mangalore, Kochi and Chennai and immigration 
counters have been set up at five major ports visited by cruise ships, thus 
facilitating the cruise passenger arrivals at the seaports.

ports, “Port Level Facilitation Committees” have been formed under the respective Chairman 
of the major ports to facilitate seamless handling of cruise ships and passengers.

a period of 10 years with effect from 6th February, 2009 without obtaining a licence from 
Director General of Shipping. This faci lity has been extended further for a period of 5years

a vast network of lakes and rivers, and a steady increase in the number of ships and

47 
 
Ministries of Tourism and Ports, Shipping and Waterways to develop India as

to Rs. 60 crore at the RE stage u nder scheme for Domestic Promotion & Publicity including 
Market Development Assistance out of which  an amount of Rs. 21.06 crore has been utilized 
(Till January 2022). An allocation of Rs. 75 crore has been made in BE 2022-23. 
 
103. The Committee has been informed that t he second wave of the pandemic  and the 
subsequent lockdowns,  had substantially affected the promotional efforts being undertaken 
by the Ministry of Tourism. Planned promotions/ campaigns/ on ground events had to be 
deferred / cancelled in the view of the fluid situation. In view of the same, the allocation 
under DPPH Head 2021-22, had to be substantially reduced from Rs 144.70 crore to Rs 60.00 
crore at RE stage.   
 
104. The proposed amount of Rs 75.00 crore for BE 2022 -23 w ould be utilized for 
undertaking various outreach programs by offices of the Ministry across the country, 
undertaking promotional campaigns on digital, print and electronic media, as per 
requirement, promotional materials, collaterals and films, organizing  tourism promotional 
events and outreach programs   by the domestic India Tourism offices, organizing specific 
campaigns for the promotion of North East, Ladakh and Jammu & Kashmir, support to 
States/UTs for fairs, festivals, etc. 
 
105. The Director General (tou rism) during his deposition before the Committee informed 

 
49 
 
that domestic tourism visits during 2020 were 610.22 milliion as compared to 2321.98 
million during 2019. 
 
106. The Committee observes that in most countries with a large population, domestic 
tourism is the foundation of a vibrant tourism industry. India also has a strong domestic 
tourism base which is evident from the fact that Domestic tourism visits were 2321.98 
million during 2019. However, owing to the prolonged COVID -19 pandemic, the 
erstwhile boomi ng tourism and hospitality sector has taken a severe beating due to 
which the number of domestic tourists slumped to 610 .22 million during 2020 
registering a negative growth of 73.3%. The trajectory of international tourism remains 
uncertain because new COVID-19 variants are emerging in some parts of the world due 
to which new restrictions are being introduced. With the rapid pace of the nation -wide 
COVID vaccination, the revival of the Indian economy has gained momentum and 
Indian tourist destinations have  risen to prominence as a result of strong pent -up 
demand and the relaxation of domestic restrictions. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the publicity campaigns of the Ministry should be focused on 
following safety protocols and helping restore confidence among tourists and promoting 
domestic tourism.  
 
107. The Committee also recommends that niche tourism avenues such as medical 
tourism, Buddhist tourism, sports tourism, ayurveda tourism, yoga tourism, spiritual 
tourism, adventure tourism, culinary tour ism, cruise tourism, etc. should be promoted 
aggressively through the media campaigns. 
 
108. The Committee observes that high net worth Indian nationals opt for foreign 
tourism instead of domestic tourism. One of the reasons behind this is the exhaustion of 
the timeworn tourist destinations and absence of new avenues. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that unexplored and unexploited tourist destinations should be 
identified, developed and marketed to revive the curiosity of high -end domestic tourists 
and the publicity campaign should aim at persuading high end domestic tourists to 
substitute domestic tourism for foreign tourism. 
 
109. The Committee recommends that on the lines of Wor ld Tourism Rankings and 

 
50 
 
"Swachh Survekshan ", a competitive Tourism Ranking System s hould be introduced 
amongst Indian cities which would provide the impetus for them to create, maintain 
and promote more and more tourist spots within their cities. This ranking system may 
be updated every year and the cities with podium finishes in varied categories may be 
incentivised. 
 
110. A very rapidly emerging trend in global tourism scenario, especially amongst the 
youth is that of Night Tourism. Though India has opened some of its monuments for 
public to visit in night, it is still in a very nascent stage. Sufficient information is also not 
available regarding the participating sites, their timings and other such details. The 
Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry should focus on night tourism and make 
more sites available for visit during night,  allow extended hours, provide exhaustive 
information on websites and social media pages and aggressively market the concept. 
This will open a new dimension of looking at our existing tourism heritage and invite 
repeat visitors.

115. The Committee notes  with concerns  that in order to  generate sufficient

establishment of Institutes of Hotel Managements and Food Craft Insti tutes. As of now

opportunities for employment generation in the tourism sector both in urban as well as rural

120. The Committee notes that tourism is a labour -intensive industry and a multi -
sector activity characterized by multiple services provided by a range of suppliers and, 
therefore, this sector has huge potential for generation of jobs and absorption of a 
substantially higher workforce. The Committee notes from the Market Pulse data 
supplied by the Min istry that the hospitality and allied sectors face huge deficit in 
trained manpower. As against annual requirement of 902890 for 2022, the total supply 
including attrition is only 84128 and the demand -supply gap is to the extent of 818762. 
Tourism sector is likely to witness a boom post pandem ic because there is lot of pent -up 
demand for travel. This boom may bring an exponential demand for the workforce at 
managerial, supervisor and skilled levels in hospitality and tourism sector. This leads 
the Committee  to the irresistible conclusion that the existing institutional capacities 
would be unable to fulfil the estimated additional requirement of manpower in the 
hospitality and allied sectors. The Committee is of the view that since training is a key 
intervention and issues of human resource development and capacity building are 
extremely important, the realization of the country's huge, barely tapped tourism 
potential cannot be realized without addressing the challenges of capacity constraints. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should adopt a proactive 
interventionist approach to give a major boost to the various initiatives relating to 
human resource development for the hospitality and tourism sector through 
convergence with the private sector.  
 
121. The Committee is of the view that there is an imperative need for the hotel 
management institutes to be updated and integrated with the hotel industry. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the complete curriculum of the hotel 
management institutes be revised. The curriculum also needs to be updated regularly to 
reflect the constantly changing dynamics of the industry in the post COVID era. 
 
122. The Committee in its 288 th Report had observed that till the year 2015 -16, the 
Hunar Se Rozgar Tak Progra mme was geared only towards the creation of employable 
skills. However, with the adoption of Common Norms on Skill Development notified by 

 
57 
 
the Ministry of Skill development and Entrepreneurship, it has been made mandatory 
on the part of the Training Provid er Institutes to arrange placement/self -employment 
for at least 70% of the certified trainees within three months of completion of the 
course." The Committee would like to be updated whether the implementing agencies 
have adjusted to this provision. The Co mmittee also desires to be apprised of the 
Training Service Provider Institutes who have lagged behind the targets set in this 
regard. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should closely put in place 
an intensive monitoring mechanism for fulfilm ent of the norms stipulated by the 
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship. 
 
123. The Committee notes that a number of programmes like Hunar Se Rozgar Tak, 
Skill Testing and Certification, Entrepreneurship Programmes, Tourism Adventure 
Courses, etc., have been launched under the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers to provi de education, training and certification to the tourism service 
providers. Though the Ministry have supplied the information regarding the number of 
persons trained and certified under the programmes of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers, it has not f urnished the annual targets fixed and the actual achievement 
made in respect thereof under the scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers in 
2021-22. The Committee, therefore, desires to be apprised of the achievements made 
vis-à-vis the targets fixed, programme-wise, under the CBSP in 2021-22. 
 
XI. ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES FOR TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE 
DEVELOPMENT:  
 
124. Development of tourism infrastructure at tourism destinations could create a critical 
mass for achieving its targeted objectives an d other socio -economic benefits to the society. 
The holistic development of tourism infrastructure at all important tourist destinations 
through Central Financial Assistance(CFA) to the States/UTs may not be possible since, 
many of the potential destinations are under the jurisdictions/ control of Central Agencies like 
ASI, Railways, Port Trusts in India, ITDC etc. and the overall development of places of 
tourist interest under their control may not be possible through their own resources and may 
require convergence of resources, expertise and experience for maintenance and management 
after development. In order to remove these shortcomings and to bring in the active 

 
58 
 
participation of the Central Agencies, the tourist interest assets owned by Central/State 
Governments/UT Administrations/Central Agencies which have potential can be developed 
through Central Agency. A total of Rs.62.85 crore has been released to various Central 
Agencies for creation of tourism infrastructure during 2020-21.  
 
125. The Committee observes that the c reation of tourism infrastructure by way of 
roads, cruise terminals, railway connectivity, and medical facilities has its multiplier 
effect in terms of overall economic growth and employment generation and acts as a 
catalyst to economic development of the country. Under the Scheme, "Assistance to 
Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development", a total of Rs. 62.85 crores 
has been released to various Central Agencies for creation of tourism related 
infrastructure. To make an assessment of the succe ss of this Scheme, the Committee 
desires to be furnished with the total number of projects sanctioned and taken up for 
implementation, along with the released amount vis -à-vis the sanctioned budget during 
the last 5 years, year-wise.  
 
Improvement of road connectivity and wayside amenities to the important tourist 
desinations with the help of Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. 
126. Ministry of Tourism (MoT) has been pursuing the matter regarding improvement of 
road connectivity to impor tant tourist destinations with the Ministry of Road Transport & 
Highways (MoRTH) and had submitted a list of 50 Tourism Destinations to MoRTH for 
taking up in the first phase. MoRTH has been requested to consider setting up of Wayside 
Amenities, prominent signages and beautification of the area, at a distance of 15 -20 km 
where good road connectivity already exists. Out of these 50 destinations, only 23 fall under 
the purview of Ministry of Road Transport & Highways/National Highway Authority of 
India, where work is in progress. For the remaining 27 tourist sites , Ministry of Tourism has 
addressed letters to the respective State Governments and PWD for improvement of 
connectivity and provision of wayside facilities as these roads did not fall under the purvie w 
of MoRT&H. Virtual meetings were held with the State/UT Tourism Departments on 24th 
and 25 th November, 2020 to get their inputs and suggestions on tourist destinations which 
require road connectivity and wayside amenities. Based on the inputs received from the State 
Governments/UTs, a list of 114 destinations has been prepared and further shared with the 
MoRT&H for improving road connectivity to these tourist sites. Further, meetings with 

 
59 
 
senior officers of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highway and the Ministry of Petroleum 
and Natural Gas have also been held in the month of November, 2021 rega rding 
improvement of road connectivity and to ensure public amenities along the national highways 
connecting the UNESCO World Heritage Sites and other prominent tourist destinations for 
enhancing smooth journey experiences of the tourists. 
 
127. The Committee o bserves that easy access to tourism destinations and facilities 
for easy movement within the destinations are prerequisites for the development of 
tourism. However, road connectivity has been one of the impediments for the growth of 
tourism in India. It is in this context that the list of 50 Tourist Destinations submitted by 
the Ministry of Tourism to the Ministry of Roa d Transport and Highways assume  
significance. The Committee notes that out of the 50 destinations selected for road 
connectivity, 23 destinations fall under the purview of Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways/NHAI where the work is going on. However, no forward movement seems to 
have been made as regards road connectivity to the remaining 27 tourist sites which are 
under the purview of the  State Governments. Though the Ministry of Tourism have 
taken up the matter with the concerned State Governments, it has not had the desired 
result. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should 
once again take up this matter at the highest level with the concerned State 
Governments and impress upon them that better connectivity to the tourist sites will 
unlock more tourism opportunities for the State and the economic benefits will flow into 
their economy in the shape of increased  State revenues and employment as road 
connectivity is one of the fundamental components for successfully developing tourism 
market. The Committee desires to be apprised of the efforts made in this regard and the 
outcome thereof. 
 
128. The Committee notes that Ministry of Tourism has shared with the Ministry of 
Road Transport and Highways a new list of 114 destinations for improving connectivity 
to these destinations. Good road, railway or air connectivity to tourist destinations is of 
paramount importance to at tract domestic as well as foreign tourists because when 
these destinations are well connected, entrepreneurs in hospitality sector, tour and 
travel operators become confident of making investments and promoting these 
destinations. The Committee, therefore,  recommends that a dedicated mechanism be 

 
60 
 
put in place for planning, coordination and completion of the road connectivity projects 
to the 114 tourist destinations. 
 
 
129. The Committee observes that last mile connectivity to several tourist 
destinations is a de terrent to promotion of tourism. Since last mile connectivity is a key 
driver for promotion of tourism, the Committee recommends that while preparing 
Master Plan for connectivity to tourist destinations, last mile connectivity should 
mandatorily be included in the concept and the Detailed Project Report. 
 
130. There is lack of good wayside amenities including toilets at several tourist 
destinations which causes inconven ience to tourists and discourages them from visiting 
such places. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should focus 
more on the improvement of wayside amenities at tourist destinations to facilitate 
travelers.

134. The Ministry has informed the Committee that it has taken several measures to 
ensure the safety and security of tourists including foreign tourists:-

freedom from exploitation of both tourists and local residen ts, in particular women and 
children. 
 
137. Ministry of Tourism has advised all the State Governments/Union Territory 
Administrations to deploy Tourist Police in the States/Union Territories. At present, a total 
number of 14 States have deployed the tourist pol ice namely Delhi, Goa, Himachal Pradesh,

138. Nirbhaya Fund, specifically designed to improve the safety and security of

Tourist Destination for Women in Madhya Pradesh‟ is being funded by Ministry of Tourism. 
Under the Project 1st instalment of Rs.6.24 crore (appr ox)has been released on 19.03.2021 
for the Financial year 2020-21. 
 
139. The Committee notes that 14 States have deployed tourist police in one form or 
the other. Keeping in mind the importance of safety and security of tourists, the 
Committee in its 275 th and 288th Reports presented to the Parliament on the 3 rd March 

 
63 
 
2020 and 9 th March 2021 respectively,  hadrecommended that the Ministry of Tourism 
should take up the matter with the remaining States. The Committee is, therefore, 
dismayed to note that no fur ther headway has been made by the remaining States 
towards creation and deployment of tourism police at major tourist destinations. Safety 
and security of the tourists are a determining factor for choosing a destination and also 
vital for providing quality services in tourism and, therefore, the destinations must have 
an image of utmost tourist safety and security. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that Tourist police should be set up in all important tourist 
destinations of ea ch State/UT and should provide travelers security through a spirit of 
courtesy and friendliness. 
 
140. The Committee is aware that the tourist police system prevails in other countries 
also. The Committee would like the Ministry of Tourism to document such best 
practices from these countries and help adopt such practices in our country. The

141. Adventure tourism in India has a huge potential for growth as India offers the 
keen adventurers a fascinating range of thrills and activities to choose from. The 
Ministry of Tourism has issued guideline s for approval of Adventure Tourism

is largely unorganized and unregulated. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is an 
urgent need to regularize the Adventure Tour Oper ators Market and promote 
registration of companies indulging in these activities on a centralized platform to 
increase credibility and enforce safety regulations.

II) ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2022-23 
The Committee notes that although there has been marginal increase in the 
budgetary outlay for the Ministry from Rs. 2026.77 crore for FY 2021 -22 to Rs. 2400.00 
crore for FY 2022-23, it is still lesser than the BE 2020-21 allocation of Rs. 2499.83 crore. 
Though the BE 2022-23 allocation is 18-41% higher than the BE 2021 -22 outlay, there is 
a substantial shortfall of Rs. 537.92 crore vis -à-vis the projected demand of Rs. 2937.92 
crore by the Ministry for FY 2022 -23 and that too at a time when this sector is reeling 
under losses in the wake of COVID -19 pandemic. The Committee notes that this 
budgetary outlay for 2022 -23 has been reduced to Rs 416 crore as compared to the BE 
2021-22 of Rs. 668.72 crore under the head - Promotion and Publicity. The Committee 
finds this reduction alarming because the tourism and hospitality sector has been hit the 
hardest by COVID-19 pandemic and with massive job and revenue losses, it is essential 
that the Government promotes India on all possible platforms, both national and 
international, as a safe and must -visit destination and for this, instilling confidence 
among tourists through use of technology with the help of skilled manpower, investment 
in skilling, reskilling and upskilling is an imperative need. The Committee, therefor e, 
apprehends that the marginal increase of Rs. 333.77 crore in the budgetary allocation for 
2022-23 is inadequate as it will be consumed by inflation. The Committee is 
simultaneously appreciative of the fiscal constraints faced by the Ministry of Finance 
due to deceleration in the growth rate in the Indian economy on account of global and 
domestic slowdown in the aftermath of COVID -19 pandemic. The Committee observes 
that with the accelerated pace of vaccine roll -out and easing of restrictions, the Indian 
economy has started to rebound and the additional resources would become available as 
a result of revenue buoyancy in FY 2022 -23. Given the fact that the activities of the 
Ministry harness the direct and multiplier effect on economic development and 
employment generation in the country and integrated development of infrastructure and 
facilities through effective partnerships and convergence with stakeholders can propel 
India to a higher growth trajectory, the Committee recommends that depending on 
better financial performance and greater absorption capacity of the Ministry, quantum 
of funding for the Ministry of Tourism be enhanced at the RE 2022 -23 stage. 
Simultaneously, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should initiate and 

 
65 
 
implement better fiscal discipline and ensure that the scarce financial resources do not 
remain parked idelling. 
(Para 19) 
From a perusal of Table No. 2, the Committee is constrained to note that there is 
a substantial underutilization of the budgeted funds during the FY 2021 -22. Against the 
RE 2021-22 allocation of Rs. 969.80 crore, only 47.70% amounting to Rs. 462.55 crore 
could be spent till the 31st January, 2022. It means that the remaining expenditure would 
have to be squeezed in the last two months of FY 2021 -22. Since as p er norms stipulated 
by the Ministry of Finance, there is a ceiling of 25% on expenditure in the last quarter, 
occurrence of huge savings is a certainty. It may be pertinent to mention here that a zero 
based budgeting exercise which requires that budget req uest be evaluated thoroughly, 
starting from zero base, is in practice and the financial outlays are earmarked based on 
factors like past trend of expenditure, stages of formulation/implementation of various 
projects, the pre-projects approvals etc. Therefore, savings of Rs. 1056.97 crore vis -à-vis 
the BE 2021-22 allocation not only betrays fiscal indiscipline by way of underutilization 
of the earmarked funds which will have an adverse bearing on infrastructure 
development oriented activities of the Ministry , but is also indicative of shortcomings in 
budgetary planning and monitoring of the budgeted funds. The Committee observes that 
a resource constrained country like India cannot afford to keep a vast chunk of its 
resources locked up and surrendered towards  the end of the financial year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that realistic projection of fund requirements should 
be given utmost priority at the highest level of the Ministry so that the Budget Estimates 
are formulated with application of proper financial yardsticks and large variations 
between the Budget Estimates, Revised Estimates and Actual Expenditure needs to be 
avoided. The Ministry must also pay attention to streamlining its monitoring mechanism 
and ensure optimal and more efficient deploy ment and utilization of its financial 
resources for smooth execution of its programmes within the approved cost and 
designated timeline. 
(Para 20) 
The Committee also takes a serious note of keeping the unspent provision of Rs. 
1056.97 crore till the close of financial year 2021 -22 despite reduction in the budgetary 
outlay at the RE 2021-22 stage, in disregard of the provisions of General Financial Rules 
requiring the unspent provisions in a grant to be surrendered to the Ministry of Finance 

 
66 
 
as soon as these  are foreseen, without waiting for the last day of the financial year. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should exercise greater fiscal 
prudence, and ensure that unspent budgetary provisions are surrendered timely in 
future.
