III) CONTRIBUTION OF TOURISM TO GDP 
 
The Committee notes that as per the World Travel and Tourism Council 
(WTTC), prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Travel and Tourism accounted for 10.4% of 
global GDP. In many parts of the world, tourism is a major engine of growth. The 
Committee in its 275th R eport presented to the Parliament on the 3rd March 2020 had 
noted that the contribution of tourism to national GDP was over 10% for most countries 
where tourism happens to be the main driver of national economy. However, in India 
which has unique endowment s of biodiversity, forests, rivers, its rich culture and 
heritage and many World Heritage sites, the tourism sector has not proved to be the 
proverbial engine of growth for our economy. This is evident from the fact that India's 
total share in global inter national arrivals remains a modest 1.57% against the target of 
3 per cent set by the NITI Aayog to be achieved by 2022. Similarly, the contribution 

 
67 
 
(direct and indirect) of tourism in the GDP and the total jobs in the country are 
estimated to be 5.16 per c ent and 15.34 per cent respectively during 2019 -20. The 
Committee is of the firm view that if India has to move towards becoming USD 5 trillion 
economy and a global economic powerhouse, as envisioned by our Hon'ble PM Shri 
Narendra Modi, then the contribut ion of tourism to India's GDP has to be raised from 
the current 5.16% to 10% in the next five years. The Committee, while welcoming the 
various measures taken by the Ministry to double the contribution of tourism to India's 
GDP, feels that the vast untappe d potential of India as a tourism destination cannot be 
realized unless tourism is included in the Concurrent List of the Constitution of India. 
Taking note of the fact that Travel and Tourism does not figure in the Centre, State or 
Concurrent Lists and si nce in a federal polity like ours, the responsibility for policy 
making and implementation of tourism projects are fragmented across different levels - 
Central and State Governments and coordination between them is often lacking due to 
absence of clearly d efined mandate, the Committee in its 288th Report had 
recommended inclusion of tourism in the Concurrent List. Since tourism is yet to be 
included in the Concurrent List, the Committee reiterates its recommendation for 
inclusion of tourism in the Concurren t List of the Constitution of India. The Committee 
is convinced that this will go a long way in channelising the development of tourism and 
positioning and maintaining tourism development as a national priority.  
(Para 30) 
The Committee observes that Emira te of Dubai does not have the abundant 
wealth of natural oil reserves and nor does it have a pre -existing plethora of natural, 
historical and internationally significant tourist sites. Despite that, it has emerged as a 
multi-billion dollar economy and amon gst the world's most visited tourist destinations, 
all based on the Government's tourism centric approach towards national policy 
making. The Committee wishes that India should also endeavour to imbibe creating 
potential for tourism in the very core of its  policy making. Although tourism is an 
important activity in India, its share in global market is extremely small and the 
potential of tourism sector in India is yet to be unleashed. The actual implementation of 
tourist projects takes place at State/UT level but in most of the States/UTs, the outlay for 
Department of Tourism is meagre. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order 
to give policy push to the tourism industry, a National Tourism Council chaired by the 
Prime Minister and composed of Chief  Ministers or Tourism Ministers of all States 

 
68 
 
should be established. This National Council should be an empowered legislative body on 
the lines of GST Council. This will enable fast -track Centre-State level tourism decision 
making, leveraging and utilising  full synergies of India's tourism potential across all our 
States. 
(Para 31) 
The Committee observes that despite the fact that India offers a diverse portfolio 
for travel and tourism, the share of India's International Tourist Arrivals (ITAs) in the 
ITAs of the world was merely 1.57 per cent in 2020. There is increased competition 
among various countries to attract foreign visitors. There is, therefore, an imperative 
need for India to prepare suitable market strategy to attract foreign visitors. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry in collaboration with a professional 
body should carry out market research of foreign tourist source markets to identify the 
expectations, requirements, psychographics, demographics and many other aspects of a 
foreign tourist willing to travel to India, thereby enabling to create a strategic plan to 
revive inbound tourism. The research should be conducted with an objective to provide 
an authentic feedback, roadmap and recommendations to the Ministry of Tourism wi th 
respect to inbound tourism in India and provide a blueprint on the various policy 
objectives and infrastructure development needed to strengthen inbound tourism in the 
country. 
(Para 32) 
 
IV) IMPACT OF COVID -19 PANDEMIC ON TOURISM, TRAVEL AND 
HOSPITALITY SECTOR 
 
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism had assigned National Council 
of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) to prepare a report on the impact of the 
COVID-19 pandemic on the tourism sector. The Ministry has shared with the 
Committee the findings of the study conducted by NCAER. The Committee notes that 
one of the key findings of the study is that due to supply -side shock, tourism economy 
saw a fall of 42.8% in April -June 2020, 15.5% in July -Sep 2020 and 1.1% in October -
December 2020. The Committee also notes that NCAER in its Study Report has made 
certain recommendations for the revival of the tourism sector. The Committee desires to 

 
69 
 
be kept apprised of the action taken by the Ministry on the findings of the NCAER. 
(Para 65) 
The Committee observes that the tourism and hospitality industry is one of the 
worst hit sectors by COVID -19 pandemic and is in huge financial distress. The highly 
infectious novel coronavirus continues to thwart the sector as new COVID -19 variants 
keep on emer ging. Apart from providing mass employment, income and foreign 
exchange for the country, this sector has an economically beneficial cascading impact 
on other sectors such as airlines, infrastructure, transportation, accommodation, 
facilitations systems, et c. As per data furnished by the Ministry, during the year 2019 -
20, this sector provided 79.86 million jobs directly and indirectly and generated 5.16% 
of India's GDP. As per the data furnished by the Ministry in the Table 9 above, the 
potential job loss in  tourism has been estimated to be 20.8% in the year 2020 falling 
from 4.01 crore in 2019 to 3.17 crore in 2020 and the total revenue loss suffered by the 
hospitality sector has been estimated to be Rs. 89,813 crore in 2020. Therefore, this 
sector needs an urgent boost for revival. The Committee notes that a proposal of the 
Ministry of Tourism regarding grant of infrastructure status to investment in hotel 
industry of Capex over Rs. 25 crore (excluding land) is under consideration of the 
Department of Economic Affairs since long. The Committee observes that construction 
of hotels is highly capital intensive and it takes long for hotel projects to reach 
operational profitability. COVID has aggravated this and the current crisis is 
threatening the existence of hotel business for organizations in the Hospitality Sector 
because availability of lending by banks and financial institutions who have turned risk 
averse, especially towards hospitality sector, have reduced for contact -intensive sectors. 
The Committee, th erefore, recommends that hotel projects with capex above Rs. 25 
crore (excluding land) be accorded infrastructure status and included in the 
Infrastructure list of the RBI so that long term funds are accessible at lower interest 
rates and the gap between return expectations and debt cost is bridged. The Committee 
is of the view that according of infrastructure status to hotel projects with capex above 
Rs. 25 crore will not only help build quality accommodation supply, but will also have 
an enormous economic  multiplier effect across the length and breadth of the country. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the policy stance of the Government in this 
matter be spelt out within three months from the presentation of this Report.  

 
70 
 
 (Para 66) 
The Committee takes note of the submissions made for relief measures for the 
survival of the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry. The Committee is aware that 
the Reserve Bank of India had constituted an Expert Committee with Shri K.V. Kamath

is already facing a third wave of infections driven by the Omicron variant and tourists'

Hospitality Sector is a major engine of economic growth in terms of growth of GDP, 
forex earnings and employment generation, it is imperative that the revival of this sector 
should be at the forefront of the efforts of the Government. There is, therefore, an 
imperative need for Government to pull this sector out of the COVID -19 recessionary 
conditions. The Committee, therefore, lends its Parliamentary support to the demand of 
the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality industry and recommends that in view of the 
adverse impact of the third wave of COVID -19 pandemic and the resultant recessionary

requirements, the deadline for achievement of all five financial parameters, i.e., (i) Total 
Outside Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net worth, (ii) Total Debt/ EBITA, (iii) Current

Ratio under the Resolution Framework relating to operational performance of

borrowing entities be deferred to September, 2023 and the repayment schedule be

Taking into account the fact that one of the bottlenecks in tapping the full 
potential of the hospitality sector is the high incidence and multiplicity of taxes in the 
country which has led to tourist packages being outpriced in comparison to those 
available in competing destinations, the Committee in its 288th Report had 
recommended that policy measures for according Industry status to hotels be initiated. 
The Committee notes that though some states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Ker ala, 
Madhya Pradesh, etc., have accorded Industry status to hospitality sector, there is no 
uniformity in the tax structure across States. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry of Tourism should work out a strategy for inclusion of Hospita lity 
Sector in the State and Central industrial policy so that this sector is conferred Industry 
Status by all the States. The Committee is of the firm view that conferring of Industry 
status will give a big boost to this Sector and help its faster recover y as it will allow the 
Sector to avail lower electricity and water tariff, lower property tax, rationalization of

in this regard and the outcome thereof. 
(Para 68) 
The Committee in its 288th Report had recommended that to provide relief to the 
tourism and hospitality sector so as to enhance export competitiveness of Indian tourism, 
the payments received by all the tourism and hospitality entities in convertible foreign 
exchange be considered as "deemed export" and exempted from GST and the concept of 
zero rating be applied to tourism foreign exchange earnings. In this connection, the 
Ministry in its action Taken Notes had stated that "…this is a policy decision to be taken 
by GST Council, a reference from Ministry of Tourism is being made to GST Council in 
this regard…" The Committee reiterates its recommendation that tourism services 
provided to foreign tourists in India on receipt of foreign exchange should be treated as 
"deemed export" and such transactions should be zero -rated for GST without stopping 
the flow of input credits. 
(Para 69) 

 
72 
 
The Committee notes that Finance Act, 2020 which wa s announced just before 
the start of COVID -19 crisis, inter alia, came up with new insertion of Tax Collected at 
Source (TCS) provisions under Section 206C (1G)(a) of Income Tax Act, 1961 pertaining 
to TCS @ 5% on foreign remittance through Liberalized Remittance  Scheme (LRS) and 
under Section 206C(1G)(b) pertaining to TCS@5% on selling of overseas tour packages 
by tour operators. The Indian Tour Operators face challenges to match the prices 
offered for outbound tours in comparison to foreign tour service providers due to 
additional burden of taxes which include GST and newly inserted TCS provisions under 
Section 206C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 because overseas agents and Online Travel 
Agents (OTAs) do not charge the same since their base is out of India. The Committee is 
of the view that the above TCS provisions will not only increase the cost of packages sold 
by Indian tour operators, they will also shift all sales of outbound tourism to overseas 
suppliers, thereby denying the Government of income tax and  GST revenue. These 
newly inserted TCS provisions, therefore, are detrimental to tourism business in India. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to allow domestic tour operators a 
level playing field in comparison with foreign tour operators in the market of outbound 
tourism, the above mentioned TCS provisions be rolled back. The Committee is of the 
view that once TCS on outbound tourism is withdrawn, it will enable the Indian Travel 
Agents and Tour Operators to stage a recovery post the pandemic. 
(Para 70) 
The Committee in its 288th Report had observed that under the Service Exports 
from India Scheme (SEIS) the Government offered domestic exports duty credit scripts 
in the range of 5% to 7% of the net foreign exchange earned depending upon the  nature 
of services and recommended that at a time when the tourism sector is faced with the 
crisis of the century, the notified services be incentivized at an enhanced rate of 10% for 
both tour operators and hotels in order to provide them with cash flow support. The 
Committee notes that the much awaited extension and the details on the Services 
Exports from India Scheme for FY 2019 -20 have been notified by the Directorate 
General of Foreign Trade vide notification No. 29/2015 -20 dated September 23, 2021. 
The Committee is, however, disappointed to note that SEIS benefits for the tourism 
sector has been granted at 5 per cent on net foreign exchange earnings as opposed to 
earlier 7 per cent. SEIS rates for hotels have been reduced to 3 per cent from earlier 
specified rate of 5 per cent. Entitlement under SEIS for services exports has also been 

 
73 
 
capped at Rs. 5 crore per exporter. The Committee observes that the reduction in 
percentage of SEIS benefits comes at a time when the tourism and hospitality industry is  
struggling to recover their losses or even to stay afloat in many cases. The Committee 
would like to point out that the travel and hospitality businesses are expected to be very 
subdued due to the decline in business scenario post COVID -19 pandemic and th ere is 
an imperative need to infuse some liquidity into this cash -strapped sector. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should take the SEIS 
rate reduction issue with the Ministry of Commerce and impress upon them that the 
dependency of the hospitality industry is high on import of goods to maintain global 
standards which warrants SEIS benefits to be lucrative to reduce the import cost and, 
therefore, the scrips generated by the travel and hospitality sector should be allowed at  
the rate of 10% vis-à-vis the existing rates and the SEIS benefits should also be extended 
for further period of two-three years for enabling cost savings. 
(Para 71) 
The Committee also observes that SEIS is the only incentive for service exporters 
and, therefore, imposing a limit on the total entitlement under the SEIS at Rs 5 crore per 
exporter will impact top revenue producers adversely. Larger organisations fetch 
volume based on higher reliability and are necessary to increase the footfall in India. 
Capping the SEIS benefit at Rs. 5 crore will force companies to split up entities to 
continue to avail full benefits which will not be helpful. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should take up with the Ministry of 
Commerce this issue so that the capping of Rs 5 crore for SEIS benefit is removed. 
(Para 72)

IX. DOMESTIC PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY (DPPH) SCHEMEINCLUDING 
MARKET DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 
The Committee observes that in most countries with a large popu lation, 
domestic tourism is the foundation of a vibrant tourism industry. India also has a 
strong domestic tourism base which is evident from the fact that Domestic tourism visits 
were 2321.98 million during 2019. However, owing to the prolonged COVID -19 
pandemic, the erstwhile booming tourism and hospitality sector has taken a severe 
beating due to which the number of domestic tourists slumped to 610.22 million during 
2020 registering a negative growth of 73.3%. The trajectory of international tourism 
remains uncertain because new COVID -19 variants are emerging in some parts of the 
world due to which new restrictions are being introduced. With the rapid pace of the 
nation-wide COVID vaccination, the revival of the Indian economy has gained 
momentum and Indi an tourist destinations have risen to prominence as a result of 
strong pent -up demand and the relaxation of domestic restrictions. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the publicity campaigns of the Ministry should be focused 
on following safety proto cols and helping restore confidence among tourists and 
promoting domestic tourism.  
(Para 106) 

 
78 
 
The Committee also recommends that niche tourism avenues such as medical 
tourism, Buddhist tourism, sports tourism, ayurveda tourism, yoga tourism, spiritual 
tourism, adventure tourism, culinary tourism, cruise tourism, etc. should be promoted 
aggressively through the media campaigns. 
(Para 107) 
The Committee observes that high net worth Indian nationals opt for foreign 
tourism instead of domestic tourism. One of the reasons behind this is the exhaustion of 
the timeworn tourist destinations and absence of new avenues. The Committee,

substitute domestic tourism for foreign tourism.

The Committee recommends that on the lines of World Tourism Rankings an d 
"Swachh Survekshan", a competitive Tourism Ranking System should be introduced 
amongst Indian cities which would provide the impetus for them to create, maintain 
and promote more and more tourist spots within their cities. This ranking system may 
be updated every year and the cities with podium finishes in varied categories may be 
incentivised. 
(Para 109) 
A very rapidly emerging trend in global tourism scenario, especially amongst the 
youth is that of Night Tourism. Though India has opened some of its mon uments for 
public to visit in night, it is still in a very nascent stage. Sufficient information is also not 
available regarding the participating sites, their timings and other such details. The 
Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry should focus on night tourism and make 
more sites available for visit during night, allow extended hours, provide exhaustive 
information on websites and social media pages and aggressively market the concept. 
This will open a new dimension of looking at our existing t ourism heritage and invite 
repeat visitors. 
(Para 110) 

 
79 
 
 
X HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
 
The Committee notes with concerns that in order to generate sufficient 
manpower in order to meet the needs of the tourism and hospitality industry, the 
Ministry extends assistance to State Governments and Union Territories for 
establishment of Institutes of Hotel Managements and Food Craft Institutes. As of now 
47 Institutes of Hotel Management and 14 Food Craft Institutes have been set up with 
the support of the Ministry and one Central IHM at Jagdishpur, Uttar Pradesh is under 
construction. Given the fact that India faces intense shortage of trained manpower at 
various levels of the travel and hospitality sector, the Committee is of the view that the 
existing institution al capacities would not be able to meet the requirement of trained 
manpower in the tourism and hospitality sector. As this sector has great potential for 
creating enormous number of jobs, the Committee recommends that the gap at the skill 
level should be b ridged and new IHMs and FCIs in the States/UTs that have not been 
covered as yet, should be established to enlarge the quality and quantity output of 
human resources required by the hospitality sector. 
(Para 115) 
The Committee also desires to be apprised o f the physical and financial progress 
in respect of the 3 Food Craft Institutes which have been sanctioned to be set up in the 
State of Madhya Pradesh. 
(Para 116) 
The Committee notes that tourism is a labour -intensive industry and a multi -
sector activity c haracterized by multiple services provided by a range of suppliers and, 
therefore, this sector has huge potential for generation of jobs and absorption of a 
substantially higher workforce. The Committee notes from the Market Pulse data 
supplied by the Mini stry that the hospitality and allied sectors face huge deficit in 
trained manpower. As against annual requirement of 902890 for 2022, the total supply 
including attrition is only 84128 and the demand -supply gap is to the extent of 818762. 
Tourism sector is likely to witness a boom post pandemic because there is lot of pent -up 
demand for travel. This boom may bring an exponential demand for the workforce at 
managerial, supervisor and skilled levels in hospitality and tourism sector. This leads the 
Committee to the irresistible conclusion that the existing institutional capacities would 

 
80 
 
be unable to fulfil the estimated additional requirement of manpower in the hospitality 
and allied sectors. The Committee is of the view that since training is a key interventi on 
and issues of human resource development and capacity building are extremely 
important, the realization of the country's huge, barely tapped tourism potential cannot 
be realized without addressing the challenges of capacity constraints. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should adopt a proactive interventionist 
approach to give a major boost to the various initiatives relating to human resource 
development for the hospitality and tourism sector through convergence with the private 
sector.  
(Para 120) 
The Committee is of the view that there is an imperative need for the hotel 
management institutes to be updated and integrated with the hotel industry. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the complete curriculum of the hotel 
management institutes be revised. The curriculum also needs to be updated regularly to 
reflect the constantly changing dynamics of the industry in the post COVID era. 
(Para 121) 
The Committee in its 288th Report had observed that till the year 2015 -16, the 
Hunar Se Rozgar Tak Programme was geared only towards the creation of employable 
skills. However, with the adoption of Common Norms on Skill Development notified by 
the Ministry of Skill development and Entrepreneurship, it has been made mandatory 
on the part of the Training Provider Institutes to arrange placement/self-employment for 
at least 70% of the certified trainees within three months of completion of the course." 
The Committee would like to be updated whether the implementing agencies have 
adjusted to thi s provision. The Committee also desires to be apprised of the Training 
Service Provider Institutes who have lagged behind the targets set in this regard. The 
Committee also recommends that the Ministry should closely put in place an intensive 
monitoring me chanism for fulfilment of the norms stipulated by the Ministry of Skill 
Development and Entrepreneurship. 
(Para 122) 
The Committee notes that a number of programmes like Hunar Se Rozgar Tak, 
Skill Testing and Certification, Entrepreneurship Programmes, Tou rism Adventure 
Courses, etc., have been launched under the Scheme of Capacity Building for Service 

 
81 
 
Providers to provide education, training and certification to the tourism service 
providers. Though the Ministry have supplied the information regarding the number of 
persons trained and certified under the programmes of Capacity Building for Service 
Providers, it has not furnished the annual targets fixed and the actual achievement made 
in respect thereof under the scheme of Capacity Building for Service Prov iders in 2021-
22. The Committee, therefore, desires to be apprised of the achievements made vis -à-vis 
the targets fixed, programme-wise, under the CBSP in 2021-22. 
(Para 123) 
 
XI. ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES FOR TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE 
DEVELOPMENT 
The Committee observes that the creation of tourism infrastructure by way of 
roads, cruise terminals, railway connectivity, and medical facilities has its multiplier 
effect in terms of overall economic growth and employment generation and acts as a 
catalyst to economic development of the country. Under the Scheme, "Assistance to 
Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development", a total of Rs. 62.85 crores 
has been released to various Central Agencies for creation of tourism related 
infrastructure. T o make an assessment of the success of this Scheme, the Committee 
desires to be furnished with the total number of projects sanctioned and taken up for 
implementation, along with the released amount vis -à-vis the sanctioned budget during 
the last 5 years, year-wise.  
(Para 125) 
The Committee observes that easy access to tourism destinations and facilities for 
easy movement within the destinations are prerequisites for the development of tourism. 
However, road connectivity has been one of the impediments for the growth of tourism 
in India. It is in this context that the list of 50 Tourist Destinations submitted by the 
Ministry of Tourism to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways assume 
significance. The Committee notes that out of the 50 destinations selected for road 
connectivity, 23 destinations fall under the purview of Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways/NHAI where the work is going on. However, no forward movement seems to 
have been made as regards road connectivity to the remaining 27 tourist sites which are 
under the  purview of the State Governments. Though the Ministry of Tourism have 

 
82 
 
taken up the matter with the concerned State Governments, it has not had the desired 
result. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should once 
again take up this matter at the highest level with the concerned State Governments and 
impress upon them that better connectivity to the tourist sites will unlock more tourism 
opportunities for the State and the economic benefits will flow into their economy in the 
shape of increased State revenues and employment as road connectivity is one of the 
fundamental components for successfully developing tourism market. The Committee 
desires to be apprised of the efforts made in this regard and the outcome thereof. 
(Para 127) 
The Committee notes that Ministry of Tourism has shared with the Ministry of 
Road Transport and Highways a new list of 114 destinations for improving connectivity 
to these destinations. Good road, railway or air connectivity to tourist destinations is of 
paramount importance to attract domestic as well as foreign tourists because when these 
destinations are well connected, entrepreneurs in hospitality sector, tour and travel 
operators become confident of making investments and promoting these destinations. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that a dedicated mechanism be put in place for 
planning, coordination and completion of the road connectivity projects to the 114 
tourist destinations. 
(Para 128) 
The Committee observes that last mile connectivity to se veral tourist 
destinations is a deterrent to promotion of tourism. Since last mile connectivity is a key 
driver for promotion of tourism, the Committee recommends that while preparing 
Master Plan for connectivity to tourist destinations, last mile connecti vity should 
mandatorily be included in the concept and the Detailed Project Report. 
(Para 129) 
There is lack of good wayside amenities including toilets at several tourist 
destinations which causes inconvenience to tourists and discourages them from visiti ng 
such places. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should focus more 
on the improvement of wayside amenities at tourist destinations to facilitate travelers. 
(Para 130) 
The Committee notes that with a view to providing enhanced amenitie s and 

 
83 
 
facilities for tourists at railway stations, 22 projects have been sanctioned by the 
Ministry of Tourism at a cost of Rs. 108.54 crores. Though more than ten years have 
elapsed since their sanction in FY 2011 -12, their full operationalization is stil l a far cry. 
The Committee is unhappy at the continuing delay in full operationalization of these 
projects and constrained to observe that the desired priority has not been accorded to 
the upgradation of facilities and amenities at the 22 railway stations selected for the 
purpose. The Committee, therefore, recommends with all the power at its command that 
concrete steps be taken to translate into reality the vision of developing top -class 
facilities at the 22 railway stations within a designated timeline. T he Committee desires 
to be kept apprised of the progress made in this regard. 
(Para 133) 
 
XII SAFE AND HONOURABLE TOURISM 
The Committee notes that 14 States have deployed tourist police in one form or 
the other. Keeping in mind the importance of safety and  security of tourists, the 
Committee in its 275th and 288th Reports presented to the Parliament on the 3rd March 
2020 and 9th March 2021 respectively, hadrecommended that the Ministry of Tourism 
should take up the matter with the remaining States. The Comm ittee is, therefore, 
dismayed to note that no further headway has been made by the remaining States 
towards creation and deployment of tourism police at major tourist destinations. Safety 
and security of the tourists are a determining factor for choosing a  destination and also 
vital for providing quality services in tourism and, therefore, the destinations must have 
an image of utmost tourist safety and security. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that Tourist police should be s et up in all important tourist 
destinations of each State/UT and should provide travelers security through a spirit of 
courtesy and friendliness. 
(Para 139) 
The Committee is aware that the tourist police system prevails in other countries 
also. The Committee would like the Ministry of Tourism to document such best practices 
from these countries and help adopt such practices in our country. The Committee 
desires to be kept apprised in this regard.  
(Para 140) 

 
84 
 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
Adventure tourism in India has a huge potential for growth as India offers the 
keen adventurers a fascinating range of thrills and activities to choose from. The 
Ministry of Tourism has issued guidelines for approval of Adventure Tourism Operators 
which is  a voluntary scheme. The Committee notes that Adventure Tourism is largely 
unorganized and unregulated. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is an urgent 
need to regularize the Adventure Tour Operators Market and promote registration of 
companies indulging in these activities on a centralized platform to increase credibility 
and enforce safety regulations.  
(Para 141)

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members to  the meeting of the Committee 
and the representatives of the Ministry of Ports, S hipping and Waterways (M/o PS&W), 
apprising them of the agenda of the meeting i.e. to  deliberate on ‘Progress made in 
implementation of Sagarmala Project.’ 
2.         Initiating the discussion, the Chairman stated that ‘Sagarmala Project’ concept was 
initially approved by the Union Cabinet in 2015 as a part of the National Perspective Plan (NPP), 
which was released by the Hon’ble Prime Minister, f or the development of India’s 7,500 km 
coastline, 14,500 km potentially navigable waterway s and maritime sector. ‘Sagarmala Project’ 
intends to enhance the capacity of major and non-ma jor ports, modernize them, strengthen port 
connectivity and evacuation infrastructure, simplif y procedures adopted in ports, promote usage 
of electronic channels for information exchange lea ding to hassle-free and seamless cargo 
movement. He asked the Secretary to apprise the Com mittee of the efforts made by the Ministry 
towards achieving port-led direct and indirect deve lopment, provision of cost-effective and 
efficient infrastructure in ports, holistic develop ment in harnessing the potential of India's 
coastline and river network and improving export co mpetitiveness. He queried about the 
challenges faced by the ports across the country in  terms of last-mile connectivity, multi-modal 
transportation, connectivity with airways, highways  and railways as envisaged in the ambitious 
Prime Minister's Gati-Shakti National Master Plan a nd measures taken thereof for their 
successful implementation. 
  
3.               It was pointed out by the Chairman  that the infrastructure plan of a country must 
seamlessly & efficiently move goods & people across  various modes of transport. However, this 
requires a coordinated approach, as roads would fee d into railway lines, which in turn would 
feed into ports, efficiently moving goods from the hinterlands to the ports. This would further 
48

 
lead to and enable the development of multiple urba n, industrial centres across India. These 
urban centres in turn, would enable balanced region al development, as multiple industrial 
clusters could sprout up across India. Both Central  as well as various state government revenues 
would be scaled up many times, enabling higher spen ding on social sectors and would have the 
spill-over effect of easing pressure on existing ur ban agglomerations, leading to a higher quality 
of life across the board. 
4.               Furthermore, while many economic z ones, industrial parks, logistics hubs and ports 
have been planned, they often fail to deliver to th eir optimal levels, owing to inefficient multi-
modal connectivity, and also due to their small siz e. The fragmented nature of decision making, 
with each department working in silos meant that a disjointed industrial network was created. 
While several issues have been sorted out, in many areas, some co-ordination issues still remain 
to be resolved and remain unconnected as well. Such  issues are responsible for the lack of scale 
in Indian manufacturing sector which coupled with r elatively inefficient logistics network has 
hampered India's global competitiveness disallowing  us to harness our complete growth 
potential. 
5.               He desired to be apprised of prepa redness of the Ministry in terms of provision of 
sustainable infrastructure to ancillary manufacturi ng clusters in port vicinity, seamless last-mile 
connectivity of ports through multi-modal transport ation, shifting movement of industrial goods 
to coastal and inland waterways, employing funding solutions for NPP and ‘Sagarmala Projects’ 
on Central, State and port level and the obstacles faced by the Ministry. 
6.         The Secretary, M/o PS&W, before making h is presentation, apprised the Committee that 
the Ministry has been working towards modernization  of ports lagging behind in terms of 
connectivity through PPP, technological development  of cargo-handling, multi-modal 
transportation to connect all ports under the PM's ‘Gati-Shakti’ programme, building energy-
49

 
efficient technology to curb waterways pollution, r egulation and operation of ports under the 
Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, planning and impr oving investment in initiatives identified 
under the Vision-2030 policy. The Committee was fur ther apprised of the Ministry’s efforts to 
achieve desired goals in  port-improvement, cargo c ost reduction, smooth and licensed cargo 
handling, maritime safety, developing coastal jetti es and fishing harbours for welfare of the 
fishermen, RORO Pax ferries for seamless transfer o f vehicles, cargo and passengers. He also 
informed the Committee of the enactment of the Majo r Port Authorities Act, 2021, the Marine 
Aids to Navigation Act, 2021 and the New Inland Vessels Act, 2021to boost the port sector. 
7.         Through his presentation the Secretary, M/oPS&W focused on the progress made in the 
‘Sagarmala Projects,’ expanding areas such as Inlan d Waterways cargo volume-growth over the 
last 5 years, coastal traffic growth of 10.2% in Indian Maritime Sector, reduction of logistic costs 
for EXIM and domestic trade, multi-modal transporta tion, monitoring of industries/ 
manufacturing centers vis-a-vis  ports, bridging skill-gap through job creation in the Indian 
maritime sector, port-led industrialization, coasta l community development, jetty/ RORO Pax 
construction in coastal and inland waterways, promo ting coastal and cruise tourism  etc. The 
Committee was apprised of the Institutional Mechani sms employed by the Ministry in 
implementation of the ‘Sagarmala Projects’ viz. Sagarmala Coordination and Steering 
Committee (SCSC) to enable coordination among vario us organizations of the government, 
National Sagarmala Apex Committee (NSAC) to guide a nd review the progress of the project, 
and State Sagarmala Committee (SSC) to oversee Stat e-level coordination over the project. The 
Committee was further apprised of the milestones ac hieved by the Ministry in completion of 181 
projects under the NPP and that the ‘Sagarmala Proj ects’ have borne fruits in the domains of last 
mile rail and road connectivity enhancement, coasta l berths fishing harbor, jetty/ Roll-on-Roll-
off (RORO) ferry construction at Major ports, holis tic development of islands/ coastal districts, 
50

 
etc. The Secretary apprised the Committee that the Ministry is pushing to ensure feasible 
implementation of projects through PPP mode and fun ding of high social impact projects with 
zero Internal Rate of Return (IRR) through Sagarmala Programme. 
8.         The Committee was also informed of the e stablishment of Technological centers/ 
institutes for Maritime and Shipbuilding research a nd training, skill development 
training,  functioning under the ‘Sagarmala Project s’ Scheme, viz. Center of Excellence in 
Maritime and Shipbuilding (CEMS), National Technolo gy Center for Ports, Waterways and 
Coasts (NTCPWC), and Center for Inland and Coastal Maritime Technology (CICMT) with the 
intent to make India a leading player in shipbuildi ng, innovative ship-designing, cryogenic cargo 
handling and renewable energy harvesting from inland waters. 
9.         The Chairman, while mentioning about the  recent Study Visit of the Committee to 
Andaman and Nicobar Islands, expressed his disappoi ntment at the lack of coordination among 
various Ministries/ Departments/ Agencies and the n eed for a master-plan thereof to tackle 
transportation issues arising in interlinking ports  with railways, airways and roadways. He also

79. While examining the Demands for Grants 1997-98, the Committee was informed 
that till the financial year 1996-97, payments made by wa)' of lease rentals for aircraft or

the exemption given under section l0(15A) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 was withdrawn.

private and public as these airlines would be required to pay a very heavy tax with the result 
the heavy burden of tax would directly affect the national exchequer also as Ind ian Airl ines 
and Air Ind ia will have to pay heavy taxes and the airlines would have to raise their f:•ir

80. The Ministry in their action taken replies had informed that the exemption 
withdrawn in the union budget for 1997-98, was later restricted only to lease agreements 
entered before 1.4.97. After this date , it implies the payment of a 48% tax by the airlines on 
the lease rentals. This will significantly discourge acquisition of new aircraft and affect th" 
viability of the sector. The Ministry has also informed that under the budget proposa l for 
1998-99 this exemption has not been provided for. The Ministry of Civil Aviation has taken 
up the matter with the Finance Minister. 
81. Tbe Committee is of the view that the exemption under section 10 (lSA) of the 
Income Ta" Act, 1961 would go a long way in improving the financial position of the Indian 
Airlines/Air India and would also be beneficial to the private airlines. The Committee, 
therefore, reiterates its e>~rlier recommendation that the proposal to withdraw this exemption 
should be reconsidered in the light of the poor health of the Indian Civil Aviation Industry.

INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Twentieth Report on  ‘Development of Tourism 
Infrastructure in the country’. 
2. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism on the subject 
on 1st November, 2021.

REPORT 
 
  India is an all year around tourist country, offering anything and everything to tourists 
from an incredible geographical diversity of lofty mountains , golden  beaches, deserts and serene  
backwaters to secluded islands , an ancient and mesmerizing cultura l history reflected in its 
myriad historical monuments including the seventh wonder of the world, the Taj Mahal, palaces 
and forts, places of interests for all religions, ancient cities, diverse art forms and lively local 
bazaars, the most diverse cuisine in the world which changes every 100 km, all of which combine 
to make India a vibrant, eclectic fusion of the traditional and the modern, the historical and the 
contemporary. Every scene evokes countless imaginations and every sight, a million more sights.  
From the northern most Jammu & Kashmir proclaimed to be ―heaven on earth‖ to the rapturously 
acclaimed ―God‘s own country‖ Kerala in the south, from the lofty peaks of the Himalayas to the 
rolling hills of the Eastern and Western Ghats, from the lush Gang etic plains to the sandy dunes 
of Rajasthan, the landscape of India is as ever-changing and diverse as its culture. 
 
“If I were to look over the whole world to find out the country most richly endowed with all the 
wealth, power, and beauty that nature can bestow – in some parts a paradise on earth – I 
should point to India.” 
~ German Philosopher Max Mueller 
 
2. There is no fall from Eden, no divide of matter and spirit in ancient Indian cosmology. 
Instead, nature flows from the Creator  as a fountain of divinit y into space and time.   India has an 
outstanding and unmatched diversity of religions, languages, and cultures. It has beautiful green 
crops, it has many rivers flowing through  its fertile soil, it has variety in flora and fauna, and it 
has the great  Himalayas as its majestic crown. The Sun plays hid e and seek in its  hill stations, 
providing relief from scorching heat.  Its western region has a potpourri of Ghats, caves while the 
southern region boasts of exquisitely carved temple architecture and beauteous beaches. India has 
something for ever yone, history buffs , spiritual seekers, adventure tourists, wildlife enthusiasts, 
tourist shoppers, luxury travelers and backpackers.   
3. Indian tourism industry contributes to around 4.7 percent of the country's GDP and 
provides employment to around 3 1.8 million of inhabitants.  By attracting a huge number of both 
foreign and domestic tourists for professional as well as holiday purpose s, the tourism industry in 
India has displayed remarkable growth. India has popularized the entire South Asia as one of the 
most spectacular tourist hotspots. International tourists bring significant income, foreign currency, 
and jobs. The more investment is there  to improve the infrastructure in the tourists  hotspots, the 

2 
more at tractive the destination will be, for both domestic and foreign  tourists. Given that the 
investment in tourism and hotel industry/ recreation facilities can mobilize the resources of the 
entire society, India‘s share in Foreign/ Inter national Tourist Arrivals at a mere 1.59% [India 
Tourism Statistics 2021] is certainly low given the huge tourist potential India has in its resources. 
It is thus evident that the vast tourism potential of India remains untapped. Foreign tourism is of 
considerable value to the I ndian Tourism and Hospitality Se ctor as is evinced by the fact that 
foreign exchange earnings from tourism in India amounted to Rs. 50,136 Crores (US$ 6.958 
Billion) in the year 2020. [Source: India Tourism Statistics, 2021].  
4. Infrastructure—both physical and soft – serves as the arteries of the industry and 
amplifies the  travel and tourism competitiveness . A country‘s tourism automatically becomes 
attractive if there are all possible alternative and reasonably priced transport and lodging facilities 
which streamlines the overall travel experience for tourists. Given that the investment in the 
tourism and hotel industry/ recreation facilities is a substantial amount requiring the mobilization 
of the resources of the entire society,  in this backdrop, the Committee decided to take up the 
subject ‗Development of Tourism Infrastructure in the country‘ for examination and report 
thereon. 
5. In this co nnection, the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Transport, Tourism and Culture heard the views of the Ministry of Tourism on the subject at  
Parliament House Annexe, New Delhi on 1 st November, 2021. Major points discussed during the 
deliberations of the Committee are:-  
(i) Tourism Infrastructure Development Schemes; 
(ii) Swadesh Darshan Scheme (SDS); 
(iii) PRASHAD Scheme; 
(iv) Assistance to Central Agencies Scheme; 
(v) Adopt a Heritage Scheme (in collaboration with Ministry of Culture and ASI); 
(vi) Development of Iconic Tourist Sites; 
(vii) Land availability and statutory clearance; 
(viii) Central Road Fund (CRF); 
(ix) Generating revenue and overall tourist satisfaction; and 
(x) Promotion and Publicity 
 
TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT SCHEMES 
6. Tourism infrastructure is the basis of tourism development and utilization of existing 
destination resources. Tourism infrastructure includes  ancillary and complementary facilities, 

3 
equipment, systems, processes, and resources necessary for functioning of every tourist 
destination, to meet the needs of the tourist and to increase their satisfaction during their stay at 
the destination. A Tourist destination is made accessible to the tourists through rail , road, air and 
port connectivity. Tourism industry st imulates investments in new infrastructure, most of which 
improves the living conditions of local residents as well as generate tourist satisfaction. 
7. The infrastructure for tourism includes basic infrastructure like airports, railways, roads, 
waterways, electricity, water supply, drainage, sewerage , solid waste disposal systems, and 
amenities like accommodation, restaurants, recreational facilities, and shopping facilities . The 
Ministry of Tourism is the nodal agency to formulate national policies and pro grammes for the 
development and promotion of tourism. Augmentation of quality tourism infrastructure 
throughout the country is a key area of functioning of the Ministry of Tourism. More than 50% of 
the Ministry's expenditure on Plan Schemes is incurred for development of quality tourism 
infrastructure at various tourist destinations and circuits in the States/UTs. To facilitate p lanning 
for sustainable develo pment of Tourism Infrastructure  and provide basic amenities in a balanced 
manner, the Ministry of Tourism with due emphasis has launched schemes like Swadesh Darshan 
Scheme (SDS), Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage Augmentation Drive 
(PRASHAD), Adopt a Heritage Site (in collaboration with Ministry of Culture and ASI), 
Development of Iconic Tourist Sites with a goal to attract tourists from every nook and corner of 
the world towards various Indian destinations through thema tic circuits, pilgrimage sites and 
excellent amenities at the hotspots.  
 
SWADESH DARSHAN SCHEME (SDS) 
8. Envisioned to synergize with other Government of India initiatives like ‗Swachh Bharat 
Abhiyan,‘ Skill India,‘ ‗Make in India‘ etc., the Ministry launched the Swadesh Darshan Scheme 
(SDS) in January, 2015 with objectives to: 
 Position tourism as a major engine of economic growth and job creation;  
 Develop circuits having tourist potential in a planned and prioritized manner;  
 Promote cultural and heritage value of the country to generate livelih oods in the identified 
regions; 
 Enhance the tourist attractiveness in a sustainable manner by developing world class 
infrastructure in the circuit/destinations;  
 Follow community based development and pro-poor tourism approach;  

4 
 Create awareness among the local communities about the impor tance of tourism for them in 
terms of increased income sources, improved living standards and o verall development of 
the area; 
 Create employment through active involvement of local communities; 
 Harness tourism potential for its effects in employment gener ation and economic 
development; 
 Make full use of the potential and advantages in terms of available infrastructure, national 
culture and characteristic strong points of each and every region throughout the country by 
development of theme-based circuits; and 
 Develop tourist facilitation services to enhance visitor experience/satisfaction. 
 
9. The site-wise detailed tourism infrastructure inventory is an important part of the DPR 
so as to get the idea of the existing tourism infrastructure, its adequacy and envis aged tourist flow 
in the future and the necessary action required to mitigate the infrastructure gap. Selection and 
evaluation criteria is divided into three levels based on the need  assessment and stakeholder 
interaction for SDS: 
I. Ministry of Tourism 
II. Central Agencies 
III. State Governments/ UT Administrations. 
10. Concept presentation would be made to MoT highlighting the potential, need, impact of  
the project by the agency proposing the p roject and its alignment to the Detailed Perspective Plan 
(DPP) prepared by the ministry. After in-principle approval, site evaluation would be carried out 
and Conceptual Detailed Project Report (DPR) would be prepared.

projects have been completed while 30 projects have been completed upto 80% and above. The 
various projects sanctioned under the Scheme are given at Annexure –I. The major interventions 
under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme are:-

currently under review and therefore no pro posals are under consideration.  State Governments

13. The Committee observes that infrastructure for tourism includes basic 
infrastructure components like roads, railways, airports, water, electricity, hotels etc.  The 
Committee recommends that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways and 
waterways should be part of the infrastructure planning process while preparing the 
Detailed Appraisal Report of any Tourism project.  Service roads and linkage of nearby 
places should also be included. Transport infrastructure plays a vital role in connecting 
origin and destination locations while ensuring safe, comfortable and efficient 
transportation to tourists. While evaluating trave l experiences, transport is one of the main 
factors which has a great bearing on trip satisfaction. The Committee therefore 
recommends that multi -modal transport should be envisaged while preparing DPR for 
facilitating tourism in the country.  This will no t only facilitate free flowing traffic but also 
serve to make tourist destinations more attractive and accessible. 
14. The Committee observes that in its earlier report, it had noted that only one of the 
fifteen thematic circuits under the Swadesh Darshan Sche me had been completed till that 
time and had recorded its disappointment about the slow progress in the projects under the 
Scheme. Now, since all the projects under the Scheme are being reviewed, the Committee 
urges the Ministry to complete the review in a  time bound manner so that the Scheme may 

6 
be completed without undue delay. Since the projects under the Scheme are spread 
throughout the country and involve local bodies, the Committee recommends the Ministry 
to hear the views of all stakeholders involved  or ensure that the agencies implementing the 
Scheme do so, and take due cognizance of local sentiment so that once streamlined the 
projects under the Scheme would be able to be implemented without any hindrance. The 
Committee also recommends that the yardstick to review the project should only be whether 
it would be truly effective in increasing the tourist potential of the area. 
15. The Committee also suggests that the Ministry should build a systematic approach 
towards restoration/ conservation of historic structures under the SDS Scheme as buildings 
of very rich historic background add character, distinctiveness, and a sense of identity to the 
places they belong to . The Committee desires t hat the Ministry promote heritage through 
branding and use it as a potential factor in tourism development. 
16. The Committee is of the opinion that  in order to successfully implement tourism 
infrastructural Schemes,  the state governments should carry out due diligence in 
consultation with the nodal agencies during conceptualizing the projects and ensure the 
completion of tendering process of projects in a time bound manner to enable the Ministry 
to release funds for such projects. The Committee recommends the Ministry to create a 
mechanism for proactive project monitoring and reviewing the same to avoid delays in 
implementation as per agreed schedules and in compliance with the approved DPRs.

ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES SCHEME 
27. The Scheme of ‗Assistance to Central Agencies ‘ (also called Central Financial

IT initiatives as marketing and publicizing their tourist products  so that they develop and upgrade 
basic tourism infrastructure with the aim to: 
a) Improve efficiency at Govt. of India tourist Offices and the Ministry Headquarters 
b) Improve Tourist information to tourists 
a) Improve Tourist facilitation 
28. This Scheme has 55 projects in pipeline with budgetary allocation of Rs. 629.06 Crores 
and has 19 completed projects  till date. The details o f projects sanctioned under this Scheme are

29. The responsibilities of Central Agencies will be to: 
(i) Ensure land availability for development; 
(ii) Implement Rehabilitation package in shifting dwellings or commercial units or provide 
assistance for construction of Tourist Reception Centres to house the displaced shops; 
(iii) Ensure any restoration work is done by experts/specialized agencies only.

promotion of unique solutions, provide for financially sustainable solutions, and to bring

LAND AVAILABILITY AND STATUTORY CLEARANCE  
45. Tourism development is highly dependent on the availability, quality, quantity and 
characteristics of land, and a plethora of issues like  land acquisition, encroachment,  use of land 
for recreation, conservation, overcrowding and disturbance of local people etc. tend to be 
magnified in developing countries like India where economic transformation and urbanization are 
rapidly going on. 
46. The Committee feels that efficient combination of sea and land accessibility is 
necessary - if not vital – to port activity and to the expansion of wider supply chain systems. 
Taking into account the  land and maritime networks  of the country , the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should focus on d eveloping port cities for lower logistics 
costs, better infrastructure, and jobs  in the Indian maritime sector . The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry take h elp of the local administration and  district authorities 
for removal of encroachments at coastline and port peripheries. 
 
CENTRAL ROAD FUND (CRF) 
47. The Central Road Fund (CRF) is used to mainta in State roads interconnecting S tates, 
railway under/over bridges, rural roads, National Highways and Waterways.  The Committee was 
informed that the process to develop highways and roads out of CRF money was ongoing process 
and some of the connectivity projects had already been undertaken by NHAI. 
48. Connectivity of tourist destinations with roads and railways decisive ly influences 
other branches of a country’s economy, without which the travel and tourism industry will 
not reach a desired place of development. The Committee expresses concern over the delay 
in formulation of master plan for roads -railway-port-air connec tivity across the country 
and desires the Ministry to set up a timeline to speed up the process. 

14 
49. The Committee feels that there is an emerging need for enhanced connectivity of 
tourist spots with road -rail-water-air, which will boost the competitiveness of  India in the 
world tourism market if proper funding and development is expedited in connectivity 
projects. 
50. The Committee is also concerned about lack of funding assistance to states in 
capacity building, which is a major hurdle in elevating India in the r anking of countries 
with maximum tourist satisfaction. 
 
GENERATING REVENUE AND OVERALL TOURIST SATISFACTION 
51. Proper revenue -generation in a developing country leads to innovation – in the 
production, services and pricing sectors, opens new gates of employment, resource sharing, 
education, empowerment of general people, improvement of political relations and 
reforming the system of food and aid distribution.  The Committee feels that identification 
and development of revenue-generating domestic tourist destinations in States is necessary. 
52. The Committee is concerned about the privately owned  culturally rich buildings, 
which are a part of Indian heritage, and therefore, recommends that an assessment and pre-
listing of such properties/ buildings be carried out and proper steps be taken towards their 
preservation. 
53. The Committee is of the view that making Tourist Information Centers accessible 
to tourists and installing signages around tourist spots will go a long way in enhancing total 
satisfaction level of the tourists, hence, it should be taken care of. 
 
PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY 
54. During the course of the oral evidences tendered in the meeting of 1st November, 2021, a 
number of issues like increasing India‘s share of global tourism market, promoting Indian tourism 
products and destinations vis -à-vis competition, functions of India Tourism Overseas Offices and 
jurisdictions covered by them, and role of  overseas diplomatic missions for promotion of Indian 
Tourism, were discussed. The Committee also deliberated upon a host of other issues like (i) 
India's low share in international tourist arrivals (ii) Measures required to be taken to tap the full 
potential of India's tourism sector and establish India as a major international tourist attraction. 
(iii) Promotion of Indian tourism in overseas markets and role and efficacy of overseas tourist 
offices and Indian Embassies and Missions in promoting Indian tou rism. (iv) Sale of miniature

replicas of historical monuments, souvenirs, and handicraft items. (v) Cleanliness and hygienic 
conditions at tourist destinations. (vi) Promotion of cruise tourism (vii) Contribution of tourism to 
India's GDP (viii) Promotion of MICE tourism (ix) Promotion of brand "Incredible India" in 
source markets. (x) Strengthening of India's role in various multi -lateral and bilateral forum. (xi) 
Partnership with SAARC and ASEAN countries to promote Buddhist circuit, Ramayana Circuit, 
Himalayan Circuit, etc. (xii) Industry -to-Industry partnerships in foreign countries to promote 
tourism fairs, exhibitions, and advertising campaigns. (xiii) Production and distribution of 
publicity material (xiv) Focus on 3-Ts, i.e., Trade, Tourism and Technology to boost tourism, etc.  
55. Based on scrutiny of the submissions made by way of Background Note and Oral 
Evidences tendered, the Committee makes the following recommendations: 
56. The Committee observes that m odern tourism industry is a key driver of socio -
economic growth through creation of jobs, infrastructure development, and the export 
revenues earned because it has potential to stimulate other sectors through its backward 
and forward linkages and cross -sectoral synergies with airlines, transport, basic 
infrastructure like hotels, guides, road connectivity , agriculture, handicrafts etc.  The 
Committee notes that despite the fact that India offers a diverse portfolio for travel, tourism 
and hospitality, the s hare of its International tourist Arrivals (ITAs) is merely 1.59% in 
2021. With the obvious that there is an increased competition among various countries to 
attract more foreign visitors, it is an imperative need for India to prepare a better 
marketing strategy by hiring marketing experts to attract foreign visitors.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should formulate an integrated marketing and 
promotional strategy in collaboration with a professional body to carry out market research 
to identify expectations, requirements, psychographics, demographics and many other 
aspects of a foreign tourist willing to travel to India, thereby enabling to create a strategic 
plan to revive the pandemic-hit tourism sector. The Committee feels that one of the effective 
steps in this direction would be re -casting the website of the Ministry in an attractive and 
user-friendly manner. 
57. Since seaports are the wealth generators of a country and the beauty of landscape 
just increases during Monsoon season, the  Committee is of the view that promoting Seaport 
tourism, Cruise tourism and Monsoon tourism will give a boost to the Indian tourism 
industry.   The Committee also is of the opinion that there is tremendous scope for 
popularizing seaplane services especially among the more affluent travelers who may prefer 
to avoid crowded airport terminals and among adventure tourists.  Seaplane services will 
benefit travelers by providing air connectivity to numerous remote, religious places and 
unexplored places adjacent to water bodies.  

16 
58. The Committee finds that hearing about a place that has never been explored 
before generates a sense of awe and curiosity am ong foreign and domestic travelers alike, 
pulling them towards that place. Curiosity plays a c rucial role in shaping attitude, 
motivation and influencing tourist loyalty. In order to magnify the role of curiosity and 
boost tourism market, the Committee rec ommends that various unexplored/ lesser -known 
tourist spots may be added/ highlighted on the homepage of the Ministry’s website portal to 
attract more tourists to such places. 
59. Tourism Police: The Committee notes that Safety and security of the tourists bot h 
domestic and foreign are paramount importance for projecting the country as a safe haven 
for tourism. There are occasional reports of incidents of misbehaviour, cheating, 
malpractices etc. at various tourist places. This gives a bad publicity for that pa rticular 
tourist destination and the country as a whole. Therefore, it is essential that the Government 
should take all the available measures to provide a safe environment for the tourists. The 
Committee therefore recommends that in every tourist place, t here should be a provision 
for tourism police, as a separate wing of the police force to provide safety and security to the 
tourists. The Committee is fully aware that law and order is a part of the State subject. 
Therefore, the Ministry of Home Affairs should issue an advisory to all the State 
Governments to create tourism police in their State to provide safety and security to the 
tourists in tourist destinations. The Ministry of Tourism should also take up the matter with 
all the State Governments for creation of separate tourism police in their respective States. 
The Committee may be apprised of the action taken by the  Ministry of Home Affairs and 
the Ministry of Tourism and the feedback received from the State Governments  in this 
regard.

RECOMMENDATIONS/ OBSERVATIONS AT A GLANCE 
 
SWADESH DARSHAN SCHEME (SDS) 
 The Committee observes that infrastructure for tourism includes basic 
infrastructure components like roads, railways, airports, water, electricity, hotels etc.  The 
Committee recommends that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways and 
waterways should be part of the infrastructure planning process while preparing the 
Detailed Appraisal Report of any Tourism project. Service roads and linkage of  nearby 
places should also be included. Transport infrastructure plays a vital role in connecting 
origin and destination locations while ensuring safe, comfortable and efficient 
transportation to tourists. While evaluating travel experiences, transport is one of the main 
factors which has a great bearing on trip satisfaction. The Committee therefore 
recommends that multi -modal transport should be envisaged while preparing DPR for 
facilitating tourism in the country.  This will not only facilitate free flowi ng traffic but also 
serve to make tourist destinations more attractive and accessible. 
(Para 13) 
The Committee observes that in its earlier report, it had noted that only one of the 
fifteen thematic circuits under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme had been comple ted till that 
time and had recorded its disappointment about the slow progress in the projects under the 
Scheme. Now, since all the projects under the Scheme are being reviewed, the Committee 
urges the Ministry to complete the review in a time bound manner  so that the Scheme may 
be completed without undue delay. Since the projects under the Scheme are spread 
throughout the country and involve local bodies, the Committee recommends the Ministry 
to hear the views of all stakeholders involved or ensure that th e agencies implementing the 
Scheme do so, and take due cognizance of local sentiment so that once streamlined the 
projects under the Scheme would be able to be implemented without any hindrance. The 
Committee also recommends that the yardstick to review the project should only be whether 
it would be truly effective in increasing the tourist potential of the area.  
(Para 14) 
The Committee also suggests that the Ministry should build a systematic approach 
towards restoration/ conservation of historic structur es under the SDS Scheme as buildings 
of very rich historic background add character, distinctiveness, and a sense of identity to the 
places they belong to. The Committee desires that the Ministry promote heritage through 
branding and use it as a potential factor in tourism development. 
(Para 15) 

18 
 
The Committee is of the opinion that in order to successfully implement tourism 
infrastructural Schemes, the state governments should carry out due diligence in 
consultation with the nodal agencies during conceptua lizing the projects and ensure the 
completion of tendering process of projects in a time bound manner to enable the Ministry 
to release funds for such projects. The Committee recommends the Ministry to create a 
mechanism for proactive project monitoring an d reviewing the same to avoid delays in 
implementation as per agreed schedules and in compliance with the approved DPRs. 
(Para 16) 
PRASHAD SCHEME 
The Committee observes that religious tourism is unlike leisure tourism in as 
much that in building a religiou s tourism product, it is essential to build in community 
participation at the given location. The participation of local nodal agencies along with State 
Governments in the PRASHAD Scheme is therefore of utmost importance and the Ministry 
should endeavour t o make all efforts to ensure their involvement and not leave it to the 
responsibility of the State Governments alone.  
(Para 21) 
The Committee is of the view religious tourists come from all economic strata and 
there is enormous need for hotels especially in the Budget and Economy categories. The 
Committee is also of the opinion that local families willing to provide homemade food and 
homestay facilities in their abodes to the tourists should be identified and given training by 
the Ministry in handling the process to promote local Indian cuisine among foreign tourists 
and at international level. The Committee is sanguine that such a novel step will unlock job 
opportunities for Indian families and generate resources for huge revenue potential in the 
Indian tourism sector. 
(Para 22) 
The Committee recommends that improvement of reception/ facilitation center for 
tourists be done with the help of travel agencies and local businesses promoting their 
products and hotel-booking tickets at lowest prices. 
(Para 23) 
The Committee is of the opinion that the rejuvenation of natural water bodies 
under the PRASHAD Scheme and building them as tourist hubs available on cheaper 
tickets will attract tourists searching for a tranquil beach -like affordable and less crowded 
environment, which will greatly benefit the Indian tourism industry and promote 
sustainable growth as well.  

19 
(Para 24) 
The Committee desires that the Ministry should reinforce sustainable 
development in Indian tourism sector through the PRASHAD Scheme by transitioning to 
the use of renewable energy features such as photovoltaic electricity, waste water re -use and 
rainwater recovery, which not only will reduce the environmental impacts, but also generate 
benefits for local communities. 
(Para 25) 
The Committ ee is of the view that approach to these destinations should be 
strengthened by proper roads, transport facilities, ticket booking facilities, lodging and 
other logistic support like reception centers etc. The role of states becomes very crucial in 
this aspect. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should play a proactive role to 
provide such facilities so as to attract tourists from every nook and corner of the world. 
(Para 26) 
ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES SCHEME 
The holistic development of tourism infrastructure at all tourist destinations 
through Central Financial Assistance to the States/ UTs may require convergence of 
resources, expertise and experience for maintenance and management after development 
since many of them are under the jurisdiction s of Central Agencies like ASI, Port Trusts in 
India, ITDC etc. and the overall development of places of tourist interest under their control 
may not be possible through their own resources. In order to remove these bottlenecks, the 
Committee suggests the Ministry to devise mechanisms to build infrastructure with the 
assistance of state governments and other agencies to bring a world standard spot with all 
the amenities. 
(Para 31) 
The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry is facilitating developmen t of 
lighthouses as tourist hotspots to provide panoramic view of scenic coastline and marking 
historic importance of their times through developing museums, open -air amphitheatres, 
cafeteria, children’s parks, and gardens in or around the lighthouses. 
(Para 32) 
ADOPT A HERITAGE SCHEME (in collaboration with Ministry of Culture and ASI) 
The Committee observes that the Ministry, with the assistance of business houses 
under the CSR, should build public amenities like public toilets, drinking water facility, ease 
of access for differently -abled citizens, standardized signage, surveillance system, night 
viewing facilities etc. in order to increase tourist footfall in the country. 
(Para 37)
