Training of Officers of Commission 
33. The Committee  was informed by CRS that  technology available with Railways is 
upgrading very fast and high speed trains, Rapid transport system etc. are being introduced  and 
officials of the Commission inspect and sanction all such systems.  Hence, upgradation of 
technical knowledge of the Commis sion officials is very essential. In the past, Railways was 
requested to include officers from the Commission for training along with the Railway officers 
on regular basis so that both Railways and Commission are on the same platform. However, 
Railways are  not institutionalizing the inclusion of Commission officials in their periodic and 
specialised training programs. Even mandatory training is not imparted to officials of 
Commission, who are on deputation from MoR. 
 
34. Committee fails to understand the lo gic of MoR behind the non -inclusion of officers 
from the Commission for training along with the Railway officers on regular basis so that 
both Railways and Commission are on the same platform  as regards technological 
advancements. The Committee recommends that immediate steps may be taken to train the 
officials of Commission including the deputationists along with the officials of the MoR and 
the training imparted should be of a global level. The Committee feels that there is a 
genuine need of the officers of Commission of Railway Safety to get exposed to the latest 
technological advancements taking place in the railway sector in India and abroad , 
otherwise there is a real danger that the technical knowledge of the officers of the 
Commission will be obsolete and they may not be able to perform their assigned duties at 
the optimum level. The Committee recommends that the officers of the Commission should 
be exposed to latest global technologies and any new technology introduced by the 
Railways through training s in the country and abroad, so that they are in a position to 
perform their role effectively.

the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety, where the matters can be discussed threadbare 
and agreements reached. While expressing their inability to accept the recommendations, 
the Railway Boa rd should invariably give detailed reasons for not accepting the 
recommendations. 
(Para 32) 
Training of Officers of Commission 
Committee fails to understand the logic of MoR behind the non -inclusion of officers from 
the Commission for training along with the Railway officers on regular basis so that both 
Railways and Commission are on the same platform as regards technological 
advancements. The Committee recommends that immediate steps may be taken to train the 
officials of Commission including the deputationists along with the officials of the MoR and 
the training imparted should be of a global level. The Committee feels that there is a 
genuine need of the officers of Commission of Railway Safety to get exposed to the latest 
technological advancements taking place in the railway sector in India and abroad, 
otherwise there is a real danger that the technical knowledge of the officers of the 
Commission will be obsolete and they may not be able to perform th eir assigned duties at 
the optimum level. The Committee recommends that the officers of the Commission should 
be exposed to latest global technologies and any new technology introduced by the 
Railways through trainings in the country and abroad, so that th ey are in a position to 
perform their role effectively.  
(Para 34) 
 

25 
 
Upgradation of post of CCRS and requirement of separate Secretariat for Commission 
The Committee appreciates the upgradation of the post of CCRS to Apex level of pay 
matrix of 7th CPC. The Committee is of the opinion that such a step will enhance the status 
of the Commission, keeping in view its important responsibility to ensure overall safety of 
Indian Railways. It would result in attracting the best available technical talent in the 
country to the Commission. The Committee also recommends that a separate Secretariat 
may be provided to the Commission to assist the CCRS in expeditious settlement of its 
work. 
(Para 36) 
The Committee notes that CCRS is working under the Administrative control  of Ministry 
of Civil Aviation.  The Committee recommends that the Commission of Railway Safety 
may be made an independent autonomous body just like many other regulatory institutions 
of the country to improve efficiency and freedom of action. 
(Para 37) 
Consequential Train Accidents 
The Committee appreciates the Railway Board for the reduction of consequential train 
accidents from 2010 -11 to 2022 -23.  The Committee also congratulates the RDSO for the 
development of indigenous Train Collision Avoidance Sys tem ‘KAVACH’, which will go a 
long way in reducing accidents through a cost -effective measure. The Committee 
recommends that KAVACH should be introduced phase -wise, through all the routes of 
India Railways. In first phase, all the routes where there are re gular cases of accidents 
should be considered and KAVACH should be installed expeditiously.  
(Para 41) 
Unmanned Level Crossings (UMLCs) 
The Committee notes the progress in elimination of such crossings by constructing RUBs 
and ROBs and hopes that the work would be expedited to eliminate all such crossings in 
near future. The Committee also hopes that sufficient budgetary allocation may be made 
for the said purpose.  The Committee also recommends that a mechanism should be 
devised to complete the construction of ROBs and RUBs in a stipulated period and in case 
of a delay, the concerned agency should be penalized.  

26 
 
(Para 44) 
Miscellaneous Safety Issues 
The Committee observes that during train accidents, the loss of life and property can be 
minimized if the Rail coaches are as per global safety standards. The Committee 
recommends that technology matching global standards should be adopted so as  to 
introduce global standards of safety for Indian Railway coaches. A railway station, a coach 
manufacturing factory/workshop and a stretch of railway track may be selected and bids 
may be invited from leading global agencies across the world for implemen tation of the 
global best standards, which may then serve as a model for other railway stations/railway 
coach factories/railway tracks across the country.  
(Para 45) 
While appreciating the efforts made by Railways and Railway Protection Force to save 
numerous lives, the Committee  recommends that urgent steps need to be taken to 
minimize the unfortunate incidents of people, especially women and children, falling on 
tracks and getting seriously injured/ killed. It should be ensured that Railway Police has 
safety training for undertaking on -the-spot rescue measures. The Committee emphasizes 
the need for delegation of powers to lower level officials also in order to enable swift action 
for addressing safety risks in Railways. The Committee also recommends that a Safety 
Task Force may be constituted in every State to respond to emergencies and that it should 
consist of young and robust personnel who have been given the necessary training and 
exposure to international best practices. The Committee feels that anoth er important 
requirement is the need to ensure that immediate and prompt help is rendered to accident 
victims. The Committee is underscoring this fact because there have been instances 
wherein railway accident victims were stuck inside boggies for hours, w ithout getting any 
help. Hence, detailed evacuation plan, in coordination with different agencies, should be 
put in place. A comprehensive safety Master Plan for improvement of safety and security 
standards in railways may be worked out and implemented in a time -bound manner. It 
should be ensured that International Organization for Standardization (ISO) Safety Audits 
are conducted periodically for all the institutions under the Ministry.  
(Para 48) 
 

27 
 
The Committee further noted the dilapidated condition of m any railway quarters across 
the country which requires urgent attention, since it is a big safety risk to the residents. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that all such railway quarters may be repaired at the 
earliest and sufficient funds may be provide d for the purpose.  Besides many Railway 
stations and goods sheds are located in congested areas, sometimes leading to accidents 
during transportation of goods by lorries. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
steps may be taken to relocate the goods sheds to safer places in order to prevent accidents. 
(Para 49)

REPORT 
India has a glorious and diverse cultural history which is beautifully showcased by the 
multitudinous historical monuments spread across the country representing its tangible cultural 
heritage. These historical monuments are a living reminder of the past a nd the guardian pillars of 
India‟s cultural splendour.  India ranks sixth in the world with 40 UNESCO World Heritage Sites 
of which 32 are cultural sites. India‟s heritage sites are an amalgamation of different styles and 
influences of various dynasties, r eligions, traditions and customs and vary from rock cut 
architecture, temple architecture, tombs, forts, palaces, minars, stupas to the monument 
complexes at Hampi, Mahabulipuram and Khajuraho.  The range and diversity of India‟s 
tangible cultural heritage is truly mind-boggling.  
2. Historical monuments act as the focal point of attraction for tourists, both domestic and 
international, and thus directly contribute to the economic growth of the country. However, while 
the iconic Taj Mahal, the Red Fort, the Qutub Minar, Fatehpur Sikri, the Ajanta and Ellora caves,  
Konark Sun Temple, Hawa Mahal, and other such renowned monuments are on every tourist‟s 
bucket list,  there are countless equally stunning masterpieces of great historical importance and 
cultural significance which languish in obscurity with even locals being unaware of their 
importance and sadly in some cases, even their existence.  As such, it is of paramount 
importance to ensure the protection of historical monuments across the country and the s ame is 
also reflected in Article 49 of the Constitution of India which states the following: 
Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance.— 
It shall be the obligation of the State to protect every monument or place or object 
of artistic or historic interest, 1[declared by or under law made by Parliament] to 
be of national importance, from spoliation, disfigurement, destruction, removal, 
disposal or export, as the case may be. 
3. Given the importance of preserving historical monument s across the country, it is a 
matter of grave concern that several Monuments of National Importance under the protection of 
Archaeological Survey of India (Ministry of Culture) have become untraceable over the years  
due to rapid urbanization, submerged by reservoirs, dams, difficulties in tracing in remote 
locations, dense forests, non-availability of their proper location etc. Besides, the present state of 
                                                
1 Subs. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 27, for ―declared by parliament by law‖ (w.e.f. 1-11-1956). 

2 
preservation and protection of even the more famous and better maintained historical monuments 
in the country often leaves much to be desired. These relics and guardians of our glorious history 
which for centuries have withstood invasions, battles, bloodshed, destruction and the vagaries of 
climate are now falling victim to pollution, negligence, apathy a nd encroachments. It is in this 
backdrop that the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism 
and Culture decided to take up the subject „Issues relating to Untraceable Monuments and 
Protection of Monuments in India‟ for detailed examination and Report thereon. 
4. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Culture; Director General, 
Archaeological Survey of India; and other senior officials of ASI on the subject in its meeting 
held on 18th May, 2022. 
5. The primary mandate of Ministry of Culture is preservation and conservation of ancient 
cultural heritage and promotion of tangible and intangible art and culture. The Ministry manages 
all the Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs) of national importance, through  the 
Archaeological Survey of India. The Ministry, in its written reply furnished to the Committee, 
informed that there are 3693 Centrally Protected Monuments and 4508 State Protected 
Monuments in the country. (Annexure-A) 
6. Established in 1861 and an att ached office of the Ministry of Culture, the Archaeological 
Survey of India (ASI) is engaged in protection, preservation and conservation of 3693 Centrally 
Protected Monuments/Sites of national importance including 24 World Heritage Property, 52 site 
museums on site, spread all over India which are directly under the ASI. The excavations of 
archaeological sites in the country are permitted in accordance with the Ancient Monuments and 
Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. 
7. The Ministry, in its backgr ound note on the subject, stated that the CAG in its 2013 
Report on “Performance Audit of Preservation and Conservation of Monuments and Antiquities” 
submitted to Parliament on 23.8.2013 had reported that 92 monuments are missing. However, 
vigorous efforts to locate/identify the reportedly untraceable monuments based on verification of 
old records, revenue maps and referring published reports were carried out by the respective field 
offices of Archaeological Survey of India. The exercise gave fruitful resul ts and many 
monuments were traced out. The status of these 92 monuments/sites is as below: 

3 
Number of monuments/sites which physically exist: 42 
Number of monuments/sites affected due to rapid urbanization: 14 
Number of monuments/sites exist submerged under reservoir/dam: 12 
Number of monuments/sites which are untraceable: 24 
8. The list of 24 untraceable monuments is placed at Annexure -B.  The Ministry stated that 
information about these 24 untraceable monuments was provided to the Parliament in reply to 
Lok Sabha Unstarred Question  No. 5913 answered on 10.4.2017.  The Ministry further informed 
that the untraceable monuments were the protected monuments, under the ASI, whose exact 
location and condition could not be determined and that this situati on arose because of various 
factors, such as rapid urbanization, non -availability of proper details about their location in the 
gazette notification, difficulties in tracing in remote locations, dense forests, etc. Such 
monuments which could not be traced on ground for a considerable time because of multiple 
factors, despite the strenuous efforts of ASI through its field offices, were referred as 
Untraceable monuments. The Ministry further stated that the chances of tracing such monuments 
with the help of s cientific tools and archival records cannot be ruled out.  Furt her, field 
explorations and periodic surveys are being conducted from time to time by the field offices of 
ASI and with the help of old revenue records, revenue maps and published reports, thes e 
monuments may also be traced out. Section 35 of the AMASR Act, 1958 has the provision to 
issue notification for such monuments which has ceased to be of national importance. However, 
this exercise of removing these 24 untraceable monuments has not been i nitiated by the ASI as 
there are chances that some of these monuments can be traced out in near future. 
9. The Committee observes that the performance audit of the CAG had included a 
joint physical inspection, along with ASI, of 1655 monuments and sites out of the 3678 
CPMs and sites spread nationwide.  The 24 monuments which are reported to be 
untraceable are from this sample of 1655 monuments.  The Committee has perused the list 
of 24 untraceable monuments submitted by the Ministry and it is perturbed to find that the 
Barakhamba Cemetery in the very heart of the Capital city is among the untraceable 

4 
monuments.  If even monuments in the Capital city cannot be maintained properly, it does 
not bode well for monuments in remote places in the country. Upon query of the 
Committee, the Ministry has informed that no further study of the remaining monuments 
has been undertaken for ascertaining how many more monuments are missi ng from the 
total number of 3693  CPMs.  The Committee is perturbed to note that having found out 
that at leas t 24 monuments are untraceable out of the sample of monuments studied, no 
further surveys were conducted for the remaining monuments, even nearly a decade after 
the original study.   
10. The Committee acknowledges the steps taken by ASI to retrace the monu ments that 
were deemed to be missing by CAG in its 2013 Performance Audit but feels that the same 
reflects at the questionable state of protection and preservation of monuments, with ASI 
being unaware of the physical untraceability of several of the Centra lly Protected 
Monuments under its ambit.  The Committee recommends that the ASI immediately 
undertake a survey of the remaining CPMs which were not inspected in the CAG Audit 
survey and ascertain whether there are any other missing monuments in the country  apart 
from the 24 monuments of the original survey.   The Committee further recommends that a 
physical survey of all the Centrally Protected Monuments must mandatorily be carried out 
by ASI from time to time as per a fixed time schedule. Digital log books may be maintained 
which may contain  textual and photographic/video record of the state of physical 
preservation of the monument, exact location coordinates and clearly demarcated 
prohibited and regulated areas in the vicinity of the monument. These digita l records may 
be made easily accessible to the general public to avoid any ambiguities and details may 
also be published regarding the date on which the last survey was conducted, due date for 
the next survey and the contact details of the ASI officials in -charge of maintaining and 
protecting the monument.   
11. The Committee further notes that out of the 92 monuments declared “missing” by 
the CAG, 42 monuments have been identified due to efforts made by the ASI and out of the 
remaining 50 monuments, 14 are  affected by rapid urbanisation, 12 are submerged by 
reservoir/dams while the location of the remaining 24 is untraceable.  The Committee feels 
that the distinction made by the Ministry regarding the monuments lost to 
urbanisation/reservoirs and 24 monumen ts which are untraceable is an academic 
distinction since monuments lost to urbanisation/reservoirs are as irrecoverable as the ones 

5 
which are presently untraceable with scant hop e of being found in future.  Moreover, the 
fact that the ASI had been unable to prevent the loss of the 14 monuments to urbanisation 
and 12 to reservoirs/dams and only located them after the study by CAG suggests that the 
ASI had no cognisance of these mon uments prior to the study. The number of monuments 
lost from public viewing must therefore be held to be 50 taking into account those lost to 
urbanisation or reservoirs.  The ASI has assured that the remaining 42 of the 92 
monuments exist physically but th e Committee would like to know whether these 
monuments exist in their entirety and undamaged or whether the ASI has only managed to 
locate some remains and ruins of such monuments.   
12. The Ministry has stated that there is no term called ―Missing Monumen ts‖ in the 
AMASR Act and the term only came into existence as it was used by the Audit team on 
their Report. The  Committee opines that the AMASR Act provides for the preservation 
and protection of ancient historical monuments and it would have been inconsi stent to 
include the concept of ―Missing Monuments‖ in the Act.  That the situation warrants the 
use of such phrases only serves to underline the apathy of the Ministry and ASI regarding 
the preservation of our historical monuments.  The Ministry has also stated that the 
exercise of removing the untraceable monuments under Section 35 of the AMASR Act has 
not been initiated by the ASI as there are chances that some of these monuments shall be 
traced out in near future. The Committee observes that Section 35 of the AMASR Act, 
1958 has the provision to issue notification only for such CPMs which have as per the 
opinion of the Central Government have ceased to be of national importance. The 
monuments which have become ―untraceable‖ have become so due to official apathy and 
may not have ceased to be of national importance had they been existing.  The situation of a 
―Missing Monument‖ cannot be automatically equated with loss of its histori cal 
importance.  The Committee recommends that the Untraceable Monuments may not be 
removed from the list of Centrally Protected Monuments by taking recourse to Section 35 
as that Section provides the exclusion only of such monuments which have in the opin ion of 
the Central Government ceased to be of national importance.   In  fact, there is the danger 
that in case of such removal, there would be no imperative to find the untraceable 
monument and it would be well and truly lost to posterity. Since untraceabl e monuments 
also cannot continue to be on the Protected list, the Committee recommends that the list of 

6 
Untraceable Monuments may be maintained as such and if necessary, the AMASR Act may 
be amended to include this terminology.   
13. The Committee observes  that the CAG audit had pointed out that the Ministry 
through the ASI had not conducted a comprehensive survey/review to identify monuments 
which were of national importance for inclusion in the list of CPMs.  Similarly, there were 
no efforts to identify t hose monuments which had lost the stature of national importance 
over a period of time.  The Committee is dismayed to note that even a decade after the 
CAG Audit Report,  the Ministry and the ASI are yet to conduct a comprehensive survey 
to identify monume nts which are of national importance or of those which had lost their 
stature of national importance. The Committee urges the Ministry and ASI to conduct 
surveys to include monuments of national importance and also those which have lost their 
importance over time.  This would ensure that the resources of the Ministry and ASI are 
utilised  in a justified manner for deserving monuments  and are not diverted to protecting 
those which are no longer of national importance.  
14. The Committee further recommends t hat the Ministry of Culture and ASI should 
undertake a survey of all the 3693 Centrally Protected Monuments to ensure that they are 
in existence and to provide adequate maintenance and protection.  
15. The Committee enquired from the Ministry regarding the steps taken by the Ministry/ASI 
to ensure that more monuments do not go missing in the future. In its written reply, the Ministry 
informed the Committee that the provisions of AMASR Act and Rules are being implemented so 
that no illegal construction or en croachment takes place near the monument/site of national 
importance. Apart from this, round-the-clock watch and ward by security personnel, both private 
and CISF and ASI staff, are being provided at the monuments and sites. Further, periodic 
inspection shall also be carried out.  
16. In the meeting of the Committee held on the subject on 18 th May, 2022, the Secretary, 
Ministry of Culture informed that the Ministry is in the process of coming up with an amendment 
to the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and that detailed 
consultations are being held with about 15 Ministries and State Governments. He informed the 
Committee that one of the changes being brought through this amendment is to remove the limit 
of 100 meters and 200 meters as prohibited and regulated area for all CPMs and have monument-

7 
wise limits instead, depending on the historical, cultural importance, geographic location of the 
monument, etc. 
17. The Committee feels that a thorough review of the AMASR Act in consul tation with 
all stakeholders and State Governments, is the need of the hour. The Committee, therefore, 
appreciates the process initiated by the Ministry of Culture to amend the AMASR Act. The 
Committee agrees with the view that having the same limits for a ll monuments for 
prohibited area and regulated area for restricting/regulating construction -related activities 
near the monument, is not a practical approach as the requirement for such limitations 
could vary a lot depending on various factors specific to each monument. The Committee, 
therefore, feels that the upcoming amendment which provides for such monument -specific 
prohibited and regulated areas is much needed and hopes that once the amendment is 
passed, all necessary steps are taken to ensure that the  monument-specific limits are 
decided upon for each Centrally Protected Monument at the earliest.  The Committee notes 
that the ASI would be surveying all 3693 monuments while delineating monument specific 
protected and regulated limits and desires that a R eport of the survey may be submitted to 
the Committee. However, the provisions of the Act may be strictly adhered to in terms of 
the prohibited areas around the monument and even Government officials violating the 
provisions should be prosecuted. 
18. The Committee reiterates the following recommendation made in para 39 of its 
311th Report on ‗Creation of Regulatory Framework for protection of Historical Sites and 
Monuments‘:  
The Committee fails to see why a person living in the Regulated Area of a CPM sho uld 
be required to seek permission from the Competent Authority under the AMASR Rules 
for carrying out innocuous maintenance activities such as filling of cracks, 
whitewashing, replacement of windows etc. The Committee feels that such uncalled -for 
interference makes lives harder for people living nearby the monuments and could 
slowly cause feelings of anguish towards the monument itself. Given the large number 
of monuments across the country and the limited budgetary resources available with 
the Government,  it is pertinent that people residing near the monuments are 
encouraged to look after the monuments and protect them. Besides, placing such 
unnecessary curbs and implementing them is a wastage of limited Government 

8 
resources and turns the focus away from w here it should be - actually protecting and 
preserving the monument itself. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may undertake a thorough review of the AMASR Act and Rules and omit any 
provisions that provide for seeking permissions for m inor works where the same is not 
actually needed and streamline the process for applying for permission in case where 
the same is actually needed. Steps may urgently be taken to make it possible for the 
entire process for seeking permission for constructio n activities in prohibited and 
regulated areas, to be completed online so as to not cause any hassle to bona fide 
residents living near the monuments. 
Assessment of security requirements at Centrally Protected Monuments 
19. The Committee sought to know from the Ministry, details regarding any audit conducted 
to gauge the requirements for security guards and CCTV cameras etc. at Centrally Protected 
Monuments across the country and the budgetary requirements/budget shortfall for posting the 
required number  of security guards at Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs) across the 
country.  The Ministry, in its written reply, informed the Committee that a meeting chaired by 
the Director General, ASI on 06.12.2021 on enhancement of security surveillance of Central ly 
Protected Monument s under ASI was held with IIT, Delhi. Pursuant to this, the Security 
Assessment for Centrally Protected Monuments is being done in collaboration with Indian 
Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi. It was further stated that the deploymen t of security guards, 
surveillance, budgetary requirements etc. shall be reviewed for implementation once the report 
submitted by IIT, Delh i. The Ministry also informed that prior to the meeting with IIT, Delhi, a 
Committee under the Chairmanship of Additi onal Secretary (Culture) had also assessed the 
details of security arrangements in ASI during a meeting held on 21.07.2014. 
20. With regard to a query made by the Committee regarding the number of Centrally 
Protected Monuments where security guards are pos ted and the number of such monuments 
where no security personnel is present, the Ministry informed the Committee that t he Security 
requirement of ASI Monuments, Sites and museums was reviewed by the Committee chaired by 
AS(C) and based on this Committee‟s recommendation a requirement of approximately 7,000 
personnel was worked out for providing security at all monuments and sites.   The security 
personnels are deployed at 248 locations i.e. monuments/sites/museums.  The requirement was 
restricted to 2578 Se curity Personnel due to budgetary constraints. In addition to above, 596 

9 
CISF personnel (317 at Red Fort, Delhi and 279 at Taj Mahal, Agra) have also been deployed for 
Security of above World Heritage Sites.  The deployment details of security personnel as well as 
approx monthly expenditure occurred on Security is given at Annexure-C. 
21. The Committee sought to know from the Ministry regarding the budgetary allocation for 
protection and safeguarding of Centrally Protected Monuments for the last 5 years. The  details 
furnished by the Ministry in this regard, are given at Annexure-D. 
22. The Committee is concerned to note that out of the 3693 Centrally Protected 
Monuments, securi ty guards are posted at only 248  CPMs/sites/museums i.e. less than  
about 6.7 percent of the total number of CPMs. The Committee notes with dismay that out 
of the total requirement of 7000 personnel for protection of Monuments , the Govern ment 
could provide only 2578 security personnel at 248 locations due to budgetary constraints. 
The Committee observes that budgetary constraints should not be an excuse for not 
providing security guards to protect our rich cultural heritage. It is the bounden  duty of 
the Government of the day to protect our cultural heritage sites. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that budget may be provided by the Government to appoint 7000 personnel 
for protection of the Monuments or as per the study conducted by IIT, Delhi. In view of 
this worrying state of affairs, the Committee is of the strong view that the budgetary 
allocation available with the Ministry/ASI for safeguarding our Centrally Protected 
Monuments needs a serious relook. The Committee recommends that the Ministry/ASI 
may conduct an urgent thorough assessment of the security requirements and budgetary 
allocation required for the same and a strong case may be made to the Ministry of Finance 
requesting allocation of additional funds for this purpose so as to ensure a basic st ate of 
protection for all Centrally Protected Monuments across the country to preserve them for 
generations to come. The Committee also recommends that the local Panchayats and police 
may be involved in safeguarding the monuments and if necessary, the AMAS R Act may be 
amended in this regard.  
23. It has also come to the notice of the Committee that various important historical 
monuments and sites such as Rama Temple at Peddathumbalam village, Adoni Taluka; 
Kethavaram Rock Arts and Belum Caves in Kurnool etc . which, although not under the 
list of Centrally Protected Monuments, are of high historical significance but devoid of any 
security guards and proper road connectivity. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 

10 
the Ministry may urgently make provisions f or posting security guards at these sites and 
adequate measures may be taken for promotion of tourism at the same, in coordination 
with the concerned Ministries/Departments. The Ministry of Culture may coordinate with 
the Ministry of Road Transport & Highw ays and State Public Works Department to 
ensure proper road/highway connectivity to these important historical sites in order to 
allow tourists to reach these sites. 
24. In response to a query regarding the steps taken by the Ministry/ASI to tackle 
encroachment of Centrally Protected Monuments, the Ministry, in its written reply, informed the 
Committee that as and when construction activities are noticed/reported in the 
prohibited/regulated area, the Superintending   Archaeologist issues a notice to the owner under 
rule 38 of the provisions of   the Ancient Monuments, Archaeological Sites and Remains Rules, 
1959 for   removal of unauthorized building. Simultaneously, help from the local police   is also 
sought by lodging a complaint and by registering  an FIR. On receipt of a report from the field 
office, the Director General, Archaeological Survey of India, issues a notice to the erring party in   
pursuance of sub -section 19(ii) and sub -rule 38(i) of Ancient Monuments and Archaeological 
Sites and Remai ns Act, 1958, and Rules, 1959 respectively for   removal of such unauthorized 
construction within a specified period.  A copy of the notice issued by the Director General is 
also sent to the District Collector with the request to demolish the illegal const ruction.  In this   
regard the assistance in containing and removing encroachments is sought from   the respective 
State Government and where there are no fruitful results,   action is initiated by filing cases in the 
court of law. 
25. The Committee takes note of the existing framework and recommends that in the 
upcoming amendment of the AMASR Act being worked upon by the Ministry, strong 
provisions may be incorporated for fixing accountability of concerned Government officials 
to ensure that necessary step s are taken timely for tackling encroachment of Centrally 
Protected Monuments. The concerned officials should be liable to be prosecuted in case of 
gross negligence of their duties with regard to tackling encroachment of CPMs. The 
Committee further recomme nds that the Ministry may examine the powers given to 
District Forest Officers (DFOs) under The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and consider 
granting similar powers to ASI officials in order to effectively curb the issue of 
encroachment of Centrally Protected Monuments 

11 
26. In response to whether there is a provision of regular meetings between the Ministry and 
the State Governments to monitor progress made in tackling encroachment of Centrally 
Protected Monuments, the Ministry stated that State Level Co -ordination Committee meetings 
are conducted periodically at the level of Secretary (Culture) of respective State Government 
27. As regard to its future plans for tackling the issue of encroachment of CPMs, the Ministry 
informed the Committee about the following plans: 
Formation of State Level Co-ordination Committee, in the States wherever not formed so 
far, taking matters with the State Level Co -ordination Committee for removal of 
encroachments, regular inspection of monuments and sites by Field office rs of ASI and 
conducting Cultural awareness programs by involving locals, etc. are proposed to be 
taken up by ASI so that such vital issues are suitably handled. 
28. The Committee feels that State Level Co -ordination Committees are a necessary 
instrument f or coordination between the Ministry of Culture and respective State 
Governments for resolving important issues such as removal of encroachment of 
monuments. The Committee may be apprised of the number of States where such State 
Level Co -ordination Committ ee has not been formed so far and the steps taken by the 
Ministry in order to ensure the formation of these Co-ordination Committees. 
29. The Committee desired to know from the Ministry whether any system is in place to 
monitor blatant neglect of historical State Protected Monuments by the State Governments and if 
there are any provisions for providing financial assistance for preservation and protection of any 
State Protected Monuments. The Ministry, in its written reply, informed the Committee that 3.33 
Crores B.E.  has been allotted to ASI for the conservation and preservation of unprotected 
monuments during the current Financial Year i.e. 2022-23 and that  ASI is making full efforts for 
conservation and preservation as per available resources and capability of Circle offices of ASI. 
30. The Committee notes that a mere Rs. 3.33 crores budgetary allocation has been 
made to ASI for the conservation and preservation of unprotected monuments during the 
current financial year 2022 -23. The Committee strongly feels that this amount seems to be 
grossly insufficient given the large number of unprotected historical monuments in the 
country, as well as a large number of State Protected Monuments which often face gross 
neglect by the respective State Governments. The Committee is of the view that the 
protection and preservation of historical monuments other than those already under the 

12 
protection of Central and State Governments, should also be looked after by the 
Archaeological Survey of India, at least to a basic extent.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may allocate a special budget for protection, preservation 
and restoration, wherever necessary, of unprotected/neglected historical monuments across 
the country. 
31. In response to a query made by the Committee regarding whether the Ministry has taken 
any steps to involve local bodies such as Panchayats and Municipalities for protection of 
historical monuments in the country, the Ministry informed the Committee that Cultural 
Awareness Programmes are being conducted by involving local bodies to protect the monuments 
for the posterity. 
32. The Committee further enquired from the Ministry regarding whether the Governm ent 
will empower the local bodies to provide security guards to the unprotected monuments, both 
Central and State, in t heir locality. The Ministry, in its written reply, informed the Committee 
that no such proposal has been received by Archaeological Survey of India in the matter so far. 
33. The Committee notes that no proposal exists at present wit h ASI for empowering 
local bodies to provide security guards to the unprotected monuments. The Committee 
feels that given their proximity and cultural ties w ith local monuments, local bodies are 
best suited to look after the protection of historical monuments especially those whi ch are 
not under the list of Centrally Protected M onuments (CPMs). Empowering local bodies to 
provide security guards at such monuments for their protection can go a long way in 
ensuring that these monuments are preserved in their present state for generations to 
come. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that provisions to empower the 
local bodies for the protection of historical monuments and to make them accountable may 
be incorporated in the amendment of the AMASR Act that is being worke d upon by the 
Ministry. 
34. The Ministry  informed the Committee that ASI had entered into an Memorandum of 
Understanding (MoU) with Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) to plot all the 
monuments/sites of national   importance indicating their protecte d , prohibited and regulated 
area boundaries on NRSC -Bhuvan Portal. However, the application of this portal is limited to   
providing NoC for construction -related activities by the National Monuments Authority (NMA) 
and Competent Authorities. 

13 
35. The Committee feels that there is a scope for using satellite imagery to monitor the 
Centrally Protected Monuments  (CPMs) across the country for encroachment and any 
illegal construction activities in the prohibited and regulated areas of the same. Satellite 
imagery should also be used to try and trace the monuments which are untraceable at 
present and to ensure that no existing CPM s become  untraceable in the future. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that ASI may approach ISRO and, if feasible, sign a 
Memorandum of Understanding with ISRO to utilize ISRO satellite imagery for the above  
mentioned purposes. 
 
Vacancies in ASI 
36. The Ministr y informed the Committee that about 2500 vacancies of Monument 
Attendants exist in ASI, out of which 2000 vacancies have already been reported to SSC under 
Direct Recruitment. Besides, three posts of Director at Zonal Cultural Centres were vacant and 
recruitment process was ongoing.  
37. Committee notes that s ince Monument Attendants are responsible for day to day 
cleaning of the monuments as well as its security,  2500 vacancies in this cadre is an 
incredible number and shows that most of the monuments are  not being secured or 
maintained on a day to day basis.   The Committee feels that while the ASI presents its staff 
shortage as one of the reasons for its apathy in maintaining monuments, it appears that the 
delay in filling up vacancies is one of the main  reasons for the pathetic state of monuments 
in the country . The Committee recommends that vacancies of Monument Attendants and 
Guards should be filled up on a war footing so that none of the CPMs is left unguarded and 
unmaintained. The Committee desires t o be informed about the recruitment status of 
Monument Attendants. The Committee does not find any reason that vacancies should be 
allowed to accumulate in thousands before action for recruitment is taken. Vacancies at 
higher levels may also be filled up a t the earliest. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may take immediate and effective action to appoint the  remaining 500 vacancies 
of Monument Attendants . The Committee recommends that the ASI may also explore the 
idea of appointing ex-servicemen to guard the monuments..    

14 
38. With regard to vacancies existing in ASI, the Committee reiterates the following 
recommendation made in para 35 of its 315 th Report on Demands for Grants (2022 -23) of 
the Ministry of Culture: 
…The Committee feels that the vacancy details reflect a very pathetic state of 
affairs in all the organizations of the Ministry. In the Archaeology Cadre of 
ASI, against the total sanctioned strength of 420, the vacant positions are 166, 
similarly in the Conservation Cadre, against the total strength of 918, there is a 
mammoth vacancy of 452 positions. The situation is not any better in other 
Cadres of ASI or other organisations of the Ministry. The Committee thus finds 
it difficult to understa nd how the Ministry can ensure the efficiency of its 
organizations and manage to meet the present human resource needs of the 
respective organisations, leave alone there being any scope for new initiatives 
by the organisations. The Committee strongly recom mends that the Ministry 
may set up a foolproof mechanism in place to ensure that the staffing 
requirements of all its organizations are met at all times, so as to enable them to 
carry out their mandate in letter and spirit. 
 
Permitting Religious Activities in Religious Historical Monuments 
39. The Committee sought to know from the Ministry the rules/guidelines at present 
regarding permitting religious activities like worshiping in religious historical monuments which 
are Centrally Protected Monuments. The M inistry, in its written reply, informed the Committee 
that as a matter of convention and decisions taken by the Cabinet on previous occasions, 
religious observances are not allowed in the monuments which were   not under the religious use 
at the time of their protection. 
40. The Committee feels that several historical monuments across the country hold 
immense religious significance to a large number of people and allowing  
pujas/worship/certain religious activities at such monuments can fulfill legitimate 
aspirations of the people. The Committee, therefore, recommends that ASI may explore the 
possibility of permitting pujas/worship/certain religious activities at historical Central ly 
Protected Monuments of religious significance, subject to the condition th at it can be 

15 
established that such activities would not have any detrimental effect on the state of 
conservation and preservation of the monument. 
 
OTHER OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS 
41. The Committee observes that the Ministry of Tourism along with the Mi nistry of 
Culture and ASI has promoted the concept of ―Adopt a Heritage‖ projects which aims to 
develop monuments, tourist and heritage sites across India, by inviting corporate entities, 
public sector companies, NGOs and individuals to  take up the responsibility of 
development and maintenance of tourist facilities and amenities at heritage sites .  The 
Committee appreciates the initiative of the Ministries and ASI as a step in the right 
direction and opines that the coronavirus pandemic has showed that the government 
cannot depend on ly on income from mass tourism to maintain historical monuments. The 
Committee recommends that the public may similarly be involved in maintenance and 
development of lesser known monuments through heritage walks and tours, local heritage 
festivals and promotion of niche tourism. The assistance of NGOs and societies like 
INTACH may be taken for tracing missing monuments. There are many monuments which 
are central to local folklore and legends and incorporating the assistance of local 
Panchayats/Municipalities in preservation of monuments in their localitie s would prove to 
be beneficial both in promoting tourism and stirring up the interest of people in their 
history and culture.  
42. The Committee finds that the website of ASI is poorly designed with many features 
as yet inoperative and a general lack of information on the work of the ASI as well as the 
built cultural heritage of India.  The Committee recommends that the A SI highlight the 
CPMs and the lesser known monuments o n its websi te and stimulate the interest of the 
public regarding their maintenance as well as raise the profile of Missing Monuments 
among the general public.

The roadblocks or constraining factors in the preparation of Heritage bye -laws of all the 
centrally protected  monuments and areas were discussed in detail during a meeting 
chaired by the Hon‟ble Culture Minister (HCM) on 2 nd November, 2021. The decisions 

19 
taken for overcoming these roadblocks or constraining factors given the volume of work 
involved, are detailed below:-  
(i) Additional number of appropriate agencies/ institutions to be empanelled for 
preparation and vetting of Heritage bye -laws: The Ministry of Culture in exercise of the 
powers vested under Section 20E(1) of Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and 
Remains (AMASR) Act, 1958 (as amended in 2010), has notified an additional 30 
(thirty) expert heritage bodies vide Gazette of India notification dated 09.02.2022, for fast 
tracking the process of framing of heritage bye-laws.

laws will henceforth be prepared by these notified heritage bodies and the role of 
Regional Directors of ASI will be of vetting such HBLs and then forwarding them to the

Proposal (RFP) document to be used by the Regional Directors of ASI for obtaining 
proposals from notified expert heritage bodies in their jurisdiction for awarding of work 
of preparation of Heritage by e-laws on least cost method. This revised strategy is 
expected to expedite the process of preparation of HBLs.  
(iii) Regional Directors are to be empowered with sufficient Manpower: Since HBLs are 
now to be prepared by the notified heritage bodies, the es timated costs to be incurred for 
hiring of qualified staff (viz. Conservation Architects, Surveyors etc.) in the offices of the 
Regional Directors will decrease since their role is now limited to supervising and vetting 
the draft HBLs. Revised staff requirements for the offices of Regional Directors are being 
examined by the Ministry of Culture.  
(iv) Heritage Consultation: The preparation of draft heritage bye -laws will henceforth be 
the responsibility of the notified heritage bodies. Once the preparation of HBLs has been 
delegated to the Heritage Bodies, a separate Heritage consultation will not be necessary. 
However, of the 101 Heritage Byelaws received and discussed in NMA, only one has 
been consulted with a Heritage body by the competent authority,  and heritage 
consultations of the rest remain outstanding. It is now proposed that the Heritage 
consultations in respect of these HBLs shall be done through the enlarged list of notified 
heritage bodies at a negotiated rate. The revised proposal is being sent to the Ministry of 
Culture for approval.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS – AT A GLANCE 
The Committee observes that the performance audit of the CAG had included a joint 
physical inspection, along with ASI, of 1655 monuments and sites out of the 3678 CPMs 
and sites spread nationwide.  The 24 monument s which are reported to be untraceable are 
from this sample of 1655 monuments.  The Committee has perused the list of 24 
untraceable monuments submitted by the Ministry and it is perturbed to find that the 
Barakhamba Cemetery in the very heart of the Capit al city is among the untraceable 
monuments.  If even monuments in the Capital city cannot be maintained properly, it does 
not bode well for monuments in remote places in the country. Upon query of the Committee, 
the Ministry has informed that no further st udy of the remaining monuments has been 
undertaken for ascertaining how many more monuments are missing from the total number of 
3693 CPMs.  The Committee is perturbed to note that having found out that at least 24 
monuments are untraceable out of the samp le of monuments studied, no further surveys were 
conducted for the remaining monuments, even nearly a decade after the original study.   
(Para 9) 
The Committee acknowledges the steps taken by ASI to retrace the monuments that were 
deemed to be missing by C AG in its 2013 Performance Audit but feels that the same 
reflects at the questionable state of protection and preservation of monuments, with ASI 
being unaware of the physical untraceability of several of the Centrally Protected 
Monuments under its ambit.  The Committee recommends that the ASI immediately 
undertake a survey of the remaining CPMs which were not inspected in the CAG Audit 
survey and ascertain whether there are any other missing monuments in the country apart 
from the 24 monuments of the original survey.   The Committee further recommends that a 
physical survey of all the Centrally Protected Monuments must mandatorily be carried out 
by ASI from time to time as per a fixed time schedule. Digital log books may be maintained 
which may contain text ual and photographic/video record of the state of physical 
preservation of the monument, exact location coordinates and clearly demarcated 
prohibited and regulated areas in the vicinity of the monument. These digital records may 
be made easily accessible t o the general public to avoid any ambiguities and details may 
also be published regarding the date on which the last survey was conducted, due date for 

28 
the next survey and the contact details of the ASI officials in -charge of maintaining and 
protecting the monument.   
(Para 10) 
The Committee further notes that out of the 92 monuments declared ―missing‖ by the 
CAG, 42 monuments have been identified due to efforts made by the ASI and out of the 
remaining 50 monuments, 14 are affected by rapid urbanisation, 12  are submerged by 
reservoir/dams while the location of the remaining 24 is untraceable.  The Committee feels 
that the distinction made by the Ministry regarding the monuments lost to 
urbanisation/reservoirs and 24 monuments which are untraceable is an acad emic 
distinction since monuments lost to urbanisation/reservoirs are as irrecoverable as the ones 
which are presently untraceable with scant hope of being found in future.  Moreover, the 
fact that the ASI had been unable to prevent the loss of the 14 monum ents to urbanisation 
and 12 to reservoirs/dams and only located them after the study by CAG suggests that the 
ASI had no cognisance of these monuments prior to the study. The number of monuments 
lost from public viewing must therefore be held to be 50 taki ng into account those lost to 
urbanisation or reservoirs.  The ASI has assured that the remaining 42 of the 92 
monuments exist physically but the Committee would like to know whether these 
monuments exist in their entirety and undamaged or whether the ASI has only managed to 
locate some remains and ruins of such monuments.   
(Para 11) 
The Ministry has stated that there is no term called ―Missing Monuments‖ in the AMASR 
Act and the term only came into existence as it was used by the Audit team on their Report. 
The Committee opines that the AMASR Act provides for the preservation and protection 
of ancient historical monuments and it would have been inconsistent to include the concept 
of ―Missing Monuments‖ in the Act.  That the situation warrants the use of su ch phrases 
only serves to underline the apathy of the Ministry and ASI regarding the preservation of 
our historical monuments.  The Ministry has also stated that the exercise of removing the 
untraceable monuments under Section 35 of the AMASR Act has not b een initiated by the 
ASI as there are chances that some of these monuments shall be traced out in near future. 
The Committee observes that Section 35 of the AMASR Act, 1958 has the provision to issue 
notification only for such CPMs which have as per the op inion of the Central Government 

29 
have ceased to be of national importance. The monuments which have become 
―untraceable‖ have become so due to official apathy and may not have ceased to be of 
national importance had they been existing.  The situation of a ― Missing Monument‖ 
cannot be automatically equated with loss of its historical importance.  The Committee 
recommends that the Untraceable Monuments may not be removed from the list of 
Centrally Protected Monuments by taking recourse to Section 35 as that Se ction provides 
the exclusion only of such monuments which have in the opinion of the Central 
Government ceased to be of national importance.   In fact, there is the danger that in case 
of such removal, there would be no imperative to find the untraceable m onument and it 
would be well and truly lost to posterity. Since untraceable monuments also cannot 
continue to be on the Protected list, the Committee recommends that the list of Untraceable 
Monuments may be maintained as such and if necessary, the AMASR Act may be amended 
to include this terminology.   
(Para 12) 
The Committee observes that the CAG audit had pointed out that the Ministry through the 
ASI had not conducted a comprehensive survey/review to identify monuments which were 
of national importance for inclusion in the list of CPMs.  Similarly, there were no  efforts to 
identify those monuments which had lost the stature of national importance over a period 
of time.  The Committee is dismayed to note that even a decade after the CAG Audit 
Report,  the Ministry and the ASI are yet to conduct a comprehensive sur vey to identify 
monuments which are of national importance or of those which had lost their stature of 
national importance. The Committee urges the Ministry and ASI to conduct surveys to 
include monuments of national importance and also those which have lo st their importance 
over time.  This would ensure that the resources of the Ministry and ASI are utilised  in a 
justified manner for deserving monuments  and are not diverted to protecting those which 
are no longer of national importance.  
(Para 13) 
The Co mmittee further recommends that the Ministry of Culture and ASI should 
undertake a survey of all the 3693 Centrally Protected Monuments to ensure that they are 
in existence and to provide adequate maintenance and protection.  
(Para 14) 

30 
The Committee feels that a thorough review of the AMASR Act in consultation with all 
stakeholders and State Governments, is the need of the hour. The Committee, therefore, 
appreciates the process initiated by the Ministry of Culture to amend the AMASR Act.  The 
Committee agrees with the view that having the same limits for all monuments for 
prohibited area and regulated area for restricting/regulating construction -related activities 
near the monument, is not a practical approach as the requirement for such l imitations 
could vary a lot depending on various factors specific to each monument. The Committee, 
therefore, feels that the upcoming amendment which provides for such monument -specific 
prohibited and regulated areas is much needed and hopes that once the amendment is 
passed, all necessary steps are taken to ensure that the monument -specific limits are 
decided upon for each Centrally Protected Monument at the earliest. The Committee notes 
that the ASI would be surveying all 3693 monuments while delineating monument specific 
protected and regulated limits and desires that a Report of the survey may be submitted to 
the Committee. However, the provisions of the Act may be strictly adhered to in terms of 
the prohibited areas around the monument and even Governme nt officials violating the 
provisions should be prosecuted. 
(Para 17) 
The Committee reiterates the following recommendation made in para 39 of its 311 th 
Report on ‗Creation of Regulatory Framework for protection of Historical Sites and 
Monuments‘:  
The Committee fails to see why a person living in the Regulated Area of a CPM should 
be required to seek permission from the Competent Authority under the AMASR Rules 
for carrying out innocuous maintenance activities such as filling of cracks, 
whitewashing, replacement of windows etc. The Committee feels that such uncalled-for 
interference makes lives harder for people living nearby the monuments and could 
slowly cause feelings of anguish towards the monument itself. Given the large number 
of monuments across the country and the limited budgetary resources available with 
the Government, it is pertinent that people residing near the monuments are 
encouraged to look after the monuments and protect them. Besides, placing such 
unnecessary curbs and implementing them is  a wastage of limited Government 
resources and turns the focus away from where it should be - actually protecting and 

31 
preserving the monument itself. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may undertake a thorough review of the AMASR Act an d Rules and omit any 
provisions that provide for seeking permissions for minor works where the same is not 
actually needed and streamline the process for applying for permission in case where 
the same is actually needed. Steps may urgently be taken to make  it possible for the 
entire process for seeking permission for construction activities in prohibited and 
regulated areas, to be completed online so as to not cause any hassle to bona fide 
residents living near the monuments. 
(Para 18) 
Assessment of security requirements at Centrally Protected Monuments 
The Committee is concerned to note that out of the 3693 Centrally Protected Monuments, 
security guards are posted at only 248 CPMs/sites/museums i.e. less than about 6.7 percent 
of the total number of CPMs. The Committee notes with dismay that out of the total 
requirement of 7000 personnel for protection of Monuments, the Government could 
provide only 2578 security personnel at 248 locations due to budgetary constraints. The 
Committee observes that budg etary constraints should not be an excuse for not providing 
security guards to protect our rich cultural heritage. It is the bounden duty of the 
Government of the day to protect our cultural heritage sites. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that budget may be provided by the Government to appoint 7000 personnel 
for protection of the Monuments or as per the study conducted by IIT, Delhi. In view of 
this worrying state of affairs, the Committee is of the strong view that the budgetary 
allocation available with the Ministry/ASI for safeguarding our Centrally Protected 
Monuments needs a serious relook. The Committee recommends that the Ministry/ASI 
may conduct an urgent thorough assessment of the security requirements and budgetary 
allocation required for the same and a strong case may be made to the Ministry of Finance 
requesting allocation of additional funds for this purpose so as to ensure a basic state of 
protection for all Centrally Protected Monuments across the country to preserve them for 
generations to come. The Committee also recommends that the local Panchayats and police 
may be involved in safeguarding the monuments and if necessary, the AMASR Act may be 
amended in this regard.  
(Para 22) 

32 
It has also come to the notice of the Committee that various  important historical 
monuments and sites such as Rama Temple at Peddathumbalam village, Adoni Taluka; 
Kethavaram Rock Arts and Belum Caves in Kurnool etc. which, although not under the 
list of Centrally Protected Monuments, are of high historical signific ance but devoid of any 
security guards and proper road connectivity. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry may urgently make provisions for posting security guards at these sites and 
adequate measures may be taken for promotion of tourism at the same, in coordination 
with the concerned Ministries/Departments. The Ministry of Culture may coordinate with 
the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and State Public Works Department to 
ensure proper road/highway connectivity to these important hi storical sites in order to 
allow tourists to reach these sites. 
(Para 23) 
The Committee takes note of the existing framework and recommends that in the 
upcoming amendment of the AMASR Act being worked upon by the Ministry, strong 
provisions may be incorporated for fixing accountability of concerned Government officials 
to ensure that necessary steps are taken timely for tackling encroachment of Centrally 
Protected Monuments. The concerned officials should be liable to be prosecuted in case of 
gross negligen ce of their duties with regard to tackling encroachment of CPMs. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry may examine the powers given to 
District Forest Officers (DFOs) under The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and consider 
granting similar powe rs to ASI officials in order to effectively curb the issue of 
encroachment of Centrally Protected Monuments. 
(Para 25) 
The Committee feels that State Level Co -ordination Committees are a necessary 
instrument for coordination between the Ministry of Culture  and respective State 
Governments for resolving important issues such as removal of encroachment of 
monuments. The Committee may be apprised of the number of States where such State 
Level Co -ordination Committee has not been formed so far and the steps tak en by the 
Ministry in order to ensure the formation of these Co-ordination Committees. 
(Para 28) 

33 
The Committee notes that a mere Rs. 3.33 crores budgetary allocation has been made to 
ASI for the conservation and preservation of unprotected monuments during  the current 
financial year 2022 -23. The Committee strongly feels that this amount seems to be grossly 
insufficient given the large number of unprotected historical monuments in the country, as 
well as a large number of State Protected Monuments which ofte n face gross neglect by the 
respective State Governments. The Committee is of the view that the protection and 
preservation of historical monuments other than those already under the protection of 
Central and State Governments, should also be looked after by the Archaeological Survey 
of India, at least to a basic extent.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may allocate a special budget for protection, preservation and restoration, 
wherever necessary, of unprotected/neglected historical monuments across the country. 
(Para 30) 
The Committee notes that no proposal exists at present with ASI for empowering local 
bodies to provide security guards to the unprotected monuments. The Committee feels that 
given their proximity and cultural ties with local monuments, local bodies are best suited to 
look after the protection of historical monuments especially those which are not under the 
list of Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs). Empowering local bodies to provide 
security guards at such monuments  for their protection can go a long way in ensuring that 
these monuments are preserved in their present state for generations to come. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that provisions to empower the local bodies 
for the protection of historica l monuments and to make them accountable may be 
incorporated in the amendment of the AMASR Act that is being worked upon by the 
Ministry. 
(Para 33) 
The Committee feels that there is a scope for using satellite imagery to monitor the 
Centrally Protected Mon uments (CPMs) across the country for encroachment and any 
illegal construction activities in the prohibited and regulated areas of the same. Satellite 
imagery should also be used to try and trace the monuments which are untraceable at 
present and to ensure  that no existing CPMs become untraceable in the future. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that ASI may approach ISRO and, if feasible, sign a 

34 
Memorandum of Understanding with ISRO to utilize ISRO satellite imagery for the above 
mentioned purposes. 
(Para 35) 
Vacancies in ASI 
Committee notes that since Monument Attendants are responsible for day to day cleaning 
of the monu ments as well as its security, 2500 vacancies in this cadre is an incredible 
number and shows that most of the monuments are not being secured or maintained on a 
day to day basis.   The Committee feels that while the ASI presents its staff shortage as one 
of the reasons for its apathy in maintaining monuments, it appears that the delay in filling 
up vacancies is one of the main reasons fo r the pathetic state of monuments in the country . 
The Committee recommends that vacancies of Monument Attendants and Guards should 
be filled up on a war footing so that none of the CPMs is left unguarded and unmaintained. 
The Committee desires to be inform ed about the recruitment status of Monument 
Attendants. The Committee does not find any reason that vacancies should be allowed to 
accumulate in thousands before action for recruitment is taken. Vacancies at higher levels 
may also be filled up at the earli est. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
take immediate and effective action to appoint the remaining 500 vacancies of Monument 
Attendants. The Committee recommends that the ASI may also explore the idea of 
appointing ex-servicemen to guard the monuments. 
(Para 37) 
With regard to vacancies existing in ASI, the Committee reiterates the following 
recommendation made in para 35 of its 315 th Report on Demands for Grants (2022 -23) of 
the Ministry of Culture: 
…The Committee feels that the vacancy details reflect a very pathetic state of 
affairs in all the organizations of the Ministry. In the Archaeology Cadre of 
ASI, against the total sanctioned strength of 420, the vacant positions are 166, 
similarly in the Conservation Cadre, against the total strength of 918, there is a 
mammoth vacancy of 452 positions. The situation is not any better in other 
Cadres of ASI or other organisations of the Ministry. The Committee thus finds 
it difficult to understand how the Mi nistry can ensure the efficiency of its 

35 
organizations and manage to meet the present human resource needs of the 
respective organisations, leave alone there being any scope for new initiatives 
by the organisations. The Committee strongly recommends that th e Ministry 
may set up a foolproof mechanism in place to ensure that the staffing 
requirements of all its organizations are met at all times, so as to enable them to 
carry out their mandate in letter and spirit. 
(Para 38) 
Permitting Religious Activities in Religious Historical Monuments 
The Committee feels that several historical monuments across the country hold immense 
religious significance to a large number of people and allowing pujas/worship/certain 
religious activities at such monuments can fulfill le gitimate aspirations of the people. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that ASI may explore the possibility of permitting 
pujas/worship/certain religious activities at historical Centrally Protected Monuments of 
religious significance, subject to the con dition that it can be established that such activities 
would not have any detrimental effect on the state of conservation and preservation of the 
monument. 
(Para 40) 
OTHER OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS 
The Committee observes that the Ministry of Tourism along with the Ministry of Culture 
and ASI has promoted the concept of ―Adopt a Heritage‖ projects which aims to develop 
monuments, tourist and heritage sites across India, by inviting corporate entities,  public 
sector companies, NGOs and individuals to take up the responsibility of development and 
maintenance of tourist facilities and amenities at heritage sites.  The Committee 
appreciates the initiative of the Ministries and ASI as a step in the right di rection and 
opines that the coronavirus pandemic has showed that the government cannot depend only 
on income from mass tourism to maintain historical monuments. The Committee 
recommends that the public may similarly be involved in maintenance and developme nt of 
lesser known monuments through heritage walks and tours, local heritage festivals and 
promotion of niche tourism. The assistance of NGOs and societies like INTACH may be 
taken for tracing missing monuments. There are many monuments which are central to 

36 
local folklore and legends and incorporating the assistance of local 
Panchayats/Municipalities in preservation of monuments in their localities would prove to 
be beneficial both in promoting tourism and stirring up the interest of people in their 
history and culture.  
(Para 41) 
The Committee finds that the website of ASI is poorly designed with many features as yet 
inoperative and a general lack of information on the work of the ASI as well as the built 
cultural heritage of India.  The Committee recommen ds that the ASI highlight the CPMs 
and the lesser known monuments on its website and stimulate the interest of the public 
regarding their maintenance as well as raise the profile of Missing Monuments among the 
general public.   
(Para 42) 
Action taken by th e Ministry on certain recommendations made in the Report of the 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India on Performance Audit of Preservation and 
Conservation of Monuments and Antiquities (Report No. 18 of 2013) 
The Committee is dismayed to note that the CAG Audit had found that no Inspection Notes 
were available without which it is impossible to ascertain when a particular site was last 
visited.  The Committee notes that the Ministry and ASI have informed that Inspection 
Notes are now regularly drawn and w orks done are published in the ASI -Annual Review.  
The Committee recommends that the Annual Review or Reports of the ASI may be 
prominently displayed on the website of the ASI for information of the general public. The 
Committee may be apprised of the peri odicity of such inspection by ASI officials for the 
various Centrally Protected Monuments and whether photographic evidence is collected 
alongside inspection notes. The Committee recommends that the ASI may categorize the 
monuments into different classes of importance and the periodicity for official inspection of 
such sites may then be decided upon.  
(Para 43.1.3) 
The Committee may be apprised of detailed guidelines, if any, issued by the Ministry/ASI 
under the AMASR Act in this regard. 
(Para 43.2.3) 

37 
The Committee is unhappy to note that the recommendation of the CAG nearly a decade 
back for a centralized database of the most important document of notification of the 
CPMs has still not been carried out.  
(Para 43.3.3) 
The Committee notes that it has been 9 years since the publication of the CAG Report. The 
Committee may be apprised of the specific action taken by the Ministry to address 
ambiguities in factual information related to the monuments by publishing correct, 
discrepancy-free information regarding the same in public domain. 
(Para 43.4.3) 
The Committee records its displeasure with the slow progress of the work of preparation of 
Heritage Bye Laws. 
(Para 43.5.3) 
The Committee feels that while all Centrally Protected Monuments are of unique cultural 
importance, World Heritage Sites are amongst the most important Centrally Protected 
Monuments and therefore, their maintenance and security requirements deserve special 
attention. The Committee recommends that due and appropriate budgetary allocation may 
be made for the protection and maintenance of World Heritage Sites and special 
monitoring mechanism may be put in place for the same. 
(Para 43.6.3) 
The Committee recommends that the conservation policy may be updated from time to 
time, incorporating necessary changes and new developments in the field of archaeological 
and historical conservation into the policy. The Committee desires to be apprised of the 
monitoring mechanism in place to ensure that log books are being maintained for each 
protected monument with detailed documentation of all conservation efforts. 
(Para 43.7.3) 
The Committee desires to be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry for framing of 
such guidelines. 
(Para 43.8.3) 
 

38 
The Committee may be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry  for such 
documentation on non -living monuments, in view of the fact that the CAG Report 
highlighted the need for this about 9 years ago. 
(Para 43.9.3) 
The Committee is surprised to note the reply furnished by the Ministry, after 9 years have 
passed since the CAG Report was laid before the Parliament. The Committee may be 
apprised of the specific action taken by the Ministry in this regard, at the earliest. 
(Para 43.10.3) 
The Committee notes that the number of antiquities retrieved are scant in comparison t o 
the huge number of antiques smuggled out from country. The Committee recommends the 
ASI and Ministry may give wide publicity to the theft of antiquities as soon as it takes place 
through newspaper advertisements etc. because such publicity will act as de terrent to 
buyers who may otherwise not know that it is stolen property.  
(Para 43.11.3) 
The Committee notes that the number of antiquities retrieved are not even the tip of the 
iceberg in comparison to the huge number of antiques smuggled out from country .   One of 
the reasons for the vulnerability of Indian antiques for smuggling is the lack of database on 
the antiques in different parts of the country.  This drawback has not been rectified even 
after the CAG pointed it out nearly a decade before. The sto len idols and antiques are 
auctioned at auctions organized by global auction houses but again as pointed out by the 
CAG, the ASI never participates or collects information on Indian antiques put on sale in 
global auctions as there is no explicit provision in the AAT 1972.  The Antiquities Act also 
does not have any penal provisions which could be a deterrent.   The Committee 
recommends the ASI and Ministry may give wide publicity to the theft of antiquities as 
soon as it takes place through newspaper advertisements etc. because such publicity will act 
as deterrent to buyers who may otherwise not know that it is stolen property.  
(Para 43.11.4) 
The Committee recommends that ASI should factor in the time it takes for the recruitment 
process on average, and rep ort anticipated human resource requirements in advance so 

39 
that vacancies do not remain unfilled for years on account of slow recruitment by 
UPSC/SSC. 
(Para 43.12.3) 
The Committee recommends that fixed timelines should be put in place for carrying out 
effective action on -ground to tackle encroachments at the earliest and any delays may 
immediately be taken up at higher levels. Accountability may be fixed on both 
Central/State officials for time -bound action for removal of encroachment at Centrally 
Protected Monuments. 
(Para 43.13.3) 
The Committee is concerned to note that out of the 3693 Centrally Protected Monuments, 
security guards are posted at only 248 CPMs/sites/museums i.e. less than about 6.7 percent 
of the total number of CPMs. The Committee notes with concern that out of the total 
requirement of 7000 personnel for protection of Monuments, the Government could 
provide only 2578 security personnel at 248 locations due to bu dgetary constraints. The 
Committee observes that budgetary constraints should not be an excuse for not providing 
security guards to protect our rich cultural heritage. It is the bounden duty of the 
Government of the day to protect our cultural heritage sit es. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that budget may be provided by the Government to appoint 7000 personnel 
for protection of the Monuments which may be later altered as per the study conducted by 
IIT, Delhi. In view of this worrying state of affairs, the Committee is of the strong view that 
the budgetary allocation available with the Ministry/ASI for safeguarding our Centrally 
Protected Monuments needs a serious relook. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry/ASI may conduct an urgent thorough asse ssment of the security requirements 
and budgetary allocation required for the same and a strong case may be made to the 
Ministry of Finance requesting allocation of additional funds for this purpose so as to 
ensure a basic state of protection for all Centrally Protected Monuments across the country 
to preserve them for generations to come. 
(Para 43.14.3)
