Greenfield Project, Brownfield Project and Defence Brownfield Project 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee noted that in the next two to three years, there would be a proposal for six 
to seven new Greenfield airports. From the recent experiences, it has been noticed that the 
Greenfield airports which were developed during the last decade have saturated on their existing 
capacities and need further expan sion and augmentation of facilities, however, lack of land 
availability is limiting the scope of expansion of Greenfield airports. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that every Greenfield airport must be planned in such a way that it should meet the 
requirements of at least next 40 years. Necessary land for the airport may be acquired based on 
the futuristic planning; construction; and development can be undertaken in the future 
depending on the requirements. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Noted. The Master Plans are developed for Airports considering the future forecast. 
However, the development plans are prepared for undertaking the construction in phases. Due to 
the dynamic nature of development, the Master Plans are reviewed regularly based on the revised 
growth forecast. Based on the futuristic traffic projections adequate facilities are  created and 
planned at the airports, such that it would be able to meet all the future traffic demand. 
 
Defence Brownfield Projects 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. In addition to the aforesaid land transfer issues between MoD and AAI, another issue 
relates to the restrictions imposed by the MoD and creation of “no fly zones” over defence 
airfields for over flying by civilian aircrafts. The Committee understands that though restrictions 
are justifiable for civilian aircrafts over flying high security defence airports, yet it feels that the 
problems faced by the civilian aircrafts must be kept in mind. The civilian aircrafts in such cases 

5 
 
have to traverse a longer route to avoid “no fly zones” which results in longer duration of flights 
and higher fuel consumption and leads to higher passenger fares. The Committee is of the 
opinion that wherever possible, the MoD should allow domestic airlines to fly over defence 
airfields in consultation with the Ministry. Hence, the Ministry should take up this issue 
expeditiously with the MoD. 
(Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Ministry of Civil Aviation in coordination with Ministry of Defence has undertaken the 
issues of FUA (Flexible Use of Airspace) under which the upper airspace of Restricted Airspace 
Volume, at and above 33,000 feet in the Northern Sector and above 25,000 feet in the Southern 
Sector, have been converted as Temporary Reserved Airspace (TRA). 119 Conditional Routes  
(CDRs) have been promulgated so far. Moreover, 24 danger areas have been de -notified in 
coordination with Army.  
 
Airports Authority of India 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee is also of the view that security and safety measures, presently available 
at the airports are generally not upto standards, due to which there are frequent security lapses. 
The ILS systems are also lacking at airports, which makes night landing and landing during 
rainy seasons risky. The Committee, therefore, recommend s that at all under construction 
airports, security and safety equipment of world -class level should invariably be installed. The 
latest ILS systems and night landing facilities should also be incorporated at the planning stage 
of airports, so that the flights can operate smoothly even in bad weather conditions, reducing the 
need for diversion of flights. The Committee is also of the view that planning for airport 
construction should be futuristic, so that there is no need for expansion and alterations for 
installation of ILS or security/ safety apparatus, at a later stage, which inconveniences the 
passengers and also disturbs the flight operations at airports. 
(Para 39) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The suggestions of the Committee have been noted and the sugge stions/ observations of 
the Committee will be adhered to, while developing airports in future.

Installation of HEPA Filters at Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that HEPA filters are not effective against 
COVID-19 virus and that it is also not technically feasible to install such systems at airports. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that as per ISHARE guidelines, UVGI systems and 
MERV-13 filters may be installed at all the airports in the country, espec ially the ones where 
there is international arrivals from countries where COVID -19 cases are still prevalent. The 
Committee desires to know the airport-wise status of installation of UVGI systems and MERV-13 
filters across the country and the action plan o f the Ministry to combat future waves of COVID -
19. 
(Para 74) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Action for installation of UVGI system and MERV -13 filters in the existing AHUs 
depending upon feasibility at AAI Airports has already been initiated in accordance with the 
guidelines issued by ISHARE on "Operating of Air conditioning and ventilation system to 
control spread of Corona Virus Disease (COVID - 19) in Residence, Workspaces and Healthcare 
Facilities". 
  
7.2 At 30 AAI airports, UVGI system has been installed, wh ile 2 AAI airports have been 
installed with MERV -13 filters. Action is being taken to install UVGI and MERV -I3 filters at 
balance airport depending upon the feasibility.  At 28 airports, installation of UVGI system and 
MERV-13 filters is not feasible due absence of centralized air-conditioning system. 
  
7.3 The airport wise details are attached Annexure - A. Status report of UVGI and MERV 13 
filters at Airport operated by State Government and PPP partners is attached under Annexure – 
A1.

Leveraging Tourism through Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee feels that airports act as a first gate of entry for both the domestic and 
international tourists visiting a particular city with iconic destinations. Hence, the visuals at the 
airports leave a lasting impact on the mind of a tourist and also create interest in them to 
explore the places of tourist interest. In view of this, the Committee feels that leveraging tourist 
places through airports assumes significance. The Committee, t herefore, recommends that 
besides offering tourist destinations suggested by Ministry of Tourism for RCS -UDAN bidding 
for promoting tourism, MoCA should also design airports to portray the local art and culture of 
the city at the airports through statues, murals, paintings and sculpture displays. The Committee 
recommends that promotional signages for promoting tourism can be explored through 
commercial concessionaires. The AAI can explore the possibility of completely removing rentals 
for Government agencie s instead of charging 50% concession on rental for promoting tourism. 
At the Jaipur airport, the Ministry may impress upon the PPP partner for synchronising the 
Master Plan of the airport, portraying the local theme, art and culture. The Ministry can also 
explore the possibility of engaging marketing personnel at airports to provide professional 
assistance and guidance, especially to the international tourists, which will help in promotion of 
tourism in the country. 
(Para 115)

Evacuation of Stranded Indians in Ukraine 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Committee notes that the Government has embarked upon a massive operation 
namely, „Operation Ganga‟, to evacuate stranded Indian nationals, especially, students, from the 
war torn region of Ukraine. Some private airlines and Indian Air Force are engaged in this 
effort, through special flights. The Committee understands that the Government of India is also 
exploring options for evacuating the stranded nationals through corridor/ cross border roads to 
neighbouring countries and thereafter bringing them back to the country by air. The Committee 
applauds this well-coordinated humanitarian efforts of the Ministries of Civil Aviation; Defence; 
and External Affairs and recommends that airlift and all the other possible means of evacuation 
efforts should continue till all the stranded Indian nationals in Ukraine are evacuated safely. 
Presumably, the Ministry would also bear the requisite cost of transport, if required and make 
arrangements for their transport to their native places. 
(Para 116) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 The Ministry of Civil Aviation notes with gratitude the words of encouragement from  the 
Committee. Around 22,500 Indian nationals returned from Ukraine to India from 1 February – 
11 March, 2022. 90 evacuation flights were operated under Operation Ganga, including 14 
Indian Air Force flights. The air fare for all the flights operated under Operation Gang a has been 
borne by the Government of India.

Greenfield Project, Brownfield Project and Defence Brownfield Project 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The committee feels that the Ministry is off mark as regards the understanding on 
creation of white paper for policy makers, as to how and why Green Field Projects are the future 
of the nation. The Ministry has had a long experience of developing airports which were owned 
by the State Governments or by Airport Authority of India. While a long time vision is always 
envisaged for an Airport project to grow for next few decades, however the Committee feels that 
the Brown Field Projects are important to enhance  the footprint of aviation network in the 
country but given an option of redoing an existing airport to that of a Green Field project, there 
should be a clear and ambitious policy of the Government to identify locations for furtherance of 
New Airports. Ind ia being a country with large population, the comparison of number of 

11 
 
aircrafts per person in India is far less than those of United States of America and China which 
have a comparable population figure and geographical area. 
(Para 20) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Greenfield airport is conventionally referred as an aviation facility being developed on 
empty land or previously undeveloped land and an airport whose commissioning, planning & 
construction process is carried out from the scratch / grass root level. 
 
2.2 Advantages of Greenfield Airports are:  
 Sites can be planned as per the governing guidelines for intended critical aircraft. Land is 
available & is comparatively cheaper than land at Brownfield airports. 
 Land for future expansion of Airport can be earmarked at initial stage & kept as reserved 
for future growth. 
  
2.3 However, to enhance the footprint of aviation network in the country, 
upgradation/modernization of existing brownfield Airports is also being done. In this regard, 
Private Airport Concessionaires and   AAI has embarked upon a CAPEX plan of more than Rs. 
90,000 crore during year 2019 -2024 for development/ upgradation/ modernization of various 
airports in the country to meet the requirement of Air traffic which includes New Greenfield 
airports, expansion/ modification of existing terminal, new terminals, expansion/ strengthening 
of existing runways, aprons, ANS works like control tower, technical block etc. Such works 
leads to more Aircraft Parking Bays, Better runway efficiency and safety, i ncrease operational 
efficiency, capacity of terminal building which will further facilitate seamless movement of 
Aircraft and enhance the passengers' experience. 
 
2.4 Government of India (GoI) has formulated a Greenfield Airports (GFA) Policy, 2008 
which provides guidelines, procedure and conditions for establishment of new Greenfield 
Airports in the country. As per the Policy, an airport developer or the respective Sta te 
Government willing to establish an airport is required to send a proposal to the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation (MoCA) in the prescribed format available at www.civilaviation.gov.in. There is a 2 -
stage process for approval of the proposal i.e., 'Site Cleara nce' followed by 'In -Principle' 

12 
 
approval.  In accordance with this policy, MoCA receives proposals from the State Governments 
or Airport Developers from time to time for establishment of airports. After due examination, the 
approval for development of a ne w Greenfield Airport is granted. The responsibility for project 
implementation such as land acquisition, project funding, obtaining other mandatory clearances, 
etc. lies with the concerned airport developer or the State Government, as the case may be. 
Under the GFA Policy, GoI has accorded 'In -Principle' approval for development of 21 
Greenfield airports, out of which 08 airports have been operationalized. 
 
2.5 Ministry of Civil Aviation launched Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) - UDAN 
(UdeDeshkaAamNagrik) to stimulate regional air connectivity and making air travel affordable 
to the masses. The primary objective of RCS is to facilitate / stimulate regional air connectivity 
by connecting unserved/underserved airports/heliports/water aerodromes. UDAN is a m arket 
driven scheme. Interested airlines based on their assessment of demand on particular routes 
submit their proposals at the time of bidding under UDAN. An airport which is included in the 
awarded routes of UDAN and requires upgradation / development fo r commencement of RCS 
operations, is developed under "Revival/upgradation of unserved and underserved 
airports/heliports/water aerodromes" Scheme. The Government of India has approved a budget 
of Rs. 4500 crore for revival of existing unserved / underserve d airports / airstrips of the State 
Governments, Airports Authority of India, Public Sector Undertakings and Civil Enclaves. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. Committee would like to clarify further this point with the example of the Patna Airport 
in which over thousand crores is being spent without adding any operational advantage and still 
continuing with all the limitations, which existed as far operations is concerned, would remain 
there even after spending a thousand crores. The reason why the Committee h as been

Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes with serious concern that out of the total MRO services turnover of 
Rs. 15,353 crores, the annual turnover of the Indian MRO industry is just Rs. 2,300 cro res, 
which is just 15% of India‟s civil MRO expense. The balance 85% MRO services amounting to a 
colossal amount of Rs. 13,053 crores are availed from MROs b ased abroad in Singapore, 
Malaysia, Middle East, EU and USA etc. The massive amount of the MRO services availed from 
abroad can be gauged from the fact that the amount is more than the total B.E. allocation of Rs. 
10,667 crores for 2022 -23. The Committee l aments the huge outgo of avoidable foreign 
exchange. It is of the opinion that Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) organizations play 
a major role in the economy of airline operations. Since, 85% of these activities are carried out 
abroad, there is a strong case to bring these MROs to India as the MRO expenditure is expected 
to grow further with the growth in civil aviation sector. The issues which come within the ambit 
of foreign suppliers can also be addressed by giving them incentives to operate in th is country. 
India with its large technical manpower base can easily provide the manpower for MRO 
services. The reasons for carrying out MRO services abroad, include tax anomaly with global 
MROs in terms of GST/ levies/ surcharges etc.; high airport charges  for land rentals, airport 
royalty, lack of availability of hangar space etc. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should take up the aforesaid issues with the Ministry of Finance and other concerned agencies 
and try to address the issues at the earliest. The issues which are within the ambit of the Ministry 
itself viz. airport charges, hangar space etc. should be expeditiously resolved by the Ministry and 
AAI. 

17

Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Keeping in view India‟s growing aviation market, technology and skill base, Government 
announced new MRO Guidelines on 1st September, 2021 with a view to create a congenial 
atmosphere in the country for the development of MRO industry for aircraft/ helicopter/ drones 
and their engines and other parts. The salient features of the guidelines are as follows: 
a. Concession fee, in any manifestation including royalty, shall not be leviable on new/ 
renewal of existing contracts. 
b. Selection of agency and procedures for allotment of land/ space under rationalized land/ 
space rental for new MRO contracts and renewal of existing MRO contracts, shall be 
through e-tender by AAI. 
c. The renewal of the existing land leases/ space license of MRO service providers/ 
Aircraft Maintenance Organizations (AMOs) shall be on the basis of bidding wherein 
Right of First Refusal (RoFR) shall be given to the existing lessee/ licensee to match the 
first rank bid in terms of the selection criteria provided its bid is within 15% of the most 
competitive bid received. 
d. The quoted/ accepted lease fee shall be escalated @15% after every 3rd year. 
e. The maximum period of contract, new or renewal, for allotment of land/ space shall be 
30 years from the date of handing over of site.

workshops in India and create a conducive environment towards making India global hub of 
MRO.

ii. Transactions sub-contracted by foreign OEMs/ MROs to domestic MRO are treated

Recommendation/Observation

strong resilience has been shown by the sector, even during the COVID -19 pandemic. The 
Committee notes the initiatives of the Ministry and recommends that all out efforts s hould be

13.1 The number of freighter aircraft deployed by Indian carriers has been increased from 7 in

carriers as promulgated vide AIC18/1992 dated 11.05.1992, and changes have been made with a

airlines and airlines registered elsewhere. The revised open sky policy has been promulgated

30 
 
Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Kolkata, Hyderabad, and Mumbai, and Operations of scheduled

I Lockdown

Rationalisation of Air Fares and Cancellation Charges in Domestic Sectors 
Recommendation/Observation 
20. As regards pricing of the tickets, the Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that at 
present, air fare is neither regulated nor fixed by the Government and airlines are free to fix the 
reasonable tariff under the provision of Sub -rule (1) of Rule 1 35, Aircraft Rules, 1937 having 
regard to all relevant factors including the cost of operation, characteristics of service, 
reasonable profit and the generally prevailing tariff. Also, as regards the concern of the 
Committee regarding extra fare for seat s election, the Ministry has stated that travel by air is a 
contractual matter between airline and passenger, which is commercial in nature. The 
Committee is of the opinion that for Civil Aviation sector to grow in an open market, it is 
justifiable that the private airline operators should be given a free hand to fix the air fares as 
they are governed by competition. However, the Committee would like to draw the attention of 
the Ministry to the provision of the  Aircraft Rules, 1937, which  specifically mention s that the 
fares should be reasonable and should maintain reasonable profit. In the above context, the 
Committee feels that the reply of the Ministry stating that air travel is purely a contractual 
matter between the airline and the passenger, is not at al l justified. The Committee is of the 

36 
 
opinion that a balance also must be maintained between the commercial interests of the airlines 
and the interest of the passengers. The Committee feels that the passengers should not be fleeced 
in the garb of commercial ization and therefore recommends that the Ministry should maintain a 
close watch on the fare pricing by the airlines to ensure that it is not exorbitant. It also 
recommends that at least for the same sector, route and duration of flight, in all the private  
airlines, the Ministry should issue guidelines so as to ensure similar or least variation in fares 
among all airlines. The Committee is also of the opinion that fixing of different fares for 
selection of seats in the same flight is arbitrary and unjustifi able. Hence, Committee on the 
principle of equity feels that all the seats in a same flight should have same fare. The Committee 
also recommends that the Ministry should strictly enforce the DGCA Charter and ensure that 
under no circumstances, the airlines  levies cancellation charges more than the basic fare plus 
fuel surcharge. The Committee may be informed about the mechanism adopted by the Ministry to 
ensure that the Aircraft Rules, 1937 and DGCA Charter is being followed in letter and spirit by 
all private airlines. 
(Para 91) 
Reply of the Ministry 
20.1 Under the provisions of Sub Rule(1) of Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, every air 
transport undertaking engaged in scheduled air services require to establish tariff having regard 
to all relevant fact ors, including cost of operation, characteristics of services, reasonable profit 
and the generally prevailing tariff. Airlines are free to charge reasonable air fares as per their 
operation viability subject to compliance of above said provision. The airli nes remain compliant 
to the Sub Rule (2) of Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 as long as fare charged by them is in 
line with fare displayed on their website. 
 
20.2 Further, fare capping was also put in place by the Government during the COVID -19 
pandemic as a special measure in order to safeguard the passengers' interest. The lower as well as 
upper air fares (excluding User Development Fee (UDF), Passenger Service Fee (PSF) and GST) 
were fixed sector -wise on the basis of duration of flight time. The far e capping is currently 
applicable on rolling basis for a 15 days' cycle. 
 

37 
 
20.3 With a view to maintain transparency, Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) 
started monitoring of airfares on certain routes selected on random basis to ensure that the 
airlines do not charge airfares outside the range declared by them.

submitted to this Ministry. KSIDC vide letters dated 29.12.2021 and 11.02.2022 had informed 
that TEFS report updation is still ongoing and the requisite information would be submitted by 
31st March, 2022. However, the updated TEFS report alongwith requisite comments are still 
awaited from KSIDC. 
 
 
 

45 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
3.3 The Committee hopes that the Ministry will take follow up action and impress upon 
the M/s KSIDC to furnish the updated Techno -Economic Feasibility Study (TEFS) Report 
at the earliest, so that a Greenfield Airport may be setup at Kottayam which will benefit 
lakhs of pilgrims visiting Sabarimala every year.   
 
Requirement of Air Traffic Controllers (ATCOs) 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee notes with serious concern that there is a huge backlog of 708 vacancies 
in the post of ATCOs. Despite this fact, most of the posts of ATCOs at different levels were 
created in 2013, 2014 and 2015 only. Since the year 2017, there has been no post creation at any 
level for ATCOs. The proposal for creation of 340 additional posts of ATCOs has been taken 
with DPE only recently. The Committee is of the opinion that the demand for ATCOs will rise 
exponentially with the growth of the aviation sector in the country and feels that the Ministry 
should have anticipated the requirement of more number of ATCOs well in advance and inducted 
ATCOs continuously over the years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that proc edural 
issues regarding manpower requirements of ATCOs should be addressed immediately to ensure 
operationalization of new airports that are being constructed in near future do not suffer due to 
lack of ATCOs. 
(Para 51) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 To address the shortage of ATCOs, AAI has already initiated the process to cover the 
present shortfall of ATCOs by filling up the existing vacant posts expeditiously.  Moreover, in 
order to mitigate the shortage of ATCOs, approval of Department of Public Enterprises has been 
obtained for creation of 340 new posts of ATCOs. AAI has been advised to take necessary steps 
to fill the posts expeditiously.  
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
4.2 The Committee reiterates its concern at the undue and avoidable delay in 
recruitment of ATCOs and strongly recommends the AAI to fill up the vacancies without 
any further delay.   

46 
 
Flying Training Organisations (FTOs) 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee notes that there would be a growing requirement of around 1000 pilots 
every year in the near future. The Committee also notes that a liberalized FTO policy has also 
been brought out, wherein new and attractive incentives have been given to pr ivate entities who 
want to start an FTO. The Committee supports the new initiatives of the Ministry as it is of the 
opinion that with the expected growth of the Civil Aviation Sector in the country, there would be 
increased demand for trained pilots. The M inistry should therefore gear up for the requirement 
of FTOs and set up FTOs in a time bound manner. The Committee also notes that the Ministry 
has taken up the issue of reduction of GST on AvGas and funding support to FTOs as a priority 
sector, with the M inistry of Finance and it has also taken up relevant issues with State 
Governments and Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. The Committee recommends that the 
issues may be forcefully taken up with the concerned stakeholders and the Committee may also 
be apprised of the progress in this regard. The Committee also recommends that keeping in view 
of the Atmanirbhar Bharat, sufficient Flight Training Organisations (FTOs) may be established 
in various parts of the country to ensure that our boys and girls are not going to foreign 
countries to get pilot training.  
(Para 55) 
5.1 Reply of the Ministry 
i) There are currently 35 DGCA -approved Flying Training Organisations (FTO) in the 
country.  IGRUA at Amethi (UP) is under the administrative control of the Central 
Government. Eight FTOs are under State Governments and 26 are owned by the private 
sector. Indian FTOs had 229 aircraft for flying training as on 30 Nov 2021.  
ii) The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) follows a five -phase certification 
process for setting up a FTO to check all the laid down rules and regulations. The 
Directorate of Flying T raining (DFT) at DGCA conducts scheduled annual inspections 
and unscheduled spot checks at FTOs.  
iii) India had 28 FTOs as on 31 st March 2016.  The number of FTOs was above 40 in 2015, 
but was reduced drastically after a comprehensive review of all FTOs by DGCA in 2015 
and subsequent closure of FTOs that did not meet the specified requirements.  

47 
 
iv) From 28 FTOs in March 2016, the number of FTOs is likely to increase to 43 by 
December 2022 and to 58 by December 2023, that is, an over 100% increase in a matter 
of two years.  
v) Airports Authority of India (AAI), on 25 September 2020, approved a liberalised Flying 
Training Organisations (FTO) policy wherein the concept of airport royalty (revenue 
share payment by FTOs to AAI) was abolished and land rental charges were 
significantly rationalised.   
vi) Under the old policy, around 13% royalty was charged on FTO revenue and land rentals 
were linked to local land rates.  These contributed to the financial distress, closure of 
training operations and long-drawn legal disputes between the FTOs and AAI.   
vii) Due to the investor-friendly liberalised FTO policy, AAI received bids for all nine FTO 
slots in March 2021 despite the airline sector going through a serious financial crisis due 
to Covid.   
viii) AAI issued award letters on 31 May 2021  and 29 October 2021 for nine FTOs to be 
established at five airports at Belagavi (Karnataka), Jalgaon (Maharashtra), Kalaburagi 
(Karnataka), Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh) and Lilabari (Assam). Soft launch of two 
FTOs at Kalaburagi was done on 15 August 2021 and at Lilabari on 12 April 2022.  
ix) In the second round of FTO creation, tender process is in progress for establishing 15 
FTOs at 10 Airports viz Cooch Behar, Tezu, Jharsuguda, Deoghar, Meerut, Kishangarh, 
Hubli, Kadapa, Bhavnagar and Salem Airports. 
x) DGCA has introduced new Online On Demand Examination (OLODE) for the AME 
and flight crew (FC) candidates with effect from November 2021. These license 
examinations provide an opportunity to the candidates to choose date and time to appear 
in the examination as per his/her choice on the available slots of the examinations. 
xi) DGCA has modified its regulations to empower Flying Instructors with the right to 
authorise flight operations at FTOs. This will help increase the flying hours and aircraft 
utilisation at each FTO and lead to faster completion of the CPL requirements. 
xii) Currently there is no shortage of pilots in the country. However, there is a shortage of 
commanders on certain types of aircraft and the same is being managed by utilizing 
foreign pilots by issuing Foreign Aircrew Temporary Authorization (FATA). Currently, 
there are 87 FATA holders in India.  

48 
 
xiii) Currently, there are around 9,000 pilots employed with various airline operators in 
India. Given the fleet projections, it is felt that India may require aroun d 1000 pilots per 
annum over the next five years.

xviii) The number of CPL holders produced by Indian FTOs in 2021 is 504, an all-time high.  
xix) The good performance by Indian FTOs in 2021 is despite severe disruptions due to the 
Covid second wave, Cyclone Yaas, Cyclone Tauktae, early onset of monsoons and a 
rising cost of imported aviation fuel. 
xx) Typically, around 40% of Indian CPL holders do their flying training at a foreign FTO.  
Based on stakeholder feedback, the cost of doing flying training abroad is around Rs. 
1.2-1.5 crore per cadet.  This works out to a direct loss of foreign exchange to t he tune 
of Rs. 500 crore annually.  The multiplier effect in terms of loss of revenue and jobs on 
account of this exodus is far higher and needs to be reversed, under the Atmanirbhar 
Bharat Abhiyan.  

49 
 
xxi) Cost of AvGas used by FTOs is a challenge. AvGas is not manufactured in India and 
hence we are completely dependent on imports. The IGST levied on import of AvGas is 
18%, additionally 18% GST is levied on the sale of AvGas.  The landed price for FTOs 
works out to Rs. 184.5 per litre as on March 9, 2022.  
xxii) Cost of AvGas is at a 98% premium to the cost price of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF), 
which is being sold to airlines at Rs. 94 per liter at Delhi, as on March 3, 2022. It may 
be noted that, to begin with, the cost of ATF in India itself is one of the highest in t he 
world. 
xxiii) In value terms, the IGST earned by the Government from AvGas imports is a mere Rs. 
3-5 crore per annum.  The tax levied on AvGas is ultimately recovered from a small 
base of flying schools. These flying schools have no option but to  charge the students. It 
increases the cost of training for students. In order to make cost of training affordable to 
children from all the sections of our society and not just the affluent, it is important to 
reduce IGST/GST on import and sale of AvGas to „Zero‟ or a bare minimum level. 
xxiv) Ministry of Civil Aviation has requested Ministry of Finance to consider requesting the 
GST Council to reduce the IGST and GST levied on import of AvGas from 18% to zero 
or one percent; This, along with various measures being undertaken by the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation will go a long way in making our FTOs stronger and India a global 
training hub by 2030. 
xxv) Under Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan, Indian Oil is planning to produce AvGas at Koyali 
Refinery located in Vadodara (Gujarat).  The first  batch of AvGas is expected to be 
dispatched in June 2022, subject to quality certification by competent authorities.  
 
 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
5.2 The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government to increase the 
number of FTOs in the country , specially  the introduction of the new liberalized FTO 
policy. The Committee desires to know whether  the second round of FTO creation for 
addition of 15 more FTOs, is progressing as per schedule . The Committee also notes that 
due to high taxation rates on AvGas, the cost of pilots training increases substantially, 

50 
 
making it affordable only for the affluent sections of the society. The Committee 
recommends that the iss ue of reduction of taxation rate on AvGas may be taken up

Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee during the course of its deliberations, raised the issue of lack of cargo 
facilities in the North -Eastern Region, especially in the States of Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh 
and Assam. The Committee is of the opinion that the economy of the North -Eastern Region is 
primarily based on horticulture, agriculture and tea cultivation, which can prosper only if 
proper markets are created for the sale of these products. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the existing Dibrugarh airport which is a major airport in the North -Eastern 
Region, may be developed as a standard airport for transport of horticulture, agriculture and tea 
products to all the regions of the country. 
(Para 62)

 At Dibrugarh, Old Terminal Building has been modified and Security Clearance has been 
applied to BCAS. The BCAS approval is awaited. 
 However, Domestic Air cargo movement facilitated through Passenger Terminal w.e.f. 
August 2021 with BCAS approval. 
 
 
 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
6.2 The Committee recommends that BCAS approval for development of Dibrugarh 
airport for transport of horticulture; agriculture; and tea products, may be expedited, 
which will result in development of the North-Eastern region.  
 
Passenger Amenities at Airports 

51 
 
Facility of Aerobridges 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee expresses its serious concern at the fact that despite charging passengers, 
PBB or aerobridge facilities are not being used by private airlines to reduce operational cost. 
Due to this, passengers, especially the aged ones have to bear the brunt and have to climb the 
stairs of the parking stand to board an aircraft. The Committee deplores this apathetic and 
unreasonable attitude of the private airlines and strongly recommends that its circular on the 
aforesaid subject may be strictly enforced. The Committee also recomme nds that regular 
surprise checks should also be carried out by the Ministry to ensure compliance of the circular 
and in case there is a default, the concerned private airlines should be penalized. 
(Para 76) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 DGCA has discussed the matter with airport &airline operators. The airlines have 
informed that the usage of Bridge Mount Equipment (such as Aerobridges) at  airports are 
attributed to commercial issues i.e. at times it adds to financial burden and increases turn -around 
time of the aircrafts and hence is not commercially viable to use such facilities at airports. Since 
this is a  commercial issue between an airport & an airline and it does not affect the safety of 
operations, DGCA/Ministry cannot issue directions for mandatory usage  of Bridge Mount 
Equipment (PCA/FEGP) at airports. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.2 The Committee notes that the DGCA/Ministry cannot issue directions to airport or 
airlines for mandatory usage of aerobridges at airports which causes major issues to 
passengers, especially the aged ones.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
the Ministry may at least issue necessary instructions to all the airports/ airlines to provide 
assistance to aged/differently abled passengers to board an aircraft  with the usage of 
passenger boarding ramps, wheelchairs and hydraulic lifts.        
 
Seaplane Policy 
Recommendation/Observation 

52 
 
8. The Committee expresses serious concern that the seaplane policy is still not in place and 
is still being finalized in consultation with stakeholders. The Committee also laments the fact that 
the first seaplane that was operationalized, was stopped due to technical reasons. It expresses 
concern at the lack of seriousness of the Ministry, as regards Seaplane policy. The Com mittee 
has repeatedly pointed out the need for Seaplane policy in view of the fact that our country is 
endowed with rivers and lakes. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a feasibility study 
may be conducted in the North -Eastern Region for operation o f Seaplanes in the big lakes and 
rivers of the North -Eastern Region. The Committee also stresses on the expeditious finalization 
of Seaplane policy. It also recommends that proper planning should be done before start of the 
operations, so that the operations are not halted. 
(Para 94) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 India has about 400 airstrips lying unused and about 7500 km long coastline. As such, 
there is vast potential to operationalise these airstrips and coastline with small aeroplanes, 
helicopters and seaplanes to provide last mile air connectivity to the common people living in far 
flung and remote areas of the country. 
 
8.2 Accordingly, Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) after extensive consultations with 
States/ UTs, Airlines and other key stakeholders of  the Industry has proposed to promote small 
aircraft operations including seaplanes and helicopters with more focus to the small aircraft 
operations for last mile connectivity and introduce a sub-scheme under UDAN. 
 
8.3 Small Aircraft Scheme (SAS) includin g the operation of seaplane has been issued by the 
Honourable Minister of Civil Aviation launched on 26.03.2022 at WINGS Hyderabad.  As per 
the provisions for Seaplanes in SAS, proposals are being invited from airlines under the special 
round of bidding UDA N 4.2 for cancelled routes of previous rounds and the Sea Plane routes 
proposed by Sagarmala. Start date of submission of the bid is 28.04.2022. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
8.4 The Committee notes that Small Aircraft Scheme (SAS) which includes the 
operation of Seaplane was launched on 26.03.2022 , however a Seaplane Policy has yet not 

53 
 
been finalized by the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation 
that a S eaplane Policy may be formulated expeditiously in consultation with various 
stakeholders, which will provide last mile air connectivity to the common people living in 
far flung and remote areas of the country. The Committee also desires to know the status of 
the bidding process for the seaplane routes proposed by Sagarmala.

Recommendation/Observation 
9. In view of the above reply, the Committee in its 308th Action Taken Report on the 
Recommendations/ Observations contained in its  Two Hundred and Ninety Seventh Report on 
the subject „Functioning of Airports Authority of India‟, had noted the proactive action taken by 
the Ministry, to ensure connectivity, and that a letter had been sent by Chairperson, AAI to Chief 
Secretaries of va rious State Governments to align and relate the City Master Plan with the 
Airport Master Plan. The Committee may also be informed of the opinion of the States across the 
country, especially as regards land acquisition, proper compensation and rehabilitatio n of the 
land owners, as it is a teething problem in infrastructure projects. The Committee may be 
informed about the views of the State Governments on the proposal of aligning City Master Plan 
with the Airport Master Plan.

9.1 None of the States has come forward with its view on the proposal of aligning City 
Master Plan with the Airport Master Plan. However, AAI has been advised to take up the issue

9.2 In the meanwhile, the Gati Shakti, National Master Plan has stressed the need to improve 
multi-modal infrastructure connectivity through convergence of developmental work and 
adoption of a holistic approach on major infrastructure projects. Accordingly, this asp ect is taken 
into consideration while planning all Greenfield projects of airport development.

54

forward with its view on the proposal of aligning City Master Plan with the Airport Master

matter with the State Governments and expedite their replies as the opinion of State 
Governments is imperative for the alignment of the City Master Plan with the Airport 
Master Plan.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes a significant gap in the overall budgetary allocation of the 
Ministry in the Financial Year ( F.Y.) 2022 -23 as compared to its projected requirements. 
Against the proposed demand for Rs. 2542.43 Crores in B.E. 2022 -23, only Rs. 1709.50 
Crores have been allocated, registering a shortfall of Rs. 832.93 Crores i.e. 32.76% of the 
overall budgetary requirement of the Ministry for the F.Y. 22-23, and is certain to have an 
adverse bearing on the implementation of various port projects of the Ministry. The 
Committee observes that under several crucial heads such as Sagarmala Development 
Company, Indian Maritime University, Kolkata Port Trust, Inland Water Transport etc., 
significantly lesser allocation/no allocation has been made against the projected demand of 
the Ministry. The Committee desires to be apprised of the different schemes/projects under its 
ambit which will be adversely affected because of the shortfall in B.E. 2022-23 along with the 
course of action planned by the Ministry to deal with this shortfall. The Committee observes 
that the growth of In dia‟s maritime sector is of paramount importance and needs to be 
accelerated to strengthen our position of eminence in the global maritime sector. Since the 
Ministry has to play a vital role in shaping India‟s maritime prowess into an engine of 
economic development, availability of adequate financial resources is a prerequisite towards 
propelling India to the forefront of the global maritime sector. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should ensure a good pace of utilization of allocated funds in 
initial quarters of F.Y. 2022-23, deploy their resources in a more efficient way and request 
the Ministry of Finance to enhance budgetary allocation at the R.E. 2022-23 stage so that the 
various programmes and projects that the Ministry has planned for F.Y. 22-23 can stay on 
course. 
(Para 6)

which are aligned with the objectives of „Sagarmala Programme.‟ Funds allocated in the F.Y. 
2022-23 will be utilized efficiently and as per the requirement additional funds will be sought 
in Revised Estimate/Supplementary Demand Stage.

3. The Committee notes that till 7 th February, 2022, under Revenue head, Rs. 726.92 
crores have been spent, i.e., about 74.4% vis -à-vis the R.E. 2021-22 of Rs. 976.57 crore

till 7 th February, 2022 is even lower with figures of 69.5% vis -à-vis the overall Capital

pace of expenditure, the Ministry will not be able to fully util ize its R.E. 2021-22 of Rs. 
1585.4 crores unless urgent corrective measures are taken. The Committee is concerned to 
note that the expenditure incurred by the Ministry during F.Y. 2021-22 under several crucial 
heads such as Assistance to Ship Building, Res earch and Development, Grants to Inland 
Water Transport Authority of India (NER), Traffic Authority for Major Ports, Indian 
Maritime University, IWAI Projects - EAP Component and Programme Component,

PERFORMANCE OF PORTS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee observes that the cargo handling capacity of Major Ports in the 
country has increased by about 79 percent between the years 2014-15 and 2020-21 (ignoring 
the incomplete data for the year 2021 -22 since it is yet to be finalized), which is an 
annualized growth rate of about 10.2 percent. As compared to this, the gross cargo handling 
capacity of Non -Major Ports has increased by on ly about 52 percent, with an annualized 
growth rate of just 7.2 percent. In terms of Traffic handled, however, Non -Major Ports 
registered a growth of about 30 percent ( ∼6.7 percent annualized) between the years 2015 -
16 and 2019 -20 (excluding the COVID affected year 2020 -21 and ongoing year 2021 -22) 
whereas Major Ports in the country only managed a minor increase of about 16 percent 
(∼3.8 percent annualized) during the same period. This data points to the fact that while 
Major Ports across the country ha ve managed to increase their capacity at a satisfactory 
pace, which is higher than that of Non -Major Ports, the statistics pertaining to traffic 
handled at ports across the country do not portray a robust picture for the Major Ports in the 
country. While N on-Major Ports have managed to increase the volume of traffic handled at 
nearly the same pace at which their capacity is increasing, Major Ports paint a contrasting 
picture with annual growth in traffic handled at a mere 3.8 percent as against the capacity  
growth rate of about 10.2 percent. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to 
review the possible reasons behind the comparative stagnancy in the volume growth of traffic 
handled at Major Ports in the country. The Ministry may also come up with an effective plan 
of action to further improve the growth rate of cargo handling capacity of Non -Major Ports 
in the country. The Committee desires to be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry in 
this regard. 
(Para 20) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1. The government has already given a strong push to port modernization, 
mechanization and digitalization, with a number of ease of doing business initiatives. Port 
modernization includes the introduction of web -based e -forms and direct port delivery, 

8 
 
installation of container scanners and radio frequency identification -based systems for gate 
automation, digitalization of land records, the launch of a single -window interface for 
facilitating trade, and integration of more seaports with the PCS.   
 
4.2. The „Sagarmala Programme, ‟ the flagship programme of the Ministry of Ports, 
Shipping and Waterways lays great emphasis on modernization and mechanization. Ports are 
looking at setting up specialized high capacity berths, supported by state-of-the-art equipment 
and skilled and trained manpower.  A roadmap has been prepared for increasing the Indian 
port capacity to 3300+ MMTPA by 2025 to cater to the Indian Ports traffic. 
 
4.3. With the objective of propelling India to the forefront of the Global Maritime Sector,  
the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has formulated Maritime India Vision 2030 
(MIV 2030), a blueprint to ensure coordinated and accelerated growth of India‟s maritime 
sector in the next decade.  MIV 2030 identifies over 150 initiatives across 10 themes covering 
all the facets of the Indian maritime sector and is a comprehensive effort to define and meet 
national maritime objectives. 
 
4.4. Since 1997, cargo-handling terminals run by government -owned ports themselves as 
well as private operators at  major ports have been required to take clearance from the tariff 
regulator (TAMP) before fixing and revising tariffs, once in two -three years, for the services 
rendered at their berths and terminals. On the other hand, Non -Major Ports are having 
operational and regulatory freedom, including the freedom to set their own tariffs, which 
gives a distinct advantage to them for attracting cargo. They also attract private investment by 
giving concession contracts, offering incentives, granting exclusivity rights,  and ensuring 
land acquisition. 
 
4.5. However, after the enactment of the MPA Act, 2021, all the Major Port Trusts are 
converted into Port Authority, except Kamarajar Port (Ennore), which will continue to 
function as a major port  under the Companies Act 20 13. This will empower the Major Ports 
to perform with greater efficiency on account of full autonomy in decision making and by 
modernizing the institut ional framework of Major Ports.  The Board of Port Authority will 
comprise 11 to 13 Members representing v arious interests. A compact Board with 
professional independent Members will strengthen decision-making and strategic planning. In 
the new Act, the Port Authority has been given powers to fix tariffs which will act as a 
reference tariff for purposes of bid ding for PPP projects. PPP operators will be free to fix 
tariffs - based on market conditions. The move to do away with the TAMP‟s tariff regulations 
will now make way for a market -driven pricing environment for PPP operators calling for a 

9 
 
level playing fi eld with their counterparts at Non -Major Ports locations. The Board of Port 
Authority has been delegated the power to fix the scale of rates for other port services and 
assets including land.  The Boards of Port Authority have been delegated full powers to  enter 
into contracts, planning and development, fixing of tariff except in national interest, security 
and emergency arising out of inaction and default.  All the above initiatives will boost cargo 
growth at the Major Ports in the coming years. 
 
4.6. Major ports are under the jurisdiction of the Government of India and governed by the 
MPA Act, 2021. Non-Major Ports comes under the jurisdiction of the respective State 
Government‟s Port Department or Maritime Boards.  At present, State Governments have the 
power to plan, develop and regulate the Non -Major Ports in the country. The improvement in 
the growth rate of cargo handling capacity of Non -Major Ports is looked after by the 
respective State Governments.

21 
 
 Major Port Authorities Act 2021: the MPA Act 2021, enacted by the parliament in 
February 2021, will provide more autonomy to ports and help them take decisions faster with 
respect to infrastructure development and changing market conditions. It is expected  to usher 
in a new era for administration of Major Ports in India in which the Major Ports will 
contribute significantly to the economic growth and provide world -class port infrastructure

nearby non major ports handling similar cargo.  
(iii) The Act also provides for formulation of an Adjudicatory Board that will adjudicate 
disputes among Major Ports, Public Private Partnership concessionaires and captive 
users. MPA Act 2021 will have enormous impact on overall maritime trade as focus

conditions and on such other conditions as may be notified by the Government.  
 
9.3 The MPA Act 2021 aims to develop the Major Ports in the „Landlord Model‟ as 
against the present „Service Model‟. Under the Landlord Model the ports would offer the 
basic available infrastructure for further development and operation by concessionaires 

22 
 
through PPP  Mode for fixed duration with clear cut revenue sharing understanding as per

by the Government. The PPP partners would bring in the latest technology and trained

attitude to compete with the best in the world. The ports would no t be required to pump in

24 
 
11.2. Comments of MA Division: 
 The National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan (NOSDCP) is a plan.  By an Office 
Memorandum of the Ministry of Defence dated 07 March 1986 and further, by 
amendment to the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 vide 
Gazette notification dated 12 th December, 2002, the Indian Coast Guard has been 
designated as the Central Coordinating Authority for combating oil spills in Indian 
waters and undertaking oil spill prevention and control. The National Oil Spill 
Disaster Contingency P lan or NOS DCP for short, together with the allocation of 
functional responsibil ities to the various Ministries and Departments of the 
Government of India for oil spill response in the maritime zones of India was 
approved by a Committee of Secretaries to the Government of India on 04 th 
November, 1993. 
 
11.3. Role & Responsibilities of Implementing NOSDCP: 
 The Ministry of Defence with administrative responsibility for the Coast Guard 
organisation is the Ministry responsible for central coordination of oil spills of 
national significance in coastal and marine environment of various marit ime zones. 
The Indian Coast Guard (ICG) is responsible for maintaining and implementing the 
National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan. The Indian Coast Guard is also 
responsible for acting as the Central Coordinating Agency for combating of oil 
pollution in various maritime zones, except in the waters of ports and within five 
hundred meters of offshore exploration and production platforms, coastal refineries, 
and associated facilities such as single buoy mooring, crude oil terminal and pipelines. 
As the Central Coordinating Authority for combating oil pollution, the Coast Guard 
will additionally:- 
a. Review the progress reports submitted by the State Crisis Management Groups; 
b. Respond to queries addressed to it by the State Crisis Management Groups and the 
District Crisis Management Groups; and 
c. Publish State -wise list of experts and officials who are concerned” with the 
handling of oil pollution incidents. 
 
11.4. MINISTRIES AND DEPARTMENTS OF THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA: An 
executive decision of the Committee of  Secretaries on 04 th November, 1993 serves as the 
reference for obligations of the various Ministries and Departments of the Government  of 
India in support of the NOSDCP. 
 

25 
 
11.5. STATE GOVERNMENTS: The State Governments of coastal states are responsible 
for coordinating the district and local administration and operation of the National Plan for 
shore line response and as per the provisions of the National Disaster Management Act, 2005. 
The State and District Authorities will provide a wide range of site -specific information and 
resources, either in relation to environmental impacts, or response activities through 
authorities, such as Transport, Conservation and Resource Management Departments, 
Environmental Protection Authorities, emergency services, port/harbour authorities, and local 
conservation groups. 
 
11.6. SUPPORT AGENCIES: The responsibilities allocated to various support agencies for 
implementation of the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan are described below. The 
Navy/coastal state authorities/ port authorities will make their communication/operation 
centres facilities available to receive and disseminate reports of marine pollution accidents. 
The Indian Navy and the Indian Air Force will provide fixed wing aircrafts or helicopters t o 
conduct aerial surveillance or provide logistic support in movement of men and materials to 
the incident site. They will also provide ground to air communication link at the site for use 
by the on scene Commander. The Port Authority will provide tugs and  pollution control 
equipment at the incident site within port limits. The Ministry of Shipping, and Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas will provide tankers or tank barges for storage of recovered oil or 
oil in water emulsions, and will arrange for stora ge and eventual disposal of recovered oil. 
The Director General of Shipping, Ministry of Shipping, will be responsible for all 
negotiations with the vessel, cargo owners, and insurers and will also conduct all negotiations 
regarding compensations and indem nification. The MoEF&CC and Ministry of Agriculture 
will provide scientific advice regarding species at risk, shore -line sensitivity, restriction of 
fishing activities, use of dispersant chemicals, beach cleaning methods, etc. The Ministry of 
Finance will provide authorization for expenditure and funds for initial response and ensure 
adequate financial records are  maintained. Coastal state authorities/ district administration/ 
departments/ public works/ civil defense corps will provide personnel and equipme nt, as 
required, for shoreline clean -up and ensure safety and protection of the local population and 
resources.

Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee observes that out of the 44 Sagarmala projects under various stages 
of development, no funds have been released for as many as 31 projects, which points to the 
lack of any substantial progress having been made for those projects. In order to be 
competitive with other leading maritime nations, the creation of best -in-class Port 
infrastructure and capacity augmentation are of utmost importance. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may analyze the diffic ulties being faced in the execution of 
these projects and take necessary remedial action to tackle the same so as to complete the 
projects on time without cost escalation and enable India to upgrade its port infrastructure to 
increase its market share. 
(Para 23) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1. The Ministry under the „Sagarmala Programme‟ release assistance to Maritime States, 
UT and Major Ports for development of infrastructure projects. In terms of funding 
guidelines, funds are released to the IA upon award of tender to avoid parking of funds. In 
some of the cased project s struck due to delay in ECs/ASI Clearance , and Local resistance 
etc. the Ministry regularly follows up with IAs to iron out the difficulties and make efforts for 
timely release and execution of projects.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation

status of  progress of  31 projects out of the total 44 projects under ‘Sagarmala.’ The

with the Committee. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee feels that having a Special Purpose Vehicle to improve the road and 
rail connectivity to Ports across the country would be very effective in addressing the 
bottleneck of poor connectivity that is faced by almost all Ports, stifling their throughput. 
Having robust rail and r oad connectivity at ports is crucial to ease congestion of cargo 
coming in and out of ports. The Committee may be apprised of the progress being made with 
regard to the creation of this proposed SPV. The proposed SPV may recruit officials having 
prior expe rience in execution of rail and road projects as well as in coordination with 
concerned agencies for this purpose. 
(Para 37) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1. The Ministry in 18 th Maritime State Development Council (MSDC) meeting held on 
24th June 2021 discussed options for implementing the road connectivity projects by forming 
SPV with the NHLML, a company formed under NHAI to take up first/ last mile connectivity 
road projects. All states and major ports were advised to coordinate with NHLML  for 
forming SPV, for executing the project on cost recovery mechanism. 
 
4.2. As of now, The Ministry has not received any proposals from state/major ports for 
forming SPV for executing road and rail connectivity.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.3. The Committee notes that MSDC meeting was held on 24 th June, 2021 and 
almost one year has elapsed since then but no response/proposal from State/Major Ports 
for forming SPV  for executing road and rail connectivity has ensued. The Committee 
therefore recommends that fresh initiatives/meeting s with the concerned stakeholders 
should be taken for speeding up the project for forming SPV.

Recommendation/Observation

Guidelines, 2014, to regulate land allotment of Major Ports. It is of the opinion that it will 
give a new direction to the regulation, operation and planning of Major Ports in India.  The 
Committee also notes that the Policy guidelines for Land/Township area management to set 
up port-based industries, is under consideration with the Government. The Committee urges 
the Ministry to expedite the framing of the policy guidelines for land Management/township 
area Management to set up port-based industries. The Committee is of the firm opinion that 
integrating the port -based and other ancillary industries in the township areas of the Major 
ports will boost the employment potential and economy of the areas near the ports. 
(Para 40)

5.1. The MoPS&W is keen on finalizing the Policy Guidelines for Land Management and 
Policy Guidelines for Land Management in Township Areas of Major Ports in order to attract

industrialization in the areas near the Major Ports.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation: 
5.2. The Committee desires to be apprised of the guidelines formulated/policies 
framed and finalized for setting up Land Management in Township Areas at Major 
Ports.

Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee observes that earlier CBIC was handling the matter of installation of 
container scanners at Major Ports. Thereafter, as per the decision of the Committee of 
Secretaries, the responsibility of procuring scanners was shifted to the Ministry of Ports, 
Shipping & Waterways in December, 2015. However, now the responsibility has again been 
shifted back to CBIC. The Committee deplores this frequent shifting of responsibility of the 
important security aspect, such as the installation of scanners, betw een the CBIC and the 
Ministry and feels that there has been no long term planning on this crucial issue. The 

37 
 
Committee desires to know the reasons for this frequent change of responsibility and 
recommends that immediate steps may be taken to resolve this i ssue. It also recommends that 
the Ministry should explore the best technical equipments available and installed at 
international ports abroad and install the same at all ports in the country. As regards 
installation of Drive through Road and Rail Scanners,  the Committee recommends that all 
the procedural and operational issues may be resolved, so that the concerned ports can 
benefit at the earliest. The Committee also recommends that a long term policy should be 
framed for installation of high tech security  apparatus at all ports in the country, in view of 
the increased security threats faced by the country. 
(Para 50) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1. Indian Customs are mandated to regulate imports and exports of goods and collects 
duties on the imported goods besi des discharging duties required under various Acts/rules to 
check smuggling of contrabands. This involves: (a) assessing duty based on the document 
submitted by the importer/exporter; and (b) examine the goods to verify the actual content 
match manifest de claration by the importer/exporter. Simultaneously, the Customs also 
checks that contraband goods of any kind do not enter the country.  
 
6.2. Need for container scanning arises from the fact that: (i) significant increase in import 
and export through cont ainers, (ii) raise in cases of contraband seizures, (iii) increased 
concern for safety and security, requiring higher percentage of examinations, (iv) physical 
examination of containers - time consuming and also result in hold up at Ports, (v) need for 
faster and non-invasive inspection of containers, etc. Hence, CBIC is primarily responsible to 
acquire, install and operate the container scanners and Ports are required to provide 
infrastructure support (like space) to the Customs in this activity. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation:

pertaining to the safety of passengers and cargo. The Committee desires to be apprised 
of the long –term policy measures framed by the Ministry for inst allation of Scanners 
and other security equipments at port and port terminals as well as the steps taken by 
the Ministry to resolve operational issues  hindering the installation process of such 
equipments. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should ensure that a 
suitable coordination mechanism exists between the CBIC  and itself on matters relating 
to infrastructure necessary for scanning of containers at ports.
