MINISTRY 
 
 
Initiatives by BCAS in Civil Aviation Security  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes the various initiatives taken by the BCAS, which is the main 
regulator for governing security in the Civil Aviation Sector in the country. It also notes the 
responsibilities and initiatives taken by various Aviation Security Groups (ASGs) like CISF, 
Airport Security Units/State Police, besides the role played by the various airlines and airport 
operators in maintaining security at Airports. The Committee also n otes the significance, the 
Government attributes to the Civil Aviation Sector, which is brought out in the policy document 
titled ‘Strategy for New India @75’, which has envisaged to expand airport capacity by more 
than five times the present capacity to h andle one billion trips a year. The Committee feels that 
this fast tracked and unprecedented growth in the Civil Aviation Sector would require parallel 
enhancement of security infrastructure in this sector as well. 
 (Para 13) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The observation of the Committee is noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The exponential growth in the sector would be a challenge for the agencies involved in 
providing security, since trained security personnel, security infrastructure and related security 
protocols, needs to keep pace with growth.   A need for close cooperation and coordination with 
all the agencies, namely Government, State Police and Private agencies and other stakeholders 
involved in providing security, would also be required.  Hence, the Committee recommends that 
the world’s best security practices should be followed to cater to the increased security 
requirements.   
 (Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The recommendation of the Committee is noted. 

3 
 
State-of-the-Art Technological Solutions for Security at Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee is also of the opinion that the Ministry should explore the feasibility of 
Biometric screening of passengers at airports, using tools such as facial recognition, fingerprint 
and retinal scans which is presently being used at many airports worldwide. The Committee 
desires that the Ministry may examine the feasibility of retinal scans for frisking passengers, as 
the retinal scan data of most of the domestic passengers are available in the A adhaar database. 
It would also like to point out that biometric security is non -intrusive and faster than 
conventional screening, which leads to faster screening of passengers and leads to less crowding 
at airports and is therefore being introduced in many airports abroad. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the global best practices for biometric scanning and screening of passengers 
should be introduced in the country. 
 (Para 54) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 In order to provide seamless and hassle free passengers journey experience on domestic 
sector, a Digi -Yatra project is underway. It is based on facial recognition technology. This is 
based on mobile wallet based identity management platform. In first phase, Digiyatra at seven 
Airports namely Varanasi, Vijayawada, Kolkata and Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Delhi are 
being implemented. 
 
Miscellaneous  
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee also feels that the Ministry should consider a policy to provide a small 
complimentary water bottle to the passengers in the aircraft, keeping in view the tradition of the 
country to give highest regard to guests and offer water on arrival. 
 (Para 64) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The recommendation of the Committee is noted. 
 
 
 

4 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Role of Various Agencies in Aviation Security  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that presently, there is a multiplicity of agencies involved in 
providing security at airports viz., the CISF, Airlines Operators, Airport Operators, State Police 
and NSG. The Committee also notes that all the aforesaid individual agencies are looking after 
the airport security functions in additio n to their other roles and responsibilities. For example, 
CISF which plays a prime role in airport security presently provides security cover to 353 
critical infrastructure facilities like nuclear installations, space establishments, seaports, power 
plants, important Government buildings, iconic heritage monuments, Delhi metro, besides 
security cover to some private corporate establishments also. The other entities such as airlines 
operators, airport operators, State police and NSG are engaged in their role  of airport security 
in addition to their main responsibilities, which is completely different from their role as airport 
security providers. The Committee recommends that the airport operators/ management should 
take the opinion of Ministry of Home Affair s, before purchasing security equipment at airports 
and also ensure that they should conform to the best standards of security worldwide.    
(Para 11) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The recommendations of the Committee are noted. The security functions associated with 
various agencies at airports are in conformity with Aircraft (Security) Rules 2011. Technical 
specifications/QRs of all the security equipment deployed/installed/to be deployed at the airport 
are issued by DG, BCAS under the Aircraft (Secur ity) Rules 2011 and National Civil Aviation 
Security Programme (NCASP). Further, these technical specifications/QRs are finalised by a 
Technical Committee of BCAS in consultation  with Central Security Agencies;  Ministry of 
Home Affairs (MHA);  Defence Resea rch and Development Organisation ( DRDO); National 
Technical Research Organisation ( NTRO); Special Protection Group ( SPG) etc. which is in 
conformity to the best standards of security. Airport Operators procures the security equipment, 
as per the minimum standard/QRs decided by BCAS. 

5 
 
Initiatives by BCAS in Civil Aviation Security 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should set up dedicated Institutions 
across the country to cater to needs for increased manpower in all  the security aspects of the 
aviation sector.  
 (Para 15) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The recommendations of the Committee noted. There is a training division in BCAS 
which administers and coordinates all tr aining requirements of increase d manpower. Trainings 
are imparted by dedicated 30 Aviation Security Training Institutes (ASTIs) across the countries. 
Further, a survey/resurvey Committee under BCAS considers augmentation proposal for CISF 
manpower requirements across airports. 
 
Categorization of airports in India  
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee notes that out of 118 operational airports, only 64 airports are under 
CISF cover, while 54 airports have no such cover. Further, out of the 28 hyper -sensitive 
airports, 21 have CISF cover; while for the 62 sensitive airports, only 39 have been given CISF 
cover. The Committee recommends that the Government should strive to bring all the 
operational airports under the ambit of CISF security cover.   
 (Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 CISF is deployed at 65 Airports out of which 21 are hypersenstive airports. The rest 
seven hyper sensitive airports are Hindustan Aeronautics Limited ( HAL) (Bengaluru), Kargil, 
Pathankot, Begumpet (Hyderabad), Juhu (Mumbai), Safdarjung (Delhi) and Thoise(J&K). Kargil 
and Thosie are mostly used to carry armed forces. HAL (Bangaluru), Begumpet (Hyderab ad), 
Juhu (Mumbai) and Safadarju ng (Delhi) have no passenger flights. Other non -CISF deployed 
airports are under security cover of State police etc. Moreover, t he CISF cover to an airport is 
decided in consultation with MHA. However, the recommendation of the Committee is noted. 
 

6 
 
Vacancy position of CISF at airports  
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee notes that though the vacancy position of CISF at airports, as compared 
to the total sanctioned strength is satisfactory, yet there is a vacancy of 1166 security personnel. 
The Committee is of the opinion that in view of the high -tech methods of intrusion used by the 
subversive elements at airports, at le ast the full sanctioned strength of CISF should be provided 
at airports in the country. The Committee also recommends that periodic surveys should be 
carried out to assess the changing threat perception at all airports in the country and 
accordingly, trained security personnel should be provided at airports in a time -bound manner. 
Continuous monitoring should also be done as regards the implementation of various security 
rules and regulations and surprise checks should be carried out to test professional ef ficiency 
and alertness of the security staff and the operational preparedness of various agencies. 
 (Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The recommendations of the Committee are noted. On the recommendation of manpower 
surveys/re-survey committee under BCAS, MHA releases the sanction for CISF manpower for 
an airport. Based on sanctioned strength, CISF deploys the manpower. Any gap between 
deployed strength and sanctioned strength  is a dynamic matter and CISF endeavours to reduce 
the gap. 
 
4.2 In order to have periodic survey to assess the changing threat perception at all airports in 
India, there is a Committee for Assessing Security and Risk Vulnerability Assessment of 
Airports in India under MHA and BCAS is its member convener.  
 
4.3 Further, there is well laid down system for regular audit, inspection, surprise 
check/dummy test as per the annual quality control function calendar issued by DG, BCAS and  
it’s a continuous and ongo ing process to test the professional efficiency  and alertness of the 
security staff  and operational  preparedness of various agencies.  
 

7 
 
Measures to Improve Airport Security by CISF  
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee notes the various roles of CISF and the various initiatives taken by CISF 
to ensure security at airports in coordination with BCAS. The Committee notes that in addition 
to imparting training on various aspects of its core duty of security at airports, the CISF also 
imparts training for soft skills to improve upon the conduct of CISF personnel involved in 
various security functions viz., appropriate behaviour patterns, language & accent, body 
language, service orientation, presentability and dressing sense etc. The Committee during th e 
course of its deliberations with the Ministry, have repeatedly pointed out the quality of the 
security staff at airports and is of the view that the security personnel are the first point of 
contact for any airline passenger after embarking from an aircr aft, be it domestic or 
international passenger. As such, the security personnel sets the first impression on the 
passenger, about the city or the country. It is especially important in case of a foreign traveller 
and leaves a lasting impression on the mind  of the tourist about the country or the behavioural 
aspects of its people. Hence, imparting training in soft skills to the passenger frisking security 
personnel, assumes great significance, especially their behaviour, proper and presentable 
uniform or body language towards the passenger. The Committee strongly recommends that the 
Ministry in coordination with the MHA should ensure that CISF and other security staff at 
airports may be sensitized adequately in soft skills, so that they perform their security  duties 
efficiently without diluting the security activities/responsibilities. The Committee notes that SOP 
for persons with special needs or ‘Divyaangjan’ has been drafted by BCAS and same will be 
finalized after receipt of comments of general public/ sta keholders. The Committee is of the 
opinion that special care should be taken to deal with passengers with special needs or 
‘Divyaangjan’ and therefore, recommends that the SOP may be expeditiously finalized.    
(Para 46) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 The observation of the Committee is noted.  Considering soft skills as an integral 
component of functioning of CISF personnel deployed at airport, CISF imparts necessary soft 
skill trainings to its personnel.   
 

8 
 
5.2 So far as SOP for persons with special needs or ‘Divyaangjan’ is concerned, BCAS has 
issued a detailed and exhaustive guideline/SOP for screening of persons with special needs 
and/or individual with reduced mobility vide Avsec Circular 01/2022 dated: 03.02.2022 (copy of 
SOP at Annexure A). 
 
State-of-the-Art Technological Solutions for Security at Airports   
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee during its deliberations with the Ministry has often pointed out that at few 
of the airports, there are long passenger queues during peak hours. In view of the Government 
guidelines for avoiding public gatherings in the context of the prevalence of Covid -19 pandemic, 
more steps may be taken to resolve the issue. The Committee also notes that the Ministry 
proposes to increase the number of flights. The Comm ittee observes that at most of the airports 
in the country, Door Frame Metal Detectors (DFMDs), Hand Held Metal Detectors (HHMDs) 
and physical frisking is done on random basis. The Committee is of the opinion that the present 
system of DFMD/HHMD, besides b eing obsolete technology, is intrusive on the privacy of 
passengers. In this context, the Committee recommends that in addition to steps taken to ease 
queues, the Ministry may also expedite its proposal for installation of Full Body Scanners at 
airports, w hich would enhance the technology of frisking of passengers and lead to faster 
clearance of queues at frisking points. Besides, the number of frisking counters may also be 
increased at airports and adequate trained personnel should be posted to man these c ounters 
effectively. 
 (Para 52) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 Sincere efforts are being made to ease congestion at airports in consultation with all 
stakeholders. The matter is deliberated at high level and all possible options have been evaluated. 
Accordingly, necessary directions on space re -alignment, manpower increase, technological 
intervention etc. have been issued to all concerned. 
6.2 BCAS has issued an AvSec Circular no 05/2019 elaborating technical specifications of 
Full Body Scanner (FBS). The setting up of FBS at al l Hyper sensitive airports are closely being 
monitored by the Ministry. Its testing at various airports is at advance stage and it is likely that 
the same will start to be set up shortly in phased manner.  

9 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry, wherein it has been stated that FBS shall 
be installed at all airports at pre -embarkation security checks in a phased manner and the 
airport operators have also been directed to install FBS replacing t he DFMD. The Committee 
notes that airport operators are obliged to procure and provide only those security equipment 
that meet BCAS specifications. The Committee is of the opinion that such an important issue, 
which has security implications, should not be left to the airport operators only as BCAS is more 
competent in technical matters regarding security as compared to airport operators. Hence, the 
BCAS should not only specify the security equipment to be installed at airports, but also engage 
itself proactively with the airport operators to train personnel to use it and also maintain them.  
 (Para 53) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 The recommendations of the Committee noted.  There is a technical specifications 
Committee headed by BCAS and comprising M embers from all stakeholders which considers 
world-wide new technology in view of the Airports functions and recommends the best 
minimum technical standards. On the basis of r ecommendation of the technical C ommittee, 
airport operators procure and install the secu rity equipments by following minimum standards at 
airports. BCAS also provides training to personnel to operate security equipment and interpret 
the results. 
 
Radiological Detection Equipment (RDE)  
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee notes the pro gress of installation and operationalization of RDE projects 
and recommends that the work may be completed as per the set deadline. The Committee may 
also be informed whether RDE projects would be implemented at remaining airports, besides the 
24 airports in Phase 1 and 2. 
 (Para 56) 
 
 
 

10 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 The RDE project was envisaged for 24 Airports in which 14 Airports were covered under 
RDE project Phase -I and 10 airports under RDE project Phase II. This is as per the minutes of 
the meeting of Group of Officers held in Cabinet Secretariat on 25.03.2014.  
8.2 The MoU was signed between BCAS & ECIL on 26 thMarch 2014 and the work of 
Supply, Installing, Training and Commencing (SITC) at 14 Airports has been completed on 31 st 
March 2020. The names of 14 Airports where Phase-I is completed, are given below:   
Amritsar, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Calicut, Chennai, Cochin, Delhi, Guwahati, Goa, 
Hyderabad, Kolkata, Lucknow, Mumbai, Trivandrum. 
8.3 The MoU for RDE phase-II at remaining following 10 airports is under finalisation:  
Mangalore, Jaipur, Coimbatore, Pune, Tiruchirappalli, Varanasi, Bagdogra, Madurai, 
Bhubaneswar, Gaya. 
8.4 At present there is no plan/Budget provision for exte nsion of this project at other airports 
apart from these 24 Airports. 

11 
 
CHAPTER-III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE 
MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad (BDDS) 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that presently BDDS is operationalised at 20 airports and non -
operationalised at 44 remaining airports and assistance of local police/ NSG is being sought for 
attending to such threats. The Committee notes that only 20 airports have BDDS cover till date. 
It is also observed that at some places where CISF does not have BDDS support, support of local 
police is being sought. The Committee is of the opini on that local police may not have the 
technical competence or the desired high -tech equipment to dispose of bomb threats. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that BDDS should be engaged at the earliest at all the 
remaining 44 airports as well to counter b omb threats in consultation and coordination with the 
MHA. The Committee also recommends that the BDDS squad should have the best international 
pedigree dogs which can be engaged for security at airports.  
(Para 31) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 There are regulatory provisions prescribed by BCAS for having BDDS at all airports 
manned by CISF. In all fresh augmentation proposals, the provision for BDDS has been 
included. Airports are also gradually extending support for BDDS. However, the 
recommendations of the Committee are noted for compliance. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
1.2 The Committee reiterates its recommendation and  expresses its concern over the 
fact that BDDS is non-operationalised at 44 airports in the country which can prove to be a 
major security hazard as absence of BDDS a s even one airport can act as a weak link for 
the entire Indian airspace. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will take up this issue 
with CISF at the earliest and ensure operationalization of BDDS at all the remaining 
airports.    
 

12 
 
State-of-the-Art Technological Solutions for Security at Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee, during the course of its deliberations with the Ministry, had stressed 
upon the need for installation of sophisticated and State -of-the-Art security equipment and best 
security practices used globally, at all the Indian airports, to ensure fool proof security. The 
Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the BCAS to install the latest security gadgets at 
airports viz., Centralized Access Control System (CACS); Full Body Scanners; Radiological 
Detection Equipment (RDE); Perimeter Intrusion Detection System (PIDS; and Automated Tray 
Retrieval System (ATRS). The Committee notes that  installation of most of the aforesaid security 
systems have been recently initiated or at planning stage only and that too, only at the major 
airports only. The Committee notes that there are a total of 118 operational airports out of 
which 28 are hyper -sensitive; 62 are sensitive; and 28 normal airports. The Committee notes 
that out of these 118 airports, a miniscule number of airports are proposed to have the security 
cover of aforesaid advanced security apparatus or gadgets. The Committee stresses upon the 
need for fool proof security cover at all the Indian airports and at least at all the 28 hyper -
sensitive and 62 sensitive airports in the near future, especially in North-Eastern Region; Jammu 
& Kashmir; and Left -Wing Extremism (LWE) Regions, keeping i n view the increase in security 
threats due to use of high -tech gadgets even by the terrorists/ extremists, to evade the security 
apparatus at the airports and create terror at airports/ airplanes and disrupt peace and progress 
of the country. In the above  context, the Committee desires to know the details of the plans for 
installation of the aforesaid security apparatus at airports and the number of airports included, 
the stages of implementation and percentage of ground work completed so far, the timeline  
which has been prescribed for the various airports, airport -wise and whether the Ministry has 
been successful in achieving the said timelines. The Committee may also be apprised of the 
deadlines, if any, by which all the airports in the country would get the aforesaid security 
apparatus.  
(Para 60) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Centralized Access Control System (CACS): Centralized Access Control System is being 
implemented at 48 Airports in the country – 23 Hyper Sensitive Airports and 25 Sensitive 
airports. At these airports Biometric AEP are being issue d. M/s ECIL provided support for 

13 
 
Hardware reader’s integration. The CACS project implementation phase will be completed on 30 
June 2022 at 48 Airports. 
 
2.2 Full Body Scanner (FBS) : BCAS mandate is to imple ment FBS initially at all Hyper -
sensitive airports and then at all sensitive airports. The installation of FBS will be in phased 
manner. The procurement process for FBS by  major Hyper Sensitive airports i.e. Delhi, 
Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and AAI has started.   
 
2.3 Radiological Detection Equipment (RDE) :  RDE is to be installed at 24 airports. Under 
Phase-I, it has been installed at 14 Airports and under Phase II, it is envi saged at remaining 10 
airports. MoU is at final stage. RDE phase- I project has been completed on 31 March 2020.  
 
2.4 Perimeter Intrusion Detection System (PIDS): BCAS has mandated to install PIDS at all 
hyper sensitive airports. Further, non-RCS Greenfield airport is to plan for installation of PIDS at 
design stage itself for the purpose of obtaining clearance of design stage security vetting from 
BCAS. PIDS has been installed at Delhi, Bengaluru (partially 4.3 Km) and Hyderabad. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
2.5 The Committee would like to again emphasize on the need of State -of-the-Art 
Technological Solutions for security at all the Indian airports which rapidly keep changing 
with advancement to technology and ensure a full proof security system. The Committee 
notes the steps being taken by the Mi nistry for installation of CACS, FBS, RDE  and PIDS 
at various airports  and urges the Ministry to expedite and complete the process at all the 
airports. The Committee al so would like to know the status of installation of Automated 
Tray Retrieval System (ATRS) at airports which is in process.  
 
ICAO Aviation Security (AvSec) Rating Procedure  
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee appreciates the high security rating of India vis -à-vis Global/ APAC 
Standards. It is of the opinion that BCAS should make it a constant endeavour to make the 
security architecture and procedures dynamic by incorporating new technological advancements 

14 
 
and best practices from across the globe.   It is further recommended that all the Aviation 
Security processes should be streamlined in consultation with the stakeholders. 
 (Para 63) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The recommendation of the Committee is noted. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
3.2 The Committee desires to know the specific steps  taken by the Ministry or the plans 
thereof to make the security structure foolproof by incorporating the best and latest 
technological advancements used at airports worldwide. The Committee also desires to 
know whether there are plans to incorporate the suggestions of all stakeholders in the 
process.  
  

15 
 
  
CHAPTER-IV 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE FINAL 
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY ARE STILL AWAITED 
 
 
-Nil -

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
ANNUAL PLAN 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee is pleased to note the trend of increasing allocation to the Ministry, 
which underscores the importance being given to expanding and improving the National 
Highways network across the country. The Committee, however, notes that the Ministry has 
not been able to attract private investment at a similar pace. This is partly the reason for the 
high IEBR component in the last few years which is mainly why the huge debt burden is 
currently being faced by NHAI. The Committee appreciates that the IEBR co mponent has 
been kept to a nominal Rs. 0.01 crore for FY 2022 -23, with the Budgetary support made to 
the Ministry covering for the shortfall in the IEBR component. The Committee, however, feels 
that neither high budgetary support alone, nor high IEBR compo nent will be able to suffice 
the investment requirements for the rapid pace of NH development across the country in the 
long run. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry may work upon 
resolving the apprehensions of the private secto r which are limiting their participation in the 
road infrastructure sector in the last few years, by working in close coordination with the 
concessionaires and financial institutions. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The position with regard to high IEBR component in the last few years and the 
budgetary support made for the shortfall in the IEBR in the current FY has been noted. The 
Committee’s recommendation is to resolve the apprehensions of the private sector which are 
limiting their participation in the road infrastructure sector in the last few years, by working 
in close coordination with the concessionaires and financial institutions. 
1.2 The Ministry has come out with several innovative funding mechanisms to increase 
private investments after 20 14. During 2007 -14, private investments were confined to only 
BOT projects. Now, apart from BOT, HAM projects, we are also getting private investments 
through monetization of National Highways under TOT, InvIT (Infrastructure Investment 
Trust) and through SPVs (Special Purpose Vehicles). The private investments during 2007-14 
were about Rs. 1,08,481 crores, which came only from BOT projects. The private 
investments has increased to Rs. 1,69,214 crores during 2014 -21 from BOT, HAM, TOT and 
SPV. 
1.3 Further a dditional steps have been taken to resolve apprehensions of the private 
sector, including but not limited to: 
   Resolving Stuck projects  – NHAI has implemented a Stuck Projects policy 
and is trying to resolve pending disputes through one -time settlement process. Through 
this process, NHAI hopes to recycle money in the infrastructure space and promote 
investment in new projects. NHAI has also introduced a Termination Projects guideline 

3 
 
to standardize the implementation of complex MCA (Model Concession Agreem ent) 
clauses. 
   Encouraging new industry categories – NHAI is encouraging new investor 
classes, like institutional investors, specialized O&M (Operation & Maintenance) 
contractors, specialized tolling agencies etc. in the roads sector to diversify the investor 
base and encourage traditional investors to focus on their core competencies. 
   Amendment in Model Concession Agreements  – NHAI has introduced 
various amendments in the MCAs for BOT (Toll), and Hybrid Annuity to encourage 
private participation and  these amendments have received positive feedback from the 
market. Innovations such as Dispute Resolution Board, sharing of traffic risk etc. have 
been appreciated. Further, NHAI is now committing 90% of Construction Zone in BOT 
Toll projects at Appointed Date. This, when added with the removal of the requirement 
of Capacity Augmentation by the Concessionaire, removes a lot of chances of disputes 
in the Contracts. 
 
 
Vacancies in NHAI 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee is highly distressed to note that despite the recommendations to the 
Ministry year after year, NHAI, with a budgetary allocation of Rs. 134,015 crores, is still 
operating with only 61.2 percent of its sanctioned strength. The Committee fails to 
understand how NHAI will be able to do justice to its mandate with more than a third of its 
sanctioned strength being vacant. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry 
should take immediate measures to fill the vacancies in NHAI in shortest possible time. 
(Para 35) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 With regard to the observation of the Committee, it is stated that continuous efforts 
for filling up the vacant posts have been made and after analysing the hindrances in filling up 
of the vacancies, various re medial measures have been undertaken from time to time. The 
following are the few important measures undertaken to fill up the vacant posts and meet the 
manpower requirements arisen from time to time: -  
 During the last two years, recruitment of 499 posts on promotion / Direct Recruitment 
(DR) / Deputation has been undertaken. 
 To overcome shortage of technical manpower and to meet the temporary requirement 
of manpower due to increased workload on account of Bharatmala projects, 449 
Technical personnel in th e category of Site Engineers / Young Professionals have 
been engaged on contract basis. Further action for recruitment of 200 Young 
Professional (Technical) based on GATE Scores is also underway. 
 To keep NHAI as a lean and thin organisation, technical manp ower was being 
engaged on deputation from other organisations and simultaneously, regular intake of 
officers is being undertaken in a phased manner at Deputy Manager level through 
GATE/Engineering Services Examination. 

4 
 
 80 posts of Deputy Manager (Technical ) based on GATE, 2020/2021 scores on DR 
mode completed. 
 69 Deputy Manager (Tech.) in 2022 based on ESE -2020 marks have been selected, 
out of which 31 have already joined. 
 The remaining unfilled vacancies would be filled -up next year based on GATE 
Score/ESE, 2021 marks. 
 Recruitment action for filling up of 193 posts is already underway. 
 In Finance Cadre, recruitment action for filling up 62 posts is underway. However, 
due to stay by the Hon’ble High Court of Odisha, the recruitment for most of these 
posts is held up. 
 The Recruitment Rules (RRs) of Technical and Finance Cadre have been revised and 
fresh recruitment based on the revised RRs has been undertaken. 
 135 vacancies will be filled in 2022 -2023, 2023 -2024 under promotion quota in 
Finance and Technical Cadre. 
 17 posts of Deputy Manager (Fin.) and 02 posts of Jr. Hindi Translator have been 
taken-up for recruitment through National Testing Agency on DR basis. Further, 13 
posts of Asst. Manager (Legal) are proposed to be filled on DR through 
NTA/NLU/BESIL. 
 RRs of Technical Cadre has been revised by the Ministry recently to attract more 
officers of State PWDs having core experience in road sector. 
2.2 Further, after analysing the reasons for non-filling up of the vacancies, comprehensive 
review of the RRs has been undertaken and the RRs are at advanced stage of finalisation. 
After the revision of the RRs, it is expected to meet the shortfall of the manpower 
requirement. 
 
Sukhad Yatra Smartphone Application 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee is concerned to note that the number of complaints received via the 
Sukhad Yatra application has not shown any uptick since 2018. The Committee is of the 
considered view that wide adoption of the application can help NHAI gain free actionable  
information regarding the issues being faced by NH users across the country, which can be 
quickly acted upon, thus ensuring a well -maintained and safe driving experience on the NHs. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may work upon impr oving the 
usability of the Sukhad Yatra smartphone application at the earliest and come up with 
innovative means to promote the application to NH users across the country. An option to 
seek feedback from the person posting a complaint using the app, may al so be added so as to 
gain insight into whether the problem pointed out by the complainant has actually been 
resolved or not. 
(Para 51) 
Reply of the Ministry 

5 
 
3.1 In last one -year, various initiatives have been undertaken to improve the user 
experience of Sukhad Yatra App as below: - 
 The usage of Google Map APIs (Application Programming Interface) extended to 
pay-as-you-use basis in a month to allow unhindered usage by road users. 
 Updated version of the App available in both iOS and Android platform with 
improved User Interface (UI). 
 Additional new options under “Report an Issue” section such as Report an accident 
(automatically dials to NH Helpline 1033 on clicking the Option), Report  non-
availability/non-cleaning of Toilets at Toll Plaza, Others, etc. 
 Regular update of all NH fee plazas, toll rates etc. 
3.2 After discussions with IIT Madras and NHAI/IHMCL, a detailed requirement has

class unified mobile App for hig hway users in India for road related information/services 
with a strong in-built highway complaint/grievance redressal & escalation mechanism. 
3.3 Further, MoRTH has also constituted a committee to suggest improvements in the 
existing App. Based on deliber ation of the Committee a draft  SOP with the detailed

3.4 The new features of the revamped mobile App to be developed are proposed under

 Compliant/Grievance Redressal mechanism 
 FASTag related services

3.5 Pursuant to internal discussion and deliberation in the Committee constituted by

DELAYED ROAD PROJECTS 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee notes that a Corridor Rating Methodology 1 for project management 
and accountability has been devised by NHAI. The Committee reiterates the recommendation 
it has previously made in para 22 of its 296 th Report on ‘Role of Highways in Nation 
Building’ regarding creation of a central database of Nati onal Highways rating scores, 
including the ones executed by State PWDs, and further recommends that those parameters 
                                                           
1 Source: https://nhai.gov.in/nhai/sites/default/files/policy_circular/Highway_Rating_Report_NHAI.pdf 

6 
 
in the Corridor Rating Methodology which pertain to the performance of road contractors, 
may be utilized to adjudge their overall performance based on all the road projects they have 
worked on across the country. The Committee feels that a lot of projects get delayed because 
of poor performance of contractors and recommends that some weightage may be given to 
the past performance of road cont ractors, in terms of timely completion and quality 
construction, during the process of awarding of road projects. 
(Para 57) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1  To assess various parameters such as efficiency, safety and user services of completed 
4/6 laned  National Highways (NHs), NHAI has initiated the exercise of Highway Rating 
twice a year. The first iteration of this exercise has been completed and was launched on 
public domain on 1st March 2021.  The NHs are managed at toll plaza level for the influenc e 
length under them which is termed as a ‘cell’. Therefore, the 'cell' is judged based on three 
major criteria i.e. Efficiency (45 marks), Safety (35 marks) & User Services (20 Marks) on a 
scale of 100 marks. These criteria are further divided into a total  of 39 parameters which 
include average speed, delay at toll plaza, accidents, incident response time, wayside 
amenities, general cleanliness etc. 
4.2 Using this rating mechanism, one can understand where and how much each ‘cell’ is 
inefficient, unsafe and  lacks in user services. Then interventions, proposals and remedial 
measures can be suggested to improve the ratings of NH. This initiative will help in setting 
standards for benchmarking and assessment of highway corridors in India. Further, this 
exercise will also help in increasing the accountability of the stakeholders involved in the 
development and maintenance of NHs. 
4.3 The use of this highway rating exercise along with other project implementation 
aspects to assess the past performance of contracto rs is being planned by NHAI for 
incorporation in assessment of the technical proposals of various firms accordingly. 
4.4 The Ministry has issued SOP for rating of 2 laning projects.  
4.5 The Ministry, vide letter dt 22.09.2022, has requested State/UT PWDs to carry out 
rating of NHs and provide details to enable performance appraisal of deployed 
Concessionaire / Contractor / Maintenance Agency. 
 
MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may look into the issue of waterlogging 
on National Highways in areas with heavy rainfall or flood -prone areas, since the same not 
only slows the movement of passengers and goods but also poses significant road safety risks. 
Necessary corrective measures may immediately be taken on the NHs facing waterlogging 
issues and research may be conducted to look into tackling the issue from the initial design 
and construction stage of new NH projects.  
(Para 77) 
Reply of the Ministry 

7 
 
5.1  The construction of National Highways (NHs) in such areas are being executed, 
following the guidelines issued vide IRC:34 -2011 – “Recommendations for Road 
Construction in Areas affected by Water Logging, Flooding and/or Salts Infestation”. 
5.2  The Ministry directed IRC on 02.06.2022 to urgently review relevant codes and 
publications related to the design criteria for embankments for the highways to ensure 
mandatorily conducting intensive hydrological studies as per of design provisions to  prevent 
flooding on one side of embankment for lack of adequate waterway and also for taking up of 
necessary mitigation measures to obviate rise in water table or HFL, etc., on account of 
highway construction. 
5.3 The Ministry also requested all its field  officers as well as State Governments / UTs, 
vide letter dt 02.06.2022, to ensure adequate advance preparedness before monsoon, timely 
actions during monsoon and floods and post monsoon rectification of damaged National 
Highways (NHs) sections and structu res for ensuring resumption of traffic movement and 
restoration of damaged highway sections of highways on priority.  
5.4 NHAI on 02.06.2022 issued directions to all its field offices: - 
a) to have a re-look on design study of all new NHs and Expressways/ acc ess controlled 
NHs with high embankments being constructed so that it does not lead to blockage of 
water flow on one side; 
b) to take data from field engineers where such issues came up in the last two years and 
provide sufficient cross drainage; 
c) to ensure pr oper drainage measures & protection works for NHs / Expressways 
projects (including in 22 Greenfield corridors under Bharatmala Pariyojana) 
conforming to design guidelines laid down in IRC Codes; 
d) use of rain water harvesting as an additional drainage and groundwater recharge 
measure; 
e) to capture drainage pattern, HFL (High Flood Level) and other hydrology aspects 
during construction period to provide additional mitigation measures (if required) 
considering usually 3 monsoon seasons are observed during construction of 
Greenfield projects; 
f) to have pre -monsoon and post -monsoon inspections carried out through project units 
and to review the same on a monthly basis at their level. 
 
5.5 NHAI is capturing the status of project highway through drone and the captured video 
is being examined at the project site level to ensure smooth flow of water during the rainy 
season.  This is also being utilized to provide additional cross drainage structures in the form 
of culvert/ minor bridge/ drain etc., wherever necessary. 
5.6 About 5 km stretch has been identified on Delhi - Vadodara Expressway, where 
ponding/ overtopping of water took place during monsoon; suitable mitigation measures for 
natural drainage is being finalized for implementation.

SPECIAL ACCELERATED ROAD DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM (SARDP) FOR 
NORTH EASTERN AREAS 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee is anguished to note that the SARDP -NE Phase -A and Arunachal 
Pradesh Package was initially targeted to be completed by March, 2014 but has faced severe 
delays, with the current target for completion in 2023 -24. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry may urgently look into the issues that led to such huge delays in the 
implementation of these projects and use the insights gained from this analysis into ensuring 
that the revised target of completion of SARDP -NE Phase-A by 2023 -24 is achieved as well  
as to mitigate delays in the execution of SARDP Phase-B once it is initiated. 
(Para 81) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 Main reasons for delay in implementation of projects under SARDP-NE (Phase A and 
Arunachal package) were delay in LA, utility shifting, clearance etc. Now, projects are 
awarded after having at least 90 % LA, all clearance in hand and utility shifting done or made 
part of scope of the contractor so that works are not delayed. Further, these reasons of delay 
and measures taken to mitigate will be utilised while implementation of SARDP-phase B. 
6.2 Out of 5,998 Km identified under SARDP-NE (Phase A & Arunachal Package), 5,721 
Km has been awarded and 4,830 km has been completed as on 31.03.2022. Various measures 
have been taken to expedite the progress to ensure timely completion of works. Government 
has set up two regional offices of MoRTH (at Guwahati and Itan agar) and Eight regional 
offices of NHIDCL headed by Executive Director level officer in each state of North Eastern 
region along with many PMUs and site offices, with a view of having a better coordination 
with the Concerned Departments of the State Gover nment, to expedite all the clearances, 
effective project monitoring and execution. Further, action against the delay caused on the 
part of Contractor/Concessionaire is taken from time to time as per contractual provisions on 
case-to-case basis, if required. 
RESEARCH, TRAINING, STUDIES AND OTHER ROAD SAFETY SCHEMES  
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee is anguished to note the poor expenditure pattern under the crucial 
head ‘Research, Training, Studies and Other Road Safety Schemes’ since the past several 
years. The various activities under this heads viz., Training of drivers, Publicity an d 
awareness, National Highways Accident Relief Service Scheme, Road Safety & Pollution 
Testing Equipment, etc. are crucial for improving the scenario of road safety on National 
Highways across the country and to offset the huge death toll faced by the coun try each year 
due to road accidents. The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons furnished by the 
Ministry for the poor expenditure pattern under this head and feels remedial measures should 
be taken to make maximum utilization of the limited funds ava ilable under this head. This 

9 
 
pattern questions the commitment of the Ministry to make earnest efforts to minimize the 
deaths caused due to road accidents each year.  The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may cull out all the issues causing under-utilization under this important head at the 
earliest so that due focus is laid on road safety in the coming years. 
(Para 88) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. The Ministry has worked 
out detailed Action Plan to e nsure optimal utilization of the funds towards ensuring Road 
Safety for FY 2022-23. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
8. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may analyze the State -wise/UT-wise 
trends of road accidents and deaths and work closely with the State Governments where an 
increasing trend is observed. Effective implementation of road safety initiatives by States 
where there is noticeable decrease in the number of road accidents/deaths, may be shown as 
a blueprint to States failing to do well in terms of road safety on NHs as well as other roads. 
(Para 91) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. The best practices adopted 
by the States for effective implementation of Road Safety initiatives will be shown to other 
States for emulation and to act upon. 
8.2 The Ministry has developed Electronic Detailed Accident Report (eDAR) [erstwhile 
Integrated Road Accident Database (iRAD)], which is a central database collation and 
management system for accident data collection across the country and a data -driven systems 
approach to road safety. eDAR (erstwhile iRAD) is a comprehensive system involving 
stakeholders like Ambulance, Blood Banks, VAHAN, SARATHI, NHAI, PWD, Courts, 
Insurance Companies, for assimilation of information on a single platform and geo-tagging of 
the same. 
8.3 The system enables a spectrum of back -end analytics to determine the root cause of 
accidents and adopting strategic remedial measures towards enhancement of Road safety.  
8.4 A success model for a similar data -driven systems approach was successfully 
implemented by State Govt. of Tamil Nadu earlier which reduced the road crash fatalities in 
the State. 
8.5 eDAR (erstwhile iRAD) project has been rolled out in 34 States/UTs and process has 
been initiated for live accident data entries by the stakeholders. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee is deeply anguished to note that against RE 2021 -22 allocation of Rs. 
229 crore for Road Safety measures, the Ministry has managed to spend only Rs. 81 crore

above, this pattern of low expenditure makes it evident that a sense of urgency and zeal is

thoroughly lacking in the steps taken by the Ministry to minimize the huge toll of deaths

(Para 95) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Observations of the Committee are noted for compliance. The Ministry has prepared a 
detailed Action Plan to ensure optimal utilization of the funds towards ensuring Road Safety 
for FY 2022-23.

Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 A corridor rating assessment was designed to improve the service levels of important 
corridors of the country. Six parameters with varying weights viz. Safety & Ride Comfort 
(40%), Mobility & Reliability (25%), Incident Management (12%),  Customer Satisfaction 
(8%), Environment (7%) and miscellaneous parameters (8%) were chosen for the study.

Recommendation/Observation 
8. It has come to the notice of the Committee that the first Recru itment Rules (RR) of NHAI 
had provisions for direct recruitment of officials up to General Manager (GM) level, both in 
Technical and Finance division. However, over time, these seats were commuted into 
promotion and deputation seats by removing the provisi on of direct recruitment from GM to 
Manager levels, which might be because of increased influence of officials on deputation in 
NHAI. 
(Para 36) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Although in the Recruitment Rules 1996, there was a provision for direct recruitment 
upto the level of GM (which was changed in 2016), NHAI has not exercised the option of 
Direct Recruitment (DR) and has rather enhanced the regular cadre by way of absorpti on of 
deputationists and in some cases lateral entry especially at the level of Manager. Keeping in 
view the dynamic nature of requirements of the organisation, the direct recruitment has been 
prescribed at the feeder grades only. Analysing the requirement  of the manpower from time 
to time, more than 20 amendments have been carried out in the Recruitment Rules since 2010 
to facilitate infusion of manpower, particularly the technical manpower. As a result of the 
effort, the technical manpower, which was 367 in 2010, has been increased to 716 as on date.  
For fresh infusion of technical competence, direct recruitment at the level of Dy. Manager 
(Technical), based on GATE scores has been undertaken since 2017, which ensured quality 
of technical manpower. More t han 200 Dy. Managers (Tech.) have been recruited, while 
recruitment for another 73 Dy.Managers based on Engineering Service Exam, 2020   has been 
concluded recently. 
Recommendation/Observation

promotion and deputation posts has caused a lot of difficulty in the efficient functioning of 
NHAI, especially in finance wing, as there is a dearth of candidates eligible for deputation 
because of various reasons, such as: 
a. NHAI follows Double Entry Accounting pattern whereas Government agencies follow 
Single Entry Accounting 
b. Disparity in pay scale as NHAI and PSUs follow different pay pattern

Manager (21 posts) level.   To ensure that the direct recruited  officers have at least two

that an arbi tral tribunal has to publish the award within a period of twelve months  from

making the award for a furt her period not exceeding six months. If the award is not made 
within the period of one and half years, the mandate of the tribunal shall terminate. 
However, power has been vested in the “Court” to extend the period.

BHARATMALA PARIYOJANA PHASE-I 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee is deeply concerned to note that though the original timeline for 
Bharatmala Phase-I targeted its completion by 2021 -22, only 20,632 km (59.28% of total) 
has been awarded while only 7,375 km (21.19% of total ) has been constructed by December, 
2022 out of the overall target of 34,800 km. This has led to the targeted timeline for 
completion now being estimated at FY27 while the estimated cost of BMP Phase -I has almost 
doubled from Rs. 5.35 lakh crores to Rs. 10.63 lakh crores. Considering that the Ministry has 
managed to construct only about 21.19% of the Phase -I length during more than four years 
since the inception of the scheme, the Committee is of the view that the targeted completion 
estimate of FY27 will p rove to be a great challenge to the Ministry. Given the direct 
correlation between delays on project cost and the positive ripple effects that the timely 
completion of BMP Phase -I will have on several inter -linked economic sectors, it is 
necessary that the Ministry undertakes all-out measures to ensure that the revised target for 
completion of BMP Phase -I is met and the bottlenecks being faced by the Ministry in the 
execution of Phase-I so far may be proactively ironed out. 

50 
 
(Para 65) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The Phase I of Bharatmala Pariyojana was approved by the CCEA in October 2017 
for development of 34,800 km of National Highway Corridors. Immediately after the 
approval, consultants were appointed to prepare detailed project report (DPRs) for ~20,000 
km in 2017 and 2018. Preparation of a high quality Detailed Project Report requires 12 – 18 
months and completing land acquisition and obtaining all statutory clearances takes another 
12 – 15 months. Accordingly, it could be seen that the implementation of P hase I has been 
proceeding at a rapid pace with 22,352 km awarded (out of 34,800 km) as of April 2022. 
Further, 521 km have been approved by the Competent Authority and are being awarded. In 
addition, preparation of Detailed Project Report is at an advance d stage for all the remaining 
length to be awarded in Phase I of Bharatmala Pariyojana wherein the Land acquisition and 
other pre -construction activity have been taken up and It has been targeted to award the 
balance length in the next two financial years, viz. by FY 2023-24.  
 
6.2 As far as implementation is concerned, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and 
its implementing agencies constructed ~24,000 km of National Highways (including 
Bharatmala Pariyojana) in FY 2020 -21 & FY 2021-22 at an average pace of ~12,000 km per 
year (33 km per day), which is unprecedented in the history of the country and is significantly 
higher than the annual highway construction in other countries. Further, the program has 
witnessed construction of works of ~9,115 km, with a majority of these works completed are 
4 Lane + National Highway corridors. It is to be noted that the flagship Delhi – Mumbai 
corridor conceptualized in 2018 is targeted to be completed and opened for traffic from June, 
2022 onwards in various stretches. In comparison, some of the world’s largest road 
infrastructure projects like 1,167 Km long Trans-Java road in Indonesia, commenced in 1995, 
took more than 2 decades to get completed in 2019. Similarly, the 217 km long Shin Tom ei 
Expressway in Japan, commissioned in the early 2000s took almost a decade for completion.  
6.3 Further, multiple agencies/steps are required to complete the project and Ministry and 
its implementing agency took multiple steps to expedite award and construction:    
 
a. Revision in scope of DPR consultants to enable deployment of retired revenue 
department officials to support the State Governments in expediting land 
acquisition 
b. Frequent reviews with the State Governments to resolve issues with land

pertaining to delays in CALA performance are comprehensively tracked in 

51 
 
review meetings at all levels including at the lev els of Secretary (MoRTH), 
Chairman (NHAI), DG (MoRTH) and Members (NHAI). 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
6.4 The Committee is glad to note that the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways and its implementing agencies have constructed about 24,000 km of National 
Highways (including Bharatmala Pariyojana) in FY 2020 -21 & FY 2021 -22 at an 
average pace of about 12,000 km per year (33 km per day), which is unprecedented in 
the history of the country and is significantly higher than the annual highway 
construction in other countries. The Committee takes note of the various steps taken

timeline of completion of road projects would help the Ministry in having more clarity

highway patrol at frequent distances etc. are often found to be lacking on National Highways. 
The Committee is of the view that ensuring such measures is not budget -intensive and feels 
that there is an urgent, pressing need to ensure that these  very basic measures are enforced 
across the entire NH stretch in the country. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends 
that the Ministry may conduct road safety audits across the entire stretch of NHs and ensure 
proper signages, streetlights and high way patrol. This would not only help women travelling 
on NHs feel safer, especially at night, but also boost the overall safety of the road passengers 
at large. Signages may prominently display helpline numbers for different emergencies in 
English, Hindi as well as local language.  
(Para 108) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 Proper signboards / highway lighting in all the development projects are being 
invariably provided. Further NHAI has also deployed Highways Patrol vehicle in all 
completed projects.  
15.2 Ministry has taken Road safety on Top Priority.   In order to take precautionary 
measures for road safety, the Ministry has issued guidelines to ensure Road Safety Audits at 
all stages (Design, construction, and operation). 
15.3 Detailed guidelines for taking up road safety audits on National Highways have been 
prepared and notified. Road Safety Audits have been made part and parcel of all National 
Highways development projects on EPC/BOT modes. Ministry has issued circular which 
makes it mandatory to carry out road safety audit for all new road projects having length of 
5 km or more at the stage of Detail Project Report (PR)/Engineering Design. 
15.4 Road safety audit has been conducted so far for about 61,086 km length of NHs, 
thereby accounting for about 43% of total NH network at present. 
15.5 All the executing agencies have been directed to ensure safety provisions for 
highways during construction. Necessary action is to be taken to ensure provision of road 
signages, construction of diversion roads and o ther requisite provisions as per NH guidelines 
and IRC standards. IRC has already issued IRC: SP:55 -2014 regarding “Guidelines on 
Traffic Management in Work Zones”. Safety of Road users is to be ensured to avoid any 
unwanted incident where construction works are going on. 
15.6 There is a provision in IRC 67-2012 – “Code of Practice for Road Signs” that the legend 
on all signboards for expressways, Urban and City roads shall be bilingual -regional/local 
language and English. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
15.7 The Committee notes the various steps being taken by the Ministry to bolster 
road safety on the NH network in India by means of provision of proper signboards, 
street lights, road safety audit etc. The Committee however desires to be apprised of the 
mechanism in place to ensure that such safety provisions are well -maintained and that 

60 
 
their implementation is checked from time to time, not just at the construction stage of 
projects. The Committee further recommends that suitable steps may be taken to 
enable citizens to report the lack of safety provisions on certain stretches of National 
Highways, through both online and offline mediums. 
 
MISCELLANEOUS 
Provisions for service roads 
Recommendation/Observation 
16. The Committee observes that the lack of service roads alongside National Highways 
causes inconvenience to local residents and is, at times, the cause of road accidents. The land 
required for development of National Highways is acquired from the local people and they 
should be given the benefits of service roads along National Highways. The Committee feels 
that service roads are an integral part of National Highways and therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry may make it mandatory to have service roads along NHs to the extent possible 
and provisions for the same may be included in the tender document for NH projects. 
(Para 117)  
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1 Service roads are generally provided at the locations wherever inter -mixing of local 
traffic with through traffic is very high resulting in conge stion. Accordingly, provision of 
service roads is made in national highway projects wherever found necessary.  
16.2 With reference to greenfield corridors developed, development of service roads would 
not stay in line with the concept of access -controlled corridors and would diminish the 
benefits of these flagship corridors. However, the Ministry takes up development of 
underpasses along the corridor to ensure un -encumbered movement of local residents with 
additional provisions made as per site requirements. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
16.3  The Committee observes that having service roads directly helps in reducing the 
number of accidents taking place on National Highways. The Ministry, therefore, 
should carry out thorough analysis of the positive i mpact of service roads in terms of 
road safety and thereafter come upon the decision of whether or not to have provisions 
for service roads in a given National Highways project. The Committee further 
recommends that cost should not be the deciding factor w hen considering the 
practicality of having service roads in a NH project and ensuring top-notch level of road 
safety should be the top priority of the Ministry / NHAI. 
 
 
Five Year Vision Plan for Infrastructure Sector 
Recommendation/Observation 
17. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take undertake concerted measures 
to achieve the ambitious goals laid out in the Five Year Vision Plan (2019 -24) for 

61 
 
Infrastructure Sector, prepared by the Sectoral Group of Secretaries, which include targetin g 
reduction of accident fatalities by at least 25%, strengthening public transport and shared 
mobility through regulatory reforms, strengthening connectivity to top 100 tourist 
destinations, development of helipads near Highways for victim evacuation and c ommercial 
purposes, development of contractors database to identify underperformers and habitual 
litigants, etc. A robust monitoring mechanism may be put in place in order to assess the 
progress being made in regard of all the goals and targets laid out un der the Five Year 
Vision Plan. 
(Para 118) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1 The Ministry and IRC have issued various codes and guidelines, from time to time, to 
implement various road safety measures so as to minimize accidents on National Highways. 
Also, Supreme  Court Committee on Road Safety, during various meetings, has issued 
direction to various State Governments for implementation of Road safety measures 
including Engineering measures. 
17.2 The Ministry has issued instructions vide circular dated 09.11.2020 to carry out All 
Stages Road safety Audit for all road projects. It is further advised that Road Safety Audit of 
all the National Highways may be carried out and follow up action may also be taken up for 
implementation of the Road Safety Audit recommendations appropriately. 
17.3 The Ministry vide OM dated 14 th September 2016 has issued directives on 
“Immediate cautionary measures for alerting road users at identified black spots”. 
17.4 The Ministry vide OM no. RW/NH-29011/2/2015/P&M (RSCE) dated 7th Decembe r 
2015 has issued directives on “Preparation and submission of proposals for rectification of 
identified road accident black spots on National Highways”. 
17.5 The Ministry, through IAHE, has signed an MoU with SaveLIFE foundation for 
implementation of “Zer o Fatality Corridors (ZFC)” on National Highways. Study on two 
stretches in UP and Maharashtra has been conducted & the action plan for implementation of 
their recommendation are under progress with respective Field Offices. Further, additional 14 
stretches in 13 States have been identified recently in December, 2021 and study on the same 
is under progress. Lately, study in Telangana has also been undertaken. 
17.6 NHAI has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Institute for Road 
Traffic Educat ion (IRTE) and Institute for Development and Communication, Chandigarh 
(IDC) to promote road safety and collaborate in the areas of traffic management through a 
programme titled “Capacity building of Road Safety Management through the Safe Systems 
Approach Programme”. The study is being implemented, examined & monitored under 
Regional Office-Chandigarh of NHAI. 
17.7 Traffic calming measures such as traffic warning signs, delineators, road studs, bar 
markings, humps at approach roads, etc. are taken at vulne rable sections of National 
Highways to reduce road accident fatalities. 

62 
 
17.8 One of the cornerstones for the development of Bharatmala Pariyojana is to 
streamline movement of freight across the country. In this pursuit, initiatives are planned to 
ensure connectivity to multiple economic nodes identified under National Master Plan as part 
of Bharatmala Pariyojana. In addition to development of greenfield corridors across the 
country. This will eventually lead to reduction in accidents as freight traffic will  be largely 
separated with passenger traffic after completion of Economic Corridors and Greenfield 
corridors. 
17.9 The Ministry is also developing 600+ wayside amenities (WSA) across the National 
Highway network to provide world class amenities like food c ourts, hotels, garages, dhabas 
and hospitals.  
17.10 One key feature of these wayside amenities (WSA) is the development of helipads to 
support in both emergency evacuation purposes and also increase aviation -based connectivity 
across the nation. Discussio ns have been held with stakeholders from DGCA to integrate 
such helipad facilities with the overall civil aviation network. Infrastructure for helicopter 
landing facility is being provided on large WSA sites (wherever feasible) along upcoming 
Greenfield Expressways. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
17.11 The Committee notes that the reply furnished by the Ministry does not make any 
mention about the steps taken by the Ministry to strengthen public transport and 
shared mobility through regulatory reforms, and to strengthen connectivity to top 
hundred tourist destinations. Given the rapidly increasing number of vehicles in the 
country as well as to tackle the issue of air pollution, promoting public transportation is 
the need of the hour. On the other hand, strong road connectivity to top tourist 
destinations in the country has a direct positive effect on the footfall attracted at these 
destinations, thereby increasing economic opportunities. The Committee, therefore, 
desires to be apprised of the action taken by the Ministry to strengthen public transport 
and to improve NH connectivity to top tourist destinations.

ANNUAL PLAN 2021-22 
 The Committee appreciates that the Ministry has utilized 93.66 percent of its 
overall Revised Estimates (R.E.) 2021 -22 allocation. However, the expenditure of 82 
percent and 84.62 percent of the R.E. 2021 -22 allocation under the important heads 
‘Development of IT’ and ‘R&D Planning Studies’, leaves much to be desired in terms of 
utilization of allocated funds. The underutilization of funds under these heads, along 
with the fact that the allocations made under these heads are already low figures given 
the vastness of the National Highway (NH) network in the country, point to the lack of 
attention given by the Ministry / National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) to these 
ancillary but important budgetary heads. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry may lay due focus on improving the expenditure figures under these heads 
in the future so as to ensure high -quality maintenance and expansion of the National 
Highway network in the country. 
(Para 1.3) 
 The Committee is concerned to note that during  the Financial Year 2021 -22, no 
separate proposal for Women Safety in Public Transport from the States/UTs has been 
received and approved under the Nirbhaya Framework. Bolstering the safety of women 
in public transport is a prerequisite to promote the use of public transport across the 
country as well as to enable women to move more freely, which also helps fuel the 
economic growth of the nation. The Committee feels that the non -receipt of proposals 
for projects under the Scheme on Women Safety on Public Ro ad Transport cannot be 
entirely attributed to the Covid -19 pandemic. The Committee recommends that urgent 
steps may be taken to encourage better participation from the State Governments under 
this scheme and to ensure that funds under this head are optimal ly utilized in the 
ongoing Financial Year. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may 
come up with other possible innovative schemes that utilize the funds under Nirbhaya 
Framework to bolster the safety of women on public road transport, besides the existing 
scheme for Vehicle Tracking Platform under this head.  
(Para 2.2) 
 
The Committee appreciates the various initiatives being taken by the Ministry to 
improve road safety, maintenance & repair of NHs, and research & development in the 
road sector. The Committee lauds the setting up of Centre of Excellence for Road Safety 
(CoERS) at IIT Madras and hopes that sufficient budgetary provisions are made to 

66 
 
CoERS to permit it to fulfill its mandate of R&D in the road sector in earnest. Research 
may be carried out into assessing the feasibility of mandating installation of advanced 
technologies such as Automatic Emergency Braking (AEC), Electronic Stability Control 
(ESC), Traction Control etc. in vehicles sold across the country. The Committee furthe r 
recommends that the Ministry may seek higher budgetary allocation under all these 
crucial heads in future so as to enable enhanced focus on the important activities 
carried out under these heads. This would significantly enhance the safety and pace of 
the transportation on the National Highway network across the country.  
(Para 3.14) 
 
 
ANNUAL PLAN 2022-23   
 The Committee notes that effectively about Rs. 5,000 crores are being 
spent annually on Maintenance & Repair of National Highways from the budget head 
of the Ministry on account of one portion of M&R being paid out of the Capital head 
and additional expenditure by NHAI on M&R. It may be noted that Rs. 5,000 crores is 
still effectively just about 2.5 percent of the overall BE 2022 -23 allocation of Rs . 
199,107.71 crores, which is a far cry from the way forward suggested by NITI Aayog to 
begin with earmarking 10 percent of its annual budget for road and highways for 
maintenance to move towards the developed country norm of earmarking 40 per cent to 
50 p er cent of the budget for roads and highways for maintenance. The Committee 
understands that the requirements of the Indian road sector are different from that of 
the developed countries but this does not mean that maintenance of the NH network of 
the coun try can be accorded a lower priority than the expansion of the NH network. 
High quality maintenance and repair of the existing network - including frequent 
monitoring of the road quality as well as carrying out preemptive repair works, where 
needed - will give a direct boost to the efforts of the Ministry to minimize the number of 
road accidents happening on the NH network across the country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may spend higher amounts on regular 
maintenance checks of the NH network across the country.  
(Para 4.14) 
 The Committee takes note of the various measures taken by the Ministry 
to minimize the number of road accidents on National Highways in the country. Given 
the extremely high number of road accidents happening i n the country, a large 
percentage of which takes place on National Highways, there is a pressing need for 
taking remedial measures on a war footing. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may evolve a robust mechanism to ensure that ample safety provis ions are in 
place on the NH network across the country and that periodic checks are made without 
fail, to ensure continued compliance of the required safety provisions throughout the 
NH network. Further, the Committee recommends that once it has been ascer tained 
that sufficient progress has been made in the rectification of black spots that have been 
identified at present, the Ministry / NHAI may review the definition of black spots on 

67 
 
National Highways to include accident-prone stretches where, say, more than 5 fatalities 
have taken place during the last three years, as compared to the present definition of 
black spots wherein only stretches where more than 10 fatalities have taken place 
during the last three years are considered to be black spots. This wou ld allow the 
Ministry / NHAI to work on the rectification of more accident -prone stretches across 
the country.  
(Para 4.15) 
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA 
Vacancies in NHAI 
The Committee is concerned to note that 114 posts out of the 317 ( i.e., 35.96 
percent) sanctioned strength of the Finance Cadre posts of NHAI are lying vacant at 
present. Given the fact that NHAI implements road projects worth thousands of crores, 
it is crucial to have close financial scrutiny of the ongoing projects of NHAI as well as its 
disputes with third parties. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that NHAI 
may take urgent steps to ensure that the vacancies existing in the Finance cadre are 
filled at the earliest.  
(Para 4A.6) 
 
PENDING ARBITRATION CASES 
The Committee notes that almost the same number of cases have been referred 
to CCIE-2 as compared to cases referred to CCIE -1 and CCIE -3 combined, while the 
number of cases resolved by CCIE -2 is much more than the combined number of cases 
resolved by CCIE -1 and C CIE-3. Speedy disposal of disputes between the parties 
(NHAI & the Concessionaire/ Contractor/ Consultant) directly enables speedier 
completion of road projects stuck due to disputes with the concessionaires. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the M inistry may look into difficulties, if any, 
being faced by certain CCIEs in timely resolution of cases and if needed, consider the 
constitution of more CCIEs to enable faster parallel processing of disputes. Further, the 
Committee desires to be apprised of  the number of cases wherein arbitration could not 
be completed within the time limit of 12 months, as stipulated by Section 29A of the 
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the number of cases wherein the "Court" 
has extended the period of mandate of the tribunal.  
(Para 5.8)

Highways and its implementing agencies have constructed about 24,000 km of National 
Highways (including Bharatmala Pariyojana) in FY 2020 -21 & FY 2021 -22 at an

the history of the country and is significantly higher than the annual highway 
construction in other countries. The Committee takes note of the various steps taken   
by the implementing agency to ex pedite award and construction of road projects in the 
country. The Committee, however, still feels that having more reasonable targeted 
timeline of completion of road projects would help the Ministry in having more clarity 
in its long -term road infrastruct ure planning as well as capital allocation. The

presently follows to estimate the projected completion date of its road projects and give

The Committee feels that the Port Connectivity Projects envisaged under the

shipping sector in the country. The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that

Connectivity Projects under Bharatmala Pariyojana. However, it is evident that the 
Port Connectivity Projects are drastically delayed, even  more so than the overall 
delayed progress of the Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase -I. While the Committee 
appreciates the increased pace of road construction per day in the country and the 
optimistic targeted timelines for ambitious projects, the Committee feel s that the

Report.
